papers.title: TimeCap: A Scalable Open-Source Pipeline for Captioning Wearable Health Time-Series Data
papers.abstract: Time-series data generated continuously across industrial, environmental, and especially health domains produce multimodal signals whose scale and heterogeneity make their processing and interpretation particularly challenging. Time-Series Language Models (TSLMs) promise scalable interpretation of these signals, yet remain bottlenecked by a fundamental lack of text-annotated time series pairs that are signal-grounded, reproducible, and extensible across modalities and schemas. Existing paired corpora are either closed or limited in scale and modality coverage. Annotation with large language models could scale them up, but its outputs cannot be regenerated exactly, which prevents others from re-deriving, extending, or auditing the resulting corpus. To address this, we release TimeCap, an open deterministic captioning pipeline with three reusable extractor tiers and a cross-channel synthesis layer that operates directly on the signal with no language model in the loop, extensible to new schemas by writing channel definitions alone. This positions TimeCap as a reproducible mechanism for future dataset generation rather than a one-off release. Applying TimeCap to OpenMHC, the MyHeart Counts wearable dataset, yields MHCap, the largest open caption layer for multimodal wearable time-series data. MHCap spans 19 Apple HealthKit channels and 7,005,763 captions over 908,944 person-days. To showcase the impact of the corpus, we train OpenTSLM, a time-series language model, on MHCap and benchmark on health-outcome prediction. Caption-augmented training (OpenTSLM-Cap) outperforms a label-only baseline on 29 of 32 per-user binary evaluations across 8 tasks.
papers.intro:
From factory machines and power grids to the human body, multivariate time series arise wherever systems are monitored over time. The volume and heterogeneity of these data make their processing and interpretation particularly challenging. Consumer health is one important example, where large volumes of wearable data can shape how people perceive and manage their health. Cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and dementia are major contributors to global disease burden, particularly in older adults [1]. Consumer wearables already capture signals that show early promise for tracking a wide range of conditions [2, 3, 4]. Given the volume of these data, realizing this promise at population scale requires robust, automated interpretation of these signals. Time-Series Language Models (TSLMs)promise to enable exactly this: models that can describe temporal patterns, support downstream prediction, and uncover structure in complex multivariate data [5]. Yet, realizing this potential requires models that can reason over these signals, and such models face three compounding gaps that jointly obstruct progress.

First, the data gap. The largest paired caption and time-series corpus for multimodal consumer wearables to date comprises 59.7M hours from 103,731 participants but remains closed [6, Table 1]. The largest open alternative is roughly four orders of magnitude smaller in recorded hours and limited to smartphone- and smartwatch-derived modalities, totaling 5,648 question–answer pairs over 60 subjects of ExtraSensory recordings [7, §3.1, §4].

MHCap is created by applying TimeCap to its 19 HealthKit channels spanning iPhone activity, Apple Watch physiology, sleep stages, and ten workout categories. With TimeCap, anyone with access to the signals can regenerate the captions. As a result, the corpus (i) can grow without silent distribution shift, (ii) stays independent of the models evaluated on it, whereas LLM-written captions partly turn evaluation into distillation of the captioning model, and (iii) can be audited, since every caption traces back to a rule and threshold that can be changed and regenerated consistently.

papers.title: PocketTSLM: Deploying an On-Device Soft-Prompt Time-Series Language Model for Privacy-Preserving Smartphone Reasoning
papers.abstract: Consumer phones and wearables increasingly collect physiological time-series data, yet most mobile systems treat these streams as summaries or text rather than as temporal evidence. This representation is poorly matched to personal health systems that need to retrieve, route, or summarize sensor evidence while preserving temporal structure. Cloud-hosted time-series language models avoid smartphone limits, but they repeatedly move sensitive physiology off the device and add latency and per-query compute cost. Mobile model alternatives that aggregate time-series data into statistical features or serialize raw samples as text either compress temporal structure or exhaust the context and memory budgets of small on-device models. We present PocketTSLM, a mobile-native deployment of OpenTSLM SoftPrompt, the soft-prompt variant of the OpenTSLM time-series language model. PocketTSLM runs fully on a consumer smartphone by injecting encoded time-series windows as embeddings instead of tokenizing time series as text. A numerical parity protocol verifies identical greedy-decoded token sequences between the Swift port and a Python reference using Apple's MLX machine-learning framework. Answers also match the PyTorch reference, although rationale wording can differ. An on-device context-economics benchmark compares the soft-prompt path with a text-serialized baseline on the same backbone. In our benchmark format, soft-prompting uses approximately 12 times fewer time-series tokens and reduces prompt-prefill cost. PocketTSLM processes 30-second Sleep-EDF electroencephalography clips for sleep staging and a 1,000-sample (10 s) 12-lead electrocardiogram clip from ECG-QA. In comparison, text-serialized baselines exceed the phone's context or memory budget at longer time-series windows. All inference runs entirely on the device, with no health data transmitted during inference.
papers.intro:
Consumer devices now collect physiological time-series data that were previously limited to clinical or research environments [1, 2]. Smartwatch irregular-pulse notifications have been evaluated for atrial fibrillation screening in large cohorts [3], phone-connected systems make electroencephalography (EEG)acquisition more accessible [4], and passive wearable streams such as heart rate, sleep, and activity have been used for infectious-disease surveillance, COVID-19 detection, and prospective health-risk assessment [5, 6, 7]. In each case, measurements are captured close to the patient, but the interpretation delivered to a patient or downstream system is often a label, score, or study endpoint. Digital biomarker pipelines make this pattern explicit: continuous measurements are translated into digital endpoints or biomarkers for evaluation and decision support [8]. Those outputs support screening, monitoring, and study endpoints, but they do not explain the source time-series window itself. Recent personal-health large language model (LLM)systems interpret wearable-derived sleep, activity, and fitness data through natural-language coaching or insight generation [9, 10]. Therefore, patient-facing assistants, clinician review tools, and supervised health agents need descriptions grounded in source time-series windows that can be retrieved, routed, summarized, or used to defer a response when the evidence is insufficient.

Time-series language models (TSLMs)are designed for this time-series-to-language interface. They couple time-series encoders to language models and generate natural-language descriptions or rationales from raw physiological time-series data such as electrocardiogram (ECG), EEG, and accelerometry [11, 12]. These outputs give software a text interface to sensor evidence while preserving the temporal structure in the model input [11]. Time Series Language Models may enable systems that reason over sensor windows rather than only aggregate features.

Time Series Language Models may enable systems that reason over sensor windows rather than only aggregate features.

Personal-health LLMsystems are important reference points, but they do not solve the deployment problem addressed here: they reason over derived wearable data with large language models rather than running a time-series-native model on the phone [9, 10]. When interpretation is served remotely, personal physiological streams or derived sensor evidence must leave the device, making privacy and secondary-use risks part of the inference pathway [13]. Server-side inference also adds a network dependency and per-query compute cost. General on-device LLMwork identifies limited device memory as a central inference bottleneck [14]. Medical LLMbenchmarks show the same tradeoff: local inference improves the privacy and cost posture, while memory and efficiency become the limiting constraints [15]. For physiological time-series data, moving inference onto the phone shifts the system boundary: raw data can remain local, offline analysis becomes possible, and cloud storage is no longer required for each query.

The main obstacle is representation rather than model size. Mobile LLMruntimes are built around token-identifier input and do not expose a path for injecting precomputed embeddings, so a time-series encoder’s output cannot be fed to the model directly. If the runtime cannot accept encoder embeddings, the time-series data must be serialized as text. Text serialization reuses an unchanged language-model interface and can cast time series as next-token prediction [16], but it expands each sample into multiple vocabulary tokens, formats or rounds numeric values, and spends the same limited context window needed for instructions and generated text. OpenTSLM soft-prompt (OpenTSLM-SP)avoids that prompt-level bottleneck by using representation-level fusion: a time-series encoder projects time-series windows into soft-prompt embeddings that are injected directly into the LLM’s embedding sequence [11]. That design is better matched to physiological time-series data, but it requires embedding-level access to the forward pass and cannot be expressed through token-only generation interfaces.

We present PocketTSLM, an on-device port of OpenTSLM-SPto MLX-Swiftthat evaluates whether the soft-prompt pathway can run on a consumer smartphone without changing the reference model’s greedy-decoding behavior. The port preserves the encoder-projector-LLMarchitecture while modifying the on-device generation path to accept projected time-series embeddings. PocketTSLM is scoped as a deployment and evaluation of on-device soft-prompt physiological time-series reasoning, not clinical validation, autonomous medical action, or behavior-change efficacy. We contribute: (1) a method for migrating soft-prompt TSLMsto MLX-Swift; (2) a numerical parity protocol that compares the on-device implementation against the reference under greedy decoding; (3) an on-device context-economics benchmark comparing soft-prompt encoding with a text-serialized baseline on the same backbone; and (4) a HealthKit-enabled iPhone demo that runs ECGand EEGreasoning locally without sending health data off-device.

papers.title: PET Quantification-Preserving Registration for Longitudinal Whole-Body PSMA PET/CT
papers.abstract: We adapt the diffeomorphic coarse-to-fine LapIRN architecture for longitudinal whole-body PSMA PET/CT registration in the Learn2Reg 2026 PSMAReg challenge. The method combines affine pre-registration, multi-modal deformable registration, and test-time instance optimization. We further introduce PET biomarker preservation losses for metabolic tumor volume (MTV) and total lesion glycolysis (TLG), including Jacobian-based constraints, and a per-structure rigidity regularization for skeletal structures. The submitted configuration achieved 81.0% DSC and 6.17 mm HD95, with MTV and TLG errors of 3.3% and 3.3%, respectively, on our evaluation protocol. Code is available at https://github.com/koegl/psmareg.

papers.intro:
Prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) PET/CT has become a central imaging modality for staging, treatment planning, radiopharmaceutical therapy, and post-therapy response assessment in prostate cancer [6]. In these settings, patients often undergo multiple scans over time, comprising a baseline scan before therapy and one or more follow-up scans. Accurate baseline-to-follow-up registration can support the comparison of disease burden, the localization of uptake changes, the assessment of lesion progression or response, dose accumulation, and quantitative longitudinal analysis [13]. For such analyses, the deformation should align anatomy without introducing artificial changes in PET-derived tumor burden measures. The Learn2Reg 2026 PSMAReg challenge [9, 8, 11] formalizes this problem as the estimation of a dense displacement field that warps each follow-up (moving) scan to its baseline (fixed) scan. The challenge evaluates registration accuracy using organ overlap and boundary distance, deformation regularity, and preservation of two PET-derived biomarkers: metabolic tumor volume (MTV) and total lesion glycolysis (TLG).

Deformable registration can be formulated as iterative optimization of a regularized objective functional [23, 1, 20], which can achieve high accuracy but is computationally demanding for whole-body images. Learning-based methods instead amortize this optimization into network weights and replace per-pair iteration with a single forward pass at inference [3, 5, 4]. We therefore build on LapIRN [17], whose coarse-to-fine Laplacian pyramid is well suited to recovering the large deformations expected between longitudinal whole-body scans while maintaining smooth and invertible transformations.

In this work, we adapt LapIRN to longitudinal whole-body PSMA PET/CT registration and extend it with PET biomarker preservation losses, local bone rigidity regularization, and test-time instance optimization.

papers.title: Uncertainty Quantification in Pairwise Difference Learning for Classification
papers.abstract: Instead of learning a mapping from instances to outcomes in the standard way, the key idea of pairwise difference learning (PDL) is to learn a function that takes two instances as input and predicts the difference between the respective outcomes. Given a function of this kind, predictions for a query instance are derived from every training example and then averaged. We propose a version of PDL for the task of classification and propose a suitable meta-learning technique for this purpose. Moreover, we address the problem of uncertainty quantification, i.e., of representing and quantifying the uncertainty of a PDL classifier's predictions in a faithful manner. Building on recent work on the decomposition of total uncertainty into aleatoric and epistemic components, we propose different ways of extending corresponding measures to the setting of PDL, depending on how and to what extent uncertainty is represented by the underlying base learner. In large-scale empirical studies, we analyze both the predictive accuracy and the uncertainty awareness of our PDL classifier.

papers.title: Greedy multiscale kernel algorithms
papers.abstract: Multiscale kernel approximation and greedy kernel algorithms are two established tools for scattered data approximation. We combine them into greedy multiscale kernel algorithms, in which every level of a multiscale residual correction is constructed by a greedy kernel algorithm. For the multiscale $f$-greedy algorithm we prove convergence rates in the number of selected centres which coincide (up to an arbitrarily small loss in the exponent) with the rates of the single-scale $f$-greedy algorithm. The gain of the multiscale construction is in the stability, and we make this precise by a two-sided estimate for the condition number of kernel matrices with rescaled kernels. The lower bound shows that any single-scale method, and in particular the $f$-greedy algorithm, pays for its convergence rate with condition numbers growing at least like a power of the number of centres. In contrast, the multiscale scaling of the kernel keeps this lower bound fixed on every level without changing the rate. The upper bound identifies the separation of the centres at the scale of the kernel as the quantity to control. We give the operation counts of all the methods considered and compare the greedy multiscale algorithms numerically with single-scale greedy and classical multiscale methods, in terms of error, time and conditioning.

Among the many developments in kernel approximation, two particularly successful directions are greedy kernel methods [35, 14, 33, 23] and multiscale kernel methods [11, 15, 30], the latter also known as multilevel, multistep, or multiresolution methods.

Greedy kernel methods originate from the thinning algorithms introduced in [12]. Their objective is to construct accurate approximations from a carefully selected subset of the data sites. Over time, the focus shifted from point removal to adaptive point insertion, leading to a variety of greedy selection rules [4, 18, 35], accompanied by a theoretical framework covering stability [32] and convergence [22, 33, 23]. Greedy kernel methods are used in numerous applications, from surrogate modeling to uncertainty quantification and scientific computing [14, 7].

Multiscale kernel methods trace their origins to the multistep interpolation schemes of [11]. Their central idea is to approximate a target function across several resolution levels by iteratively correcting the residual of the previous levels: starting from a coarse set of centres, progressively finer point sets and progressively narrower kernels are used. The framework was originally motivated by compactly supported kernels [28], for which a scaling of the support proportional to the fill distance yields sparse and well-conditioned system matrices. Convergence was established in [15, 30] with later refinements in [26, 31], and the development of adaptive multiscale schemes is an active topic, see [31, Algorithm 3] and the recent preprints [13, 17, 8].

Although greedy and multiscale kernel methods pursue different strategies, they share a common objective, namely the construction of efficient kernel approximations from large data sets. Greedy methods achieve this through adaptive centre selection, multiscale methods through a hierarchy of resolutions. In this paper we combine both ideas and introduce a class of greedy multiscale kernel algorithms in which every level of the multiscale hierarchy is built by a greedy algorithm. Since the PP-greedy algorithm produces asymptotically quasi-uniformly distributed centres [32], the classical multiscale construction on quasi-uniform sets can be seen as a PP-greedy multiscale algorithm11 1 To be precise, [32] establishes quasi-uniformity for a fixed shape parameter. It remains to check whether this result extends uniformly to a range of shape parameters., while target-dependent rules such as ff-greedy yield genuinely adaptive multiscale approximations.

(i) For the multiscale ff-greedy algorithm we prove convergence rates in the number of selected centres, see Theorem 4.8. The rate coincides, up to an arbitrarily small loss in the exponent, with the rate of the single-scale ff-greedy algorithm of [23]. (ii) We prove a two-sided estimate for the condition number of kernel matrices with rescaled kernels, see Proposition 4.10 and Theorem 4.12. (iii) We combine the multiscale contraction lemma behind all convergence proofs, Lemma 4.5, with the stability estimate into one theorem, Theorem 4.13, valid for any construction of the levels. papers.title: Teaching DINOv3 About Partial 3D Geometry: A Self-Supervised Geometry-Aware Approach
papers.abstract: Partial shape matching is a crucial yet underexplored problem in 3D vision, with significant relevance to real-world scenarios where shapes are often only partially observed. Existing feature descriptors face difficulties in this setting, as traditional representations either struggle with the boundaries of partial shapes or heavily depend on the shape's spatial position. While existing approaches have employed DINO features for partial shape matching, these features are not inherently suited for handling partial observations. In this work, we propose a method to refine DINO features using LoRA-based self-supervised learning, enabling the generation of feature descriptors that are robust to partiality. Our features substantially improve performance on partial shape matching compared to traditional or vision foundation features. Additionally, when integrated into existing partial shape matching pipelines, we achieve state-of-the-art results on partial shape matching and left-right prediction benchmarks.

papers.intro:
Finding dense correspondences between 3D deformable shapes is a fundamental step in understanding geometric data, enabling several downstream tasks, including information transfer and learning statistical models. Specifically, when the geometries do not share the same identity (e.g., different humans) and undergo non‑rigid deformations (e.g., different poses), establishing such correspondences remains an open research problem. The challenge is further exacerbated when one (or both) of the shapes comes from partial observations, a common real-world case due to occlusions, acquisition noise, or local errors in the 3D reconstruction.

Scholars have relied on handcrafted descriptors [55, 5, 57] for decades, both standalone and as input to deep learning pipelines. Such descriptors demonstrate powerful capabilities for full shapes, but they often rely on theoretical premises (e.g., watertight meshes with the same topology) that make them impractical for partial use cases. Recently, the emergence of foundation models like DINO [14, 44, 53] or Stable Diffusion [50] has introduced a new class of features. Trained on billions of images in a self-supervised manner, these models demonstrate an impressive ability to characterise points semantically, while being robust across deformations and identities. Such features have been applied to various computer vision tasks, including detection [40, 63], segmentation [36, 60], and, more recently, 3D shape matching [19]. However, these models have a limited understanding of 3D geometry, often exhibiting geometrical confusion, such as left-right mismatches and occlusions/disocclusions. These problems persist even in the most advanced foundation models (DINOv3 [53]), as we will demonstrate in our experiments. While recent works have explored 2D-based fine-tuning strategies [30], models trained solely on single-view images lack true 3D grounding. Achieving this physical understanding requires incorporating 3D information directly into the training process.

While training a new foundation model for 3D shapes from scratch would require a huge amount of data and resources, we propose a more natural and elegant solution that injects 3D awareness into 2D foundation features. We propose GeoLoRA (Geometry-Aware Low-Rank Adaptation), a new self-supervised approach that, using only synthetic data, informs the backbone 2D foundation features of the 3D structure. Our idea is to start from full shapes and generate synthetic partial versions of them, using procedures to simulate real occlusions or artefacts. Since the partial shapes originate from the full ones, they also enjoy a natural 3D correspondence. We use this information to supervise a lightweight LoRA [33] module on top of the 2D foundation model, rendering multiple images for both the full and partial shapes, and optimising the features to be aligned between the two. Finally, unlike fully 2D approaches, since we have access to the 3D geometry of the shapes that generated the image, we incorporate a geodesic penalty into our contrastive loss, providing a strong geometric cue. In practice, we learn a feature space where dissimilar points are pushed away proportionally to their distance on the object surface.

As a result, we achieve the best features for partial-to-full shape matching available to date. We surpass handcrafted and 2D foundation feature alternatives across different partiality classes and datasets, both in partial-to-full and partial-to-partial settings (some results are shown in Fig. 1). The refined features integrate seamlessly with state-of-the-art matching methods, boosting their performance. They also show better chirality (left-right disambiguation) than the original backbone features, suggesting that partial-to-full matching can be a useful auxiliary task for enhancing the geometrical understanding of foundation models. papers.title: Putting a Temperature on Electron Correlation
papers.abstract: It is common wisdom that a better understanding of how to quantify electron correlation should lead to more efficient treatments of the correlation problem. Here, we not only substantiate this view but turn it into a concrete, systematic framework for ground states. Since prominent correlation measures such as the nonfreeness depend only on the one-particle reduced density matrix, modeling the correlation energy as a function of such a measure naturally places the framework within reduced density matrix functional theory, while keeping the cost at mean-field level. Strikingly, the variable conjugate to the measure emerges as a ``correlation temperature'', thereby connecting correlation measures, functional theory, and effective temperatures. The framework rationalizes methods such as i-DMFT, and we illustrate its key concepts analytically for the Hubbard dimer and numerically for small molecular systems. This brings a fundamental question within reach: how much of the correlation problem can be solved at mean-field cost?

papers.intro:
Describing electron correlation is one of the central challenges of quantum chemistry, condensed matter physics, and materials science, particularly for strongly correlated systems [1]. Its difficulty stems from the exponential complexity of the many-electron wave function [2, 3]. In quantum chemistry, the most common starting point for tackling this correlation problem is the Hartree–Fock (HF) method. By restricting the wave function to a single Slater determinant, HF reduces the problem to self-consistent one-particle equations at so-called mean-field cost. Moreover, HF is rarely the end point: perturbative, coupled-cluster, configuration-interaction, and many multireference approaches typically build on the HF reference state and its orbitals. HF thus constitutes the natural first step for most quantum-chemical treatments of electron correlation.

HF thus constitutes the natural first step for most quantum-chemical treatments of electron correlation.

A remarkable insight due to Lieb [4, 5] is that, for positive interactions, the HF method can be recast as the minimization of a functional of the one-particle reduced density matrix (1RDM) over all ensemble NN-representable 1RDMs. HF thereby becomes the simplest approximation within reduced density matrix functional theory (RDMFT) [6, 7, 8, 9, 10], whose exact functional differs from the HF functional only by the correlation functional ℱc\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{c}}. Despite well-developed foundations [11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16], however, approximations to ℱc\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{c}} are still less mature than in density functional theory (DFT), and their systematic improvement remains a central challenge.

Quantum information theory offers a complementary perspective, starting from a more basic question: what is electron correlation in the first place? Since electrons do not constitute proper subsystems in the operator-algebraic sense, the standard paradigm based on local operations and classical communication does not apply, and no unique measure of electron correlation exists [17]. Instead, it can only be quantified ad hoc, for instance by the prominent nonfreeness, the distance of a state from the set of mean-field states [18, 19]. Remarkably, for pure states the nonfreeness is a simple function of the 1RDM. Moreover, these mean-field states are precisely those whose two-particle reduced density matrix underlies the HF functional. Both perspectives thus single out the 1RDM and rest on the same notion of uncorrelated states.

Yet it leaves open how a correlation measure could actually be put to work in a computational method. In this perspective, we not only substantiate this view but turn it into a concrete, systematic framework for ground states. The guiding idea is simple: if a correlation measure captures the essential correlation of the NN-electron wave function, as compressed into its 1RDM, then the correlation energy should be expressible through the measure alone, at least within a specific class of systems, such as a molecule along its dissociation coordinate. Following this idea through naturally places the framework within RDMFT, while keeping the computational cost at the mean-field level. Most importantly, it reveals that three seemingly distinct concepts are intimately connected: correlation measures from quantum information theory, RDMFT, and effective temperatures, whose thermal occupation numbers mimic those of correlated states (Fig. 1). This connection, a central result of this work, gives such temperatures a clear conceptual origin: unlike the occupation smearing used to improve numerical convergence [20, 21], they follow directly from quantifying electron correlation.

papers.title: Auditable and Deployable Multi-Agent Motion Planning via Posetal Games from Legal Guidelines
papers.abstract: When robots are deployed in the real-world, they must interact with other agents and accomplish their own goals while adhering to legal constraints. These potentially conflicting objectives are often only partially prioritized, making scalarized objectives or fully specified hierarchies unsuitable. We present a framework for multi-agent motion planning under legal requirements based on games with partially ordered preferences (posetal games). Scenario-independent legal guidelines order abstract legal concerns, from which we automatically derive agent preferences and a legal game for any concrete scenario. Agents may refine their legal preferences with private objectives, and regulators may refine the guideline as laws evolve. We prove that such customizations can only remove equilibria and thus preserve legality. To coordinate agents without explicitly communicating private preferences, we introduce belief play, which provably recovers the true equilibria from conservative local games, and a distributed iterative best-response protocol requiring less information. We apply the framework to maritime navigation, systematically lifting pairwise traffic rules to multi-vessel encounters. On seven encounters with up to four vessels, every rule violation of the committed equilibria is certified as forced by the legal hierarchy or unsatisfiable, and defectors are identified from public information in all tested cases. These results indicate that guideline-based posetal games offer an auditable route from partially specified laws to multi-agent motion planning.

papers.intro:
Robots that share roads, waterways, or airspace with other agents must plan their motion subject to many potentially conflicting objectives. These objectives often include legal requirements imposed by regulators, which take precedence over individual objectives. Since not all objectives can be satisfied simultaneously in general, minimum-violation planning prioritizes them and systematically violates lower-priority objectives when necessary to satisfy higher-priority ones [1, 2]. Legally compliant multi-agent motion planning is nevertheless difficult for at least three reasons. First, some objectives are incomparable, in the sense that one cannot assert that either objective is more important than the other. This is particularly relevant for legal regulations, where authorities typically specify only a partial priority order [3]. Second, many traffic laws are stated as rules between pairs of agents, so the obligations of an agent depend on which other agents are present, and obligations toward different agents might conflict (Fig. 1). Third, in multi-agent settings, agents respond strategically to the actions of other agents [4], whose private objectives are typically unknown. Taken together, these obstacles call for a framework that derives the preferences of the agents from the law for every scenario, preserves the partial priorities of the law, and coordinates the agents without requiring them to disclose their private objectives.

Second, many traffic laws are stated as rules between pairs of agents, so the obligations of an agent depend on which other agents are present, and obligations toward different agents might conflict (Fig. 1). Third, in multi-agent settings, agents respond strategically to the actions of other agents [4], whose private objectives are typically unknown. Taken together, these obstacles call for a framework that derives the preferences of the agents from the law for every scenario, preserves the partial priorities of the law, and coordinates the agents without requiring them to disclose their private objectives.

A particularly important instance of this problem is motion planning for autonomous vessels in the maritime domain. The International Code of Safety for Maritime Autonomous Ships [6], adopted in 2026, requires autonomous vessels to comply with the maritime traffic rules laid out in the Convention on the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea (COLREGS) [5]. However, the COLREGS are only defined for pairs of vessels which may lead to conflicting requirements in encounters involving more than two vessels, as shown in Fig. 1. While the COLREGS prioritize collision avoidance over strict compliance with the encounter rules [5, Rule 2], they do not specify which rules should be violated when conflicts arise.

Considering these challenges, we identify auditability, customizability, and deployability as key requirements for a multi-agent motion planning algorithm under legal constraints. Auditability requires agents to exhibit predictable behavior and provide explanations for their actions, particularly when not all conflicting objectives can be satisfied. Customizability enables regulators to revise legal priorities and manufacturers to refine priorities that laws leave unspecified. Moreover, any deployable algorithm has to allow agents to coordinate despite their limited knowledge of the private objectives of other agents. To meet these requirements, we present, to the best of our knowledge, the first systematic method for automatically constructing legally compliant motion-planning games from scenario-independent legal guidelines. Our framework represents objective hierarchies as partially ordered preferences, resulting in posetal games [4], for which we provide solution protocols that operate under limited information. The key idea is to separate what the law prescribes from what a scenario instantiates. Regulators specify a guideline, i.e., a partial order over abstract legal concerns such as collision avoidance, and every concrete scenario inherits the preferences of its agents by matching their legal metrics to these concerns. Since every customization of the resulting preferences is a refinement, and refining preferences can only remove equilibria, legality is preserved by construction. We demonstrate the practical applicability of the framework through a case study of COLREGS-compliant motion planning for multi-vessel encounters.

Formal specifications, initially used primarily for offline monitoring and runtime verification, have become core components of learning, synthesis, and control methods [7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14]. They provide interpretable representations of objectives and constraints and, in multi-agent settings, requirements governing interactions among agents. For example, autonomous-driving systems must satisfy specifications ranging from lane-keeping requirements to appropriate responses to emergency vehicles [15, 16]. In unstructured environments, interaction requirements are commonly expressed through pairwise rules or fixed priority structures, which favor concise representations at the expense of completeness. For instance, the airborne collision-avoidance system ACAS-X determines priorities for pairwise aircraft encounters and relies on heuristics to combine the resulting evaluations [17, 18]. Even in this pairwise setting, the precomputed lookup tables are sufficiently large to motivate dedicated compression methods [19]. This scalability challenge is further amplified in domains such as warehouse navigation and maritime robotics, where agents and interactions are more diverse [20, 21, 22, 23]. Rulebooks [3, 24] reduce the need for exhaustive specification by prioritizing objectives and permitting lower-priority objectives to be violated when necessary to satisfy higher-priority ones. Our framework builds on this principle and extends it to multiple strategic agents whose obligations depend on the scenario.

papers.title: Adding Temperature to the Adiabatic Connection: Hybrid Functionals for Static and Dynamic Correlation
papers.abstract: Capturing static and dynamic electron correlation simultaneously at manageable computational cost remains a key challenge in electronic structure theory. Motivated by the recurring role of effective temperature in self-consistent field methods we extend the adiabatic connection mechanism from density functional theory to include a temperature dimension. This gives rise to thermally enhanced hybrid functionals, in which static correlation is captured via fractional occupations generated by an effective "correlation temperature" within thermal Hartree-Fock, while dynamic correlation is described by established density functional approximations. The framework formally unifies information-density matrix functional theory (i-DMFT) and thermally-assisted-occupation (TAO-)DFT as special cases, clarifying their theoretical basis and the respective prescriptions for the temperature parameter. We assess the performance of several thermally enhanced hybrids for different cases where i-DMFT was previously shown to fail. Furthermore, we discuss and test different schemes for determining the correlation temperature and investigate the accuracy of different such choices for a benchmark set derived from biphenyl. The results help to clarify the achievable balance of accuracy, generality, and efficiency, establishing thermally enhanced hybrids as a systematic route toward low-cost treatment of both correlation types.

Within the RDMFT framework, fractional occupation numbers alone already offer a promising route to capturing static correlation at mean-field cost. The i-DMFT method [89] achieves this via a conjectured linear relation between cumulant energy and 1RDM entropy [24, 95, 90], leading to a thermal Hartree-Fock picture [67]. In both cases, the central challenge is determining θ\theta appropriately – various approaches have been proposed, from matching high-level occupation numbers [20] to orbital-energy based criteria [63]. Related efforts to combine density-functional and occupation-dependent correlation treatments have also been explored. This repeated occurrence of effective temperatures in electronic structure methods motivated us to investigate the theoretical foundations of those methods, mainly DFT, that can actually be formulated as a thermodynamic theory. This viewpoint (Section II) then very naturally leads to a novel adiabatic connection that extends the usual coupling-strength integration [44, 9, 10, 70, 1, 82], to include a temperature dimension, providing a rigorous definition of why an electronic temperature and exact HF exchange emerge simultaneously. The resulting “thermally enhanced” hybrid functionals (Section III) operate at mean-field cost, covering static and dynamic correlation and the transition between them. We demonstrate how known failures of i-DMFT in densities, occupation numbers, and dissociation barriers are systematically resolved (Section IV), and critically discuss existing strategies for determining correlation temperatures, arguing that neither fully universal values nor highly system-specific methodologies are satisfactory, while proposing new alternatives (Section V). Benchmarking on a set of organic molecules then tests the transferability of these ideas across chemically similar systems (Section VI), before we conclude with an outlook towards future development and applications (Section VII).

papers.title: Knowledge That Is Linear Before Fine-Tuning Generalizes After It
papers.abstract: Not all facts a language model can recall support further learning equally well. We distinguish active facts, which support generalization beyond their own recall, from inert facts, which can be recalled but do not support such generalization in a given task. We study this distinction by constructing new relations from existing ones. Take the relation that maps a place to its continent (Paris -> Europe) and assign each of its answers an arbitrary new label (Europe -> crab, Asia -> zebra). The new relation then maps Paris -> crab. We fine-tune the model on the new relation for a subset of subjects, without telling it the original relation or the relabeling rule, and test whether it assigns the corresponding labels to held-out subjects that share an answer in the original relation. Having learned Paris -> crab, does it answer Munich -> crab? Across eleven language models and 70 relations, how linearly readable the original relation is in pretrained representations strongly predicts this generalization. Within each model, the two correlate across relations at Pearson r = 0.87 to 0.92. This association persists when controlling, separately and jointly, for the number of fine-tuning subjects and answers, the model's accuracy on the original relation, and how often the subjects occur in pretraining text. It is also robust to re-randomizing the label assignment and fine-tuning seed, and to replacing the animal labels with labels from thirteen other semantic categories. When we map a fine-tuned model's wrong label back to the original answer it was assigned to, Munich -> zebra becomes Munich -> Asia. Answers recovered this way are more often among the linear probe's top answers for the subject than among the pretrained model's own. Whether a new relation generalizes depends less on whether its facts can be recalled than on how readily their shared structure can be read out linearly.

papers.intro:
Imagine that the pretraining text describes Mary as having grown up in France, attending French schools, writing books in French and working in French-speaking institutions, but never states her native language. A language model should still assume that Mary is a native speaker of French. We call this statistical generalization of facts. The model infers a new fact from facts it knows, by a statistical rule that the pretraining text rarely states explicitly and that is not always true. It differs from entailment, where the new fact follows necessarily from the known ones, and from paraphrase, where the same fact is merely worded differently (Section 2). Statistical generalization is an important part of what makes language models useful beyond recalling what they were told. Prior work has asked whether models draw such inferences from facts they are trained on (Feng et al., 2025; Treutlein et al., 2024), but, to our knowledge, no prior work has asked which of a model’s facts support them.

papers.title: A Benchmark for Controllable Speaking-Style Captioning in Audio-Language Models
papers.abstract: Speaking-style captioning (SSC) aims to generate natural language descriptions of how speech is delivered, capturing paralinguistic attributes such as vocal timbre, prosody, and expressivity. Many downstream applications, including conversational AI agents, controllable speech generation, and large-scale audio annotation, require dimension-specific style captions that describe targeted aspects of speech (e.g., speaker traits, emotion, or delivery style), rather than a single undifferentiated description. However, existing work lacks a unified formulation for controllable speaking-style captioning. We address this gap by formulating SSC as an instruction-following audio-language task, where explicit instructions specify the speaking-style dimensions to be described. We introduce StyleInstructCaps, the first standardized benchmark for controllable speaking-style captioning in audio-language models. StyleInstructCaps provides a dataset and evaluation framework that measures metadata groundedness, hallucination, instruction-following ability, generalization to unseen instructions and audio datasets, and speaker-style consistency. Across nine state-of-the-art audio-language models, we find that strong instruction-following ability does not necessarily imply grounded speaking-style understanding, and that SSC-specific instruction-diverse training substantially improves groundedness, controllability, and speaker consistency.

(2024). Despite growing interest, SSC still lacks a unified task formulation and evaluation paradigm.

Researchers in audio understanding often treat SSC as an extension of speech comprehension, emphasizing communicative intent and discourse-level meaning Jing et al. (2024); Chandra et al. (2025); Zhang et al. (2025b). In contrast, speech synthesis and generative modeling communities typically view speaking-style captions as controllable descriptions of vocal characteristics for expressive text-to-speech Wang et al. (2025a); Guo et al. (2023) and voice conversion systems Kuan et al. (2023); Hai et al. (2024). These differing perspectives reflect a deeper challenge: speaking-style is inherently subjective Adigwe et al. (2024), spanning multiple interacting paralinguistic factors such as speaker identity, affect, prosody, and contextual delivery. As a result, existing SSC systems often capture different notions of style, making evaluation and comparison across models difficult.

Conventional SSC approaches typically produce a single holistic description of speech, often entangling speaker traits, emotion, prosody, and delivery characteristics, making captions difficult to interpret or evaluate systematically. In contrast, controllable SSC conditions generation on explicit style instructions, enabling the same utterance to yield multiple targeted and complementary descriptions depending on the task objective.

Despite their effectiveness on narrowly defined objectives, existing SSC models often adopt a single view of speaking-style, typically focusing on speaker-centric or emotion-centric attributes, which limits generalization to broader stylistic phenomena. Since speaking-style depends on downstream context, SSC models must be controllable and generate captions conditioned on explicit style instructions. StyleInstructCaps evaluates generated captions along five dimensions: (1) metadata groundedness, (2) hallucination, (3) instruction-following ability, (4) generalization to unseen speech data and prompts, and (5) speaker-style consistency.

papers.title: EviGround-CT: Sentence-to-Volume Grounding for Verifying LLM-Generated Chest CT Reports
papers.abstract: Chest computed tomography (CT) reports generated by large language models (LLMs) can describe positive findings that lack localized evidence in the scan. We propose EviGround-CT to verify these findings after report generation. A deterministic extractor identifies positive finding sentences, and a 3D grounding model predicts an evidence mask for each sentence. Using the full sentence retains anatomical location, laterality, and descriptive modifiers in the grounding query. We evaluate report generation on CT-RATE, and grounding and verification on a held-out 100-case ReXGroundingCT subset. Using the available annotations, sentence-grounded verification raises evidence-supported precision (ESP) from 0.263 to 0.365 across 137 extracted in-scope positives, compared with category conditioning. The corresponding unsupported positive finding rate falls from 0.737 to 0.635. The paired case-level bootstrap ESP difference is +0.102 (95% confidence interval: [0.028, 0.181]). The predicted masks associate individual report statements with spatial evidence that can be inspected alongside the CT.

papers.intro:
Full-volume chest computed tomography (CT) report generation must summarize hundreds of slices containing abnormalities that may be small, diffuse, or spatially distributed. Recent volumetric datasets and CT-oriented systems enable report generation from these scans [1, 2]. Spatial correspondence is also central to multimodal image-guided systems [3, 4, 5]. Evaluating the generated findings requires checking where their evidence lies. For a statement such as “a small pulmonary nodule is present in the right upper lobe,” the relevant evidence is a nodule in the specified lobe. Lexical similarity and finding-level agreement assess text or labels without explicitly testing this spatial correspondence. Category agreement, for example, treats mentions of a nodule in different lobes alike. Sentence-to-volume grounding includes the stated location in the evidence query.

papers.title: Planet forming disk populations and their connection to the environment
papers.abstract: Existing sub-mm observatories such as ALMA have provided statistics on the planet-forming mass reservoirs within circumstellar disks around stars in stellar clusters out to distances of $\sim$400pc. However, these disks are not where most planets form. Many stars, and hence planets, form in more massive clusters, which are only found at larger distances. Environmental conditions that affect disks - such as UV radiation field, ambient gaseous mass reservoir, and stellar density - change significantly as a function of cluster mass, implying that our current knowledge of the disk population from current facilities is severely biased. Characterising planet formation in stellar clusters towards the peak of the cluster mass function requires determining the distribution of planet forming disk masses out to $\sim$3kpc, which encapsulates the nearby parts of the Sagittarius arm of the Milky Way and contains multiple massive stellar clusters. ALMA2040 will provide the leap in sensitivity needed to move beyond detections of only a handful of disks and robustly measure the slope and median of the disk mass distribution at these distances. This will mark the transition from studying individual detections to population-level studies of planet formation across diverse cluster environments. This has synergy with existing and upcoming measurements of accretion rates in these distant clusters, which combined provide a measure of the accretion timescale, enabling us to distinguish various evolutionary pathways and assess how they depend on cluster mass and star-forming environment.

papers.title: Wandering intermediate-mass black holes and off-nuclear tidal disruption events from early star clusters
papers.abstract: Off-nuclear tidal disruption events (TDEs) reveal evidence for massive black holes outside galactic centers, but the origins of this wandering population remain uncertain. We investigate wandering intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs) formed through runaway stellar collisions in dense, high-redshift star clusters and predict their TDE signatures across cosmic time. Our semi-analytic model samples clusters associated with low-mass subhalos at $7<z<20$ and uses merger trees from the IllustrisTNG TNG50 simulation to follow the assembly of 15 elliptical galaxies with stellar masses of $10^9-10^{11}~M_\odot$. We compare two models for high-redshift cluster formation: a maximal model taken from a high-resolution simulation and a conservative model calibrated from local cluster relations. Off-nuclear TDEs produced through this mechanism occur in bursts within 10-100 Myr of IMBH formation as the loss-cone surrounding the black hole is depleted. We estimate the rate of off-nuclear TDEs expected across time per galaxy, and characterize these events as typically occurring between $10-10^3$ kpc from their host galaxy centers. Event rates increase with galaxy mass; in the maximal model, the progenitors of the most massive galaxies reach peak off-nuclear TDE rates of approximately $5\times10^{-4}-4\times10^{-2}~\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$ per galaxy at $7\lesssim z\lesssim13$. This work provides a framework for constraining the early population of star clusters that form IMBHs through runaway collapse via their contribution to the rate of off-nuclear TDEs in the high redshift Universe.

Off-nuclear tidal disruption events (TDEs) offer a direct way to uncover massive black holes outside galactic centers, where weak persistent accretion can make them difficult to detect [67, 44, 45, 36, 89, 75]. The four candidates analyzed by Guolo [29] are associated with massive, early-type parent galaxies with stellar masses M⋆∼1011M_{\star}\sim 10^{11} M⊙. These events bring a long-standing theoretical prediction into observational reach: hierarchical galaxy assembly can leave massive black holes outside galactic nuclei when the orbital decay of black holes accreted during mergers is inefficient [27, 82, 35, 9, e.g.,]. Furthermore, off-nuclear TDEs may provide the opportunity to probe intermediate-mass black holes formed in early star clusters, provided their formation and subsequent stellar dynamics translate into off-nuclear TDE activity as galaxies assemble.

Dense star clusters in the early Universe provide a promising environment for forming intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs), here defined as black holes with masses 10210^{2}–10510^{5} M⊙. Observations at z≳8z\gtrsim 8 reveal compact, young stellar systems with masses and sizes comparable to present-day globular clusters, or with even higher stellar densities [2, 53]. In sufficiently dense clusters, runaway stellar collisions can build a very massive star that subsequently collapses into an IMBH [93, 25, 70, 26, 78, 87, e.g.,]. The surrounding cluster also supplies stars that may be tidally disrupted after the black hole forms. The TDE activity of this population therefore depends on both IMBH production and the subsequent evolution of the stellar orbits that populate their loss cones.

Cosmological simulations that include black hole seeding prescriptions and allow black holes to evolve on independent orbits provide a framework for studying wandering populations during galaxy assembly. Examples include ROMULUS [77] and ASTRID [57, 91]. Studies based on these simulations predict substantial off-nuclear populations: ROMULUS finds that wandering black hole abundance increases approximately linearly with halo mass, while ASTRID shows that mergers can redistribute black holes away from galactic centers, causing central and wandering occupation fractions to evolve differently [68, 67, 20, 29, 84] . Their adopted seed masses, however, do not sample the full IMBH regime, and the stellar collisions and loss-cone dynamics that govern cluster-born IMBH formation and TDE production remain unresolved. papers.title: An Attenuation Bump at z=9.3: Probing Dust Diversity at Cosmic Dawn
papers.abstract: We report the identification of a UV attenuation bump in the Black Pearl, a galaxy at a spectroscopic redshift of 9.3335 observed with JWST/NIRSpec as part of the ZENITH and EMBER surveys. This is the highest-redshift UV bump reported to date, probing dust properties only approximately 500 Myr after the Big Bang. The feature is directly detected as a broad depression in the rest-frame UV continuum and is well described by a local Drude profile, with a central wavelength of 2132+/-17 Angstroms, an FWHM of 413+/-54 Angstroms, and a peak attenuation of 0.21+/-0.02 mag. Joint spectrophotometric modeling with a flexible attenuation law independently recovers a pronounced UV bump without imposing its presence a priori, regardless of the adopted star-formation history. The modeling indicates a relatively low-mass, actively star-forming galaxy, with a logarithmic stellar mass of 8.35 (+0.09/-0.08) in solar units, a star-formation rate of 2.36 (+0.54/-0.42) solar masses per year, and a visual attenuation of 0.34 (+0.12/-0.11) mag. Rest-frame optical emission-line diagnostics indicate a hard ionizing spectrum and allow for a moderate AGN contribution, but provide no evidence for a powerful AGN capable of dominating the observed UV continuum. The bump is blueshifted by 43+/-17 Angstroms (approximately 2.5 sigma) relative to the canonical Milky Way 2175 Angstrom feature and by 127 +/- 17 Angstroms relative to the few UV bumps currently known at redshift approximately 7, while its width is consistent with the broad distribution measured along Milky Way sightlines. The displaced central wavelength therefore provides the clearest evidence for a nonstandard UV-bump profile at redshift 9.3335, pointing to substantial diversity in the properties of UV-bump carriers at early cosmic times, with both PAHs and small graphite grains remaining plausible candidates.

papers.intro:
The rapid enrichment of galaxies with metals and dust during the first billion years of cosmic history is emerging as one of the major discoveries enabled by the James Webb Space Telescope [43, JWST,]. Recent spectroscopic observations have revealed galaxies with intense nebular emission, hard ionizing radiation fields, and substantial metal abundances already in place during the epoch of reionization and beyond, only a few hundred million years after the Big Bang [28, 41, 86, 29, 33, e.g.,]. At the same time, Atacama Large Millimeter Array observations have demonstrated that significant dust reservoirs and obscured star formation are already present in some galaxies at z∼7​–​8z\sim 7\mbox{--}8 [30, 49, 97, 36, 1, 9, e.g.,], as well as in host galaxies of luminous quasars at similar epochs [107, e.g.,]. Evidence for substantial dust enrichment is now emerging at even earlier epochs: the spectroscopically confirmed galaxy EGS-z11-R0 at z=11.45z=11.45 exhibits a remarkably red UV continuum and significant dust attenuation, demonstrating that dust-enriched systems can already be in place within the first ∼400​Myr\sim 400\,\mathrm{Myr} of cosmic history in a massive log10⁡(M⋆/M⊙)∼9.2\log_{10}(M_{\star}/M_{\odot})\sim 9.2 galaxy 85, but see also 31 and 72. Together, these results are transforming our understanding of the time scales of metal production, dust growth, and interstellar medium (ISM) processing in the early Universe and their interplay [68, 75, 17, e.g.,].

At the same time, Atacama Large Millimeter Array observations have demonstrated that significant dust reservoirs and obscured star formation are already present in some galaxies at z∼7​–​8z\sim 7\mbox{--}8 [30, 49, 97, 36, 1, 9, e.g.,], as well as in host galaxies of luminous quasars at similar epochs [107, e.g.,]. Evidence for substantial dust enrichment is now emerging at even earlier epochs: the spectroscopically confirmed galaxy EGS-z11-R0 at z=11.45z=11.45 exhibits a remarkably red UV continuum and significant dust attenuation, demonstrating that dust-enriched systems can already be in place within the first ∼400​Myr\sim 400\,\mathrm{Myr} of cosmic history in a massive log10⁡(M⋆/M⊙)∼9.2\log_{10}(M_{\star}/M_{\odot})\sim 9.2 galaxy 85, but see also 31 and 72. Together, these results are transforming our understanding of the time scales of metal production, dust growth, and interstellar medium (ISM) processing in the early Universe and their interplay [68, 75, 17, e.g.,].

In this context, the ultraviolet (UV) extinction bump centered approximately at 2175​Å2175\,\AA represents a particularly powerful diagnostic of dust composition and grain evolution [39, 22, 32, e.g.,]. The feature is the strongest structure in the interstellar extinction curve in the Milky Way and is also observed in nearby galaxies and in absorption systems over a broad range of redshifts [44, 77, 45, e.g.,]. The UV bump is widely attributed to small carbonaceous grains or molecules, although the precise identity and physical properties of its carriers remain uncertain. The proposed candidates include small graphite grains, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), amorphous carbonaceous materials, and related aromatic carbonaceous particles [61, 32, 14, 79, 65, e.g.,]. The formation, survival, and processing of these carriers depend on the physical conditions of the ISM, making the presence and detailed profile of the UV bump a potentially sensitive probe of dust evolution.

The diversity of the observed UV-bump profiles may provide important information on the physical properties of early dust. In the Milky Way, the central wavelength of the bump is remarkably stable, whereas its width and strength exhibit substantial variations among different sightlines [39]. At high redshift, the still limited number of spectroscopic detections already appears to span a broader range of bump properties, raising the possibility that the carriers and/or their processing state differ among galaxies. In this perspective, the central wavelength, width, and strength of the UV bump become complementary observables that can help constrain the composition, size distribution, and local processing of the underlying grain population.

papers.title: A model for the ongoing subcluster interaction in Centaurus
papers.abstract: Intracluster globular clusters (GCs) preserve the hierarchical and chemical history of galaxy cluster assembly. The nearby Centaurus cluster is believed to be undergoing an interaction between two subclusters, Cen 30 and Cen 45, which should leave an imprint on its intracluster GCs. We aim to characterise the GC population in Centaurus and constrain its recent assembly history, ultimately constructing an interaction scenario consistent with the observational evidence. Using deep VLT/FORS imaging in the $V$ and $I$ bands, we select GC candidates around the cluster centre based on morphology and colour criteria. We use a Voronoi tessellation approach to study the GC spatial distribution and density profiles, demonstrating its advantages over traditional annuli-based methods. We then constrain the evolution of the galaxy luminosity function using the GC specific frequency and colour distribution. The GC spatial distribution shows significant substructure. As in other clusters, red GCs are concentrated on the brightest galaxies, whereas blue GCs trace a more extended structure. We confirm and quantify the previously reported 'bridge' of GCs connecting NGC 4696 and NGC 4709, showing that it hosts twice as many GCs as expected from the projected GC systems of the two galaxies alone. The inferred evolution of the galaxy luminosity function agrees with previous results for Hydra I, yielding a faint-end slope of $α=-1.87_{-0.06}^{+0.06}$ for the galaxy population that assembled the Centaurus core. We propose a nearly head-on collision scenario in which Cen 45 recently passed through Cen 30, with the two subclusters moving approximately along the line of sight. This scenario explains the large line-of-sight velocity difference between the subclusters, the hot X-ray-emitting gas between them, the GC bridge, and the puffed-up GC system of NGC 4709.

papers.intro:
The hierarchical assembly process of galaxy clusters produces a stellar component that is not bound to any individual galaxy, but rather to the cluster potential as a whole. This component consists of individual stars, known as intracluster light (ICL, Montes 2022), as well as intracluster globular clusters (GCs, White 1987; Hilker et al. 1999). Since the ICL and ICGCs originated in the galaxies that assembled the cluster, their properties can be used to constrain the dynamical history of the cluster and the evolution of its galaxies (Montenegro-Taborda et al., 2025). The ICL is particularly difficult to observe due to its low surface brightness (μg≳26\mu_{g}\gtrsim 26 mag/arcsec2) and the contamination from the light of individual galaxies. In contrast, GCs are more easily detectable as they are observed as point sources which can be as bright as g∼g\sim 20 mag20\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{a}\mathrm{g} (Chaturvedi et al., 2022). Thus, GCs can serve as excellent tracers of the ICL, as they are typically found in the same regions of space and share similar kinematic properties (e.g. Arnaboldi et al. 1996; Schuberth et al. 2008; Chaturvedi et al. 2022). Still, the study of these faint components is restricted to the nearby universe, motivating our work in the nearby Centaurus cluster (∼\sim 35.6 Mpc35.6\text{\,}\mathrm{M}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{c}, Tully et al. 2016).

The dominant subcluster, denoted Cen 30, recedes at 3041 km s−13041\text{\,}\mathrm{km}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1} with a velocity dispersion of 586 km s−1586\text{\,}\mathrm{km}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1} and has 2.5 times more galaxies than the smaller one, Cen 45, which is moving at 4570 km s−14570\text{\,}\mathrm{km}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1} with dispersion of 262 km s−1262\text{\,}\mathrm{km}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1}. Cen 30 and Cen 45 host the two brightest cluster galaxies (BCGs), NGC 4696 and NGC 4709, respectively. Their properties are summarised in Tab. 2. Despite the large velocity difference, Lucey et al. (1986) argue that the two subclusters are within the same cluster as suggested by their U−VU-V colour-magnitude diagrams, galaxy size distributions and luminosity functions. They favour a merging scenario, where Cen 45 is falling into Cen 30 along a direction close to the line-of-sight, which would explain the 1500 km s−11500\text{\,}\mathrm{km}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1} velocity offset. They note, however, that some Cen 45 members probably belong to a background group of galaxies located in the Hubble flow. A similar case is found in the Virgo Cluster, where M86 is thought to be falling into M87 at a comparable relative velocity (Binggeli, 1999).

Centaurus has been extensively studied in X-rays using a variety of instruments. Using ASCA and ROSAT data, Churazov et al. (1999) showed that the X-ray emission in the cluster is not symmetric, but rather shows an excess emission centred on NGC 4709 and exhibits a filamentary structure. They argue that this temperature excess is likely the result of gas heating due to the infall of Cen 45 into Cen 30. This excess temperature and filamentary structure was later confirmed with XMM-Newton (Walker et al., 2013) and eROSITA (Veronica et al., 2025), who also showed an asymmetric distribution of metals around NGC 4696, supporting their sloshing scenario for this galaxy. Finally, recent XRISM observations confirm the gas sloshing in the core of Cen 30 happening along the line-of-sight (XRISM Collaboration et al., 2025).

Additional evidence for an ongoing interaction between the two subclusters is provided by the spatial distribution of GCs in the Centaurus cluster, studied in Federle et al. (2024) and Federle et al. (2025) using wide-field imaging with the Magellan telescope. In Federle et al. (2024), the authors reported that the GC system of NGC 4696 is not azimuthally symmetric, but rather shows an excess of GCs in the direction of NGC 4709 and NGC 4696B. Similarly, in Federle et al. (2025) they show that the GC system of NGC 4709 is also asymmetric, with an excess of GCs in the direction of NGC 4696, further supporting the scenario of subcluster interaction. More interestingly, in the same work, they identify the existence of a ’bridge’ of GCs that connects NGC 4696 and NGC 4709, at least in projection. Such a connecting structure has been reported in other galaxy clusters (Bassino et al., 2006; D’Abrusco et al., 2016; Ennis et al., 2024) and may be indicative of an ongoing interaction (Chaturvedi et al., 2022).

Although the interaction scenario between the two subclusters is generally accepted, their exact geometry is still debated. The two BCGs in Centaurus, NGC 4696 and NGC 4709, lie approximately 15 arcmin15\text{\,}\mathrm{a}\mathrm{r}\mathrm{c}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{i}\mathrm{n} apart in projection on the sky, which corresponds to a projected separation of around 155 kpc155\text{\,}\mathrm{k}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{c}. However, the individual distances to the two galaxies are still debated, making the exact geometry of the cluster uncertain. Previous works estimated the distances to the two galaxies using surface brightness fluctuations (SBF) and the GC luminosity function (GCLF) as distance indicators, and concluded that NGC 4709 is closer than NGC 4696 by several Mpc (Mieske and Hilker, 2003; Mieske et al., 2005; Federle et al., 2025). In particular, Federle et al. (2025) proposes that the reported GC bridge connects the two galaxies and extends for ∼\sim8.5 Mpc8.5\text{\,}\mathrm{M}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{c}. Other works, however, place NGC 4709 farther away than NGC 4696 using the DnD_{n}–σ\sigma, fundamental plane and Tully-Fisher methods (Faber et al., 1989; Blakeslee et al., 2001; Theureau et al., 2007). papers.title: mm-jets in the multi-messenger era
papers.abstract: Jets and outflows operate across the full cosmic mass scale from young stellar objects (YSOs) and X-ray binaries (XRBs) to active galactic nuclei (AGN), gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), and tidal disruption events (TDEs), shaping many time-domain and multi-messenger transients. Key questions concern on how jets are launched, accelerated and collimated; where and how they dissipate energy and accelerate particles; and how they couple to their environments to set electromagnetic counterpart diversity and feedback. Millimeter and sub-millimeter observations uniquely address these questions by tracking the evolving synchrotron turnover for robust calorimetry and Lorentz-factor constraints, providing full-Stokes polarization and Faraday diagnostics close to the jet base, and enabling high-resolution imaging from Galactic ejecta to event-horizon-scale AGN jet bases via global Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI). We describe the jet and outflow science enabled by ALMA2040, a next-generation mm/sub-mm interferometer combining an order-of-magnitude sensitivity gain with rapid-response observing, simultaneous multi-band coverage, full-Stokes polarimetry, and integration with global VLBI networks. These capabilities will enable statistically controlled, trigger-driven samples spanning XRB outbursts, early GRB afterglows, protostellar disk winds and jet launching, AGN jet bases, and jetted TDEs, establishing mm/sub-mm astronomy as a cornerstone of time-domain and multi-messenger jet physics in the 2040s and beyond.

papers.title: Intern Lumina U2: A Multi-Codebook Diffusion Large Language Model for Omni-Visual Understanding and Image Generation
papers.abstract: Unified multimodal generation covers discrete, continuous, and hybrid paradigms. Discrete approaches with single-codebook visual tokenizers align naturally with text modeling but have limited representational capacity. Continuous and hybrid approaches retain richer visual representations, but they model text and images in heterogeneous spaces with different training objectives, potentially introducing optimization conflicts between modalities with misaligned representation spaces. These choices expose a central question: how to efficiently model high-capacity visual representations alongside textual content in a shared optimization space within a single backbone. We present Intern Lumina U2, to our knowledge the first diffusion language model to represent multi-codebook visual tokens in a fully discrete space. Each visual position is represented by a group of codes from complementary codebooks, increasing its representational capacity while preserving compatibility with discrete text modeling. At the input, the embeddings are concatenated at each position; at the output, a lightweight multi-codebook autoregressive head predicts the codes within each position sequentially, while the diffusion backbone processes all positions in parallel. Built on the unified 4D representation of AToken, Intern Lumina U2 supports image, video, and 3D inputs within a single backbone and achieves leading performance among unified models in visual understanding, image generation, and image editing. We further build a full-stack training, inference, and evaluation system on both Ascend and NVIDIA platforms to verify the cross-platform effectiveness of our model. We also improve the inference efficiency through a stability-aware sampling strategy, which combines confidence-plateau-guided unmasking approach with drift-triggered cache refreshing mechanisms, accelerating image generation by 4.45x.

papers.intro:
Unified multimodal models integrate visual understanding and generation within a single model (Chameleon Team, 2024; Deng et al., 2025; Tian and others, 2026). However, architectural sharing alone does not constitute complete unification, since understanding and generation may still rely on separate representations and training objectives (Qiu et al., 2026). To go beyond architectural unification, we identify two principles for unifying understanding and generation more comprehensively. First, text and visual content should be mapped into a shared optimization space under a single objective. Although hybrid designs (Deng et al., 2025; Fan et al., 2025; Tian and others, 2026) can achieve high visual fidelity by retaining continuous visual states and delegating synthesis to a continuous decoder, they optimize visual generation with a continuous objective distinct from the text objective and often adopt separate visual encoders for understanding and generation, leading to optimization difficulties. Second, the generation process should respect the intrinsic structure of each modality. Text follows a natural sequential order, whereas visual content has no canonical generation order: each region depends on both its local neighborhood and long-range global context. The generation process should therefore decode text sequentially while refining visual content in parallel with bidirectional context.

Second, the generation process should respect the intrinsic structure of each modality. Text follows a natural sequential order, whereas visual content has no canonical generation order: each region depends on both its local neighborhood and long-range global context. The generation process should therefore decode text sequentially while refining visual content in parallel with bidirectional context.

Discrete masked diffusion provides a natural basis for satisfying the requirements above. It applies a masked-prediction objective to discrete text and visual tokens, thereby optimizing both modalities within a common discrete space. Under this formulation, each task is specified by partitioning the token sequence into observed conditioning tokens and masked prediction targets. Understanding and generation are thereby cast as distinct conditional queries to the same model, rather than as separate tasks with task-specific objectives. Moreover, masked diffusion decodes tokens in parallel through iterative refinement without imposing a fixed generation order (Nie et al., 2025; Chang et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2025; Xin et al., 2025), allowing each spatial position to be refined with bidirectional access to both local and global context. However, existing discrete unified models (Xin et al., 2025; Xie et al., 2025a; Yang et al., 2025) remain limited in visual representation capacity, as single-codebook tokenization compresses the visual information at each position into a single discrete code. Such a compact representation is insufficient both for faithful reconstruction and for covering the full range of visual tasks (Ma et al., 2025a). This motivates us to design a unified discrete framework that carries a high-capacity visual representation in a shared space under a single training objective, while modeling it efficiently with a unified backbone.

Intern Lumina U2 encodes images, videos, and 3D assets into a unified 4D code space and organizes these visual tokens together with text tokens in a unified packed-sequence format, so that understanding and generation across all these modalities are formulated over the same sequence representation and handled by a shared backbone. Each visual position carries KK complementary codes: independent embedding tables concatenated at the input preserve codebook identity for efficient training, while a lightweight multi-codebook autoregressive head models the dependencies among the codes within each position. Extensive experiments on image, video, and 3D understanding, as well as image generation and editing, demonstrate the effectiveness of this unified design. Trained on data curated by a unified pipeline that organizes heterogeneous sources under a common protocol, the model achieves leading performance among unified multimodal models across our evaluations. papers.title: Idea2Prior: Auditable Paper Retrieval and Ranking from Research Ideas
papers.abstract: Finding a paper from an informal research idea requires more than matching topic words: relevant work may use different terminology, and its distinguishing mechanism may be absent from the abstract. We present IDEA2PRIOR, an auditable literature-search system built on PaperArena. It combines multi-source discovery, identity verification, facet-based abstract assessment, semantic citation expansion, and joint Expert ranking. A retrieval-only mode ranks up to five papers from a shortlist of at most 60, using complete available abstracts and locally selected PDF evidence from five fixed acquisition attempts, without generating a long-form report. In a historical comparison covering ten queries from each of EASY, MEDIUM, and HARD, aggregate reported Hit@5 is 53.3% for IDEA2PRIOR, 43.3% for ChatGPT web Deep Research, and 36.7% for Gemini web Deep Research under the documented accounting convention. The advantage is concentrated in EASY and MEDIUM; ChatGPT leads on HARD. Selected IDEA2PRIOR runs average 8 minutes 53 seconds, compared with user-reported web averages of 5.2 and 4.7 minutes. A separate nine-query API sample averages $0.0945 per task; this is a historical cost observation, not a matched comparison with web subscription costs. Pairwise Top 5 coverage ranges from 6% to 34%, showing differing returned evidence sets. The system also exposes optional implementation analysis and citation-evolution tools. These results support targeted idea-to-paper retrieval while leaving general web research, forum search, and broader relevance evaluation open.

Researchers often remember an idea before they remember a title: a neighborhood with uncertain boundaries, a circuit transformation with a particular constraint, or an assistant that recognizes when a complex task changes. Recovering relevant prior work from such descriptions is difficult because vocabulary, application setting, and the level of technical detail can differ substantially between a query and a paper. A useful assistant must retrieve candidates, establish their bibliographic identities, and distinguish a close conceptual match from work that merely shares a topic.
