papers.title: Self Calibrated Galaxy Groups from the DESI DR1 Bright Galaxy Survey
papers.abstract: We present a galaxy group catalog built from Data Release 1 of the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) Bright Galaxy Survey, using the Self Calibrated Group Finder. The algorithm uses clustering data from the observed sample to calibrate the Group Finder's free parameters, rather than simulations. The catalog contains 2,229,741 galaxies from ~$2680$ deg$^2$ of sky with 3-pass coverage and $r$-band fluxes $\lt 19.5$. The catalog classifies all galaxies in the flux-limited sample as centrals or satellites and estimates host dark matter halo masses. We show the satellite fraction $f_{\rm sat}$, luminosity halo mass relation, stellar halo mass relation and halo occupation distributions (HODs) from the catalog. We find these non-parametric HODs can be fit by standard HOD models, with satellite power-law index $α$ values around 0.75 for star-forming galaxies and around 1.1 for quiescent objects. In agreement with recent results, we find that the quenched fraction of central galaxies depends mostly on halo mass and is nearly independent of central galaxy stellar mass for galaxies more massive than $10^{10.3}$ $M_\odot h^{-1}$ and halos more massive than $10^{12.2}$ $M_\odot h^{-1}$. In an appendix, we introduce a new Hybrid Nearest Neighbor (HNN) technique to mitigate systematics from fiber incompleteness. HNN uses photometric redshifts and multiple on-sky neighbors to assign redshifts to unobserved targets. Calibrated on DESI Survey Validation 3 data, our technique yields correct redshifts $\sim 50\%$ of the time and produces unbiased halo occupation statistics.

papers.intro:
In the modern cosmological paradigm, galaxies form in the centers of collapsed dark matter halos. Both galaxies and halos then grow via mergers and accretion into the diverse masses and morphologies we observe today. Because of these intertwined histories, the galaxy-halo connection is a critical piece of any theory of galaxy formation, as well as a tool to improve our ability to probe cosmology from galaxy surveys.

In the modern cosmological paradigm, galaxies form in the centers of collapsed dark matter halos. Both galaxies and halos then grow via mergers and accretion into the diverse masses and morphologies we observe today. Because of these intertwined histories, the galaxy-halo connection is a critical piece of any theory of galaxy formation, as well as a tool to improve our ability to probe cosmology from galaxy surveys.

Many approaches have been used to explore the galaxy-halo connection (see Wechsler and Tinker 93 for a review). Hydrodynamic simulations offer a theory-first model, by attempting to resolve or otherwise include as much physics as possible. On the other end of the spectrum is data-driven modeling, where the most common model is the Halo Occupancy Distribution (HOD), a probabilistic statement about which galaxies occupy which halos [74, 100, 101, 102, 98].

Many approaches have been used to explore the galaxy-halo connection (see Wechsler and Tinker 93 for a review). Hydrodynamic simulations offer a theory-first model, by attempting to resolve or otherwise include as much physics as possible. On the other end of the spectrum is data-driven modeling, where the most common model is the Halo Occupancy Distribution (HOD), a probabilistic statement about which galaxies occupy which halos [74, 100, 101, 102, 98].

Here we take an intermediate approach: halo-based galaxy group finding. Galaxy group finders attempt to determine which galaxies in a sample are in bound gravitational systems together. When focused on massive clusters, methods such as MaxBCG [47, 46] and redMaPPer [71, 72, 88] have been applied to photometric surveys, enabling a variety of applications. Percolation-based methods such as friend-of-friends [43] have also been applied to many galaxy samples, including the Sloan Digital Sky Survey [11] and the Galaxy and Mass Assembly survey [68]. In contrast, halo-based group finders employ our knowledge of the halo mass function and other halo properties to aid in group finding. As with most HODs, halo-based group finders operate in a central-satellite paradigm, asserting that one galaxy sits in the center of the dark matter potential well, and other group members are satellites residing in subhalos. As a result, halo-based group finders provide group membership and an assignment of dark matter halos to galaxies, making them models of the galaxy-halo connection across several decades of halo mass. Compared to the HOD, group finders offer a non-parametric model, avoiding the need to specify a fixed functional form. Instead of using a 1-dimensional summary statistic to capture the relation (as in HODs), group catalogs use the actual observed distribution of galaxies in specifying the galaxy-halo connection.

The first halo-based group finder was introduced in [94]. The method made use of the abundance matching technique, ordering galaxies/groups by luminosity (or stellar mass) and assigning halo masses from an assumed halo mass function. Many group finder variations have been developed; see [18] for a review. Other variations include a 2nd-turnaround radius based group finder [89], a halo-based method for processing the entire DR8 Legacy Survey using mostly photometric redshifts [96], and a neural-network based approach to group finding [53].

One of the advantages of the [94] algorithm is that there is only one free parameter: BsatB_{\rm sat}, a threshold to determine if a galaxy is a member of a nearby group. In [94] this was calibrated by mock catalogs to balance completeness and purity of the groups. However, this low-parameter approach led to several issues: 1) systematic misclassifications of quiescent satellite galaxies, 2) an inability to differentiate the halo masses for subclasses of galaxies at fixed group luminosity, and 3) insufficient scatter in the halo mass at fixed group luminosity. As the first Stage-IV spectroscopic galaxy survey, DESI is providing the largest redshift-space map of the nearby universe to date. BGS, which we use here, is a flux-limited survey with an rr-band magnitude limit of 19.5, almost two magnitudes deeper than SDSS, achieving a median redshift of z∼0.2z\sim 0.2 across the final survey footprint of ∼17,000​deg2\sim 17,000\rm~deg^{2} [39]. However, due to the limited patrol radius of the fiber positioners, the program is unable visit every target in dense regions of the sky, creating a non-trivial fiber incompleteness systematic. Here we develop a new methodology to handle this important systematic, which is stronger than in SDSS. Our goal is to produce a galaxy group catalog capable of exploring the galaxy-halo connection into the fainter regimes made possible by DESI BGS.

papers.title: A model for the image structure and spectral energy distribution of relativistic jets
papers.abstract: Upcoming advances in high-frequency VLBI promise to enable spatially resolved studies of astrophysical jets across an increasingly large source population. We present here a Python implementation of the semi-analytic model from Tsunetoe et al. (2025) for self-consistently interpreting the spatial and spectral structure of the synchrotron emission from such jets. The model is based on an axisymmetric force-free jet solution supplemented with a prescription for nonthermal electron heating, synchrotron cooling, pitch-angle anisotropy in the electron distribution, and radiative transfer along straight rays. We use this model to explore how the predicted spectral energy distribution depends on the model parameters, identifying approximately self-similar scalings with black hole mass, accretion rate, and electron heating efficiency. We also compare the model predictions against observations of M87 and Sgr A*. For M87, a single fiducial parameter set qualitatively reproduces VLBI images across multiple frequencies and matches the observed longitudinal intensity profile, while also yielding a broadband SED that is quantitatively consistent with the observed radio through X-ray measurements. For Sgr A*, a fit to the quiescent-state SED demonstrates that emission from a collimated jet with comparable nonthermal heating efficiency to M87's is quantitatively consistent with the observed radio through X-ray measurements, predicting a compact jet whose radio size decreases inversely with frequency, consistent with VLBI constraints.

papers.intro:
Relativistic astrophysical jets provided some of the earliest evidence for the existence of black holes, and they remain one of the clearest observational signatures of supermassive black hole (SMBH) ubiquity. The canonical picture for these jets holds that magnetic fields threading the event horizon of a spinning black hole extract energy and angular momentum from the hole, powering an outflow containing relativistic particles that we observe via their synchrotron emission [14, 13, 15]. Because of the high brightness temperature of this synchrotron emission, relativistic jets have been the target of very long baseline interferometric (VLBI) radio observations since the development of the technique [9, 24]. Jetted active galactic nuclei (AGN) were the first sources to be imaged with VLBI [127, 114], and they remain among the most frequently observed VLBI targets.

Jetted active galactic nuclei (AGN) were the first sources to be imaged with VLBI [127, 114], and they remain among the most frequently observed VLBI targets.

One of the most well-known and spectacular examples of relativistic jets is found in the M87 galaxy and associated with the M87∗ black hole, whose proximity and large mass have made it the target of increasingly high-resolution VLBI observations for decades [128, 78, 3, 149, 93, e.g.,]. The M87∗ jet has now been imaged with VLBI over a large dynamic range in spatial scales, revealing a broad opening angle near the base, an approximately parabolic collimation profile, and a persistent limb-brightened morphology [81, 110]. However, M87∗ is an exceptional case; for the majority of jetted systems, VLBI primarily provides only longitudinal information such as core shifts and brightness temperature profiles. The transverse structure – and particularly the structure of the innermost regions of the jet – is only resolved in a relatively small number of nearby systems [16, 87, e.g.,].

That situation is changing as (sub)millimeter VLBI capabilities grow, providing more routine access to ever-finer angular scales. The Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) has already observed multiple AGN jets [82, 72, 71, 77, 131], and this trend is set to accelerate substantially in the coming years as the EHT continues to expand its capabilities [143]. The next-generation EHT (ngEHT) project will improve the EHT’s sensitivity through increased bandwidths and the addition of multiple new telescopes to the array [41, 74], while also implementing simultaneous multi-frequency observing capabilities to push the angular resolution frontier by enabling routine observations at the highest observing frequencies [70, 130]. The Black Hole Explorer (BHEX) mission will sharpen the angular resolution of the array even further via the addition of a spaceborne element [73]. These upgrades will bring a population of partially and fully resolved jetted sources into view [126, 90, 79, 103], shifting the science focus from individual case studies to demographic considerations.

A rich collection of tools exists for simulating the emission from AGN jets. General relativistic magnetohydrodynamics (GRMHD) codes [55, 121, 91, 123, e.g.,] and ray-tracing and radiative transfer pipelines [111, 42, 38, 124, 23, 102, e.g.,] provide general-purpose physics packages that cover important parts of the jet emission problem; such tools are widely used for, e.g., interpretation of the near-horizon emission observed by the EHT [120, 58, 151, 122]. Special relativistic MHD codes such as PLUTO [99] have likewise been extensively used to simulate the dynamics and structure of relativistic jets on larger scales (see, e.g., Komissarov and Porth 85, for a review). However, the existing jet modeling capabilities are largely distributed across specialized workflows. GRMHD codes and radiative transfer pipelines typically require substantial expertise and nontrivial post-processing of simulation products, while semi-analytic or phenomenological packages tend to be optimized either for broadband SED fitting or for image-plane morphology rather than providing a self-consistent treatment of both. For rapid population studies and parameter space exploration, there thus remains a need for end-to-end tools that are fast to evaluate and easy to deploy while retaining physical interpretability. papers.title: Integer-Free Control Synthesis for Signal Temporal Logic via Ranked Implicants
papers.abstract: This paper proposes an integer-free method for control synthesis of nonlinear discrete-time systems under finite-horizon Signal Temporal Logic (STL) constraints. Instead of introducing integer variables, we consider the discrete choices of the specification in a ranked order and solve a standard nonlinear program for each selected choice until a satisfying trajectory is found. We first define implicants as sets of timed atomic constraints whose joint satisfaction is sufficient to satisfy the specification. A reference trajectory obtained from a smooth approximation of the STL robustness is used to rank these implicants. Fixing one implicant turns the problem into a standard nonlinear program with no auxiliary weights or bilinear terms. If the solution does not satisfy the specification, the next implicant will be considered. We prove soundness and completeness of our method relative to the nonlinear programming solver. Numerical evaluation on nonlinear multi-agent systems shows that our proposed method identifies satisfying trajectories where the exact continuous reformulation fails, and moreover, it is faster than a mixed-integer formulation of the same specification.

papers.intro:
Signal Temporal Logic (STL) [1] is a formal language for specifying spatio-temporal requirements of dynamical systems. Its quantitative semantics, a.k.a. the robustness function [2], assigns a real value to a trajectory, where a positive value implies satisfaction, allowing STL requirements to be included in trajectory optimization problems. The robustness function is built from nested min\min and max\max operators and is generally nonsmooth and nonconvex. For linear systems and predicates, STL constraints can be encoded exactly using mixed-integer linear programming [3], and more compact encodings introduce binary variables only at the disjunctive choices of the formula [4]. For nonlinear dynamics, however, the same encodings lead to nonlinear mixed-integer problems, which can be significantly harder to solve. Smooth approximations of the robustness function [5] allow gradient-based solvers, scaled to high-dimensional nonlinear systems by differential dynamic programming [6], but they introduce approximation error. In all of these gradient-based methods, the discrete choices of the specification stay inside one nonconvex program. A local solver can therefore settle on an infeasible choice [6].

Optimization techniques based on the robustness function have also been extended to stochastic settings [7, 8]. Control barrier function (CBF) techniques can also be used to enforce STL specifications [9], reducing online computation, but these methods require the barrier functions to be constructed in advance. More recently, exact continuous reformulations rewrite the min\min and max\max operations using continuous weights on simplices [10], or rewrite arbitrary logical constraints through their conjunctive normal form into max-min constraints [11]. Both remove the binary variables without approximation error. However, we show that the simplex-weight reformulation of [10] remains sensitive to initialization.

Contributions. First, we show that the exact simplex-weight reformulation in [10] is sensitive to initialization. Although binary variables are removed, the discrete choices remain encoded in the continuous simplex weights. We characterize this failure mechanism and show why several natural initialization strategies do not resolve it. Second, building on the disjunctive view of STL satisfaction [12, 13, 14], we formalize implicants for arbitrary finite-horizon STL formulas, including nested operators and until. We prove that STL satisfaction is equivalent to the satisfaction of at least one implicant and express the STL robustness exactly as the maximum of the margins of these implicants. This separates the discrete choices of the specification from the continuous trajectory optimization. Third, we propose ranked implicant synthesis. One smooth robustness problem provides a reference trajectory for ranking the implicants, and each selected implicant is enforced through a smooth nonlinear program (NLP) with no simplex weights or bilinear terms. We prove soundness and completeness relative to the NLP solver and demonstrate improved feasibility and speed in multi-agent problems.

The proposed search is related to relax-and-fix methods in integer programming [15] and to Logic-Geometric Programming in task and motion planning [16]. Closer to our approach, [12] and the graph-of-convex-sets planner for STL [13] exploit the disjunctive structure of restricted STL settings to guide sampling-based and convex optimization, respectively. Closely related, [14] rewrites STL into a strengthened disjunctive normal form and heuristically selects a single branch for planning. In contrast, our implicants represent the specification exactly and are ranked, rather than selected. A single smooth reference trajectory orders them by predicate margin, and the resulting NLPs are tried in that order until a feasible one is found. Thus, an inaccurate ranking affects efficiency but cannot discard a feasible implicant, yielding completeness relative to the NLP solver.

papers.title: Vectorized and Symbolically Optimized Seminumerical Exchange for Large-Scale Quantum Chemistry
papers.abstract: We present a seminumerical exchange algorithm (SNK) based on the sn-LinK method [Laqua et al., J. Chem. Theory Comput. 16, 1456 (2020)], optimized for modern multi-core central processing units with single instruction multiple data vector instructions and report its implementation into the Q-Chem quantum chemistry program. Vectorization and memory management strategies for the Boys function and 3-center-1-electron (3c1e) integral kernels are given. Several new considerations are made in the computation of the 3c1e integrals: the Head-Gordon Pople horizontal recurrence relations, same-center optimizations, and multishell optimizations, all implemented symbolically employing the SymPy symbolic algebra library and exported as optimized C++ code leveraging common-sub-expression elimination (CSE) optimization techniques. A general scheme for choosing optimal integral kernels is developed through rigorous timing benchmarks. The resulting implementation is tested against traditional 4c2e exchange for several systems and basis sets, showing 1-2 orders of magnitude speedups for systems of practically relevant sizes (100-500 atoms, 2000-10000 basis functions). For smaller molecules, comparisons are also made against the more efficient occ-RI-K method showing a break-even point around 50-100 atoms beyond which SNK dramatically outperforms due to its superior sub-quadratic (between linear and quadratic) time complexity as well as its effectively negligible memory demand.

Hartree-Fock[20, 11] exact exchange (K) has proven to be an indispensable tool for modern electronic structure theory. Particularly in Kohn-Sham Density Functional Theory (DFT), the addition of K via global hybrids[4] and range-separated hybrids[25] has shown great success,[54] making hybrid density functionals the de facto standard for obtaining accurate energies and molecular properties. However, the computation of K is expensive and typically represents the rate-limiting step in any SCF calculation.

Particularly in Kohn-Sham Density Functional Theory (DFT), the addition of K via global hybrids[4] and range-separated hybrids[25] has shown great success,[54] making hybrid density functionals the de facto standard for obtaining accurate energies and molecular properties. However, the computation of K is expensive and typically represents the rate-limiting step in any SCF calculation.

This is in large part due to the canonical dependence of K on the 4-center-2-electron (4c2e) atomic orbital (AO) integrals[71] whose number scales as 𝒪⁡(M2)\mathcal{O}(M^{2}) with respect to the system size MM (number of atoms) when leveraging the fast spatial decay of Gaussian type AOs. For fixed molecule size, the number of 4c2e integrals rises steeply as 𝒪⁡(Nbasis4)\mathcal{O}(N_{\text{basis}}^{4}) with respect to the number of basis functions NbasisN_{\text{basis}}. This steep scaling is 𝒪⁡(L8)\mathcal{O}(L^{8}) with respect to the highest angular momentum LL of the basis set when computed in the Cartesian Gaussian basis. Thus, traditional 4c2e K becomes prohibitively expensive for large systems and large AO basis sets.

Therefore, several more efficient methods for the computation of K have been developed, largely falling into two categories: First, resolution-of-the-identity (RI) methods such as RI-K[15, 84] and occ-RI-K[52] instead transform the 4c2e integrals into 3c2e integrals by means of an auxiliary basis. This has the benefit of reducing the basis scaling to 𝒪⁡(Nbasis2)\mathcal{O}(N_{\text{basis}}^{2}), although the asymptotic time complexity with respect to system size increases to 𝒪⁡(M4)\mathcal{O}(M^{4}) and the work-space (memory) complexity increases formally to 𝒪⁡(M3)\mathcal{O}(M^{3}). The workspace can be reduced asymptotically (for large enough systems exploiting the locality of Gaussian-type AOs) to 𝒪⁡(M2)\mathcal{O}(M^{2}). The system-size scaling and workspace requirements restrict the usefulness of RI-based K builds to smaller systems (<<100 atoms).

The second class of methods are given by the seminumerical approach, in which computation of the 4c2e integrals relies on performing one integration analytically while the other is performed via numerical quadrature with a real space grid. The advantages of seminumerical methods are in part due to their use of 3c1e integrals, which scale only as 𝒪⁡(Nbasis2)\mathcal{O}(N_{\text{basis}}^{2}) and 𝒪⁡(L4)\mathcal{O}(L^{4}), making them much more viable for large basis sets. In addition, seminumerical methods also scale only as 𝒪⁡(M3)\mathcal{O}(M^{3}) formally (𝒪⁡(Nbasis2⋅Ngrid)\mathcal{O}(N_{\text{basis}}^{2}\cdot N_{\text{grid}}) without exploiting any sparsity/locality) and can be implemented in an asymptotically linear scaling fashion via efficient integral screening techniques. Seminumerical methods are also naturally suited for local hybrid[34, 49] and locally-range-separated local hybrid density functionals,[50, 51] which use position-dependent admixtures of semi-local and exact exchange and require the numerical integration of quantities involving the exact exchange energy density. Finally, as Ngrid≫NbasisN_{\text{grid}}\gg N_{\text{basis}}, the majority of the work involved in seminumerical methods is branchless and highly uniform as identical operations are applied to different grid points, meaning such methods are naturally suited for modern CPUs and GPUs supporting single-instruction-multiple-data (SIMD) vector instructions.

Development of seminumerical algorithms for K began with Friesner’s pseudospectral method.[12, 13, 14] The pseudospectral method was implemented in the Jaguar quantum chemistry package, including several extensions to property calculations.[86, 38, 70, 57, 19] While efficient, the implementation itself is highly sophisticated, involving several corrections and optimizations for specific basis sets. This prompted the development of more generally applicable seminumerical methods, such as the chain-of-spheres exchange (COSX) algorithm of Neese and coworkers,[58, 24] the SENEX implementation in the TURBOMOLE package by the Weigand and Kaupp groups,[68, 3, 2, 36, 37] and various independent implementations by others.[48, 32] More recently the preLinX[41] and sn-LinK[43, 42, 40, 76, 77, 78] methods implement new screening techniques based on the locality of the exchange interaction for insulating systems, allowing for the efficient evaluation of K for systems with thousands of atoms and quadruple zeta basis sets.

Beyond the two main classes of algorithms already mentioned is a third class, which is based on a different type of approximate tensor decomposition of the 4c2e integrals, such as tensor hypercontraction (THC), or the closely related interpolative separable density fitting (ISDF). THC was first proposed for electron correlation methods,[30, 63, 31, 64, 28, 29, 65, 66, 39, 73, 75, 74] and was later applied to K.[27] The ISDF approach is a way to systematically improve the accuracy of THC and forms the basis of the adaptively compressed exchange (ACE) algorithm,[47, 33] which was designed for plane-wave basis sets. ISDF was subsequently applied to K builds in atomic orbital basis sets.[44] Due to the underlying approximate tensor decomposition, ISDF yields formal 𝒪⁡(M3)\mathcal{O}(M^{3}) scaling without exploiting numerical sparsity. Efforts to gain improved precision within the ISDF formalism continue, with promising developments.[87] However, due to the accuracy and scaling challenges,[44] THC and ISDF are not yet employed in production quantum chemistry codes.

Beyond the two main classes of algorithms already mentioned is a third class, which is based on a different type of approximate tensor decomposition of the 4c2e integrals, such as tensor hypercontraction (THC), or the closely related interpolative separable density fitting (ISDF). THC was first proposed for electron correlation methods,[30, 63, 31, 64, 28, 29, 65, 66, 39, 73, 75, 74] and was later applied to K.[27] The ISDF approach is a way to systematically improve the accuracy of THC and forms the basis of the adaptively compressed exchange (ACE) algorithm,[47, 33] which was designed for plane-wave basis sets. ISDF was subsequently applied to K builds in atomic orbital basis sets.[44] Due to the underlying approximate tensor decomposition, ISDF yields formal 𝒪⁡(M3)\mathcal{O}(M^{3}) scaling without exploiting numerical sparsity. Efforts to gain improved precision within the ISDF formalism continue, with promising developments.[87] However, due to the accuracy and scaling challenges,[44] THC and ISDF are not yet employed in production quantum chemistry codes.

papers.title: GRADS: Graph-Regulated Agentic Data Synthesis with Controllable Difficulty
papers.abstract: Deep research agents are increasingly deployed to retrieve precise information from large corpora, yet multi-hop, long-horizon tasks remain challenging. Synthetic data generation has emerged as a scalable solution, with existing pipelines typically expanding seed tasks to increase their apparent depth and breadth. However, this expansion does not reliably translate into necessary reasoning: newly introduced evidence may be only weakly coupled to the answer, creating a mismatch between intended and empirical difficulty. To address this problem, we introduce GRADS, a graph-guided agentic data synthesis framework with explicit difficulty control. GRADS runs a closed loop of seed selection, evidence expansion, question--answer construction, and verification while maintaining a graph of the evidence and inference dependencies required to derive each answer. At each step, it conditions generation on a relevant subgraph, preserving indispensable inference without accumulating irrelevant context. Experiments across security, software-engineering, and scientific-document domains show that GRADS consistently generates verified tasks with empirically separated difficulty distributions, as measured by independent solvers. Moreover, under matched training budgets, post-training on this data delivers consistent gains at every level: SFT raises the solution-termination rate to over 95% while cutting tool calls and turns by up to 75%, RL trims tool use by up to a further 19.5%, and on our held-out, domain-specific benchmarks, the resulting 4B model matches Sonnet~4 on software engineering and surpasses it on the scientific and security domains.

Specialized knowledge is often distributed across domain-specific record collections that are too large to inspect manually. Deep search agents have emerged as a promising way to exploit such collections: LLM-based agents that iteratively plan, issue search queries, read retrieved documents, and reason over them to answer complex, multi-hop information needs (Huang et al., 2025b; Li et al., 2025b; Li et al., 2025c). Post-training, including supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL), has proven to be effective in teaching models when and how to invoke search tools during reasoning (Jin et al., 2025; Song et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2025). A rapidly growing body of work demonstrates that synthetic question–answer data is sufficient to train strong deep search agents through SFT and RL (Wu et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025a; Gao et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2025b; Sun et al., 2025a; Liu et al., 2025). The quality of such agents is therefore bounded by the quality of the data they are trained on, and in particular by how reliably that data exercises genuine multi-step reasoning.

To make synthetic data sufficiently challenging, most pipelines impose an explicit structure intended to raise the latent inference complexity of each question. Representative strategies include depth- and width-based task extension (Shi et al., 2026), set-theoretic formalization of information-seeking tasks (Tao et al., 2026), graph sampling combined with information obfuscation (Li et al., 2025a; Wei et al., 2025), recursive construction of hierarchical research trees (Xia et al., 2025a), and bottom-up composition of single-hop questions (Trivedi et al., 2022). These methods share a common premise that complexity accumulated during synthesis translates into complexity of the reasoning required at solution time. But this premise does not reliably hold. A long line of analysis shows that nominally multi-hop questions are frequently answerable through shortcuts or disconnected reasoning that bypasses the intended chain (Min et al., 2019; Jiang and Bansal, 2019; Trivedi et al., 2020). When evidence is added to a question without regard to whether it is necessary, it may be only weakly coupled to the answer. The intended difficulty of the resulting item then diverges from its empirical difficulty, and the difficulty label ceases to be a reliable signal for evaluation or curriculum design. This motivates the central questions of this work: can we synthesize data whose difficulty is realized in the solver’s reasoning, not merely claimed? Is such data effective for post-training?

We approach these questions by defining the evidence graph of a QA pair, whose nodes are source-grounded claims and whose edges are necessary inference steps, so that its depth estimates the reasoning an answer requires. Building on this structure, we introduce GRADS, a graph-regulated agentic data synthesis method with controllable difficulty. GRADS departs from two prevailing strategies. The first piles ever more explicit evidence into a question, extending tasks with additional constraints, entities, or obfuscated clues until they appear harder (Shi et al., 2026; Tao et al., 2026; Li et al., 2025a; Liu et al., 2025). The second builds or samples a knowledge graph to broaden the raw material from which questions are drawn (Chen et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2025; Xia et al., 2025a). Both increase the apparent size of a question, but neither guarantees that the added evidence is required to reach the answer. GRADS instead deepens a question within an agentic loop by regulating the structure of its evidence graph. It decouples exploration from difficulty control, and is designed to ensure that each question attains its required reasoning depth.

Applying this idea to real domain knowledge, such as GitHub issue trackers and scientific experiment notes, raises two further challenges. First, the underlying corpora are too large to be explored exhaustively, so an agent must locate relevant evidence efficiently. Second, LLM-synthesized answers are prone to hallucination (Huang et al., 2025a), and an incorrect answer is more damaging in training data than an easy one. To address scale, we clean and cluster the raw records and expose unified local and online search tools to the agents. To address correctness, each answer carries a rubric of atomic claims tied to verbatim source spans (Gao et al., 2023; Min et al., 2023), and verification subagents check every item before acceptance (Dhuliawala et al., 2024; Manakul et al., 2023; Du et al., 2024).

We evaluate GRADS on three heterogeneous domains: GitHub issue tracking, experimental particle physics, and security. For each domain, we construct a representative benchmark and a post-training corpus. Compared with three synthesis baselines, GRADS is the only method whose delivered reasoning depth increases monotonically with the requested difficulty, and correspondingly the only one whose solver scores decrease monotonically from Easy to Hard. This ordering is preserved across solvers of three capability tiers. The resulting data is also effective for training: supervised fine-tuning a 4B model on GRADS trajectories yields large gains over the untrained model in every domain and outperforms every baseline at matched sample count and optimizer steps. Although SFT accounts for most of the post-training margin, subsequent RL further improves tool use and the model’s ability to terminate with an answer, bringing the 4B model to the level of the mid-sized Sonnet 4 solver.

papers.title: The Birth and Early Feedback of Massive Star Clusters Across the Local Universe
papers.abstract: Young massive star clusters (YMCs; ${\gtrsim}10^4\rm\,M_\odot$) represent a distinct, extreme mode of star formation and the closest present-day analogues of the environments in which globular clusters and Cosmic Noon stellar populations assembled. Given the extreme dust extinction in the earliest phase of YMC formation, (sub-)millimeter observations are the only means of probing their assembly and early feedback. Pioneering works with ALMA are limited to individual region studies and to the most massive YMCs in them, leaving many open questions about the initial conditions of YMC formation, the integrated star and cluster formation efficiencies, the dominant pre-supernova feedback channels, and the prevalence and reach of cluster-driven outflows. ALMA2040 will enable mass-complete, resolved surveys in hundreds of host galaxies, transforming the study of massive cluster formation and feedback from individual case analyses into statistical measurements across the full range of galactic environments.

papers.title: Unveiling star formation at sub-solar metallicity with ALMA2040
papers.abstract: A fundamental question in astrophysics is whether the processes governing star formation are universal or depend on the physical conditions of their local galactic environment. The Milky Way and the Magellanic clouds offer ideal laboratories to explore this question, as the gas conditions in them span up to orders of magnitude in metallicity, gas surface density, ambient pressure, dust abundance, radiation field, and cosmic-ray flux. In particular, both the outer Milky Way and the Magellanic clouds provide the closest low-metallicity environments with conditions similar to those of metal-poor galaxies, while remaining sufficiently close to soon allow spatial resolution of individual star-forming cores and disks. Recent observations with ALMA and other facilities have begun to unveil the physical and chemical properties of star-forming regions in low-metallicity environments. Yet, their distances from the Sun still require transformational gains in current ALMA capabilities to address fundamental open questions: (1) Are the properties of prestellar cores universal? (2) Does cloud fragmentation, and the resulting stellar IMF, depend critically on metallicity? (3) How does dust evolution depend on metallicity, and what is the impact in the survival of protoplanetary disks? (4) Is the reduced amount of metals and dust shielding at low metallicity critical for the formation and survival of molecules? ALMA2040 will identify similarities and differences between solar- and sub-solar-metallicity star-forming regions, and answer the question: how do different environmental conditions influence the physical and chemical pathways leading to star formation?

papers.title: Honesty is the Best Policy ... or is it? Demand Management for Probabilistic Service Options
papers.abstract: To enable well-informed customer choices and redistribute demand across service options, providers can display probabilities regarding predicted service levels at the time of booking, effectively offering probabilistic service options. In many service settings, the underlying truthful probabilities endogenously depend on the system state, rather than being static product attributes controlled by the provider. While customers rely on this information when making decisions, they cannot readily verify its accuracy. Consequently, providers may be tempted to manipulate the displayed probabilities to guide customers' choices in their favor, creating a novel lever for demand management. In this work, we model the resulting problem as a sequential decision process, define truthful probabilities recursively, and introduce transparency constraints that limit their distortion. Because the exact computation of truthful probabilities is intractable for realistic settings, we develop an adapted reinforcement learning algorithm to approximate them. Furthermore, we propose a sampling-based mixed-integer program to optimize the information communicated by the provider in each state. Our framework enables providers to gauge the benefits of dynamically disclosing probabilistic information at the time of booking and sheds light on incentives for manipulation. Our computational study is motivated by out-of-home delivery, i.e., the delivery to parcel lockers or shops, and reveals a trade-off between individual-level transparency and aggregate customer utilities.
papers.intro:
Services are fundamentally characterized by the active participation of customers in the value creation process (Bordoloi et al. 2023, Chapter 1). From the provider’s perspective, this introduces substantial uncertainty regarding the available capacity given that the amount or duration of resources being blocked may also depend on customers’ behavior. Consequently, guaranteeing service provision for every advance reservation would require a conservative definition of feasibility based on worst-case assumptions regarding resource availability, which entails high costs in the form of foregone revenue and underutilized capacity (Sailer et al. 2026).

From the provider’s perspective, this introduces substantial uncertainty regarding the available capacity given that the amount or duration of resources being blocked may also depend on customers’ behavior. Consequently, guaranteeing service provision for every advance reservation would require a conservative definition of feasibility based on worst-case assumptions regarding resource availability, which entails high costs in the form of foregone revenue and underutilized capacity (Sailer et al. 2026).

To sidestep strict feasibility requirements at the time of booking, service providers have devised strategies to deal with insufficient capacity ex post at the time of service provision. On the one hand, providers may deny the originally promised service, resorting to backup options or compensation schemes. Examples include widespread overbooking practices in the travel industry, preemptible instances in cloud computing, or the rerouting of parcels in out-of-home delivery networks. On the other hand, providers may still accommodate all customers at the cost of degraded service quality, such as throttled speed at electric vehicle charging stations or standing passengers on public transit. In both cases, customers systematically prefer one service outcome (receiving service, higher quality) over the other.

On the one hand, providers may deny the originally promised service, resorting to backup options or compensation schemes. Examples include widespread overbooking practices in the travel industry, preemptible instances in cloud computing, or the rerouting of parcels in out-of-home delivery networks. On the other hand, providers may still accommodate all customers at the cost of degraded service quality, such as throttled speed at electric vehicle charging stations or standing passengers on public transit. In both cases, customers systematically prefer one service outcome (receiving service, higher quality) over the other.

While these strategies enable providers to efficiently manage uncertainty, they shift most of the associated risks and inconvenience to customers, causing dissatisfaction. To mitigate this, the provider can share information on predicted service levels at the time of booking, thereby unlocking two key advantages: First, communicating predicted congestion or availability supports well-informed customer choices that align with individual preferences and risk tolerance. Second, the information simultaneously serves as a demand-shaping instrument because it induces customers to redistribute themselves across service options, reducing inefficient demand concentration and the need for ex post interventions.

Second, the information simultaneously serves as a demand-shaping instrument because it induces customers to redistribute themselves across service options, reducing inefficient demand concentration and the need for ex post interventions.

In this work, we provide such information in the form of probabilities, thereby constructing probabilistic service options. The probabilities are displayed to dynamically arriving requests at the time of booking and represent the likelihood of receiving a capacitated premium outcome (the higher quality level or not being denied service altogether) at the time of service provision. With the remaining probability, the customer receives the service option’s base outcome. Essentially, the provider offers an assortment of probabilistic service options to each incoming request. In response, the customer selects one of them (possibly including the alternative not to book), turning the request into an order. At specific points in time, service outcomes are allocated to orders. We allow for resources to be reusable, i.e., customers make use of the capacity for a (potentially random) duration, and it becomes available again afterward. In total, we consider three sources of uncertainty: request arrival, customer choice, and usage duration.

From a conceptual perspective, these probabilistic service options resemble probabilistic products (Fay and Xie 2008, Gönsch 2020), i.e., an offering that comprises multiple component products, each associated with a probability. Existing research on probabilistic products investigates probabilities as a static design choice, set exogenously by the provider prior to selling. In contrast, the stochasticity of the realized outcome in service settings is not the provider’s deliberate choice, but naturally emerges from the uncertain availability of capacity. Such uncertainty may stem from random capacity usage durations, customer no-shows, or orders displacing earlier arrivals if allocation decisions do not follow the first-come-first-served principle. As a result, the truthful probabilities endogenously depend on the state of the system, potentially including the characteristics of the current request, and vary dynamically during the selling horizon.

Unlike traditional supervised learning, simply estimating the probabilities from historical data would lead to biased predictions because the data reflects customers’ choices under probabilities displayed in the past. Once the provider communicates newly estimated probabilities, customers’ choices adapt in response, and hence the underlying true probabilities change, resulting in a feedback loop. To communicate accurate probabilities to sequentially arriving requests, the provider must forecast demand, anticipate choice behavior of future requests in response to probabilities expected to be displayed in subsequent periods, predict allocation decisions, and account for units already sold along with current utilization. For realistic problem sizes, a vast space of possible states paired with the continuous probability space and customers’ expectation to receive probabilities in real time pose significant challenges.

To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to study endogenously probabilistic products, thereby enabling providers to assess the benefits and implications of dynamically communicating probabilistic information. Moreover, because customers cannot readily verify their accuracy, providers may be tempted to manipulate the displayed probabilities to guide customers’ choices in their favor. Beyond controlling product availability or prices, this creates a novel, information-based lever for demand management that may call for regulation. In response, we propose transparency constraints that limit the deviation between displayed and truthful probabilities, with full transparency referring to the case where the provider is honest and always reports probabilities equal to the truthful ones. Our work provides methodology to quantify the extent of the provider’s incentive for distortion and assess how transparency constraints affect the involved stakeholders.

papers.title: V-SHARE: Provable Convergence Guarantees for Advantage-based Algorithms
papers.abstract: In reinforcement learning, advantage-based value-learning methods, unlike standard Q-learning, share information across actions by decomposing the action-value function into a state-dependent value component and action-specific advantages. While this mechanism has proven effective in both tabular and deep reinforcement learning, its theoretical understanding remains incomplete. We introduce V-SHARE, an advantage-based value-learning algorithm that combines cross-action value sharing with an importance-weighted Bellman-residual correction. To our knowledge, we provide the first complete theoretical characterization of an advantage-based algorithm, including both asymptotic convergence and non-asymptotic finite-sample guarantees. We identify a regime in which V-SHARE mitigates the rare-action bottleneck of asynchronous Q-learning and uncover a contraction--variance tradeoff between stronger deterministic contraction and increased importance-weighting noise. Motivated by this tradeoff, we develop decreasing residual-preconditioning schedules that combine faster early contraction with lower asymptotic noise. We further develop a two-timescale analysis that removes the single-timescale residual-weight threshold while preserving convergence guarantees. Experiments on discrete Markov decision processes (MDPs) and deep reinforcement-learning benchmarks corroborate our results.

papers.title: A Systematic and Validated Translation of the Perceived Empathy of Technology Scale to Chinese
papers.abstract: The Perceived Empathy of Technology Scale (PETS) allows evaluation of empathic behavior in intelligent systems, a concept increasingly applied in human-AI interaction, particularly in emotional and mental health support applications. To support intercultural research and development, PETS is already available in multiple languages, as research suggests cultural and language-based differences in the expression and perception of empathy. Given the substantial Chinese-speaking population and the growing focus on cross-cultural HCI research, we present a validated translation of PETS into Putonghua (Mandarin) with Simplified Chinese. Based on established back-translation methodologies as used in previous PETS translations, our process included multiple independent translations, expert panel reviews, and empirical testing with a total of N=400 participants from an English and a Chinese sample. Through confirmatory factor analysis and invariance testing we show that the Chinese PETS retains the original two-factor structure with high reliability, with support for configural, metric, and scalar invariance. Beyond validation, empathic system behavior was rated equivalently across languages, while non-empathic behavior drew substantially higher ratings from Chinese participants, suggesting its absence is read less consistently across cultures than its presence. This validated Chinese version enables researchers and practitioners to assess empathy perceptions among Chinese-speaking users, supporting culturally appropriate empathic technology development.

papers.intro:
Intelligent artificial agents are increasingly required to express empathic behavior, especially in the context of well-being, digital health support, and social care (Park and Whang, 2022; Jeong et al., 2023; Paiva et al., 2017), where empathy can affect user trust, engagement (Yoon and Lee, 2021; Plank et al., 1996; Johanson et al., 2023), and emotional support (Bae Brandtzæg et al., 2021; Bickmore and Picard, 2005; de Gennaro et al., 2019). Technological advances in generative AI and affective computing now enable systems to process and express emotional states (Park and Whang, 2022; Elyoseph et al., 2023; Liu and Sundar, 2018; Daher et al., 2020) in a way that, in some cases, even exceeds human empathy abilities (Ayers et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024a; Yonatan-Leus and Brukner, 2025). Evaluating how users actually perceive that behavior therefore becomes a prerequisite for designing such systems responsibly. To evaluate the empathic capabilities of artificial systems, Schmidmaier et al. (2024) introduced the Perceived Empathy of Technology Scale (PETS). The PETS was developed and validated in English, and Schmidmaier et al. (2025) subsequently published a German version, motivated by evidence that emotional perception and empathic response vary with cultural background (Pavlenko, 2012; Ward and Ragosko, 2025; Keysar et al., 2012) and native language (Dewaele, 2010; Schmitt et al., 2020). Such variation is particularly pronounced in Chinese contexts, where empathy relies heavily on nonverbal cues and contextual sensitivity rather than explicit emotional expression, reflecting Confucian values of emotional moderation and face-conscious interaction within relationship networks (“guanxi”, 关系) (郭景, 2024; Liu et al., 2024b). Chinese individuals also tend to experience greater self-focused distress when confronted with others’ suffering and to prefer practical advice over direct emotional validation, contrasting with Western patterns of other-oriented empathic concern (Cassels et al., 2010; Trommsdorff et al., 2007). Yet no instrument for perceived empathy of technology has been validated for Chinese-speaking populations. Given how widely empathic systems are deployed in China, this leaves a substantial body of work without a comparable measure. We therefore developed and validated a Chinese version of the PETS, targeting Putonghua ( 普通话) and Simplified Chinese ( 简体中文). We closely followed the translation and validation process applied by Schmidmaier et al. (2025), which builds on work by Brislin (1970); Klotz et al. (2023) and Jones et al. (2001). Confirmatory factor analysis established measurement equivalence with the English PETS across configural, metric, and scalar levels, with high reliability throughout. Unlike the German translation, where the trust item U3 loaded lower than in English (Schmidmaier et al., 2025), the Chinese version showed a stronger loading for that item. Comparing scale behavior across languages further revealed an asymmetry, as ratings of empathic system behavior were equivalent across samples while non-empathic behavior was rated substantially higher by Chinese participants, which may indicate that the absence of empathy is interpreted less consistently across cultures than its presence. This work thus contributes a validated Chinese PETS for cross-cultural research on empathic technologies, together with evidence that cultural differences in perceived empathy surface where empathic behavior is absent rather than where it is present. Additional information on how to apply the PETS can be found at https://perceived-empathy-of-technology-scale.com.

(2025) subsequently published a German version, motivated by evidence that emotional perception and empathic response vary with cultural background (Pavlenko, 2012; Ward and Ragosko, 2025; Keysar et al., 2012) and native language (Dewaele, 2010; Schmitt et al., 2020). Such variation is particularly pronounced in Chinese contexts, where empathy relies heavily on nonverbal cues and contextual sensitivity rather than explicit emotional expression, reflecting Confucian values of emotional moderation and face-conscious interaction within relationship networks (“guanxi”

关系) (郭景, 2024; Liu et al., 2024b). Chinese individuals also tend to experience greater self-focused distress when confronted with others’ suffering and to prefer practical advice over direct emotional validation, contrasting with Western patterns of other-oriented empathic concern (Cassels et al., 2010; Trommsdorff et al., 2007). Yet no instrument for perceived empathy of technology has been validated for Chinese-speaking populations. Given how widely empathic systems are deployed in China, this leaves a substantial body of work without a comparable measure. We therefore developed and validated a Chinese version of the PETS, targeting Putonghua (

普通话) and Simplified Chinese (

简体中文). We closely followed the translation and validation process applied by Schmidmaier et al. (2025), which builds on work by Brislin (1970); Klotz et al. (2023) and Jones et al. (2001). Confirmatory factor analysis established measurement equivalence with the English PETS across configural, metric, and scalar levels, with high reliability throughout. Unlike the German translation, where the trust item U3 loaded lower than in English (Schmidmaier et al., 2025), the Chinese version showed a stronger loading for that item. Comparing scale behavior across languages further revealed an asymmetry, as ratings of empathic system behavior were equivalent across samples while non-empathic behavior was rated substantially higher by Chinese participants, which may indicate that the absence of empathy is interpreted less consistently across cultures than its presence. This work thus contributes a validated Chinese PETS for cross-cultural research on empathic technologies, together with evidence that cultural differences in perceived empathy surface where empathic behavior is absent rather than where it is present. Additional information on how to apply the PETS can be found at https://perceived-empathy-of-technology-scale.com.

papers.title: A Shell Collision Scenario for EP251222b/GRB 251222A: Connecting Prompt Emission and Double-Peaked Afterglow
papers.abstract: GRB 251222A is a long-duration gamma-ray burst at a spectroscopic redshift of $z=3.171$. It was detected by the EP as the soft X-ray transient EP251222b before and during the gamma-ray emission. We performed a multi-wavelength (EP/WXT, fermi/GBM, swift/XRT and optical/NIR) investigation of this event. Its prompt soft X-ray and gamma-ray features, together with two afterglow rebrightenings, allow us to examine a possible connection between the prompt ejecta and the afterglow. We consider a multiple-shell scenario in which a faster, narrower shell catches up with a slower, wider shell. We assume that the selected pulse groups trace different ejecta and that the late X-ray flare marks their collision. Under these assumptions, we represent the post-collision outflow by an effective merged core and an outer annular component. A joint fit to the multi-band afterglow gives a Lorentz factor of $Γ_c\approx293$ for the merged core and $Γ_{1,w}\approx228$ for the outer component. The sample-wise collision mapping gives an energy release of $E_{\rm diss}=(1.6^{+2.1}_{-0.9})\times10^{52}$ erg and a dynamical dissipation efficiency of $0.37^{+0.07}_{-0.14}\%$. EP251222b can therefore be used to test a prompt--afterglow connection through shell collisions, although it does not uniquely establish this interpretation.

Gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) are among the most luminous transient phenomena in the Universe, serving as vital subjects for research in time-domain astronomy and high-energy astrophysics. GRBs release tremendous amounts of energy in the form of gamma-rays associated with the collapse of massive stars or the merger of compact objects [30, 63, 61, 106, 12], where the prompt emission is believed to be produced by internal shocks or magnetic reconnection in the relativistic jets launched by the central engine [16, 95, 62, 84, 114]. The simplest forward-shock model predicts smooth power-law evolution, but many afterglows contain complex features like flares, plateaus, and rebrightenings. Proposed explanations include refreshed shocks caused by late shells [87, 66, 92, 51], late energy injection from a magnetar central engine [25, 112], angularly structured or two-component jets [89, 113, 52], density variations in the external medium [76], and late internal dissipation [33]. A useful discriminator is whether the prompt pulse sequence, late high-energy activity, and afterglow peaks can be described by one dynamical history rather than by unrelated components.

Recent work has begun to connect complex prompt activities and the late-time afterglow structure within a common evolution of multiple ejecta. High-energy variability and structure in the later afterglow may arise from the same dynamical sequence if the central engine releases relativistic material more than once. A newly launched outflow can produce high-energy emission before or during its encounter with earlier ejecta, whereas the redistribution of energy and momentum in that encounter subsequently modifies the external-shock emission. GRB 240529A showed two prompt episodes separated by a quiescent interval of about 400 s, followed by an apparent X-ray plateau and optical rebrightening [100]. By combining the prompt analysis with numerical modeling of the optical afterglow, Sun et al. [99] interpreted these features as two distinct shocks launched during separate episodes of central-engine activity. Using the timing of the prompt pulses and flares together with multiwavelength afterglow modeling, Geng et al. [43] identified three ejecta shells whose successive collisions produced the X-ray flares, while the resulting fast narrow component and slower hollow component generated the two later afterglow bumps.

papers.title: Probing fundamental physics with ALMA2040 mm-wavelength observations of neutron stars
papers.abstract: Bursty or (rotation-induced) pulsed coherent radio emission from pulsars, magnetars, and fast radio transients originates in some of the most extreme environments in the Universe. However, the exact physical mechanism behind the scenes remains poorly understood. ALMA2040 will allow for systematic exploration of the millimeter-wavelength spectral window for pulsars and fast radio transients for the very first time, offering unprecedented opportunities to discover new observational phenomena and advance our understanding of emission physics. Beyond this, ALMA2040 provides a unique means to unveil the neutron-star population in the Galactic Centre (GC), enable novel tests of fundamental physics in the vicinity of the supermassive black hole Sgr A*, probe the potential existence of dark matter in the GC, and investigate the dense, highly dynamic interstellar and magnetic environment of this region.

papers.title: LOADBench: A Large Open Analog Dataset and Benchmark for Machine Learning in IC Design
papers.abstract: Machine learning (ML) for analog IC design is constrained by limited open data and the absence of standardized evaluation: results reported in different papers are typically obtained on bespoke, often closed, datasets and with ad-hoc metrics, leaving comparisons across methods unreliable. We address both gaps with a large opensource dataset and a suite of standardized benchmarks. The dataset contains more than 100 operational amplifier (opamp) topologies (1-, 2-, and 3-stage) in the SkyWater130 PDK, each shipped with structural and functional annotations, topology-specific sizing constraints (symmetry and sizing rules), an Ngspice testbench, and a multi-objective NSGA-II sizing run producing around 103 Pareto-optimal and 106 intermediate sizing-performance pairs per topology. On top of this data we define six benchmark tasks with precise protocols: inverse sizing, topology selection, sub-circuit classification, structural circuit generation, Pareto-membership prediction, and multi-objective optimization. Thus, the data presented here constitutes the most comprehensive dataset for ML development in over four decades of analog IC design automation. The dataset, ground-truth annotations, and reference implementations of the metric-defining routines are released under an open license, enabling reproducible and directly comparable evaluation across heterogeneous analog design automation methods.

Machine learning has been applied across the analog design flow. LLM-based methods have been explored for topology selection/sizing and code/netlist generation (Vijayaraghavan et al., 2024; Lai et al., 2024; Nguyen and Liu, 2025). Related non-LLM generative approaches include RL-based and evolutionary circuit generation (Uhlich et al., 2024; Uhlich et al., 2025), as well as variational autoencoders (Poddar et al., 2024). For circuit sizing, surrogate models such as artificial neural networks (ANNs) (İslamoğlu et al., 2019; Budak et al., 2022; Vaz et al., 2022) and decision trees (Martins and Lourenço, 2024) replace expensive simulator calls within optimization loops, while (Mueller-Gritschneder et al., 2009) targets the Pareto-optimal front (POF) directly. The inverse sizing problem, mapping target specifications back to parameters, has been tackled through direct one-shot prediction using regression (Lourenço et al., 2018; Beaulieu et al., 2023), dense neural networks (Leibl and Graeb, 2024), or generative models such as LLMs (Nguyen and Liu, 2025) and diffusion models (de Azevedo et al., 2025; Azevedo et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025). Reinforcement learning has also been explored as an optimization-style alternative (Costa et al., 2025; Taşkıran et al., 2025). Beyond the circuit level, graph neural networks (GNNs) have been applied to placement-quality prediction (Li et al., 2020), circuit classification (Kunal et al., 2020a), topology generation (Dong et al., 2023) and symmetry-constraint identification (Kunal et al., 2020b; Gao et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2024).

Open benchmarks and datasets have emerged in response, but each leaves parts of the design space uncovered (Table 1). AnalogGym (Li et al., 2024) ships only two of its five circuit categories in an open-source PDK. AICircuit (Mehradfar et al., 2024; Mehradfar et al., 2025) is built on commercial tools, restricting comparison to predicted-performance metrics on a closed test set. AMSBench (Shi et al., 2025) and AnalogCoder (Lai et al., 2024) target LLM schematic perception and code generation respectively, and are therefore confined to LLM-based approaches. The datasets OCB (Dong et al., 2023), AnalogToBi (Lee et al., [n. d.]) and the EDA-Opamp-Database (Leibl, [n. d.]), although extensive in number of netlists, have no sizing or complete structural annotations, the former two being built on commercial tools as well. None combines an open-source workflow, broad topology coverage, a benchmark suite spanning multiple stages of the analog IC design flow, and metrics applicable across a broad range of ML methodologies relevant to analog IC design. Furthermore, only AICircuit provides precomputed sizing data, at modest scale and behind a commercial PDK; methods developed against the other benchmarks must still generate their own training set, recreating the data-hunger problem that motivated open benchmarks in the first place. Moreover, when evaluation depends on a fixed dataset as in inverse sizing or classification, leaving its creation to the user undermines cross-method comparability.

papers.title: A first look at the protoplanet WISPIT 2 b with VLTI/GRAVITY+
papers.abstract: Confirmed observations of young protoplanets actively undergoing the process of formation have remained rare to date. In this Letter, we present new insights into the nature of the recently identified protoplanet WISPIT 2 b (age $\sim$ 5 Myr) from VLTI/GRAVITY+ observations. Through the analysis of the spectral energy distribution (SED) and astrometry of WISPIT 2 b, with the inclusion of new GRAVITY+ data, we investigate the nature of the protoplanet's thermal emission and orbital properties. We performed an orbit fit with the inclusion of new high-precision GRAVITY+ astrometry to provide an updated orbital solution. We also analyzed the medium resolution GRAVITY+ K band spectrum in combination with new VLT/SPHERE and literature photometry, exploring both the atmospheric properties and the constraints on the circumplanetary environment. Finally, we checked for any signal from a resolved circumplanetary disk in the GRAVITY+ data. We detected the protoplanet WISPIT 2 b at $\sim$322 mas separation from its host star. The new GRAVITY+ astrometry prefers an orbit with a moderate eccentricity. Analysis of the SED reveals an effective temperature in the 900 to 1300 K regime and a slight preference for atmospheric models including clouds over pure blackbody emission. While the GRAVITY+ observations do also not resolve a circumplanetary disk, we place an upper limit on the possible spatial extent of such a disk. The new GRAVITY+ observations independently confirm WISPIT 2 b as a self-luminous and point-like companion residing inside the gap of the transitional disk at $\sim$60 au from its host star. Further observations - either at higher signal-to-noise ratio or at longer wavelengths - are required to characterize the atmosphere and examine the presence of circumplanetary material from thermal emission of the dust.

papers.intro:
The characterization of newborn planets provides key benchmarks to inform planet formation and evolutionary models. Many class II stars have been found to host so-called transitional disks (Andrews et al., 2018, e.g.,), which are circumstellar disks with gaps or inner cavities. While transitional disks have often been postulated as signposts of ongoing planet formation, only a small number of protoplanets and protoplanet candidates have so far been discovered in the gaps and inner cavities of these disks (Biller et al., 2014; Keppler et al., 2018; Haffert et al., 2019; van Capelleveen et al., 2025a; Close et al., 2025; Lagrange et al., 2025; Crotts et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025, e.g.,). Arguably, the most well-established protoplanets discovered to date are PDS 70 b and c (Keppler et al., 2018; Müller et al., 2018; Haffert et al., 2019), which both exhibit continuum point-source emission and Hα\alpha line emission, which traces active accretion onto the planets. Other protoplanet candidates include, but are not limited to, PDS 70 d (Christiaens et al., 2024; Hammond et al., 2025), AB Aur b (Currie et al., 2022), and HD 169142 b (Hammond et al., 2023). In a case very similar to the PDS 70 system, WISPIT 2 was recently discovered to host a high confidence accreting protoplanet (van Capelleveen et al., 2025a; Close et al., 2025).

Similar to PDS 70 in both architecture and effective temperature, WISPIT 2 is a classical T Tauri star (M⋆∼1.1​M⊙M_{\star}\sim 1.1\,\rm{M}_{\odot}, Teff∼4400T_{\mathrm{eff}}\sim 4400 K), located in the nearby, young co-moving population Theia 53 (Kounkel and Covey, 2019; Kounkel et al., 2020; Hunt and Reffert, 2023, ∼5\sim 5–10 Myr, ∼130\sim 130 pc,), hosting a multi-ring transitional disk, with an embedded protoplanet (van Capelleveen et al., 2025a, WISPIT 2 b,) and an additional inner protoplanet candidate (Close et al., 2025). WISPIT 2 b was detected inside the innermost (known) gap of the transitional disk across multiple wavelengths, allowing for the planetary signal to be disentangled from the circumstellar disk. Detection of strong Hα\alpha emission robustly confirmed the protoplanetary nature of WISPIT 2 b, implying an accretion rate of M˙≈(2CLOSE\dot{M}\approx(2–OPEN6)×10−9​MJup​yr−16)\times 10^{-9}\,\mathrm{M_{Jup}\,yr^{-1}} (Close et al., 2025), similar to the accretion rates of the PDS 70 protoplanets (Wagner et al., 2018). In addition to the measurement of Hα\alpha, which likely traces accretion, only H and K band photometry of the companion is available in the literature. Therefore, observations with ideally both a larger wavelength coverage and a higher spectral resolution than the existing photometry are needed to characterize the atmosphere and circumplanetary environment of WISPIT 2 b.

In this Letter, we present the first Very Large Telescope Interferometer (VLTI)/GRAVITY+ observations of the protoplanet WISPIT 2 b, providing an updated astrometric position and KK band (∼2.0\sim 2.0–2.4​µm2.4\,\text{\textmu m}) spectrum of the actively accreting protoplanet. In Sect. 2, we present the new GRAVITY+ observations along with a brief discussion of the literature photometry used in our analysis of WISPIT 2 b. We then provide the GRAVITY+ astrometry and discuss an updated orbit fit in Sect. 3.1. We made use of the medium resolution R∼500R\sim 500 KK band spectrum to investigate the nature of the thermal emission of WISPIT 2 b in Sect. 3.2, and explored the spatial extent of the circumplanetary environment in Sect. 3.3. In Sect 3.4, we discuss the prospects for future observations of WISPIT 2 b at mid-infrared wavelengths and present our conclusions in Sect. 4.

papers.title: Conditional Mean Flows: Few-Step Densities for Simulation-Based Inference
papers.abstract: Flow matching has emerged as a powerful generative family for simulation-based inference (SBI). However, sampling and density evaluation require numerical integration at inference time. This makes posterior sampling in neural posterior estimation costly. More importantly, it can make repeated likelihood evaluation prohibitively expensive and impractical for Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling, which may require thousands of repeated density evaluations. Here, we develop conditional mean flows for posterior and likelihood approximation, combining few-step sampling with tractable density evaluation. We show that the mean flow objective identifies conditional flow maps and that independent masking enables direct estimation of marginal likelihoods. We evaluate both posterior and likelihood estimation across several tasks and show that conditional mean flows retain the flexibility of flow-based density estimators while significantly reducing inference time. In particular, single-step conditional mean flow density evaluation yields estimation error comparable to 200-step flow matching while enabling about 200-fold faster downstream MCMC sampling.
papers.intro:
Mechanistic simulators are used to describe processes ranging from cognitive science (Ratcliff et al., 2016) to disease modeling (Ye et al., 2025). Yet, while practically important, their likelihoods are often unavailable in closed form. Simulation-based inference (Sisson et al., 2018; Cranmer et al., 2020; Deistler et al., 2025; Arruda et al., 2026, SBI;) addresses this challenge by using simulated parameter-observation pairs (𝜽,𝐲)(\bm{\theta},\mathbf{y}) to infer unknown parameters, and amortized methods reuse the trained network across datasets (Bürkner et al., 2023).

Mechanistic simulators are used to describe processes ranging from cognitive science (Ratcliff et al., 2016) to disease modeling (Ye et al., 2025). Yet, while practically important, their likelihoods are often unavailable in closed form. Simulation-based inference (Sisson et al., 2018; Cranmer et al., 2020; Deistler et al., 2025; Arruda et al., 2026, SBI;) addresses this challenge by using simulated parameter-observation pairs (𝜽,𝐲)(\bm{\theta},\mathbf{y}) to infer unknown parameters, and amortized methods reuse the trained network across datasets (Bürkner et al., 2023).

Two popular forms of SBI are neural posterior estimation (NPE) and neural likelihood estimation (NLE). NPE learns a posterior model q𝝍​(𝜽∣𝐲)q_{\bm{\psi}}(\bm{\theta}\mid\mathbf{y}) which can sample from the approximate posterior directly. NLE, instead, learns a likelihood model q𝝍​(𝐲∣𝜽)q_{\bm{\psi}}(\mathbf{y}\mid\bm{\theta}) which requires Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) to sample from the posterior. NPE amortizes over datasets but is usually tied to the prior and data format used in training, whereas NLE needs MCMC for every dataset, but allows the prior to be changed after training and composes exchangeable likelihoods across any number of i.i.d. observations (Cranmer et al., 2020).

Many SBI methods demand neural estimators that are both flexible and inexpensive to evaluate. In NLE, MCMC requires thousands of likelihood evaluations per posterior, making each evaluation a practical bottleneck. Further, hierarchical approaches (Arruda et al., 2024) or self-consistency objectives that improve NPE (Schmitt et al., 2024a; Mishra et al., 2026) and enable model comparison (Kucharský and Bürkner, 2026) rely on density evaluation during training or inference.

So far, normalizing flows have been a standard choice in these applications because they evaluate densities in a single pass (Papamakarios et al., 2021; Dinh et al., 2017; Durkan et al., 2019). However, their transformations must remain invertible with tractable Jacobians, which restricts how inductive biases can be built into the architecture (Chen et al., 2025). Autoregressive flows based on causal transformers (e.g., TARFlow and STARFlow) relax this restriction (Zhai et al., 2025; Gu et al., 2025), but impose a fixed variable ordering and require sequential inversion for sampling. Moreover, tractable joint densities do not generally imply tractable marginals, which are required with missing observations (Yalavarthi et al., 2024).

Yet, their densities require solving an ordinary differential equation (ODE), which can take hundreds of network evaluations and makes repeated likelihood calls during training or within MCMC costly. Few-step generative models reduce the sampling cost, but consistency models, for instance, provide no tractable density (Song et al., 2023; Schmitt et al., 2024b). To overcome this limitation, we present conditional mean flows for SBI, which learn the average velocity between two times, so that one network evaluation defines a finite-time map based on mean flows (Geng et al., 2025; Geng et al., 2026). papers.title: Transferable conditional brain charts link cortico-subcortical structure to Alzheimer's disease progression
papers.abstract: Normative models chart how brain measures vary across the lifespan, expressing each individual as a deviation from a healthy reference. However, most regional models of cortical thickness disregard dependencies between cortical and subcortical anatomy, and transferring them to a new site typically requires retraining or a recalibration of location and scale alone. We condition lifespan norms of cortical thickness on subcortical volume, such that each deviation indicates whether an individual's cortex lies within the healthy range given their subcortical anatomy, and make them transferable. In 21,351 healthy individuals from 216 sites, conditioning on ten subcortical structures improved out-of-sample prediction on average, most for the amygdala and hippocampus. Refitting only the intercepts of all four distributional parameters on about 20 healthy individuals, as implemented in our open-source package NormGAMLSS, calibrated most of six unseen sites without retraining, for base and conditional models. In the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, global deviation and structural dissociation (the reduction in mean absolute deviation under conditioning) predicted conversion to mild cognitive impairment and dementia beyond the Clinical Dementia Rating and dissociation added beyond global deviation for dementia, even at similar clinically recorded impairment. Conditional norms thus provide relevant, individual-level information.

papers.title: Tracking the flow of interstellar gas across scales: from galaxies to star clusters
papers.abstract: While the baryon cycle of the interstellar medium - and its ability to form stars - plays a key role in galaxy evolution, unravelling the physical processes driving its evolution remains a critical challenge, given that present-day observing facilities are unable to map entire galactic ecosystems down to the scales of individual star-forming clumps. Here, we outline the technical requirements that would enable, for the first time, to connect the small (pc) scale physics of star formation, to the large (tens-of-kpc) scales of galaxies, enabling an effective tracking of the flows of matter and energy across a vast range of environments, and answering the long-standing question of what regulates star formation across cosmic time.

papers.title: How language model agents reshape price competition
papers.abstract: Repeated Bertrand competition is a stringent benchmark for algorithmic pricing: in homogeneous-goods markets, standard learning procedures typically select the stage-game Nash outcome with prices near marginal cost. We show that LLM pricing agents can escape this benchmark, depending on deployment decisions. LLMs outperform standard online learners through faster adaptation, but this advantage largely disappears against full-information learners. An extracted surrogate algorithm illustrates how LLMs in specific deployments profit from regularly undercutting slower learners. Agents that post one price every period from raw market histories that include rival prices can sustain supracompetitive regimes in self-play. Agents that periodically emit probability distributions from summarized histories of their own profits instead move toward the competitive region in self-play. Markets mixing these interfaces can generate dynamic regimes in which LLMs establish a high-price anchor and regularly undercut it to capture demand. These regimes can keep both competitors' prices above marginal cost. Deployment choices shape these outcomes, shifting the focus from stationary equilibria to dynamic pricing regimes.
