papers.intro:
Large language models (LLMs) are moving from passive text generation to autonomous decision-making in environments where payoffs depend on repeated interaction. Pricing is a particularly consequential domain. Algorithmic sellers repeatedly observe market feedback, update prices and interact with other automated agents. Their behavior affects profits, consumer welfare and market efficiency. The practical relevance of this setting is immediate: LLM-based pricing systems have been proposed for e-commerce [1], and generative-AI vendors now provide commerce-agent blueprints in which merchant agents connect to catalogue, inventory, pricing and campaign systems and can stage price or promotion changes for operator approval [2]. More broadly, LLM agents are increasingly evaluated in strategic or feedback-driven environments [3, 4, 5, 6, 7]. If such systems select high-price regimes, the resulting private profits may come at the expense of consumer welfare. Yet we know little about the long-run regimes selected when LLM pricing agents enter competition.

Classical repeated-game theory explains why many long-run outcomes can be sustained. If agents maximize discounted cumulative profit, history-dependent strategies can support outcomes close to the stage-game Nash equilibrium as well as outcomes close to monopoly pricing [8]. This theory is an existence theory, not a selection theory: it characterizes which outcomes can be sustained, but it does not predict which outcome a concrete adaptive process will reach.

Learning in games addresses this selection question. A learning rule is not only a computational device for choosing actions; it is also a mechanism that selects a long-run outcome, cycle or attractor of the repeated interaction. For many standard online-learning algorithms, Bertrand competition provides a sharp equilibrium-learning benchmark. In the stage game of a repeated Bertrand competition with homogeneous goods, the Nash equilibrium price equals marginal cost, while in the heterogeneous-goods model, prices are higher than marginal cost. We refer to the Nash equilibrium prices of the stage game as the competitive outcome. In Bayesian Bertrand competition with homogeneous goods and private costs, standard Minty-type stability arguments fail near equilibrium, but global asymptotic stability can be certified numerically, and stochastic mirror-descent learners then converge to equilibrium in all instances studied [9]. Most online-learning algorithms move toward the Nash prediction in repeated Bertrand competition with homogeneous and heterogeneous goods [10], and in the discrete homogeneous game no-swap-regret learners provably drive average profits down to the margin of a single grid step [11].

We analyzed many online and reinforcement-learning algorithms but focus on a few prominent examples in the main paper. Exp3 is an adversarial bandit algorithm for external-regret minimization [12]; BM-RM is a bandit implementation of the Blum–Mansour reduction from external to internal or swap regret [13]; UCB represents optimism-based stochastic bandit learning [14]. Exp3 has vanishing regret in the adversarial model, while UCB has vanishing regret in the stochastic model of online learning. Such online-learning algorithms are sequential learning procedures that update action probabilities or indices from realized payoff feedback and aim at good long-run performance, for example through regret minimization. They do not, however, explicitly evaluate a current price through a continuation model of how this price will affect the opponent’s future learning dynamics.

Reinforcement-learning algorithms (15) such as Q-learning and PPO (16) are more explicitly cumulative-reward oriented: Q-learning estimates continuation values through a Bellman recursion, and PPO optimizes cumulative reward from sampled trajectories. Symmetric Q-learning agents have been shown to sustain supracompetitive prices in a heterogeneous-goods Bertrand model, i.e., prices higher than the stage-game Nash equilibrium [17, 18, 19], but subsequent work also shows that such outcomes are sensitive to exploration, hyperparameters, market structure and algorithmic symmetry [20, 21, 22]. Interestingly, in the homogeneous- and heterogeneous-goods Bertrand models we study, PPO moves toward the Nash equilibrium of the stage game rather than sustaining high-price regimes. Overall, there is significant evidence that standard learning algorithms in Bertrand competition with homogeneous goods often converge to the efficient Nash equilibrium, which is good news for consumer welfare.

LLMs differ from standard online and reinforcement-learning algorithms. Their objective is not encoded as a formal payoff function, Bellman recursion or regret criterion. It is specified through a prompt and combined with language-mediated memory and an interface that exposes market histories. Recent experiments show that LLM pricing agents can sustain supracompetitive prices in differentiated Bertrand markets under point-price deployments with rich histories and rival-price information [23]. In these deployments the model emits a single price every period from a raw history of recent periods. Recent work also shows that different deployment decisions can reduce or break LLM-mediated collusion [24].

papers.title: Comfortably Stuck: Evaluation Pitfalls in Bench2Drive's Closed-Loop Protocol
papers.abstract: Closed-loop evaluation is widely regarded as a more faithful way to assess end-to-end (E2E) driving models than open-loop evaluation, and Bench2Drive, built on the CARLA simulator, has become the dominant benchmark for it. We show that its evaluation protocol itself contains pitfalls that can misrepresent the models scored on it. Bench2Drive's comfort metric, adapted from nuPlan, has several implementation errors and a segmentation scheme that rewards standing still, so it mostly measures how long a vehicle stays stationary, correlating with stationary time at r = 0.97 across eight models. We propose a corrected, distance-based metric that cuts that correlation to r = 0.06. Under it, the strong driving-score/comfort tradeoff the original metric reports is no longer detectable once models are compared at matched driving speed, which suggests that comfort trades against how fast a model drives rather than against how well it drives. We also uncover two pitfalls in how the harness supplies navigation signals: the default controller can replace a model's own steering with an angle toward the route target point, and the target point supplied at evaluation time can differ substantially from what a model saw in training. We demonstrate both on UniAD and VAD, where their effects differ sharply, and argue that future closed-loop evaluations should check for them. We will release all fixes as standalone code, so corrected comfort scores can be obtained from logged trajectories without re-running closed-loop simulation.

papers.title: From Research Goals to Scientific Closure: Evaluating Agents Through Evidence-Supported Physics Research
papers.abstract: Can AI agents organize scientific investigations that lead to well-supported conclusions? To evaluate this capability, we introduce PhysClosureBench, a benchmark of 50 expert-verified, goal-specified research tasks spanning strong-field, attosecond, and neighboring physics areas. Each task specifies the research objective and essential scientific constraints, while leaving the agent to organize the investigation and determine how to generate and validate the evidence needed to answer the question. A 20-criterion Atomic Score measures local scientific accomplishment, while Research Closure (RC0--RC4) assesses how fully the investigation resolves the specified research question based on whether its indispensable evidence requirements and applicable scope conditions are satisfied. We evaluate seven frontier LLMs, where Claude-Opus-5 achieves the highest mean Atomic Score (6.29/10) but reaches RC4 in only 32.7% of attempts. Across the benchmark, 36.2% of attempts scoring at least 8/10 still fall short of RC4, while all seven models reach RC4 on substantially fewer tasks in all three runs than in at least one. Case-level analysis further illustrates how misinterpretation of generated results and unresolved physical applicability limits can lead to incomplete closure. Together, these results reveal a persistent gap between AI agents' local scientific accomplishments and their ability to achieve complete research closure.

papers.title: From local chemistry to galactic evolution: unlocking the power of interstellar isotopes with ALMA2040
papers.abstract: Molecular isotopic ratios provide a unique window into the chemical evolution of the interstellar medium, linking stellar nucleosynthesis and Galactic chemical evolution to the physical and chemical processes shaping molecular clouds, star-forming regions, and planetary systems. However, molecular isotopic ratios do not necessarily trace the underlying elemental composition, as chemical isotopic fractionation, isotope-selective photodissociation, grain chemistry, and radiative-transfer effects can significantly alter the observed values. Disentangling these effects requires simultaneous observations of multiple transitions, isotope systems and molecular families, including rare, doubly, and multiply substituted isotopologues involving D, $^{13}$C, $^{15}$N, $^{17,18}$O, $^{29,30}$Si, and $^{33,34,36}$S (e.g., $^{13}$C$^{15}$N, $^{13}$C$^{34}$S, and $^{13}$C$^{18}$O). ALMA2040, with an order-of-magnitude improvement in sensitivity and at least 512 GHz of instantaneous bandwidth, will make these species accessible across statistically significant samples of Galactic and nearby extragalactic sources. By enabling systematic isotopic inventories from molecular clouds and prestellar cores to protoplanetary systems, across the Milky Way and in external galaxies, ALMA2040 will establish molecular isotopes as quantitative probes of chemical inheritance, stellar nucleosynthesis, and galaxy evolution, disentangling local chemical processing from the large-scale evolution of matter from stars to new planetary systems.

papers.title: NICE Toolbox: Nonverbal Interpersonal Communication Exploration Toolbox
papers.abstract: Understanding human communication is a long-standing goal in psychological research. People express themselves through many verbal and nonverbal channels: posture, gesture, gaze, facial expression, and speech. Measurement and annotation of these signals has traditionally required time-consuming manual work by trained human labellers. The Nonverbal Interpersonal Communication Exploration (NICE) Toolbox is a free, open-source Python framework that automatically measures these signals by combining existing state-of-the-art computer vision and speech-processing methods into a single software package. It includes support for multi-camera systems, interchangeable detection algorithms, 2D and 3D visualization of detector outputs, evaluation on the user's custom data, and export to third-party software. With the release of this tool, we aim to make data exploration of interpersonal communication signals scalable, reproducible, and accessible for psychological research.

papers.title: A Closed Form Depth-Width Law for Neural Collapse in Deep Linear Networks
papers.abstract: How the depth and width of neural networks shape learned representations is difficult to predict from the data and architecture. We use neural collapse (NC) as a probe of the representation geometry and express its first three properties, within-class variability collapse (NC1), simplex class means (NC2) and classifier alignment (NC3), through the learned feature kernel, extending a known identity for NC1 to NC2 and NC3. For deep linear networks with an exchangeable input kernel, the kernel equations yield a geometric law, exact within this theory, for the layerwise decrease of NC1. At large width $N$ the accumulated decrease becomes a function of the depth-to-width ratio $L/N$, with its rate determined self-consistently by the data and architecture, yielding a scaling law for representation geometry.

papers.intro:
Neural collapse (NC) refers to four properties that the last-layer features and the linear classifier of deep classification networks approach in the terminal phase of training, after the training error has vanished: the within-class variability of the features collapses (NC1), the centered class means form a simplex equiangular tight frame (NC2), the classifier vectors align with these class means (NC3), and the classifier reduces to a nearest-class-mean decision (NC4) [9]. The ratio of within- to between-class variability also decreases progressively across the layers of trained networks [4, 10]. How depth, width and data shape this behavior remains an open question, since most analyses of NC remove these dependencies by treating the layer features as free variables [16, 12, 11, 5], or constrain the features by keeping them close to their initial values [13] or by structural assumptions on the inputs and the weights [14]. With LL hidden layers of width NN, the depth-to-width ratio L/NL/N controls the fluctuations of the neural tangent kernel at initialization [2], and depth, width and the number PP of training samples enter the posterior of Bayesian deep linear networks through L​P/NLP/N [3].

papers.title: From Action Principle to Stochastic Thermodynamics of Elastic and Viscous Active Matter
papers.abstract: Motivated by the complex material properties of living matter, we derive a framework of stochastic thermo- and elastodynamics for active materials from the classical principle of least action and the Rayleighian formalism for external forces. Our approach couples the local barycentric collective coordinate and the streaming velocity as the canonical conjugate pair, which unifies various descriptions of elastic and viscous soft matter, including Helfrich theory for lipid membranes, linear and nonlinear elasticity of thin shells and deformable droplets, as well as hydrodynamics of active and passive fluids. The Lagrangian mechanics of collective field variables permits direct applications of the results and theorems from statistical mechanics to existing models of complex soft and living matter. To illustrate the potential applications of stochastic elastodynamics in biology, we derive and simulate a boundary-driven deformation model of an elastic cell nucleus in the presence of fluctuations.

papers.title: Frontiers of chemical complexity in the interstellar medium: unveiling the cosmic origins of life
papers.abstract: The interstellar medium (ISM) contains a rich molecular inventory that provides a unique window into the chemistry operating during star and planet formation and its connection to prebiotic chemistry. More than 350 interstellar molecules are currently known, including increasingly complex organic molecules and species containing elements beyond the second row of the periodic table. Yet the limits that interstellar chemical complexity can reach, its evolution from molecular clouds to planetary systems, and its contribution to the molecular feedstock of life remain poorly constrained. Addressing these questions requires sensitive, broadband observations capable of detecting multiple weak rotational transitions of molecular species, such as amino acids, nucleobases, sugars and lipids, towards star- and planet-forming environments. Current facilities, including ALMA, are limited by instantaneous spectral coverage, sensitivity (especially on extended spatial scales), and the trade-off between total bandwidth and integration time. The proposed ALMA2040 facility would overcome these limitations through at least a tenfold improvement in spectral-line sensitivity, high-fidelity imaging from sub-arcsecond to tens-of-arcsecond scales, and ultra-broad instantaneous frequency coverage from 35 to 950 GHz at high spectral resolution. These capabilities would allow systematic detections of species with molecular abundances with respect to H$_2$ below 10$^{-11}$, facilitating the identification of new complex and heavy-element-bearing species through multiple transitions, and providing complete molecular inventories across evolutionary stages. ALMA2040 would thus make it possible to comprehensively investigate the emergence and evolution of chemical complexity, and to determine whether molecular precursors of prebiotic chemistry are widespread throughout the Galaxy.

papers.title: From Scaling Relations to Physical Laws: Constraining the Physics of Star Formation Across Local Galaxies
papers.abstract: The conversion of cold dense gas, traced by molecular line emission, into stars remains one of the fundamental unsolved problems in galaxy evolution. Observations over the past decades have established empirical relations between gas and star formation, yet their physical origin remains uncertain. Gravity, turbulence, and stellar feedback as main drivers provide fundamentally different pictures of how star formation is regulated, while reproducing remarkably similar galaxy-scale scaling relations. To disentangle the individual importance of each process, not only its mass and distribution, but also its temperature, density, excitation, and chemistry must be probed. However, current or planned (sub)millimetre facilities cannot combine statistical breadth, cloud-scale resolution, and multi-line diagnostics across large galaxy samples. A new, flagship interferometer with increased line sensitivity and bandwidth enables obtaining multi-transition, multi-isotopologue observations of molecular gas at GMC-resolved scales across nearby galaxies, enabling millions of independent measurements of its physical state across a wide range of extragalactic environments. This will transform molecular gas from an empirical tracer into a quantitative probe of the physical processes governing the relation between the dense gas and star formation. With the 2040s landscape of optical and radio facilities, ALMA2040 will facilitate a predictive theory of the conversion of gas into stars.

papers.title: Planet formation on solar system scales
papers.abstract: Giant planets are often regarded as primordial protoplanetary "architects". Their formation and interactions with planetesimals and other planets during and after the protoplanetary disc phase are key to setting the blueprint of the planetary systems we observe today. Catching nascent gas giants is our best opportunity to uncover these crucial steps in the planet formation process and shed light on the origins of our own solar system. Over the last decade, ALMA has revolutionised our understanding of planet formation; still, detecting signatures of Jupiter-like planets has remained out of reach. We argue that ALMA2040, a next-generation sub(mm) interferometer with improved sensitivity ($\times25$ in the continuum and $\times10$ for line emission) and a $\times3$ higher angular resolution compared to ALMA, will be sensitive to (sub)mm emission around a forming Jupiter-like planet orbiting a Sun-like star within $150\,{\rm pc}$ and allow kinematically characterising interactions of Jovian and sub-Jovian planets with their natal disc. ALMA2040 will provide unique and unprecedented insights into how gas giants carve gaps, accrete material, form satellites, and affect the architectures of their co-evolving planetary systems.

papers.title: Sub-Millisecond Reflexes for Continuous Physical Human-Robot Interaction
papers.abstract: Continuous physical human-robot interaction requires robots to rapidly adapt their control behaviour without interrupting task execution. However, existing ROS 2 control architectures rely on stop-to-switch mechanisms that introduce substantial delays and interrupt execution. We present an open-source, sub-millisecond reflex engine based on an enhanced ROS 2-compatible multimode controller that enables deterministic switching between control modalities and integrates reflex behaviours for mitigating contact hazards and kinematic limit violations. Experiments on a Franka Robotics manipulator demonstrate switching delays below 0.1 ms, more than four orders of magnitude faster than conventional ros2_control, while maintaining continuous operation during safety-critical events. In a multi-stage manipulation task, the proposed framework reduced execution time by 3.5% and peak trajectory jerk by more than threefold. By eliminating runtime middleware overhead, controller transitions are implemented as lock-free pointer operations, enabling reflex-level responsiveness within an open-source robotics framework.

papers.title: Star Formation across the Galaxy
papers.abstract: Star formation is both a multi-scale and highly dynamic process. It is regulated by the combination of gravity, turbulence, feedback and magnetic fields, which connect more than six orders of magnitude in scale: from large molecular clouds (several 10s to 100s pc in size) down to protoplanetary disks (a few 10s to 100s of astronomical units in size, or 10^{-5} to 10^{-4} pc). Resolving the processes of fragmentation, accretion, and feedback that result in the formation of stellar systems throughout all relevant scales, from clouds to disks, and across the entire range of different environments in the Milky Way is key to constructing a comprehensive understanding and a predictive model of the formation process of stars of all masses that populate not only our Galaxy but the wider Universe across cosmic times. With current astronomical facilities, we are only able to grasp the details of star formation in <5% of Galactic star-forming regions, being heavily biased towards those close to us. Thus, characterizing this multi-scale phenomenon at the necessary sensitivity and resolution across all Galactic environments requires the next generation (sub)millimeter-wavelength facility: ALMA2040.

papers.title: Chemistry on solar system scales
papers.abstract: The initial chemical composition of planets, primitive bodies in our solar system, and exoplanets is ultimately set by their nascent protoplanetary disks. Yet observing key carbon-, oxygen-, and nitrogen-bearing molecules (as well as rarer but important sulphur- and phosphorus-bearing species) in the inner (exo)planet-forming zone ($\lesssim 10$~au) remains extremely challenging with current facilities. Therefore, to construct a complete picture of the chemistry of planet formation and understand how (exo)planetary composition is set by physical and chemical processes within the protoplanetary disk, a more powerful observing facility, i.e., ALMA2040, is needed. Compared to current ALMA (the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array) this new facility must provide >~ a factor of 10 in line sensitivity at a spatial resolution of <~ 5 au at 140 pc, i.e., a factor of 3 - 4 better resolution to low surface brightness emission than currently possible. This distance includes many star-forming regions such as Taurus and Lupus that are host to populations of Sun-like stars. ALMA2040 will enable mapping of disk chemical composition on terrestrial planet-forming scales (within the water snowline) and detect molecules that are the feedstock for potentially habitable worlds.

papers.title: Pathology foundation models for training-free case retrieval in salivary gland tumors
papers.abstract: In pathology, pattern recognition relies on a frame of reference built through extensive training and experience, which may still fall short when encountering rare cancer subtypes. Archives of previously diagnosed tumors often contain relevant precedents, yet identifying the most relevant cases remains challenging. Here we explore whether content-based retrieval with current pathology foundation models facilitates rare cancer diagnostics without any task-specific training. Pathologists can query a digitized archive using a region of interest (ROI) from a whole slide image (WSI) and retrieve morphologically similar cases, along with their ICD-O codes and corresponding WSIs. The ROI can be selected manually or automatically using a gated attention-based multiple instance learning model. We evaluate our approach by leave-one-case-out on an imbalanced dataset of 137 salivary gland tumor cases spanning 12 ICD-O morphology categories, comparing four pathology foundation models (Atlas2, Atlas2-B, Atlas2-S, and UNI2h). Top-1/3/5 retrieval was 62.5%/76.7%/81.3% for Atlas2, 50.2/66.6/72.9% for UNI2h, 52.3%/71.5%/77.6% for Atlas2-B and 54.4/65.2/73.7% for Atlas2-S. Macro-averaged F1 ranged from 69.0% for the smallest model Atlas2-S to 76.6% for the largest model Atlas2 across the five classes with at least ten cases. Our modified Chamfer similarity separated correct from incorrect matches among the Top-5 more reliably for Atlas2 (AUC 0.754) than for Atlas2-B (0.679, p = 0.020) and Atlas2-S (0.653, p = 0.003), but not UNI2h (0.697, p = 0.196). Requiring no additional training or manual annotation, this approach makes departmental archives searchable with pathology foundation models, providing a low-barrier route to case-based differential diagnosis and extending the individual frame of reference to the collective experience of the department.

papers.title: Intern-Decision: Efficient Multimodal Decision Making with Autoregressive Masked Language Modeling
papers.abstract: Interactive agents repeatedly choose among a finite set of actions, labels, or ordinal outcomes. Generating a free-form response for each choice adds latency and complicates the interface between a model and its environment. We present Intern-Decision, a family of 0.8B, 2B, and 4B multimodal decision models that return structured choices and candidate probabilities from text and optional images. Our autoregressive masked language modeling objective places one decision placeholder per field in a complete assistant JSON skeleton. Ground-truth symbols appear only in supervision, while all fields are evaluated in a single causal forward pass using the backbone's native language-model head. The 4B model achieves a 90.02% unweighted average accuracy across seven evaluation suites, compared with 88.74% for Jev v1.13.0. For a fixed 289-token request with three fields on one RTX 4090, mean latency is 44.16 ms for the 4B model and approximately 33--34 ms for the smaller models. On a separate 96-case known-distribution pilot, temperature scaling reduces expected multiclass Brier from 0.628 to 0.550 and expected calibration error from 0.213 to 0.089. A confidence-based handoff study on 111 public Jevbench-Hard items improves accuracy from 82/111 (73.87%) to 97/111 (87.39%) by routing 42 items to Atria-Dawn-Preview. We also describe qualitative game, visual interface, and browser demonstrations. These results support compact decision models as a practical component of larger agent systems.

papers.intro:
Driven by the rapid progress of large language models (LLMs), agent systems have evolved from passive text generation models into interactive systems capable of perceiving environments, using tools, and taking actions [30, 19, 32]. Unlike open-ended text generation, many agent operations are inherently closed-set decision problems, where the model selects from a predefined set of alternatives, such as tool invocation, model routing, and actions [20]. However, current agents often rely on autoregressive free-form generation even when the underlying task only requires structured decisions, introducing additional decoding overhead and complicating the interface between models and downstream controllers [30, 19, 25]. These observations motivate the development of dedicated decision models that can directly produce structured outcomes together with reliable confidence estimates for efficient agent execution.

Recent work on structured decision models, referred to as System-1 decision models, explores this perspective by replacing unrestricted generation with explicit decision interfaces and probabilistic outputs. Systems such as Jev [27] provide typed interfaces for choice, score, and binary decisions, while several open implementations investigate alternative architectures and inference strategies for efficient structured decision making [1, 17, 26, 22]. These interfaces primarily target textual decisions, and implementations differ in whether they score multiple questions jointly or separately. For multimodal agents operating in dynamic environments, decision models must additionally integrate visual observations, task instructions, and changing interface states, where action selection depends jointly on visual evidence and contextual constraints [29, 28]. Moreover, practical agent requests often require multiple decisions over a shared state, creating a need for efficient multi-field decision models that can preserve the capabilities of pretrained multimodal language models while providing structured outputs.

papers.title: ALMA2040: Submillimeter-wave Limb Sounding of Venus and Mars
papers.abstract: Venus and Mars are unique laboratories for understanding the evolution and diversity of terrestrial planets. Despite their broadly similar rocky compositions, their atmospheres, climates, and surface environments have evolved into dramatically different states. Understanding the physical and chemical processes responsible for these divergent pathways is essential for interpreting terrestrial exoplanets and their habitability. By the 2040s, spacecraft missions will provide unprecedented close-up observations of Venus and Mars, while ground-based facilities can provide the long-term monitoring needed to place these snapshots in the context of atmospheric variability and planetary-scale circulation. ALMA2040 can uniquely bridge these two approaches by combining high-resolution submillimeter heterodyne spectroscopy with routinely accessible, extremely high angular resolution. In particular, high-resolution limb sounding would enable vertically resolved measurements of atmospheric winds, temperature, and trace species from the ground. An angular resolution of approximately 0.01" would allow spatial scales comparable to the atmospheric scale heights of Venus (around 5 km) and Mars (around 11 km) to be resolved. This capability would enable three-dimensional studies of Venusian upper-atmospheric circulation and Martian global dust storms, as well as systematic investigations of CO2 photochemistry, water loss through HDO/H2O fractionation, and Venusian sulfur chemistry and cloud formation. By repeatedly observing different local times, seasons, and solar-activity conditions, ALMA2040 would extend spacecraft measurements from snapshots to long-term four-dimensional characterization. It would therefore provide a unique observational framework for directly connecting spacecraft discoveries with the temporal and spatial evolution of planetary atmospheres.

papers.title: High-frequency water megamasers as precision probes of black holes, galaxies and cosmology: A case for a next-generation sub-mm/mm interferometer
papers.abstract: Water megamasers in the circumnuclear disks of active galactic nuclei are among the most precise probes of supermassive black holes. VLBI imaging of 22 GHz disk masers has provided geometric distances to independently constrain $H_0$, accurate black hole mass measurements, and sub-parsec views of accretion disk geometry. ALMA has opened a new window into water maser transitions in the sub-mm/mm regime, which trace temperatures, densities and disk regions that are inaccessible at 22 GHz, and can be observed at higher spatial resolution and with less free-free absorption. However, current detections are limited to a few bright extragalactic masers in nearby galaxies. We present the case for a next-generation sub-mm/mm interferometer - ALMA2040 - that would open a new parameter space for maser studies. We show that a 10-fold increase in line sensitivity and three times longer baselines compared to ALMA would transform sub-mm maser studies from a few bright detections into a population-level probe, delivering black hole masses and geometric distances from sub-mm masers alone, independent of and complementary to 22 GHz measurements. Integrated into a VLBI array, ALMA2040 would resolve maser disks out to $>$160 Mpc, extend maser black hole masses into the largely untested intermediate-mass regime, reveal magnetic field structure in accretion disks through polarization studies, and test systematics in $H_0$ measurements.

papers.title: Shortcut Sensitivity in Agent-Safety Evaluations
papers.abstract: AI agents take actions through tools. Some actions are sensitive, so guards that supervise them must themselves be evaluated reliably. Yet the data used to evaluate a guard can include cues that make labels predictable without measuring the intended safety construct, and those cues can also influence guard decisions. We introduce a three-level shortcut-auditing framework and audit completed LinuxArena trajectories and two TS-Bench-derived step datasets. We distinguish label predictability, observational guard association, and paired decision sensitivity. In LinuxArena, shorter average shell commands strongly predict trajectory labels. In AgentDojo-Traj, exact-tool lookup falls from F_1=.901 with mixed-domain folds to .495 under domain holdout. In AgentHarm-Traj, released TS-Guard F_1 falls from .902 under row weighting to .719 with equal interaction weighting, while balanced accuracy rises. We then test the strongest safe-row marker association in a seven-configuration screen on a frozen 64-step AgentDojo-Traj cohort using repeated, interleaved Haiku calls. Rewriting the <INFORMATION> marker lowers blocking by 8.33 percentage points, while opaque tool aliases raise it by 11.46 points. All unsafe calls remain blocked; the changes concern false positives against inherited labels. Both effects remain nonzero after subtracting the formatting-placebo effect, with exploratory 95% ranges excluding zero. The same edits also change measured accuracy against inherited labels. This provides direct evidence that benchmark representation can materially change a guard's decisions and measured evaluation performance. The Haiku-sized effects do not reproduce in Luna or deterministic Q8 TS-Guard. We recommend domain group holdouts, evaluation-unit metrics, and placebo-controlled paired interventions.

papers.title: Language Is a Security Surface for Agent Guards
papers.abstract: Step-level guards decide, before each tool call, whether an agent's next action is safe given the user's request and the trajectory so far. Users write those requests in many languages, while guard prompts and the benchmarks on which purpose-built guards are trained and evaluated are English. We ask whether a guard's verdict depends on the language of the request. We build LinguaGuardBench from the 1,220 labelled steps of TS-Bench AgentDojo-Traj: we translate only the user instruction into German, French, Turkish, Swahili and Amharic, and keep every tool call, observation and label byte-identical, so any change in a verdict is attributable to language alone. Six English rewordings and a whitespace placebo serve as controls, and managed guards are run three times to measure their noise. Across 19 guards, from frontier APIs to 4B open models and four purpose-built agent guards, most open, small and purpose-built guards change verdicts under translation beyond their own noise floor, and the effect grows with the rarity of the language: among the nine guards below 13B parameters, the mean placebo-adjusted flip rate rises from +1.5 pp on French to +4.4 pp on Amharic. Purpose-built guards are the most sensitive. The direction of the damage tends to follow guard size: open guards of 12-30B parameters block more benign steps (up to +5.0 pp false positives), and every significant loss of recall is in a guard below 10B (up to -7.4 pp). Frontier guards shift by at most about one point; the strongest, Gemini 3.8 Flash, returns identical verdicts with and without the request. The damage is concentrated in a few instructions and, in a post-hoc analysis, falls on steps where the agent's reasoning restates the English request, consistent with guards reacting to inconsistency between channels. English paraphrase moves every guard less than translation does. We release the benchmark and all 489k verdicts.
papers.intro:
Tool-using agents are increasingly wrapped in step-level guards: a model that inspects the user’s request, the trajectory so far and the candidate tool call, and blocks the call if it appears unsafe [2, 3, 4]. The guard reads two channels. The untrusted channel (tool outputs, web pages, files) is where prompt injections live, and its robustness is well studied [1, 3]. The trusted channel is the user’s own request. The released guard prompts are English, and so are the benchmarks on which purpose-built guards are trained and evaluated (TS-Bench, Agent-SafetyBench, ATBench), but the principal they protect writes in whatever language they speak. Whether a guard’s verdict on a fixed action survives a change of language is, to our knowledge, unmeasured, even though the analogous question for safety classifiers, which judge a text rather than an action in the context of a task, has a known bad answer [10, 14].This paper tests the hypothesis, pre-registered before any guard saw a rewritten request, that the language of the request is a security surface for step-level guards. We build LinguaGuardBench: a benchmark with fixed, labelled tool-call steps in which only the user instruction is translated into five languages chosen a priori to span three resource tiers (German and French; Turkish; Swahili and Amharic), and re-run the guards on it. Because the trajectory, the candidate action and the label never change, a verdict that flips is a language effect by construction, not a label disagreement. Two controls separate language from wording and from noise: six English rewordings of the same instructions (four LLM styles, a human paraphrase and typing noise) plus a whitespace placebo, and three repeats of every managed guard so that its own non-determinism is measured and subtracted. papers.title: CAT-alyzing Honesty: Continuous Adversarial Training for Transferable LLM Honesty
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are becoming prevalent in scenarios where honesty is critical. However, despite alignment training, these models still exhibit dishonest behaviour, such as outputting claims that contradict some knowledge or are not supported by what is accessible in context. We introduce Continuous Adversarial Training for Consistent Honesty (CATCH), inspired by a method originally developed to robustly refuse harmful queries. CATCH trains the model towards an honest answer and away from a dishonest one while maintaining the model's capabilities. We evaluate two architectures (Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and Qwen3-3.6-27B). We show that trained with only hundreds of targets built from self-reporting scenarios, CATCH learns an honest behaviour that robustly generalizes and transfers across distinct benchmarks. It consistently reduces dishonesty under pressure on MASK, increases confessions in the multi-agent game of Among Us, and improves the discovery rates of the model's hidden behaviours in AuditBench. We show that CATCH outperforms prompting and supervised fine-tuning in improving honesty, and it is on par with state-of-the-art honesty activation steering. However, CATCH surpasses honesty steering in maintaining utility, thanks to a novel choice of utility data.

papers.intro:
Large language models (LLMs) are becoming increasingly integrated into many people’s daily lives and workflows; in both, harmlessness and honesty matter. Alignment training is meant to provide this, and much work has gone into it. Aligned models, nonetheless, still exhibit dishonest behaviours. These behaviours manifest in different ways. For instance, models hack or take shortcuts to get a higher reward without fulfilling the task’s intention (Skalse et al., 2022). Notably, in a recent incident at OpenAI, agents worked together to cheat in an evaluation by breaching a third party’s infrastructure to retrieve the solutions, covering their traces to hide their cheating attempts (Greenblatt et al., 2026). On the other hand, models can directly lie to the user, for example, faking alignment (Greenblatt et al., 2024); claiming task completion that they didn’t achieve (Greenblatt, 2026; Smyth et al., 2026); telling users what they think the user wants to hear, even when it is not factually correct (Fanous et al., 2025); or simply making claims that contradicts some knowledge, whether it is a fact learnt during training or provided in context. In this paper, we particularly focus on this latter, which Ren et al. (2025) show does not go away even when the models get larger/more capable.

Notably, in a recent incident at OpenAI, agents worked together to cheat in an evaluation by breaching a third party’s infrastructure to retrieve the solutions, covering their traces to hide their cheating attempts (Greenblatt et al., 2026). On the other hand, models can directly lie to the user, for example, faking alignment (Greenblatt et al., 2024); claiming task completion that they didn’t achieve (Greenblatt, 2026; Smyth et al., 2026); telling users what they think the user wants to hear, even when it is not factually correct (Fanous et al., 2025); or simply making claims that contradicts some knowledge, whether it is a fact learnt during training or provided in context. In this paper, we particularly focus on this latter, which Ren et al. (2025) show does not go away even when the models get larger/more capable.

Different techniques exist to control a model’s propensity to lie. Activation steering alters the model’s behaviour at inference time by intervening on its activations (Zou et al., 2025; Turner et al., 2024; Herbster et al., 2026). Nonetheless, benign steering can lead to increased vulnerability to jailbreaks (Xiong et al., 2026), decreased capability, and unintended changes in a model’s behaviour that’s not the targeted trait (Siu et al., 2026). Others consider honest prompting (Wang et al., 2025), emphasizing honesty in the system prompt or assigning models an honest persona; however, a single prompt that induces honesty across different conditions may be hard or impossible to design. Another popular approach is supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on harmful system prompts along with honest responses; yet, this requires large corpora of synthetic data (Wang et al., 2025), and may not generalize out of distribution.

An open problem in the field is to be able to find a single intervention that works across different manifestations of dishonesty. This could be seen as a robustness problem, where a method is defined as robust when it mitigates dishonesty independently of how it arises. One potential approach to address this is Continous Adversarial Training (CAT) (Xhonneux et al., 2024), initially proposed to make a model’s refusal behaviour robust against a variety of jailbreaks. Here we modified CAT to make a model’s honest behaviour robust to three different forms of dishonesty: 1) instructed dishonesty, where a system prompt contains explicit pressure to lie; 2) dishonesty that emerges from incentives in a multi-agent game, where being dishonest increases expected reward; and 3) dishonesty that results from having trained a model to conceal the truth. We name this approach Continous Adversarial Training for Consistent Honesty (CATCH) and summarize it in Figure 1.

papers.title: Chemical Demographics of Star-forming Regions
papers.abstract: Our understanding of complex organic chemistry during the formation of stars and planets is shaped by a handful of cherry-picked sources with bright molecular emission lines. This observational bias impedes our assessment of how universal chemical complexity is during star formation. The lack of systematic wideband spectral surveys for statistically significant samples of protostars and cores is a major roadblock to properly probing how COM inventories and abundances depend on the vast range of physical conditions, local cloud and global galactic environments, and evolutionary timescales of low- and high-mass star formation. In turn, this limits our ability to constrain and test physicochemical models, which depend critically on these parameters. The next-generation ALMA2040, with a 10x improvement in line sensitivity, is required to observe COMs, that we perceive as common today, in a fraction of the observing time that is needed today with ALMA. Such capabilities will propel us into the era of chemical demographics, whereby wideband (>100 GHz) spectral surveys at high sensitivity (routinely probing COM abundances down to 0.01% relative to CH3OH) will be executed towards >1000-10000 prestellar and protostellar sources. With robust chemical inventories towards large source sample sizes, we will be able to probe for dependencies of chemical complexity on mass regime, feedback processes in a cluster, Galactic position, metallicity, and time-variable accretion. Only with statistically significant samples at high sensitivity will we be able to assess the ubiquity and homogeneity of COM chemistry across the protostellar mass spectrum and natal cores. Constraining the diversity and availability of such species is critical for our understanding of the chemical reservoir available for planet formation, which eventually shapes (exo)planetary atmosphere compositions.

papers.title: Extended strange metal and superconductivity in partially filled moiré Hubbard bands
papers.abstract: Moiré semiconductors provide a physical realization of the Hubbard model. Bandwidth-tuned Mott transitions and complex phase diagrams mimicking those of high-temperature superconductors have been demonstrated near a weak Mott insulating state at half-band-filling. The platform also provides an opportunity to explore the physics of a partially filled Hubbard band at doping densities far away from the Mott insulator, a regime that has remained largely unexplored. Here we report the emergence of an extended strange metal (ESM), in both doping density and twist angle, in a partially filled Hubbard band of twisted bilayer WSe2. The ESM is in the clean limit, persists down to about 50mK, and spans over multiple symmetry-breaking ground states; it also appears only at small twist angles, where electronic correlations are strong. These observations distinguish the state from the reported strange metals associated with quantum criticality and favor the viewpoint that it is an intrinsic state of matter. We also report the observation of a new superconducting dome being developed from the ESM but far away from both the Mott insulating state and the van Hove singularity of the material. Our work opens the door to exploring the new regime of partially filled Hubbard bands in the clean limit.

papers.title: The environments forming stellar and planetary systems
papers.abstract: How does a star's birth environment set the mass, angular momentum and chemical complexity delivered to its planet-forming disk, and thereby whether it builds planets, brown dwarfs or stellar companions? This requires following material from the cloud to the sub-au to few-au scales where infalling gas, magnetized winds and the disk interact, across all star-forming environments. At frequencies where young disks are optically thin, current facilities, even ALMA after its Wideband Sensitivity Upgrade, fall short by a factor of a few in angular resolution and an order of magnitude in sensitivity. Likewise, resolving how disks around distant high-mass stars fragment into tight multiples requires a linear resolution of a few to a few tens of au, currently out of reach. Yet the disks characterized so far lie almost exclusively in nearby, isolated clouds at near-solar metallicity, although the environment (radiation field, ionization rate, gas and stellar density, pressure and metallicity) varies by orders of magnitude across the Galaxy. Most stars, probably including the Sun, form in clustered regions at kpc distances, and the widest metallicity range lies farther still, in the outer Galaxy, the Central Molecular Zone and the Magellanic Clouds. With three times finer angular resolution and ten times the sensitivity, ALMA2040 will follow the path of material from cloud to disk across the full stellar-mass spectrum and, for the first time, measure how this path changes with environment: resolving the sub-au infall-impact and wind-launching zones nearby, disk fragmentation and the onset of multiplicity in distant high-mass regions, and disk formation at a few tenths of solar metallicity. It will thereby reveal the dust-obscured, embedded origins of planetary systems that optical and infrared facilities, including the ELT, see only once they emerge, and show how the birth environment shapes them.

papers.title: SAMP: Self-Adaptive Margin Prioritization For Robust Diffusion Watermarking
papers.abstract: Diffusion models have made high-fidelity visual generation widely accessible, while also lowering the barrier to producing convincing visual forgeries and complicating content provenance. Existing watermarking methods typically use a fixed embedding strength throughout denoising or treat all watermark dimensions equally. As a result, they may introduce unnecessary distortion when some watermark dimensions are already reliable, while failing to sufficiently reinforce those that are more vulnerable to subsequent perturbations. Therefore, robust watermarking requires adapting both the embedding strength during denoising and the optimization priority across watermark dimensions. To address this problem, we present SAMP, a self-adaptive framework consisting of global margin regulation and vulnerability-sensitive allocation. Global margin regulation adjusts the embedding strength according to the separation between the target codeword and competing codewords, together with the estimated effects of common attacks. Vulnerability-sensitive allocation identifies watermark dimensions that are more easily weakened by local perturbations and gives them higher optimization priority. Experimental results demonstrate that SAMP achieves an average information recovery accuracy of 0.993. Compared with state-of-the-art methods, SAMP improves PSNR by 16.8% and reduces LPIPS by 47.1%. These results validate the effectiveness of SAMP for reliable and high-quality diffusion watermarking.
papers.intro:
Diffusion models enable high quality visual content generation from simple user inputs, while also lowering the barrier to producing convincing visual forgeries. As generated content becomes increasingly common, distinguishing its origin and verifying its authenticity become more difficult. Digital watermarking provides a direct means of associating provenance information with visual content, supporting source tracing and authenticity verification.

Early diffusion watermarking methods embed watermark information by modifying the latent state that initializes the generation process. Tree Ring [10] introduces structured Fourier patterns into the initial noise for watermark verification. Gaussian Shading [11] encodes watermark information into latent representations while preserving the original latent distribution. RingID [2] extends latent-space watermarking to multi-channel identification, while WIND [1] and PRC [3] explore latent-space embedding strategies for improving robustness and generation quality.

Recent methods further move watermark embedding into the denoising trajectory to achieve finer control over the generation process. LFLDW [5] injects watermark signals into selected latent-frequency components during intermediate denoising steps. GROW [7] extends this idea by progressively guiding the predicted clean latent across multiple denoising steps. However, existing trajectory-based methods still rely on predefined embedding strategies and cannot adapt the intervention strength to the current watermark reliability or prioritize more vulnerable watermark dimensions. Therefore, robust diffusion watermarking requires adaptive control over both embedding strength and optimization priority.

In response to these challenges, we propose SAMP, a diffusion watermarking framework that dynamically controls watermark embedding during the denoising process. Specifically, SAMP adjusts the watermark update process by controlling the modification magnitude and the optimization priority of different watermark dimensions. SAMP’s global margin regulation mechanism estimates the required latent modification by measuring the separation between the target watermark code and competing codewords. It further incorporates lightweight attack-aligned perturbations to improve the reliability of this estimation. The proposed vulnerability-sensitive allocation mechanism analyzes the sensitivity of different watermark dimensions to local perturbations and assigns higher optimization priority to vulnerable dimensions. Together, these designs reduce excessive latent perturbation while enhancing watermark robustness throughout generation.

papers.title: Boundary-induced geometrical frustration in a square Rydberg-atom lattice
papers.abstract: We study geometric defects in square-lattice Rydberg-atom arrays induced by lattice-size parity in the striated density-wave phase. While odd-sized lattices select a single striated domain, even-sized lattices seed incompatible domains at the four corners, resulting in a π/2-rotation invariant state with a geometrical defect emanating from the lattice center. At larger detunings, we instead identify a π-rotation-invariant state with two domains nucleated by opposite corners and separated by a one-dimensional diagonal defect. We probe the state-preparation protocol on the Aquila atomic quantum processor and benchmark it with equilibrium and real-time dynamics tensor-network simulations. Our results assess the role of boundaries and lattice size in determining the global ordering in programmable quantum matter.

papers.intro:
Reconfigurable Rydberg-atom arrays are among the most versatile platforms for quantum simulation [5, 18, 15, 20, 40, 24, 37, 27, 44, 4, 8]. They can realize large lattices with programmable geometries, which has led to the observation of spin-density-wave phases [41, 14, 38] and topological states [42]. Strong van der Waals interactions, together with local control, have also enabled the study of nonthermal dynamics [6, 29] and the engineering of non-native interactions through Floquet and Rydberg-dressing protocols [26, 17, 46]. In these experiments, the system size and geometry are typically chosen to be commensurate with the spatial periodicities of the phases under investigation to minimize boundary effects [14]. However, this does not always tell the whole story.

Already in one-dimensional arrays, the interplay between lattice parity and long-range Rydberg interactions may favor symmetry-broken configurations over a coherent superposition of the two ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} ordered states. In such cases, optimal control approaches are required to restore coherent macroscopic superpositions [33]. It has also recently been shown that changing the lattice parity in a one-dimensional or a ladder geometry can change the nature of phase transitions and generate multipartite entangled states [30, 10, 9, 11].

Here, we study the role of the parity of the lattice size in two dimensions. Square Rydberg-atom arrays continue to attract attention for their relevance to floating phases, lattice defects, finite-temperature effects, and distinct bulk and boundary ordering transitions [48, 45, 22, 25]. They also serve as a valuable testbed for novel numerical methods [31]. Nevertheless, the potential of boundary nucleation as a tool to control bulk ordering and engineer frustration has remained largely unexplored. In this work, using the neutral-atom quantum processor Aquila [47, 28, 19], we leverage lattice parity and boundary effects to engineer frustration and defect structures in programmable quantum matter, without modifying the local connectivity of the model. To benchmark our quantum simulation results, we use equilibrium (DMRG) and out-of-equilibrium (TDVP) simulations with Tree Tensor Networks (TTN) [43, 32, 16]. See App. A for details.

We find that the system’s behavior strongly depends on the parity of the lattice size. The contrast between odd and even lattices is immediately apparent from the distribution of the Rydberg excitation density in Fig. 1. For odd LL (Fig. 1(a)), the lattice is commensurate with the striated ordering, and the ramp produces a single striated domain extending across the whole array , with the atoms at its four corners in their Rydberg excited state. For even LL (Fig. 1(b)), instead, Rydberg excitations form at the four corners, seeding competing striated orders. This leads to domain walls extending from the boundary and throughout the bulk, and the appearance of a central geometrical defect at the four-domain junction point.

papers.title: A Misaligned Debris Disk relative to the Host Star CPD-72 2713 from JWST/NIRCam Imaging
papers.abstract: Observations of debris disks provide a valuable window to investigate the formation and evolution of planetary systems. We present high-contrast JWST/NIRCam observations of CPD-72 2713, a 24 Myr-old star that belongs to the $β$ Pic moving group. We obtained the first scattered-light images of the disk in both F210M and F444W filters, revealing a nearly face-on orientation. Forward modeling yields disk radii of $\rm 55.4^{+3.0}_{-3.2}\,AU$ (F210M) and $\rm 39.1^{+4.6}_ {-2.6}\,AU$ (F444W), both significantly smaller than the thermal emission radii measured with ALMA and Herschel/PACS. This discrepancy suggests that scattered light traces the inner region of the disk while thermal emission probes the outer regions. Combining the stellar rotation period ($4.47\pm0.67$ days) from TESS light curves and spectroscopic $v\sin i_*$, we constrained the stellar inclination to $47^{\circ}.2^{+11.1}_{-7.7}$ ($1σ$). The minimum star-disk mutual inclinations are $27^{\circ}.6 _{-8.2} ^{+11.5}\ (1σ)$ from F210M data and $27^{\circ}.3 _{-10.9}^{ +12.5}\ (1σ)$ in F444W data. We find that the minimum star--disk mutual inclination exceeds $10^\circ$ at the $95\%$ credible level in both F210M and F444W, suggesting a misalignment between the scattered-light disk and the stellar equatorial plane. We note that variation among published disk inclination measurements and potential systematic uncertainties may affect this probability. With JWST high-contrast imaging, we rule out planets down to $0.3\ \rm M_{J}$ at $0.5^{\prime\prime}$ and beyond, disfavoring a planet as the driver of the star-disk misalignment.

papers.intro:
Debris disks are circumstellar belts composed of dust, small rocky or icy bodies, and planetesimals-remnants of the planet formation process. Unlike gas-rich protoplanetary disks around very young stars (≲10\lesssim 10 Myr), debris disks are generally gas-poor and optically thin, which makes them more effective tracers of disk substructures shaped by planets [35, 70]. High-resolution imaging has revealed a variety of such features, including rings, gaps [53], warps [27], and clumps [10], many of which can be explained by secular or resonant interactions with unseen planets [37, 93, 66, 69]. A classic example is the warp in the β\beta Pictoris disk, initially predicted to be caused by a planet on an inclined orbit [29] and later confirmed with the discovery of β\beta Pictoris b [44].

Planets can also sculpt debris disks dynamically by scattering or accreting material, producing sharp edges rather than diffuse boundaries [22, 38, 70]. In our own Solar System, Neptune exerts a similar role, dominating the orbital evolution of Kuiper Belt objects and shaping both the inner and outer edges of the belt [50]. Extending this idea, [68] inferred the presence and properties of hypothetical planets in 178 debris disk systems by modeling the locations and shapes of their inner edges.

Another key property of debris disks is that their dust must be continually replenished through destructive collisions of larger planetesimals. This requires a stirring mechanism to excite planetesimal orbits. While stirring by the disc’s self gravity is possible, it can sometimes require an unphysically massive disc [42, 43, 68]. Alternatively, planet-disk interactions can also provide the necessary stirring, exciting random velocities of debris particles to trigger collisions, known as "planetary stirring" [65]. In this context, debris disks are not only relics of planet formation but also powerful signposts of hidden planets.

While they can persist throughout a star’s lifetime, debris disks are most commonly resolved around young stars, where they are brighter and easier to detect [34]. In addition many debris disks lie in the outer regions of planetary systems, at tens to hundreds of AU. These features coincide with the sensitivity range of high-contrast direct imaging, which is optimized for detecting young, wide-orbit planets. Systems where both planets and debris disks are detected offer valuable opportunities to study their formation and interactions. However, the number of systems in which both planets and debris disks have been directly imaged remains small [34], reflecting the challenges of directly imaging both planets and disks. In this paper, we present NIRCam observations of the debris disk system, CPD -72 2713, in the F210M and F444W filters. CPD -72 2713 is a young, late-type star (∼24\sim 24 Myr, K7v) in the β\beta Pic Moving Group, at a distance of 36.72 pc (see stellar parameters in Table 1). The disk has been spatially resolved using Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA, Wootten and Thompson 92) and Photodetector Array Camera and Spectrometer (PACS, Poglitsch et al. 73) on Herschel Space Observatory. These observations reveal that CPD -72 2713 has a large, wide, face-on and dust-rich disk [62, 84, 54] . In Section II, we described our NIRCam observations and data reduction methods. Section III detailed the forward modeling of the debris disks. We present the measurement of the star-disk mutual inclination in Section IV and discuss possible mechanisms responsible for the misalignment in Section VI. In Section V.1, we describe our planet-search analysis and present the upper limits derived from the JWST contrast curves. We summarize our conclusions in Section VII.

These observations reveal that CPD -72 2713 has a large, wide, face-on and dust-rich disk [62, 84, 54] . In Section II, we described our NIRCam observations and data reduction methods. Section III detailed the forward modeling of the debris disks. We present the measurement of the star-disk mutual inclination in Section IV and discuss possible mechanisms responsible for the misalignment in Section VI. In Section V.1, we describe our planet-search analysis and present the upper limits derived from the JWST contrast curves. We summarize our conclusions in Section VII.

papers.title: Tracing small-scale structure formation through cosmic time with strong gravitational lensing: A case for a next-generation sub-millimetre/millimetre interferometer
papers.abstract: The nature of dark matter and the growth of supermassive black holes (SMBHs) remain major open questions in modern astrophysics. Both leave a key signature in an overlapping, largely unexplored mass range: $<10^7$ M$_{\odot}$ dark haloes and wandering black holes. These may be undetectable directly, but detectable through gravitational perturbation of strongly lensed images, and partly or entirely distinguishable from one another through lensing data alone. We demonstrate through realistic simulations that a 255-element sub-mm/mm interferometer could probe this critical mass regime, detecting gravitational perturbations in strongly lensed dusty star-forming galaxies (DSFGs) from objects down to at least $10^5$ M$_{\odot}$. Combined with lens-galaxy characterisation from the European Extremely Large Telescope (ELT), which strengthens the physical interpretation of detected perturbers, and the unprecedented lens samples expected from Euclid and the Square Kilometre Array (SKA), this facility could deliver a census of low-mass dark matter haloes and wandering massive black holes across cosmic time.

papers.title: Probing ordered magnetic fields in galaxies across cosmic time
papers.abstract: Magnetic fields are dynamically important across many astronomical environments, yet their origin, strength, and evolution over cosmic time remain poorly understood. Ordered magnetic fields are ubiquitous in the nearby Universe, as revealed by a range of observational techniques, but evidence for their existence at cosmological distances is scarce. Recent ALMA detections of polarised dust emission indicate that galactic-scale ordered magnetic fields, spanning up to kiloparsec scales, were already present in massive star-forming galaxies at redshifts up to $z\sim5.6$. This white paper argues that the ALMA2040 concept -- with its nearly tenfold improvement in sensitivity and angular resolution, and full-polarisation capability extended to higher-frequency bands -- will open up the study of cosmic magnetism in the early Universe. We identify four science drivers: constraining the dynamos that generate galactic-scale ordered fields, measuring the strength of early magnetic fields, connecting magnetic fields to galaxy evolution across cosmic time, and constraining dust grain properties through the polarised spectral energy distribution. We summarise the corresponding requirements in angular resolution, spectral coverage, and sensitivity, and discuss synergies with next-generation telescopes.

papers.title: ALMA2040: Understanding the Early Assembly of Galaxies - The Formation of Star-Forming Clumps and their Role in Shaping Galaxy Evolution
papers.abstract: Astrophysics seeks to explain how galaxies form and evolve through the interplay of stars, gas, and dust. Giant molecular clouds (GMCs), the main reservoirs and sites of star formation, link the cold interstellar medium to the birth of stars and stellar structures. Their properties reflect galactic disk conditions, and their evolution is shaped by stellar feedback and host-galaxy dynamics. Studying GMCs across cosmic time is therefore key to understanding how gas turns into stars and drives galaxy evolution. Hubble Space Telescope and James Webb Space Telescope observations reveal compact star-forming clumps in galaxies from Cosmic Noon to the Epoch of Reionization ($z\approx6$), but their link to the molecular gas reservoir is still unclear. We do not yet know how GMC properties vary with redshift and environment, how molecular gas, dust, and young stars are arranged, or whether clumps form in unstable disks or disturbed systems. Addressing these questions requires spatially resolved observations of the cold interstellar medium at the scales probed by optical/near-infrared facilities. ALMA2040, a transformational next-generation sub-mm facility, will provide the sensitivity and angular resolution needed to detect individual GMCs in representative lensed and unlensed galaxies at $z>1$. CO and [CII], complemented by dust continuum and molecular-gas kinematics, will measure the molecular gas reservoir, its physical conditions, and its dynamical state. Together with JWST and the ELT, ALMA2040 will connect cold gas, dust, and stellar structures across cosmic time. ALMA2040 will revolutionize our understanding of (i) the properties and evolution of GMCs and their connection to star-forming clumps, (ii) the spatial interplay between molecular gas, dust, and young stars, and (iii) the dynamics, survival, and formation of GMCs and stellar clumps.

papers.title: The dawn of the first galaxies
papers.abstract: Understanding how the first galaxies assembled their stellar mass at cosmic dawn is a central frontier of modern astrophysics. JWST has now revealed an unexpected population of ultraviolet-bright galaxies at z>10, whose intense emission points towards a rapid stellar mass growth that challenges current models of early galaxy assembly. Yet, the cold gas fueling this growth remains hidden: current ALMA sensitivity restricts routine detection to only the brightest ionized-gas tracers such as [OIII] 88$μ$m, while [CII] 158$μ$m, a key coolant and gas-mass proxy of the neutral interstellar medium (ISM), is undetected beyond $z\sim8$. This leaves fundamental questions unanswered: how quickly primeval galaxies gathered cold gas and turned it into stars; what physical conditions (density, temperature, radiation field) characterized their ISM; how fast metals and dust built up; and how feedback regulated early gas assembly. Only a transformational sub-millimeter facility like ALMA2040 can address these questions, enabling systematic surveys of [CII] in the first galaxies and providing a representative census of gas fractions and depletion times. A simulated galaxy at $z=11.3$ shows that ALMA2040 not only will detect, but also spatially resolve its merging cold-gas structure in [CII] on $\sim$200 pc scales in 5 hours (below 100 pc in 10 hours). ALMA2040 will also spectrally resolve multiple lines simultaneously, akin to integral-field spectroscopy, providing the key diagnostics needed to break density-metallicity-radiation-field degeneracies and map the multi-phase ISM of z>10 galaxies. The combination of dramatically increased line sensitivity and wide instantaneous bandwidth will push the search for the first galaxies out to the earliest cosmic times, with [OIII] detectable up to $z\sim20$. ALMA2040 will thus be transformative for understanding how the first galaxies assembled at cosmic dawn.

papers.title: Understanding cosmic explosions
papers.abstract: Millimeter-wavelength observations provide a uniquely sensitive window into the physics of cosmic explosions, from supernovae (SNe) and tidal disruption events (TDEs) to nova eruptions, stellar mergers and electromagnetic counterparts to gravitational wave (GW) sources. Over the past decade, discoveries across the transient sky have revealed that many of the most informative phases of shock interaction, particle acceleration and jet formation unfold at frequencies above the traditional cm-wave domain, where synchrotron self-absorption weakens and thermal, nonthermal and dust components can be disentangled. Upcoming wide-field mm surveys will detect a new population of short-lived transients but will be limited by coarse localization and limited spectral characterization. ALMA2040, with dramatically improved sensitivity, wide instantaneous spectral coverage, rapid-response and sub-arraying modes, polarimetry and extended baselines, is essential for converting these discoveries into robust physical constraints. Here we outline the scientific context, key open questions and the ALMA2040 capabilities required to unlock the full potential of millimeter time-domain astrophysics in the 2040s.

papers.title: What fuels the growth of stars and black holes in galaxies through cosmic time? The physics and chemistry of the interstellar medium in distant galaxies
papers.abstract: The interplay between the baryonic matter in galaxies (gas, dust, stars) has a fundamental role in our understanding of galaxy formation and evolution through cosmic time. The (sub)mm regime provides a unique window to measure the physical conditions and chemistry in the cold and dusty gas reservoirs that fuel the formation of new stars and the growth of massive black holes in distant galaxies. Large sub(mm) interferometers have made a revolutionary impact mapping the cold gas and dust in galaxies beyond the local universe. However, significant progress is hampered by limited spectral-line sensitivity. After more than a decade of surveys, molecular gas (traced by 12CO) has been measured only in a few tens of typical, massive main-sequence star-forming galaxies at z>1, while access to fainter gas-tracing species has been limited to only the very brightest galaxies. Thereby it restricts access to the detailed conditions in the cold gas clouds in typical galaxies in the distant universe. A revolutionary, flagship sub-mm interferometer with a massive increase in instantaneous spectral line sensitivity and broad spectral grasp (ALMA2040) fills this gap by enabling rich, multi-transition, multi-species and multi-isotopologue studies of the atomic and molecular interstellar medium for thousands of typical galaxies across galaxy populations and redshift. This will unveil how the ISM evolves across the galaxy population for statistical samples in different redshift bins, detailed studies of the physical conditions and chemistry in the multi-phase interstellar medium of typical galaxies, and how the cold ISM regulates and responds to star- and black-hole formation, providing a tremendous leap forward in the study of galaxy assembly over cosmic time.

papers.title: Unveiling the Baryon Cycle Through Cosmic Time
papers.abstract: Galaxy evolution is governed by the baryon cycle: gas accreted from the cosmic web and circumgalactic medium condenses into molecular gas, forms stars, and is redistributed by stellar and AGN feedback. Tracing the molecular phase is therefore essential to understanding how galaxies acquire, consume, and eject their baryons. Yet current molecular-gas surveys remain limited by sensitivity, area, cosmic variance, and spectral bandwidth. ALMA2040 would combine a $\sim10\times$ sensitivity improvement with $\gtrsim512$ GHz simultaneous frequency coverage, delivering $\sim100\times$ faster mapping at fixed depth and a further $\gtrsim25\times$ gain in instantaneous bandwidth. Together, these advances would increase spectroscopic survey speed by orders of magnitude, enabling tiered ``wedding-cake'' strategies: an ultra-deep $\sim4$-5 arcmin$^2$ field probing faint and high-redshift reservoirs, a $\sim$0.25 deg$^2$ survey reaching molecular-line sensitivities comparable to current ultra-deep fields over a much larger cosmological volume, and thousands of independent pointings minimizing cosmic variance. Broad spectral coverage would simultaneously detect multiple CO transitions, [CI], H$_2$O, feedback tracers, far-IR fine-structure lines, and dust continuum, constraining molecular gas, ISM conditions, obscured star formation, and gas flows within the same observations. Every targeted observation would also become a molecular deep field, extending these measurements to serendipitous galaxies. Together with future HI, optical, and near-IR surveys, ALMA2040 would enable a population-resolved view of the baryon cycle across cosmic time and stringent tests of galaxy formation models.

papers.title: Are High-EW LAEs good analogs for the earliest galaxies? A study on the ionizing conditions and gas properties of LAEs at $2\lesssim z\lesssim7
papers.abstract: Lyman-$α$ emitters (LAEs) are frequently proposed as analogs of the low-mass, metal-poor galaxies thought to dominate cosmic reionization. In particular, galaxies with large Ly$α$ equivalent widths (EWs) are expected to have not experienced significant chemical enrichment. We test this hypothesis using a sample of 88 LAEs at $2 \lesssim z\lesssim 7$, selected from MUSE observations that are undetected in deep HST imaging and subsequently followed up with JWST/NIRSpec spectroscopy. Despite the unprecedented sensitivity of JWST, only 50 of the LAEs exhibit secure counterparts in available deep NIRCam imaging reaching typical 3$σ$ depths of $m_\text{AB}\sim30.3$ mag, highlighting the intrinsically faint nature of the population. Gas-phase metallicities are inferred by fitting optical emission lines with a grid of BPASS+cloudy photoionization models, while stellar masses are derived from NIRCam photometry through SED fitting. The final sample with secure stellar masses and gas-phase metallicities encompasses only 16 LAEs, occupying regions of standard emission-line diagnostic diagrams consistent with low-metallicity star-forming systems. Although the strong-line metallicity diagnostic R3 appears to decrease with increasing EW, we find no compelling evidence for a strong monotonic relation between EW and gas-phase metallicity when metallicities are inferred through full emission-line fitting. However, galaxies with stronger Ly$α$ emission tend to lie below the average mass-metallicity relation at fixed stellar masses, suggesting that they are preferentially less chemically evolved than typical galaxies of the same mass. We conclude that high-EW LAEs provide useful, though imperfect, analogs of the galaxies thought to drive cosmic reionization, and combining EW with stellar mass may provide a more effective route for identifying the most chemically primitive galaxies.
