papers.intro: A key prevailing question in extragalactic astronomy is understanding how the Universe underwent its last major phase transition: reionization. The onset of reionization is associated with the formation of the first stars and galaxies, and therefore fundamentally related to our understanding of galaxy formation and evolution (Dijkstra, 2014). Fully characterizing the sources responsible for reionization requires the observation of primordial galaxies. Deep imaging obtained with the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) has allowed us to study in detail the post-reionization Universe, abundant with star-forming galaxies and largely transparent to light by a redshift of z=5.5z=5.5, approximately one billion years after the Big Bang (Stark, 2016). The launch of the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has immensely facilitated the discovery of galaxies past the end of reionization, out to redshifts z≳10z\gtrsim 10 (see e.g. Finkelstein et al. (2023); Labbé et al. (2023); Mason et al. (2023); Carniani et al. (2024); Scholtz et al. (2024)). This extremely high redshift galaxy population exhibits large masses, large star-formation rates (SFRs), and is unexpectedly UV bright, with some galaxies showing high ionization emission lines, often with anomalously high equivalent widths (EWs) and/or unexpected line ratios such as GN-z11 (Bunker et al., 2023), exhibiting strong emission in NIII]λ1750\text{NIII}]\lambda 1750 and CIII]λλ1907,1909\text{CIII}]\lambda\lambda 1907,1909 as well as super-solar N/O ratios, which are seemingly at odds with the young age of the Universe at a redshift of z∼11z\sim 11, given the timescales of nitrogen enrichment (Cameron et al., 2023). Emission lines originating from HeII (54.4 eV), CIV (49.9 eV), or CIII]\text{CIII}] (22.4 eV) require a significant amount of energy to be raised into an excited state, indicating extreme conditions in the gas, such as high temperatures or highly energetic irradiation. Stellar population synthesis models tuned to low-redshift galaxies struggle to explain these extreme conditions and peculiar chemical enrichment patterns that have been progressively uncovered in the era of JWST. Despite these recent observational advances into the high-redshift Universe, low-mass galaxies, which recent works suggest may be primarily responsible for reionization (Atek et al., 2024), continue to largely evade observations. While gravitational lensing has enabled the discovery of a small number of intrinsically faint, low-mass galaxies, a statistically representative sample remains beyond current observational capabilities. Identifying sources at redshifts z>9z>9 typically requires galaxies to have already built up a significant amount of stellar mass and to be MUV\text{M}_{\text{UV}} bright, leaving the youngest and lowest-mass galaxies largely undetected. It is thus still beneficial to look to analogous low-metallicity galaxies with low mass but highly ionizing properties at intermediate redshifts (2<z<62<z<6), analyzing their stellar and gas properties to gauge the contribution of these early, extreme sources to the reionization process. The characteristics of the hot interstellar medium (ISM) in these early galaxy analogs can be pinpointed utilizing rest-frame optical emission lines (Nakajima et al., 2023). Some emission lines and line ratios depend purely on the temperature of the gas, such as the [OIII]​λ​4363/[OIII]​λ​5007[\text{OIII}]\lambda 4363/[\text{OIII}]\lambda 5007 ratio, while others probe the density of the medium, such as the [SII]​λ​6716/[SII]​λ​6731[\text{SII}]\lambda 6716/[\text{SII}]\lambda 6731 ratio (Stasińska, 2009). Combining emission lines of different species permits the constraint of further properties of the ISM; for example, the BPT diagram (for Baldwin, Phillips, and Terlevich Baldwin et al. (1981)) allows for the characterization of the hardness of the ionizing radiation. Further diagnostic diagrams, such as the [OIII]​λ​5007/H​β[\text{OIII}]\lambda 5007/\text{H}\beta vs [SII]​λ​λ​6716,6731/H​α[\text{SII}]\lambda\lambda 6716,6731/\text{H}\alpha (Veilleux and Osterbrock, 1987) diagram, help to gauge the ionization state, density, and metallicity of objects. With the launch of JWST, we now have an unprecedented view of the high-redshift universe, extending the range of redshifts at which rest-frame optical emission lines are observable beyond z≈2−3z\approx 2-3, the limit for ground-based instruments. Nevertheless, the optical emission lines in the highest redshift sources remain elusive; another reason why it remains paramount to identify and study analogous, highly ionizing galaxies at intermediate redshifts. A good candidate for intermediate redshift analogs to primordial galaxies is Lyα\alpha emitters (LAEs), as they have been determined to be highly star-forming, low-metallicity, and low-mass objects (Maseda et al., 2018; Maseda et al., 2023). A galaxy is typically considered a LAE if the rest-frame EW is EW0≳20\text{EW}_{0}\gtrsim 20 Å (Ouchi et al., 2020). Central Lyα\alpha emission occurs mainly due to ionization by young, hot, and massive stars or the presence of an AGN. As Lyα\alpha originates from a transition into the ground state, it may undergo resonant scattering. Thus, Lyα\alpha emission indirectly traces the distribution and dynamics of HI gas in galaxies, allowing us to probe the neutral hydrogen gas in and around high-redshift objects, which is generally hard to investigate otherwise (Wisotzki et al., 2018). Additionally, some recent studies have shown that strong Lyα\alpha emission traces galaxies with high ionizing photon escape fraction fescLyC\text{f}_{\text{esc}}^{\text{LyC}}, which is necessary for galaxies to ionize their surrounding IGM during the EoR (Begley et al., 2024). Theory predicts that high equivalent width LAEs (EW0, Ly​α≳200\text{EW}_{0,\text{ Ly}\alpha}\gtrsim 200 Å) are galactic systems that have yet to experience significant chemical enrichment, as Lyα\alpha emission is boosted in the surrounding gas (Raiter et al., 2010; Zackrisson et al., 2011), analogous to primordial galaxies. Recent observational studies have shown evidence that the Lyα\alpha EW of galaxies may indeed be used as a selection criterion for extremely low metallicity systems (Maseda et al., 2023). Observations of nearby star-forming regions suggest that binary and higher multiplicity stellar systems are the norm even for low-mass stars (Duchêne and Kraus, 2013), and latest findings show that the presence of massive stars in close binaries is ubiquitous even at low metallicity (Sana et al., 2025). Therefore, the effect of stellar multiplicity is important when modeling the evolution and properties of young stellar populations (Eldridge et al., 2017), and may explain the excess of highly ionizing radiation observed in many star-forming systems. The inclusion of binary evolution can lead to older stellar populations appearing more blue due to the contribution of interacting binaries (Eldridge and Stanway, 2009), indicating higher amounts of ionizing radiation at later times. While observations cannot yet be perfectly matched, including the effects of binary evolution, like the stellar population models BPASS(Eldridge et al., 2017), appears to yield models that more accurately represent reality. Combining these models with photoionization codes such as cloudy (Chatzikos et al., 2023) assuming a range of abundance patterns (such as varying C/O and N/O ratios, which have been increasingly identified at high redshift (Romano, 2022; Isobe et al., 2023)) may help to illuminate the nature of the gas properties in highly ionizing intermediate redshift galaxies and thus primordial galaxies in the EoR. In this work, we test whether high-EW LAEs satisfy the physical criteria expected of analogs to the low-mass galaxies thought to dominate reionization: exhibiting low stellar masses, low metallicities, and extreme ionization conditions. We analyze the properties of 88 galaxies that exhibit Lyα\alpha emission in the MUSE HUDF (Bacon et al., 2023) or MUSE Wide survey (Herenz et al., 2017; Urrutia et al., 2019), and determine their Lyα\alpha EW0\text{EW}_{0} utilizing NIRCam F090W observations to estimate the continuum emission as described in section 2. Using NIRSpec MSA observations, optical emission line fluxes were measured to constrain ISM properties such as the metallicity, density, and ionization parameter (section 4) by fitting to an emission line diagnostic grid produced using BPASS v2.2.1 and cloudy v23.01 as described in section 3. The results and discussion are presented in section 4 and 5, followed by a summary and main conclusions in section 6. Throughout this article, we adopt a solar abundance of Z⊙=0.01524\text{Z}_{\odot}=0.01524 corresponding to 12+log⁡(O/H)=8.6912+\log(\text{O/H})=8.69 and a solar C/O ratio of (C/O)⊙=0.44(\text{C/O})_{\odot}=0.44 (Gutkin et al., 2016). Where needed, we adopt the Planck 2018 flat Λ\LambdaCDM cosmology (Planck Collaboration et al., 2020) with H0=67.7​ km s−1​ Mpc−1H_{0}=67.7\text{ km s}^{-1}\text{ Mpc}^{-1}, ΩM=0.31\Omega_{\text{M}}=0.31, and ΩΛ=0.69\Omega_{\Lambda}=0.69.

papers.title: Resolving the Assembly of Disk Galaxies from the Epoch of Reionisation to Cosmic Noon
papers.abstract: Most of the mass and angular momentum of today's disk galaxies assembled at $z>1$. Yet, it remains unclear how these galaxies acquired their gas, how their baryons and dark matter coevolved, and how feedback and radial gas transport shaped their disks. Addressing these gaps requires resolved observations of cold gas, which carries most of the mass and angular momentum involved in galaxy assembly. By resolving CO and [C II] at kpc scales, ALMA revealed a surprising population of rotation-dominated disks, even at $z>2$, exhibiting kinematic signatures consistent with spiral arms, bars, and tidal tails. Yet, these studies are limited to massive ($M_\star>10^{10.5}$ M$_\odot$) and highly star-forming (SFRs$\gtrsim 100$ M$_\odot$yr$^{-1}$) galaxies, the progenitors of today's most massive elliptical and disk galaxies. To understand how most present-day spirals (like the Milky Way) assembled, it is crucial to resolve their low-mass progenitors, which dominate the star-forming galaxy population by number at $z>1$. Achieving this goal demands a tenfold increase in line sensitivity and hence a next-generation sub-/millimetre facility: ALMA2040. This leap in sensitivity will enable routine resolved studies of hundreds of $M_\star>10^9$ M$_\odot$ galaxies, including those on and below the main sequence of star-forming galaxies, providing representative, statistical galaxy samples with sub-kpc constraints on the cold gas kinematics and morphology. By uniquely providing resolved CO, [C I], and [C II] observations across $z=1-6$, ALMA2040 will trace a much larger fraction of the cold-gas reservoir than is accessible today, extending resolved studies from rare massive and/or lensed systems to representative galaxy populations. In this way, ALMA2040 will transform our understanding of how galaxy disks formed and evolved.

papers.intro:
Galaxy assembly is governed by the flow of baryons through dark matter (DM) halos. Gas accreted from the cosmic web acquires angular momentum, settles into rotationally supported disks, and promotes star formation. Throughout their assembly, DM halos shape the gravitational potential in which galaxies evolve, whereas baryonic processes such as accretion, feedback, and radial gas transport alter the distribution of mass and angular momentum (Somerville and Davé 2015; Naab and Ostriker 2017). Together, these processes regulate key galaxy properties, including size, stellar mass, and star formation rate (SFR). Yet understanding how these processes interact and collectively govern galaxy evolution remains a major challenge in modern astrophysics.

The epoch at z>1z>1 spans two key phases of galaxy evolution: the initial assembly of galaxies at z>3z>3 and their subsequent growth and dynamical transformation at Cosmic Noon (z∼1−3z\sim 1-3). Yet despite major observational progress at z>1z>1, several fundamental questions remain unanswered. • How do galaxies acquire gas and angular momentum? • When do dynamically cold disks become a common and stable outcome of galaxy assembly? • How do baryons and DM halos coevolve, establishing the dynamical scaling relations, dark matter fractions, and DM halo structures observed in galaxies today? • Once disks are in place, how do gravitational instabilities, feedback, and non-axisymmetric structures redistribute mass and angular momentum within galaxies? Answering these questions requires resolved (sub-kpc scale) observations of cold (molecular and atomic) gas, which carries most of the mass and angular momentum involved in disk assembly. Crucially, such observations must extend to the low-mass galaxies that dominate the population by number and represent the progenitors of today’s L⋆L_{\star} spiral galaxies, including the Milky Way.

Sub-/millimetre observations of cold-gas tracers such as CO, [C i], [C ii], and [O i] provide a powerful means of probing gas accretion, disk dynamics, and angular-momentum transport at z>1z>1. These cold gas tracers directly probe the turbulence and radial flows that regulate star formation in disks, complementary to ionised-gas tracers, which more sensitively probe energetic processes like outflows (Ejdetjärn et al. 2022; Kohandel et al. 2024). For dusty, gas-rich systems, cold-gas tracers provide a unique window into heavily obscured regions where ionised-gas tracers like Hα\alpha are strongly attenuated, enabling kinematic studies across the full extent of the gas disk. Resolved observations of the main atomic gas tracer, H i, remain inaccessible beyond the local Universe; even with the increased sensitivity of the Square Kilometre Array (SKA), such studies will be limited to massive galaxies at z∼<1z\lower 2.0pt\hbox{$\,\mathrel{\mathop{\kern 0.0pt\scriptstyle\sim}\limits^{\scriptstyle<}}\,$}1 (Lelli et al. 2026). Thus, sub-/millimetre observations provide a critical window on the gas reservoirs and kinematics that govern disk assembly at z>1z>1.

Over the last 15 years, ALMA has revolutionised studies of disk assembly at z>1z>1. By resolving cold gas at kpc scales, it has revealed a population of massive, highly star-forming galaxies that are more rotation-dominated than expected from ionised gas observations or simulations (Neeleman et al. 2020; Lelli et al. 2021; Roman-Oliveira et al. 2023; Lelli et al. 2023; Rizzo et al. 2024). Several of these systems also exhibit evidence of spiral arms, bars, and tidal interactions (Hodge et al. 2019; Tsukui and Iguchi 2021; Amvrosiadis et al. 2025; Kaasinen et al. 2026). Extending these studies beyond rare starbursts to representative samples of massive main-sequence galaxies has required several large program-scale investments. For example, the large program “CONDOR” has dedicated 230 hours of ALMA time to resolve the gas kinematics and surface-density distributions of just ∼10\sim 10 massive (M⋆>1010.5{}_{\star}>10^{10.5} M⊙) main-sequence galaxies at z=1−3z=1-3. Together with the high-mass parameter space covered at z>3z>3 (Fig. 1), this highlights that ALMA lacks the sensitivity required to resolve the dominant population of lower-mass galaxies.

A complete view of disk assembly requires CO, [C i], and [C ii] to be mapped jointly, as their relative distributions and kinematics reveal how mass and angular momentum are partitioned between different phases of the cold interstellar medium (ISM) (Sec. 3). Mapping [C i] and [C ii] becomes increasingly critical at low masses, as they are expected to remain detectable over a larger fraction of the disk than CO. However, with its current sensitivity, ALMA takes several tens of hours to resolve [C i] or [C ii] at z∼<3z\lower 2.0pt\hbox{$\,\mathrel{\mathop{\kern 0.0pt\scriptstyle\sim}\limits^{\scriptstyle<}}\,$}3, even for the most massive galaxies, limiting such studies to a handful of extreme and/or lensed galaxies (Lamarche et al. 2018; Rooney et al. 2025). Although ALMA’s unique site and frequency coverage make it the only facility capable of covering CO, [C i], and [C ii] across z=1−6z=1-6, jointly observing all three still requires separate time-intensive observing programs. Hence, most multi-line studies are limited to fortuitous line combinations covered by the same receiver (Tadaki et al. 2019; Gómez et al. 2025; Kaasinen et al. 2026). A next-generation sub-/millimetre interferometer with 10×10\times the line sensitivity of ALMA and instantaneous coverage of all receiver bands (Fig. 2) is therefore essential to resolve the key processes that fuel and shape the dominant population of galaxies, from z∼6→1z\sim 6\to 1. This facility is ALMA2040.

papers.title: Dust at cosmic dawn: unveiling the onset of dust and obscured star formation at $z\gtrsim8$
papers.abstract: Although less than 1 percent of the baryonic mass budget of a galaxy, cosmic dust profoundly alters the multi-wavelength appearance of galaxies across cosmic time. The (sub)millimeter wavelength regime is uniquely capable of weighing these dust reservoirs, and revealing the total extent of galaxy evolution that remains hidden behind them. With current facilities, however, doing so at $z > 8$ is largely out of reach. ALMA2040, a next-generation (sub)millimeter interferometer, is set to change this. Through an order-of-magnitude increase in sensitivity compared to ALMA, ALMA2040 is a transformational facility that will be able to routinely detect dust emission from galaxies at $z > 8$ and, through simultaneous multi-band characterization, accurately measure their dust masses, temperatures, and infrared luminosities. Combined with ancillary metallicity measurements -- including from the far-infrared lines detected by ALMA2040 itself -- this will establish the relative roles of supernovae and grain growth in building up dust in the earliest galaxies. Simultaneously, ALMA2040 will measure the fraction of star formation that is obscured by dust at cosmic dawn, and thereby the extent to which rest-UV and optical surveys miss early galaxy build-up. Without a 10$\times$ upgrade to ALMA -- comparable to the leap from the VLT to the ELT -- we will not be able to capitalize on the momentous advances enabled by JWST, and will remain blind to the cold and obscured component of galaxy formation in the $z > 8$ Universe.

papers.title: Probing cold gas and dust in quiescent galaxies across cosmic time
papers.abstract: The discovery of massive quiescent galaxies at high redshift by JWST has revealed that star formation can cease rapidly in the early Universe, yet the physical mechanisms responsible for quenching remain unknown. A key missing element is the systematic measurement in statistically representative quiescent samples of the cold gas and dust content, which are crucial for distinguishing quenching mechanisms and evolutionary pathways. Such observations are currently not feasible because state-of-the-art sub-millimeter facilities (e.g., ALMA) cannot routinely detect the faint molecular gas and dust reservoirs of quiescent galaxies, nor pinpoint outflowing molecular gas. A next-generation facility (ALMA2040) capable of providing transformative access to the cold interstellar medium of quiescent galaxies across redshift is therefore essential. In particular, it will allow the community to probe the molecular gas content of quiescent galaxies at cosmic noon and beyond by targeting the CO, [CI], and [CII] emission lines, as well as unveiling the physical conditions of the cold interstellar medium by constraining the CO spectral line energy distribution. It will also reveal the dust content of the passive population, a crucial ingredient to constrain the different quenching mechanisms. Finally, it will enable probing the molecular gas kinematics and identify molecular outflows driven by supermassive black holes. When combined with the rich legacy of JWST, ELT, and SKAO surveys, ALMA2040 will deliver a comprehensive, multi-phase view of feedback and quenching, allowing us to establish when, how, and why galaxies shut down their star formation across cosmic time.

papers.title: Direct measures of black hole masses through cosmic time
papers.abstract: Supermassive black holes (BHs) are thought to reside in all massive galaxies. They play a fundamental role in shaping galaxy evolution by suppressing star formation and halting the stellar growth of the most massive galaxies via feedback mechanisms. However, to date, measuring even their most basic property, their mass, is still challenging. The mass of BHs carries information on the growth history and the mutual interplay with the host galaxy. Uncertain BH masses leave many key questions on galaxy evolution wide open. Here we show that a transformational facility such as ALMA2040 would open a new window to measure BH mass by directly observing the kinematics of cold gas in galaxy cores from the local Universe up to very high redshift, irrespective of BH activity. This would revolutionise our understanding of BH formation, growth, and their role within galaxy evolution.

papers.title: AGN Feeding and Feedback: Resolving the Torus
papers.abstract: Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) play a key role in galaxy evolution by regulating star formation within their host galaxies. It is therefore crucial to understand how the central supermassive black holes (SMBH) are fueled by material from the galactic disk, and how AGN feedback impacts the surrounding gas. Most information so far comes from very nearby active galaxies (z < 0.008; D < 35 Mpc), providing the best spatial resolution and revealing randomly oriented dusty molecular tori that fuel SMBHs. A facility such as ALMA2040, offering significantly higher sensitivity and better angular resolution than current ALMA, would enable progress in two fundamental areas that remain beyond the capabilities of all existing and planned observatories: (i) probing the dynamics of the material feeding the AGN down to the accretion disk in nearby galaxies; and (ii) spatially resolving the tori and circum-nuclear regions of more energetic and cosmologically significant AGN, such as local quasars (z ~ 0.1 and Lbol > 10^45 erg/s).

papers.title: Molecular atlas of nearby galaxies through sensitive high-resolution multi-band molecular line surveys
papers.abstract: Star formation and associated feedback processes play a key role in galaxy evolution. Astrochemistry is a powerful tool for characterising the physical conditions of dense star-forming gas and understanding the reciprocal relation between stellar feedback and the interstellar medium (ISM): from the way feedback influences the ISM to how the ISM conditions regulate the formation of new stars. The advent of large spectral surveys of a few individual galaxy centres have demonstrated the potential of molecular gas inventories to reveal the physical conditions of star-forming gas in great detail. A next-generation (sub)mm facility in the 2040s would extend this science to the local star-forming galaxy population, providing for the first time a comprehensive view of the physical and chemical conditions of the molecular ISM in the local universe.

papers.title: WALTzER: Wide-band Atmospheric Laboratory for Transiting Exoplanet Research
papers.abstract: Understanding the origin and evolution of planetary atmospheres, and the connection between their lower and upper atmospheric layers, remains a fundamental challenge in exoplanet science. Addressing these questions requires observations spanning a broad wavelength range, from the ultraviolet to the near-infrared, together with the ability to simultaneously characterise planetary and stellar variability. The Wide-band Atmospheric Laboratory for Transiting Exoplanet Research (WALTzER) is an ESA F3 mission candidate designed to address this need through simultaneous low-resolution spectroscopy and high-precision photometry of transiting exoplanets. WALTzER covers simultaneously the near-ultraviolet (NUV: 240--325 nm) and visible (VIS: 450--820 nm) bands with two medium resolution spectrographs and the near-infrared (NIR: 900--1700 nm) range with a broadband photometer. We outline the main science drivers and present the mission concept and instrument design. WALTzER's broad, simultaneous wavelength coverage enables the detection and characterisation of the atmospheres of more than 30 gas-rich exoplanets and provides data relevant for a broad range of Solar System and Galactic astrophysics science cases. The payload consists of a 35 cm Cassegrain telescope feeding three co-aligned channels (i.e. NUV, VIS, NIR), sharing a common optical train to minimise instrumental systematics, while maximising observational efficiency.

papers.intro:
The discovery of exoplanets has opened an exciting new field in astrophysics and has completely transformed our understanding of planets. Transiting exoplanets, that is planets passing in front of their host star as seen from Earth, enable comprehensive studies of the atmosphere of these foreign worlds through transmission spectroscopy. More than 6000 exoplanets are currently known and thousands more are expected to be soon found by space-based surveys (Ricker et al., 2015; Rauer et al., 2025, e.g. TESS, PLATO;) explicitly dedicated to the search for transiting planets orbiting bright stars, and thus providing opportunities for detailed atmospheric characterisation.

The discovery of exoplanets has opened an exciting new field in astrophysics and has completely transformed our understanding of planets. Transiting exoplanets, that is planets passing in front of their host star as seen from Earth, enable comprehensive studies of the atmosphere of these foreign worlds through transmission spectroscopy. More than 6000 exoplanets are currently known and thousands more are expected to be soon found by space-based surveys (Ricker et al., 2015; Rauer et al., 2025, e.g. TESS, PLATO;) explicitly dedicated to the search for transiting planets orbiting bright stars, and thus providing opportunities for detailed atmospheric characterisation.

Gas-rich transiting exoplanets are key laboratories for investigating planet formation and evolution. Owing to their close proximity to their host stars, they also provide extreme environments in which to study atmospheric composition and fundamental atmospheric processes such as cloud formation and atmospheric escape. Infrared (IR) and visible observations probe the lower atmosphere (∼\sim1–10-6 bar), enabling the reconstruction of its chemical inventory (Kempton and Knutson, 2024, e.g.) and the characterisation of ubiquitous aerosols (Pont et al., 2013; Kreidberg et al., 2014; Sing et al., 2016, e.g.). Transmission spectra of some planets show clear atmospheres with prominent Na (∼\sim580 nm), K (∼\sim770 nm), and H2O (∼\sim1.4 μ\mum) absorption features, while others surprisingly lack one or both of the Na and K signatures (Sing et al., 2016, e.g.). The hottest planets can additionally exhibit strong TiO features, which are thought to contribute to the formation of atmospheric temperature inversions (Sedaghati et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2021a, e.g.). Ultraviolet (UV) observations, in contrast, probe the extended upper atmosphere (<<10-6 bar), where atoms and ions are continuously lost to space (Vidal-Madjar et al., 2003; Fossati et al., 2010; Haswell et al., 2012; Ehrenreich et al., 2015; Sing et al., 2019, e.g.). Atmospheric escape is expected to play a key role in the long-term evolution of planetary atmospheres and may therefore be an important driver of the observed diversity of exoplanetary systems (Owen and Wu, 2016; Kubyshkina and Fossati, 2022; Guillot et al., 2023; Snellen, 2025, e.g.).

Despite the complementary information provided by observations at different wavelengths, a coherent characterisation of exoplanet atmospheres remains challenging because existing observations are inevitably incomplete in wavelength coverage and/or disjointed in time. Even in the few cases where both the lower and upper atmospheres have been observed, the measurements have generally been obtained at different epochs and with different facilities, and are therefore subject to different instrumental systematics and potentially different stellar activity states. Combining such heterogeneous observations can complicate the construction of a consistent picture of the atmospheric structure and evolution, and can introduce additional uncertainties into their interpretation (Giacobbe et al., 2021; Xue et al., 2024; Blain et al., 2024; Bachmann et al., 2025; Verma et al., 2025; Finnerty et al., 2025, e.g.). For example, the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) is enabling studies of atmospheric composition, thermal structure, and molecular signatures in the near- and mid-IR, while ESA’s Ariel mission (Tinetti et al., 2018) will provide a large statistical survey of transiting exoplanet atmospheres. In parallel, the Pandora SmallSat (Hoffman et al., 2022) aims at disentangling stellar variability from planetary atmospheric signals through simultaneous visible (imaging) and near-IR (spectroscopy) observations. However, their capabilities are somewhat limited. The general observatory nature of JWST limits the number of targets that can be observed and its instruments do not cover the blue-optical and UV bands, while Ariel and Pandora lack optical and UV spectroscopic coverage. This calls for a stable and efficient facility simultaneously covering the UV to the near-IR, further enabling connecting its data with those of other facilities covering longer wavelengths. WALTzER is designed to probe the lower (near-IR and visible) and upper (near-UV) atmospheres of transiting exoplanets with a single instrument, providing a temporally and instrumentally coherent view of their atmospheric properties.

WALTzER will simultaneously obtain near-UV (NUV; 240–325 nm) and visible (450–820 nm) transmission spectra at a resolving power of R∼\sim3000, plus near-IR (NIR; 900–1700 nm) high-precision photometry of more than thirty transiting gas-rich exoplanets. The space-based platform and mission architecture dedicated to the characterisation of exoplanetary atmospheres ensures that WALTzER will survey a significant number of transits (≈\approx20) of each system, thus uniquely enabling the investigation of variability and its origin. WALTzER will increase the number of systems with UV-to-IR observations by a least a factor of ten, while uniquely providing simultaneous UV-to-IR wavelength coverage. Its broad wavelength coverage and spectral resolution will give simultaneous access to tracers probing lower and upper atmospheric structure and composition (e.g. Fei, Feii, Mgi, and Mgii in the NUV; Nai, Ki, and TiO in the optical) and enables constraining the altitude and inferring the composition of aerosols, while the near-IR (NIR) imager will cover a number of water bands. As part of its core survey, WALTzER will provide the observational material needed to answer the mission’s core science questions: 1. What is the origin of planetary atmospheres and how do they evolve? 2. How do lower and upper atmospheric layers interact?

papers.title: ALMA2040: The High-Redshift Circumgalactic Medium. Imaging the fueling and feedback of galaxies in the early universe
papers.abstract: Galaxies do not form in isolation, but rather as part of a wider interconnected web mediated at their interface by an extended gaseous atmosphere - the Circum-Galactic Medium (CGM). This dynamic and multiphase region is fed and shaped by gas inflows and mergers from the intergalactic medium and by feedback-driven outflows and radiation from the central galaxy. The CGM is imprinted by the past, present and future evolution of its central galaxy and environment. The cool atomic and molecular phases are of particular interest as they dominate the mass budget of outflows and provide a reservoir of direct star forming fuel for the galaxy to accrete. In the early universe where accretion rates, mergers, and feedback processes peak, the cycle of gas through the CGM is most vigorous. Sub-mm observations have detected cold gas in extended halos and gas flows around high redshift galaxies but are thus far limited to the most massive, extreme or gravitationally lensed sources, using just a handful of the strongest emission and absorption lines. A significant increase ($5-10\times$) in spectral line sensitivity compared with the current ALMA is needed to push physical scales, densities and properties to a new regime. We present three key scientific cases for an ALMA2040 telescope: (i) direct imaging of extended [CII]-traced CGM halos around Milky-Way-progenitor galaxies at $z=4$-8; (ii) resolved detection of cold, clumpy outflows on $\sim$100 pc scales tied to individual star-forming clumps; and (iii) multi-species/-transition emission and absorption diagnostics that jointly constrain the density, chemistry, and radiation fields permeating the cool CGM and its multiphase gas flows.

papers.title: Planetary system architectures in the final stages of planet formation
papers.abstract: The processes in the last stages of planet formation determine the final assembly and composition of planets. After the protoplanetary discs dissipate, a system of planets and planetesimals -- analogues of the Asteroid and Kuiper Belts -- remains. Ongoing collisions between these bodies produce second-generation dust and gas that form a debris disc. Resolved images of such belts allow us to trace the dynamical history of these systems, including giant impacts and planet-belt interactions, during the crucial era from 10 to a few 100 Myr of terrestrial planet formation. High-resolution mm and optical/near-IR imagers have revolutionised our view of the brightest planetesimal belts, providing first glimpses of diverse structures, many of which show plausible planet imprints, while ALMA has revealed gas in a growing number of systems. Yet these results are strongly biased toward the brightest, mostly young belts around early-type stars, and even for these, crucial details remain undetectable at the required resolution due to their typically low surface brightness. A future (sub-)mm facility with an order of magnitude leap in continuum sensitivity and 10x higher line sensitivity would transform our understanding of late-stage planet formation by enabling the first statistically meaningful surveys of faint outer planetesimal belts across all spectral types, imaging planetary collisions in the inner regions of planetary systems, and gas measurements that trace volatile delivery to terrestrial planets. For the first time, this would reach the faint majority of belts, rather than only the rare bright discs accessible today.

papers.title: Multi-wavelength Polarization as a Probe of Planet Formation
papers.abstract: Polarization reveals details of circumstellar disks that are not readily available from total intensity observations. Via multi-wavelength polarimetric observations of disks, we can trace how planets form, how dust grains evolve at the onset of planet formation, and how magnetic fields (B-fields) influence accretion. Since polarized emission from these disks is typically at levels from 0.5% to a few percent of the total emission, very high sensitivities are needed. Current ALMA capabilities make these key measurements of protoplanetary disks challenging due to (1) long integrations with separate observations to measure multi-wavelength polarization of substructures, (2) prohibitive time requests to observe large samples of disks, (3) limited sensitivity and frequency coverage for polarization in spectral lines; and (4) insufficient calibration of polarization in all the Stokes parameters. An ALMA2040 with large collecting area, increased bandwidth with multi-band capabilities, and accurate polarization calibration will provide a great leap in our understanding of the formation of protoplanets through polarization. Specifically, such an ALMA2040 can use polarized emission from the continuum and spectral lines to: (A) provide stringent tests of streaming instabilities; (B) accurately constrain grain shape, size, porosity, and alignment; (C) resolve polarization of substructures for a large sample of disks with resolutions less than 5 au; (D) quickly survey 100s of disks; and (E) measure the B-field strength and morphology of disks.

papers.title: Stellar Mass Census of $S^4G$ Local Bars
papers.abstract: Bars are stellar structures commonly found in disk galaxies and important agents of secular evolution. Quantifying the stellar mass content of bars provides a physically motivated approach to assess how bar growth depends on galaxy mass and internal structure. We perform a GALFITM multi-band mid-infrared two-dimensional decomposition of 344 barred galaxies from the Spitzer Survey of Stellar Structure in Galaxies ($S^4G$) in the 3.6 and 4.5 $μ$m bands. We estimate the stellar mass associated with each structural component (i.e., disk, bulge, bar, and nuclear point source) and investigate how bar properties correlate with global galaxy characteristics. Our final models consist of 2-4 components per galaxy, with the simplest configuration (disk + bar) typically associated with low-mass systems. We find that more massive galaxies with prominent bulges host more massive bars and higher median bar-to-total stellar mass ratios. These bulges generally present Sérsic indices below 2, consistent with a photometric signature of nuclear stellar disks. Additionally, when we consider the relative bar lengths at a fixed galaxy mass, we find a bimodal distribution where galaxies with bulges host relatively longer bars compared to their bulgeless counterparts. These findings could be the result of different evolutionary paths, possibly linked to different disk formation epochs, allowing bars more time to grow in size and mass. Our study indicates that bar evolution may follow distinct pathways across different galaxy mass regimes, and is likely influenced by secular processes and environmental effects.

papers.intro:
Decades of numerical studies have shown that bars can form naturally in dynamically cold stellar disks [36, 58, 2, 3, e.g.,]. Observationally, dynamically cold disks appear to be a necessary, although not a sufficient, condition for bar formation, since some cold disks remain unbarred [74]. This intrinsic susceptibility of cold stellar disks to bar formation is reflected observationally in the high fraction of barred systems among disk galaxies, reaching approximately two-thirds in the local Universe [15, 55, 9, e.g.,]. However, which physical processes regulate the growth of bars are still not fully understood. Observational studies suggest that formation of bars follows the standard downsizing scenario, in which more massive galaxies formed their bars earlier [73, 47]. In this scenario, the bar has sufficient time to slow down and grow in length. This interpretation is consistent with observational studies showing that longer and stronger bars are preferentially found in quiescent galaxies [30], that bars are longer in more massive systems [19, 42], and that older bars are generally longer [43, 44, 13].

Studies point out that bars play a role in the secular evolution of their host galaxies. The formation and evolution of bars involve the exchange of angular momentum between the inner disk, the outer disk and dark matter halo [3, 4]. Once formed, bars can drive gas toward the central regions through shocks along their leading edges [65, 64, 76], leading to central gas concentrations and enhanced nuclear star formation [71, 33, 35, 76]. This process can build up a central gas reservoir [67, 76] and contribute to the formation and growth of central stellar structures, such as nuclear disks [7, 23, 69]. Observational studies have pointed to nuclear disks increasing in size and mass together with bar length [24] and age [14], suggesting that these structures grow synchronously. However, these evolutionary processes may operate differently in lower-mass galaxies. In Verwilghen et al. [78], using hydrodynamical simulations, they find that in low-mass systems the supernova-driven feedback can disrupt gas inflows, leading to clumpier bar morphologies and preventing the formation of stable central gas reservoirs. Differences in bar properties linked to galaxy mass are observed across cosmic time. Observations at low redshift (z<1<1) find that absolute bar length increases with galaxy stellar mass, especially for massive systems [19, 42, i.e., log⁡(CLOSE\log(M⋆/{}_{\star}/M)⊙∼10.1{}_{\odot})\sim 10.1,], while JWST findings show constant values along galaxy stellar masses to high redshifts [50]. This epoch-dependent shift may suggest that bars formed with significant lengths regardless of their host galaxies’ stellar masses in the early Universe, in agreement with simulations showing that bars forming at high redshift tend to be born longer than those forming at later epochs [22, 83]. However, these findings could also be driven by larger and more massive disks acquiring the conditions for bar formation earlier, resulting in an observed bar population biased toward larger structures. Together, these results may point to bar growth pathways are not universal, but instead depend on galaxy mass, environment, and cosmic epoch.

Quantifying the stellar mass contained in bars therefore provides a physically motivated avenue to investigate how bar growth varies with galaxy mass and internal structure.

In this work we investigate how much stellar mass is contained within bars in the local Universe, how the bar stellar mass varies with galaxy stellar mass and the presence of a central stellar component, and how these relations depend on other global galaxy properties. We aim to explore what these trends can reveal about the different pathways of bar growth. We organize this paper in the following manner. In Section II we present our sample selection. In Section III we explain our methodology for decomposing the light of each component and then convert the light to stellar mass. In Section IV we show our analysis and our main results. Section V is our discussion. Section VI is the summary of our study.

papers.title: ALMA2040: Mapping the Spatially Resolved Dust and Star Formation Physics Driving High-z Galaxy Assembly
papers.abstract: Interstellar dust reprocesses approximately half of the starlight emitted across cosmic history. However, dust temperature, which is essential to convert continuum flux into dust mass, molecular gas mass, and obscured star-formation rates, remains largely unconstrained on sub-galactic scales at high redshift. While single-band ALMA imaging has characterized continuum sizes for hundreds of z>1 galaxies, single-frequency measurements cannot separate the dust mass column from the local dust heating. To date, spatially resolved (<0.5-arcsec) multi-band dust temperatures exist in the literature for only ~10 extreme systems (quasars, hyperluminous starbursts, or strongly lensed galaxies) at z>1, with ongoing programs within a few years adding at most a few dozen submillimeter or UV-bright galaxies. This still leaves typical main-sequence disks largely unexplored across cosmic history. With an anticipated ~30 times improvement in continuum sensitivity (compared to the current ALMA), simultaneous multi-band receivers, and (sub-)kpc angular resolution, ALMA2040 will transform resolved dust thermometry into a systematic survey science. Here, we present the scientific rationale and technical requirements, highlighting a future statistically meaningful survey with > 100 representative main-sequence galaxies across cosmic epochs. Realistic visibility simulations demonstrate that ALMA2040 measures radial temperature gradients with ~0.5-4 K precision (L_IR~10^{12} L_sun in 2 h on-source at z~2). These measurements will break the degeneracy between intrinsic compactness and temperature gradients, deliver the first extinction-free, temperature-calibrated resolved star-formation relations, and uniquely trace radiative feedback and disk maturation from cosmic noon to cosmic dawn.

papers.title: A counterexample to the generalized Viterbo conjecture on the spectral distance in a disc cotangent bundle
papers.abstract: We prove the unboundedness of the spectral distance on the space of Lagrangians Hamiltonian isotopic to the zero section within the disc cotangent bundle of a closed manifold satisfying some topological assumptions. This disproves the generalization of a conjecture due to Claude Viterbo. The proof relies on a direct computation of the spectral distance between the zero section and its image by a magnetic Hamiltonian diffeomorphism via generating functions. We also classify all surfaces for which the conjecture holds over $\mathbb{Z}_2$ via a Floer-theoretic argument for covering spaces.

papers.title: Fundamental Groups and Coregularity: Klt Pairs with Trivial and Nef Log-Anticanonical Class
papers.abstract: In this article, we study how the absolute coregularity of a projective log pair reflects on its fundamental group. More precisely, we show that for a projective klt log pair $(X,D)$ of absolute coregularity $c$ and arbitrary dimension the fundamental group $π_1^{\rm reg}(X,D)$ admits a normal abelian subgroup of finite index and rank at most $2c$. We reduce this statement to klt Calabi-Yau pairs with standard coefficients of dimension $c$. In the cases $0\le c\le2$ and fixed dimension, we can furthermore bound the index of a solvable normal subgroup. Combining the reduction with the recent regular-locus theorem of Fu-Guo-Song-Wang, we prove the coregularity bound in every dimension. In particular, for a projective klt pair $(X,D)$ with $-(K_X+D)$ nef, the orbifold fundamental group of the smooth locus is virtually abelian of rank at most $2\, {\rm dim}X$.

The fundamental group as a topological invariant gains its importance from viewing smooth projective varieties as Kähler manifolds. As such, it is long known that Fano manifolds are simply connected and projective manifolds with trivial or antinef canonical divisor have almost abelian fundamental group; see [Pau97] for the latter case. During the last few years, many of these statements have been generalized to orbifolds and to varieties with Kawamata log terminal (klt) singularities, with respect to the orbifold fundamental group and/or the fundamental group of the smooth locus. While proofs in the orbifold case mostly mimic the differential-geometric proofs from the smooth case using orbifold charts, in the klt case, often new techniques and insights are needed. In particular, the transfer from the fundamental group of the whole space to the one of the smooth locus often requires the local finiteness result from [Bra21], which simultaneously proved the finiteness of the orbifold fundamental group of the smooth locus of klt log Fano pairs.

papers.title: Effect of deuteration on methane cluster stability
papers.abstract: The evaporation from clusters of mixed deuterated and protonated methane molecules has been studied experimentally and theoretically. Only loss of the two components CH$_4$ and CD$_4$ is observed, showing the absence of hydrogen scrambling. The branching ratio of the two channels scales with the mole fractions of the isotopologues, corresponding to a fixed ratio of 1.5 for the CH$_4$ and CD$_4$ rates. The number is explained by the combined effect of the zero-point energies found in quantum chemical calculations and the use of detailed balance to describe the evaporation process, the latter by incorporating the moment of inertia of the two isotopologue molecules and their rotational degrees of freedom. The difference in evaporative activation energies is determined to be 6.1~\% and 6.8~\% from two experimental determinations and 8.7~\% theoretically with B3LYP+GD3BJ, corresponding to 5--7~meV. The same theory finds the CH$_4$ activation energy to be 83.8 meV, close to the experimental bulk value of 84.7 meV. Differences in Helmholtz free energies of decay products are extracted from the experimental data, yielding the molecular mixing as the only contribution to the entropy term.

papers.intro:
Deuterium substitution is a widely used technique for probing reactions of biological molecules and of other hydrogen-containing molecules that exhibit hydrogen bonding, because hydrogen scrambling is easily monitored with mass spectrometry. The clearest form of hydrogen bonds is arguably found in water. Collisional experiments on water clusters with heavy water molecules have shown a strong degree of hydrogen scrambling on time scales as short as tens of microseconds, at least for sufficiently large clusters [1, 2]. More recently, it was shown that water reaches bulk thermal properties already at cluster size N=9N=9 [3], demonstrated by scaling of evaporation branching ratios of water molecules. This result was observed concurrently with the observation of complete hydrogen scrambling. The water study has recently been extended to ammonia clusters [4], which showed a similar scaling behavior.

papers.title: Learning to Think and Explore in 3D World
papers.abstract: We study how vision-language models (VLMs) can learn to think and actively explore in 3D space. Instead of providing multi-view images, videos, or 3D representations to the model, we preserve the native visual encoding of VLMs, i.e., a single image, one at a time, just like humans, and treat the 3D representation only as an environment with which the model can interact through actions (e.g., move left) and observations (rendered images). Each rollout begins from an initial first-person view and a visual question. The model can then iteratively reason, navigate, and reorient its viewpoint before committing to a final answer. Following an initial trajectory-supervised finetuning, we apply reinforcement learning (RL) with rewards driven primarily by final-answer correctness. Crucially, RL provides no direct supervision over which viewpoints the model should visit or which exploration actions it should take. Instead, the model must learn an effective exploration policy solely from the extent to which its interactions improve performance. Across six 3D benchmarks, our model ACT3D achieves an average accuracy of 53.2% that improves its base Qwen model by 22.0% and surpasses proprietary Gemini 3.6 Flash. ACT3D also outperforms existing open-source 3D methods while using 50-70% fewer input frames, and generalizes to unseen domains with an average improvement of 5.9% over its supervised initialization. Further analysis reveals adaptive, question-conditioned exploration. Performance gains over the base model increase from 0.6% on questions answerable from the initial view to 16.3% on those requiring extensive exploration. ACT3D searches for occluded targets, avoids unnecessary exploration, and acquires complementary viewpoints for spatial comparisons. These findings demonstrate that outcome-based RL enables VLMs not only to reason over visual evidence, but also to learn when and how to acquire it.

papers.intro:
Despite substantial progress in 3D vision-language models, much of the existing work studies spatial reasoning under observations that are specified a priori, providing models with complete RGB-D scans (Azuma et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2025), multi-view images (Yang et al., 2025), videos (Zheng et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2026a), or explicit 3D scene representations such as point clouds and meshes (Hong et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2024b). Yet under partial observability, a fundamental challenge remains: the model must not only reason over the evidence currently available, but also determine how to act in order to acquire the evidence that is missing. This motivates the central question of our work: can a vision-language model learn to actively explore and acquire task-relevant visual evidence as an integral part of the 3D reasoning process?

Yet under partial observability, a fundamental challenge remains: the model must not only reason over the evidence currently available, but also determine how to act in order to acquire the evidence that is missing. This motivates the central question of our work: can a vision-language model learn to actively explore and acquire task-relevant visual evidence as an integral part of the 3D reasoning process?

We address this question by first formulating reasoning in 3D as an interactive visual decision process under partial observability. Rather than providing the VLM with a complete 3D representation, the 3D scene is kept external to the VLM and serves as an interactive environment that the model accesses through sequential action-observation interactions. Starting from a fixed initial egocentric view and a visual question, the model alternates between reasoning and interaction, iteratively acquiring observations through navigation and viewpoint control before committing to a final answer. This entire episode of interaction constitutes a policy rollout, in which the model jointly determines what information to acquire, how to interact with the environment, and how to reason over the accumulated evidence. To learn a policy that integrates visual information acquisition, spatial interaction, and reasoning, we adopt a two-stage training procedure: trajectory-supervised fine-tuning first establishes the interaction protocol, after which reinforcement learning optimizes the full interactive policy over the rollout described above using rewards driven primarily by final-answer correctness. During reinforcement learning, no direct supervision is provided for intermediate viewpoints, actions, or exploration trajectories. Effective exploration must instead be learned through credit assignment from task performance. This formulation enables us to examine whether task-level supervision alone can induce task-directed visual information acquisition during 3D reasoning.

Building on this formulation, we present Act3D, a vision-language model that jointly learns to acquire visual evidence and reason over observations. Experiments across six 3D benchmarks show that Act3D achieves an average accuracy of 53.2%, outperforming all evaluated prior methods and baselines. It improves upon its base Qwen model by 22.0% and surpasses Gemini 3.6 Flash by 1.0%. Act3D also outperforms existing open-source 3D methods while using 50–70% fewer input frames and lower-resolution observations. These gains generalize to out-of-distribution beyond the training domains, with an average improvement of 5.9% over the supervised initialization across four out-of-domain benchmarks. Beyond accuracy, we observe the emergence of adaptive exploration behaviors where models learn to explore more with increasing interaction steps on questions that require more exploration, leading to pronounced improvements when target objects are initially occluded or far away from the initial camera position. We further qualitatively illustrate that Act3D learns to search for hidden objects, limit unnecessary exploration when relevant evidence is already visible, and gather complementary viewpoints to resolve spatial relationships. Together, these findings demonstrate that RL enables VLMs not only to reason over visual observations, but also to adaptively acquire the evidence needed for 3D reasoning.

papers.title: The Glacier Model Intercomparison Project (GlacierMIP): Towards standardisation of global glacier projections
papers.abstract: The Glacier Model Intercomparison Project (GlacierMIP) provides an international framework for the coordinated evaluation and comparison of global glacier evolution models and their projections of glacier change. Its fourth phase, GlacierMIP4, updates previous global glacier projections through a standardised experimental design. For the first time, the protocol includes simulations extending to 2300 and an overshoot scenario for a subset of climate projections and requires monthly output of individual mass-balance components such as melt, accumulation and refreezing, in addition to annual results for glacier mass and area. While permitting model-specific approaches to calibration and other aspects of model implementation, the protocol prescribes common atmospheric forcing data, inventory boundary conditions, and reporting conventions to enable consistent analyses of inter-model differences. Here, we describe the GlacierMIP4 experimental protocol, including the simulation domain, initialisation, atmospheric forcing, and standardised output requirements. More broadly, we emphasize the need for standardised terminology, units, sign convention and file formats in global glacier modelling to improve the traceability, interoperability, and comparability of results, and recommend this protocol as a blueprint for future global glacier modelling studies.

The Glacier Model Intercomparison Project (GlacierMIP) is a Targeted Activity of the Climate and Cryosphere (CliC) project of the World Climate Research Project (WCRP). Its overall goal is to provide a framework for coordinated intercomparisons of global-scale glacier evolution models and their decadal-to-centennial projections, to provide community-based projections, e.g., to inform international assessments such as the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), to foster model improvements and to reduce uncertainties in projections of global glacier change. GlacierMIP focuses on all glaciers outside the ice sheets in Greenland and Antarctica but includes those in their periphery.

GlacierMIP complements the Ice Sheet Model Intercomparison Project (ISMIP), an umbrella framework under which several ice-sheet model intercomparisons have been coordinated, for example, ISMIP-HOM (Pattyn et al., 2008), ISMIP-HEINO (Calov et al., 2010) and most prominently ISMIP6 (Seroussi et al., 2020; Goelzer et al., 2020; Nowicki et al., 2016, e.g.,). ISMIP was endorsed by the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6, Eyring et al. (2016). Consequently, only few glacier models, capable of supplying global-scale projections (Raper and Braithwaite, 2006; Radić and Hock, 2011) had been developed prior to the release of the first version of the Randolph Glacier Inventory (Pfeffer et al., 2014, RGI, ). The RGI subsequently spurred the development of several global glacier models and large-scale projections within just a few years (Marzeion et al., 2012; Slangen et al., 2011; Hirabayashi et al., 2013; Giesen and Oerlemans, 2013; Radić et al., 2014). Its first phase (2015-2019) focused on a comparison of the glacier volume and area projections 2015-2100 from six previously published modelling studies including 214 global model runs based on four emission scenarios (Hock et al., 2019a). Because of this post-hoc approach, there was no standardisation of initial and boundary conditions. The results were used in the Special Report on the Ocean and Cryosphere in a Changing Climate (SROCC) by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) (Hock et al., 2019b).

In GlacierMIP2 (2019-2020), all participating modelling groups were required to submit annual glacier volume and area projections until 2100, based on standardised experiments. Models had to cover at least one of the 19 primary RGI regions, and use projections from ten prescribed General Circulation Models (GCMs) forced by at least two emission scenarios (Representative Concentration Pathway RCP2.6 and RCP8.5 (Van Vuuren et al., 2011). Regional initial ice volumes were prescribed based on RGI 6.0 (Huss and Farinotti, 2012). Results based on an ensemble of 288 unique projections from 11 glacier models were used to partition the total uncertainty into individual contributions caused by glacier models, GCMs, RCPs, and natural variability (Marzeion et al., 2020). Results also informed the glacier projections used in the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report (Fox-Kemper et al., 2021).

The stabilisation experiments were based on eight glacier models forced with 80 prescribed constant climatic scenarios derived from five GCMs, and were run for 2000 to 5000 years (Zekollari et al., 2025).

Thus, for the first time, the GlacierMIP protocol requires the submission of individual mass-balance components (e.g. accumulation, melt, runoff) in addition to annual glacier mass and area. papers.title: Parafermions in polarized $ν=2/3$ Fractional Quantum (Anomalous) Hall Heterostructures
papers.abstract: Motivated by recent experimental signatures of fractional Chern insulators in 2D quantum materials, we investigate the realization of $\mathbb Z_3$ parafermion zero modes (PZMs) on edges of spin-polarized $ν=2/3$ fractional quantum Hall states which are proximitized by superconductors. Unlike the spin-unpolarized Halperin state, the polarized $ν=2/3$ edge contains counterpropagating electron and fractional quasihole modes, giving rise to a plethora of competing tunneling and pairing processes. We focus on the vicinity of the fixed point where these modes reorganize into decoupled charge and neutral sectors, with the neutral sector describing an emergent dipole degree of freedom. Using bosonization and renormalization group analysis, we lay out the parameter space in which the interedge dipole interactions gap the neutral sector to stabilize one dominant tunneling and one dominant pairing channel resulting in a double sine-Gordon model in the charge sector which supports $\mathbb{Z}_3$ PZMs at domain walls. We discuss both clean and disordered systems. In clean systems this mechanism requires a certain degree of control of the interaction strength and range. In contrast, disorder can provide a more generic route: While short-ranged, edge-uncorrelated disorder % on the two edges suppresses the simultaneous pinning required for stable parafermion modes, when the disorder on the two edges is sufficiently correlated, as expected for smooth disorder potentials, the parameter regime hosting PZMs increases.

papers.intro:
The realization of topologically ordered phases and the associated detection of exotic anyonic quantum particles remains a major focus of modern condensed matter physics [69, 70, 89, 38, 97, 50, 51, 81, 6, 35, 80, 59, 53, 31]. Beyond its inherent scientific value, this endeavor is fueled by the dream of an intrinsically robust topological quantum computer. In this framework, quantum information is encoded in anyonic fusion channels whilst quantum braids are the physical processes underlying quantum gates. [71, 52] A famous example includes Majorana-based topological quantum computation [4, 2, 1], corresponding to Ising topological order. In this case, however, the set of quantum gates is too restricted to enable universal gate operations. As a possible remedy, parafermionic generalizations of Majorana zero modes to fractionalized systems with richer ℤn\mathbb{Z}_{n} degrees of freedom have been put forward [29, 25, 26, 67]. In suitable coupled architectures, they can provide a route toward Fibonacci anyons – a platform for universal topological quantum computation [68, 93, 3].

Parafermion zero modes (PZMs) have been proposed to emerge at interfaces between differently gapped regions of fractional quantum Hall (FQH) edges [62, 17, 15]. The topic has received substantial theoretical attention and has been extensively studied [68, 92, 93, 18, 19, 82, 61, 84, 60, 23, 10, 88, 87, 37, 73, 11, 102, 105, 8, 12]. A major experimental challenge is the simultaneous realization of a robust fractional topological phase and superconductivity [39, 83, 45, 54, 104, 91, 90]. Conventional FQH states require strong magnetic fields, which complicate their integration with superconductors (SCs). Fractional Chern insulators (FCIs) provide an attractive alternative: they realize fractionalized topological order in partially filled Chern bands and can occur without an externally applied magnetic field [79, 72, 63]. Their recent observation in 2D quantum materials [9, 103, 75, 99, 46, 78, 65, 14, 64, 20], therefore, opens new possibilities for realizing parafermions in experimentally accessible platforms.

Twisted bilayer MoTe2\mathrm{MoTe}_{2} (tMoTe2) is particularly promising in this respect. Top and bottom gates tune the sample into the spin-polarized ν=2/3\nu=2/3 FCI, while a narrow finger gate locally changes the filling and induces superconducting or insulating regions. Fractional superconducting and insulating regions can thus, in principle, be defined electrostatically without an additional material interface.

With the prospect of such a single-material realization, we here theoretically delineate the parameter space in which ℤ3\mathbb{Z}_{3} parafermion modes may be realized based on 1D heterostructures of SCs and the edge states of spin-polarized ν=2/3\nu=2/3 phases. Our study includes an in-depth analysis of interaction and disorder effects. We find that for clean samples, interaction effects need to be externally controlled to stabilize quantum phases with parafermion edge states. In contrast, for disordered interfaces, the tuning can be avoided. If the disorder potential is long ranged (e.g. Coulomb impurities), the parafermionic phase is stable over a large portion of the phase diagram. However, if the disorder potential is very short ranged and at the same time the tunneling interface is smooth, the phases including parafermions are suppressed.

II by giving a brief review of how PZMs can appear in FQH–SC heterostructures as a low-energy theory of a double sine-Gordon model. Thereby, we identify the unresolved question of ℤ3\mathbb{Z}_{3} PZMs in a ν=2/3\nu=2/3 spin-polarized FQH state. In Sec. III, we introduce the model and define all relevant objects needed to derive the effective low-energy theory. In Sec. IV, we first demonstrate our approach in a fine-tuned case in which the edge reorganizes into two counterpropagating decoupled modes, one neutral and one carrying charge 2​e/32e/3. Subsequently, in Sec. V, we discuss the more realistic case of correlated and uncorrelated edge disorder for multiple disorder scenarios and demonstrate a ℤ3\mathbb{Z}_{3} PZM phase without the necessity of fine-tuning. Finally, in Sec. VI, we summarize and discuss our results.

papers.title: Coexistence of Altermagnetic and Compensated Ferrimagnetic Motifs in a Noncollinear Multiferroic
papers.abstract: Collinear compensated magnets with nonrelativistic spin splitting comprise altermagnets (ALMs), whose rotation- or mirror-related opposite-spin sublattices produce momentum-selective splitting that vanishes at $Γ$, and compensated ferrimagnets (CFIMs), whose symmetry-inequivalent sublattices allow splitting throughout the Brillouin zone, including at $Γ$. Here, we show that the coplanar noncollinear magnetic state of multiferroic boracite Ni$_3$B$_7$O$_{13}$Cl hosts both motifs on distinct Ni sublattices in real space. The electronic structure and spin texture exhibit coexisting $d$-wave-like and $s$-wave-like spin-polarization components associated with the ALM and CFIM motifs, respectively. Opposite ferroelectric states exhibit reversed band-resolved spin polarizations, indicating magnetoelectric coupling, and sign reversals of linear shift and circular injection currents.

papers.title: CLIS-MPPI: Closed-Loop Model Predictive Path Integral Control With Initial-State Sampling Under Execution Delay
papers.abstract: Sampling-based motion planning such as Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control has become attractive for robotics due to its ability to handle nonlinear dynamics and non-smooth objectives without gradient information, while leveraging parallel rollout computation for real-time performance. However, in real-world robotic systems, the optimized control input is often applied after a non-negligible planning delay, causing a mismatch between the state used in forward simulation and the actual state at control execution, which can significantly degrade planning accuracy and may even lead to unsafe behavior such as collisions. This paper proposes Closed-Loop MPPI with Initial-State Sampling (CLIS-MPPI), which explicitly addresses execution-time state mismatch by modeling planning delay as a distribution over plausible execution-time initial states, performing rollout optimization from sampled initial states, and applying a rollout-based local feedback correction during control execution. The proposed method is validated through real-world experiments on a 6-DoF UR5e manipulator in a narrow-passage task involving obstacle avoidance and end-effector target reaching. Across 5 real-world runs of the same task, standard MPPI collided in 2 runs, whereas CLIS-MPPI remained collision-free in all 5 runs. Averaged over all collision-free runs for each method (3 for MPPI and 5 for CLIS-MPPI), CLIS-MPPI reduced the average task completion time from 25.4s to 24.4s and the average end-effector path length from 0.456 m to 0.425 m. It also reduced the overall joint-position and joint-velocity root mean square errors (RMSEs) from 0.100 rad and 0.108 rad/s to 0.017 rad and 0.011 rad/s, respectively. These results demonstrate improved safety, planning-execution consistency, and motion smoothness.

papers.intro:
With the rapid growth of computing hardware, sampling-based motion planning methods [1, 2], especially Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control [3], have emerged as a powerful framework for real-time robotic motion planning and control. MPPI repeatedly samples stochastic control rollouts, performs forward simulation, evaluates trajectory costs, and refines the control sequence through a path-integral weighted update over a receding horizon. Compared with traditional gradient-based model predictive control (MPC) [4], MPPI does not require differentiable cost functions, making it particularly suitable for robotic systems with nonlinear dynamics, obstacle-rich environments, and complex non-smooth objectives [5]. Furthermore, unlike learning-based methods such as reinforcement learning [6], which typically depend on large-scale offline training, MPPI is a fully online planning method and can leverage GPU-parallelized rollout computation [7] to enable real-time decision-making.

With the rapid growth of computing hardware, sampling-based motion planning methods [1, 2], especially Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control [3], have emerged as a powerful framework for real-time robotic motion planning and control. MPPI repeatedly samples stochastic control rollouts, performs forward simulation, evaluates trajectory costs, and refines the control sequence through a path-integral weighted update over a receding horizon. Compared with traditional gradient-based model predictive control (MPC) [4], MPPI does not require differentiable cost functions, making it particularly suitable for robotic systems with nonlinear dynamics, obstacle-rich environments, and complex non-smooth objectives [5]. Furthermore, unlike learning-based methods such as reinforcement learning [6], which typically depend on large-scale offline training, MPPI is a fully online planning method and can leverage GPU-parallelized rollout computation [7] to enable real-time decision-making.

Despite these advantages, the performance of MPPI in real-world robotic systems can be significantly degraded by execution-time delay. In particular, the quality of MPPI critically depends on the accuracy of its forward simulation and cost evaluation, since both are used to determine the control update at each planning cycle. However, forward simulation is typically the most computationally expensive step in MPPI, and the resulting planning latency can introduce a substantial mismatch between the state used for optimization and the state at which the optimized control is actually applied. As illustrated in Fig. 1, at planning time tiplant_{i}^{\mathrm{plan}}, MPPI starts forward simulation from the measured robot state xirefx_{i}^{\mathrm{ref}}, and the rollout costs are evaluated based on this state. During the planning interval τi\tau_{i}, however, the robot continues executing the previous control command ui−1u_{i-1}. Consequently, when the newly optimized control uiu_{i} becomes effective at tisendt_{i}^{\mathrm{send}}, the actual robot state has already evolved to xiapply≠xirefx_{i}^{\mathrm{apply}}\neq x_{i}^{\mathrm{ref}}. As a result, the control command uiu_{i} is no longer applied to the state on which it was optimized, leading to a delay-induced state mismatch. This issue becomes particularly critical in high-frequency control settings or when the robot operates with large control actions, where even a small planning delay may produce a significant state deviation. In safety-critical tasks such as obstacle avoidance in narrow spaces, such mismatch can cause severe performance degradation and even collisions, despite the fact that the planned rollouts themselves are collision-free during forward simulation.

To address the delay-induced state mismatch, we propose closed-loop MPPI with initial-state sampling (CLIS-MPPI), as illustrated in Fig. 2. The key idea is to explicitly convert execution delay into an initial-state uncertainty at each planning cycle, and to compensate for the resulting mismatch through a closed-loop control update. Instead of assuming that the control optimization starts from a single measured state, CLIS-MPPI samples a distribution of perturbed initial states around the currently measured state to represent the possible system evolution during the planning interval. For each sampled initial state, perturbed control sequences are generated and parallel forward simulations are performed to obtain rollout trajectories and their associated costs. Based on the weighted rollout distribution, a nominal state-control trajectory is constructed, from which a local feedback gain is further extracted in a rollout-based manner. The final control input is then computed as a closed-loop combination of the MPPI feedforward update and a state-feedback correction term. In this way, the proposed method enables the applied control command to better match the actual robot state at execution time, thereby improving consistency between planning and execution, motion smoothness, and safety in delay-sensitive real-world tasks.

MPPI was originally introduced for aggressive autonomous driving tasks, where its sampling-based formulation demonstrated strong capability in handling high-speed, nonlinear systems under complex objectives [3]. Since then, MPPI has been extended to a wide variety of robotic platforms, including robotic manipulators [5, 8, 9], aerial robots [10], and legged systems [11]. In robotic manipulation, STORM [5] and RAMP [8] showed that GPU-accelerated MPPI can achieve real-time obstacle avoidance and goal-reaching on 6–7 Degrees of Freedom (DoF) manipulators in cluttered environments. For dynamic environments, Zhou et al. [9] proposed a parallel MPPI framework for manipulators that improves computational efficiency and incorporates a gradient-velocity modulated signed distance field cost for dynamic obstacle avoidance. Zhai et al. [10] developed a perception-aware MPPI method for quadrotor navigation in unknown environments, where perception-driven objectives are integrated into the planning process to promote exploration and path recovery under occlusion.

papers.title: napari-TurboBox: Interactive Multi-Viewer Bounding Box Annotation for AI-Guided Volumetric Bioimaging
papers.abstract: Promptable segmentation models turn one 3D bounding box into an instance mask. Box placement therefore limits how fast microscopy volumes with thousands of objects are annotated. Each box must be checked in several synchronized viewers, but napari-bbox shares no state between viewers. An edit must update every viewer and slows down with more boxes. napari-TurboBox instead holds one shared copy of the boxes for all viewers. In a four-viewer layout, napari-TurboBox needs a few milliseconds per mouse move to update the three slice viewers up to $10^4$ boxes. The same update in napari-bbox leaves the 33 ms budget beyond about $10^3$ boxes and takes 159 ms at $10^4$. Boxes stay axis-aligned and export to COCO and YOLO as per-slice 2D boxes. napari-TurboBox is a pure-Python plugin for napari 0.6.6 to 0.9. The code is available at https://github.com/N-Friederich/napari-turbobox under the Apache 2.0 licence, and version 0.1.0 is archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23090828 on Zenodo.

papers.intro:
Dense volumetric biomedical imaging routinely resolves hundreds to hundreds of thousands of objects per volume (Amat et al., 2014; Schmitz et al., 2017; Lin et al., 2021; Long et al., 2022; Long et al., 2009; Weigert et al., 2020; Achard et al., 2024). Because 3D structures span multiple optical slices, manual voxel-level segmentation is prohibitively slow. Promptable deep learning models substantially reduce this burden: a single axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) enclosing a target structure provides sufficient spatial guidance to generate an instance mask (Kirillov et al., 2023; Ma et al., 2024) (Fig. 1A). An imprecise box yields an imprecise mask (13), so accurate AABB placement directly determines downstream quality.

Placing a 3D box precisely is intrinsically a multi-view task. An object’s zz-extent is invisible in any single X​YXY slice yet decides whether the box encloses or clips the object, and depth in a projected 3D rendering is ambiguous under occlusion (Tory and Möller, 2004). Established volumetric annotation tools (e.g., ITK-SNAP (Yushkevich et al., 2006), webKnossos (Boergens et al., 2017), CVAT (CVAT.ai Corporation, 2023)) therefore commonly provide synchronized orthogonal slice views (X​Y/X​Z/Y​ZXY/XZ/YZ) alongside a 3D rendering for live verification (Fig. 1A). We call each such synchronized window a viewer and use the four-viewer layout X​YXY/X​ZXZ/Y​ZYZ/3D throughout this work.
