The napari viewer (napari contributors, 2019), widely used for Python-based bioimaging, can host several viewers side by side (synchronizing them is left to the application), with image data and annotations directly accessible as NumPy arrays (Harris et al., 2020). This ecosystem increasingly integrates promptable deep learning models such as nnInteractive (Isensee et al., 2025) and μ\muSAM (3) as interactive plugins. However, existing bounding-box tools like napari-bbox (Bauer, 2023) share no state across viewers, so each open viewer holds its own layer with the full coordinate state. Consequently, translating or resizing a single box must be applied to the layer of every viewer, and each of these updates costs time that grows with NN, i.e. 𝒪⁡(N⋅V)\mathcal{O}(N\cdot V) per edit. In a standard four-viewer layout (V=4V=4), this overhead causes response times to exceed the interactive 33 ms threshold (≥30​Hz\geq 30\,\text{Hz}) (Card et al., 1991; MacKenzie and Ware, 1993; Jota et al., 2013) beyond about N=103N=10^{3} boxes, reaching about 160 ms at N=104N=10^{4} (Fig. 3a). To address these limitations, we present napari-TurboBox, a lightweight plugin built on napari’s own Shapes layer, designed for responsive multi-viewer 3D bounding box annotation via a shared-state architecture. A single in-memory store holds one authoritative copy of the boxes and propagates each edit to all viewers without duplicating the array. napari-TurboBox therefore needs about 2 ms per mouse move to update the three slice viewers up to 10410^{4} boxes, well within the 33 ms budget. Dense volumes with thousands of objects can thus be edited as a whole rather than in crops, whose boundaries clip objects and remove the depth context a box must be checked against. Every bounding box remains a strictly valid AABB during interaction and can be directly exported on demand to standard COCO (Lin et al., 2014) and YOLO (Redmon et al., 2016) formats for downstream segmentation and detection workflows (Fig. 1).

papers.title: Semantic Latent Alignment for Flow Matching with Invertible Bi-Lipschitz Adapters
papers.abstract: Pretrained latent spaces trade compression, reconstruction, and the learnability of the coordinates a downstream generator has to work in, which complicates adapting these spaces to different domains or tasks: continued training is expensive, and without a new alignment objective it often fails to improve downstream generation. We instead leave the encoder and decoder fixed and change only the coordinates between them, using an invertible bi-Lipschitz adapter aligned offline to a semantic teacher and frozen during class-conditional flow matching. Invertibility preserves compatibility with the pretrained autoencoder, while the bi-Lipschitz constraint limits how far alignment can distort its latent geometry. This provides a simple way to improve semantic organization while retaining the compression and reconstruction properties of the original latent space. On two medical imaging datasets, constrained latent adaptation improves feature metrics, seed stability and counterfactual edit strength, while remaining competitive on downstream classification. In contrast, unconstrained adaptation can become highly anisotropic and sensitive despite remaining invertible, highlighting the importance of controlling geometric distortion. Our results suggest that carefully constrained post-hoc adaptation offers a parameter-efficient and tuning-free alternative to jointly modifying the representation during generative training.

papers.intro:
Latent generative models, including latent diffusion (Rombach et al., 2022) and flow matching (Lipman et al., 2023), operate on compressed representations produced by pretrained variational autoencoders (VAEs) (Kingma and Welling, 2013). VAEs are typically optimized for a rate-distortion trade-off between compression and reconstruction fidelity (Alemi et al., 2018; Bozkurt et al., 2021). However, a representation that reconstructs well is not necessarily easy for a downstream model to learn (Skorokhodov et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2026; Dombrowski et al., 2026). Latent representation design therefore involves a third axis: downstream learnability. We define learnability as the ease with which a bounded-capacity learner can recover task-relevant structure from a representation under the measurement process used by the downstream pipeline. It depends not only on which information the representation retains, but also on how that information is arranged (Yao et al., 2025; Black Forest Labs, 2025).

Fine-tuning the autoencoder can adapt the representation, but it also changes the decoder coordinates, requires a new latent cache, and adds a costly adaptation stage, with the adapted latents often still showing low learnability (Dombrowski et al., 2026). Meanwhile, methods such as REPA (Yu et al., 2025) align features inside the generative model during training. They improve the generator instead of the latent representation and repeat the alignment cost for each training run. We study a post-hoc alternative: adapt the latent coordinates once, then reuse them across flow-matching models.

Flow matching consumes the adapted latents, while the adapter inverse returns generated samples to the coordinates expected by the pretrained decoder. Under exact inversion, the encoder-decoder reconstruction mapping remains unchanged. An unconstrained invertible map can still produce essentially collapsed latents, so we use a bi-Lipschitz design that bounds the distortion in both directions with a single scalar, estimated from the data.

We evaluate generation on two medical imaging datasets, using sample quality, semantic coverage, train-on-synthetic utility and counterfactual generation. Comparisons include the unchanged latent space, online generator alignment, autoencoder adaptation, and less constrained invertible maps.

Our contributions are: 1. We propose a post-hoc latent adapter that is invertible and bi-Lipschitz by construction, aligned offline to a semantic teacher via CKA and frozen during flow matching. It leaves the autoencoder and the flow-matching objective unchanged, while a single scalar λ\lambda bounds its distortion in both directions with a closed-form certificate. 2. We make the adapter tuning-free: λ\lambda can be estimated from a necessary condition on teacher triplets and the teacher from label geometry on training data, both fixed before any generator is trained. On both datasets the teacher choice agrees with the downstream results, and the method works across an eightfold range of λ\lambda. 3. On our tested datasets, the adapter is competitive with online generator alignment and autoencoder adaptation, has the lowest seed variance in domain FID among the adaptation methods, and produces stronger counterfactual edits, at 405×405\times fewer parameters than REPA’s projection head and a fraction of the compute of autoencoder fine-tuning. 4. We show that invertibility alone is insufficient: invertible maps without Lipschitz control become nearly rank-deficient and fail as generators, and adapting only the clean endpoint instead of the whole flow path gives good but unreliable runs.

papers.title: Receiver-Specific Interventional Valuation of Semantic Atoms for Budget-Constrained Multi-Agent Communication
papers.abstract: Cooperative multi-agent semantic communication requires deciding not only how a transmitter encodes its observation, but also which resulting semantic content should be delivered to each receiver under a limited link budget. We introduce an encoder-agnostic transmitter-side framework for receiver-specific valuation of independently selectable semantic units, termed semantic atoms. Each atom is assigned a signed value that quantifies whether delivering it is expected to improve or degrade the intended receiver's downstream decision. We formulate this effect through a controlled-delivery utility and identify it via prospective randomized payload delivery before the receiver acts. A shadow receiver estimates this utility using only transmitter-available information, from which receiver-specific leave-one-out (LOO) and Shapley atom values are computed. Experiments on a four-receiver intersection benchmark show 68.4% accuracy in recovering the sign of non-negligible LOO atom effects and a Spearman correlation of 0.302 between estimated and reference LOO values. Under limited budgets, we show that receiver-specific selection consistently outperforms shared and random alternatives, demonstrating the benefit of adapting semantic ranking to the intended receiver. At full affordability, exhaustive subset selection also outperforms full-payload transmission, showing that transmitting all available content need not maximize receiver utility. Overall, our results show that receiver-specific semantic valuation can support effective budget-constrained communication despite imperfect atom-value estimation.

papers.intro:
Future wireless systems will increasingly connect vehicles, robots, sensors, and autonomous agents that exchange information to support decisions rather than merely reproduce source samples. Prior work on semantic and task-oriented communication has established this shift toward transmitting information according to its relevance to the downstream task [1, 2]. More recently, generative semantic communication has extended this direction by using foundation models, diffusion models, and multimodal priors for more efficient semantic representation and reconstruction [3, 4]. While these advances improve semantic representation and recovery, an additional challenge arises in cooperative multi-agent systems: when an agent shares its observation with multiple receiving agents, it must determine which extracted semantic information to communicate to each receiver under a constrained link budget.

Future wireless systems will increasingly connect vehicles, robots, sensors, and autonomous agents that exchange information to support decisions rather than merely reproduce source samples. Prior work on semantic and task-oriented communication has established this shift toward transmitting information according to its relevance to the downstream task [1, 2]. More recently, generative semantic communication has extended this direction by using foundation models, diffusion models, and multimodal priors for more efficient semantic representation and reconstruction [3, 4]. While these advances improve semantic representation and recovery, an additional challenge arises in cooperative multi-agent systems: when an agent shares its observation with multiple receiving agents, it must determine which extracted semantic information to communicate to each receiver under a constrained link budget.

Consider a cooperative intersection in which a roadside agent and several connected vehicles form a multi-agent team. At a given epoch, the roadside agent may observe a pedestrian trajectory, an occluded cyclist, and a congestion cue, while the other agents differ in their routes, local observations, and decision states. Consequently, different receiving agents may require different parts of the same shared observation. Communicating the full representation to every agent can consume the limited per-link communication budget on redundant information, whereas communicating one common subset cannot account for these heterogeneous information needs. Thus, even when agents share the same source of semantic information, the communication relevance of its contents can differ across the team.

Existing semantic communication research has advanced learned semantic representation [1], task-oriented transmission based on feature importance [5], and adaptive communication resource allocation [6]. Generative semantic communication has further improved semantic reconstruction from compact representations through learned priors [3, 4], while task-oriented multi-agent communication has used value of information to adapt the precision of shared observations [7]. These approaches guide task-relevant encoding or resource assignment, but they do not directly address assigning independently selectable components of one transmitting agent’s observation differently to multiple receiving agents according to their individual information needs.

Generative semantic communication has further improved semantic reconstruction from compact representations through learned priors [3, 4], while task-oriented multi-agent communication has used value of information to adapt the precision of shared observations [7]. These approaches guide task-relevant encoding or resource assignment, but they do not directly address assigning independently selectable components of one transmitting agent’s observation differently to multiple receiving agents according to their individual information needs.

A closely related line of work studies learned communication and credit assignment in cooperative multi-agent systems. Targeted messaging and social-influence methods learn whom to communicate with or measure how communication affects other agents’ behavior [8, 9], while counterfactual and Shapley-based approaches assign value to communicated messages [10, 11]. These works provide important foundations for communication valuation, but primarily operate at the message or link level rather than valuing independently selectable semantic content for different receivers under explicit communication budgets. We address this gap with a receiver-specific semantic valuation framework for budget-constrained multi-agent communication. Rather than using one importance measure across receivers, we evaluate communicated content with respect to the intended receiver and its downstream decision. The framework links semantic valuation directly to receiver-specific payload construction while remaining independent of the underlying encoder, making it applicable to the outputs of generative, multimodal, or conventional semantic representation models. It therefore enables receiver-specific selection of independently selectable semantic content under explicit per-link budgets, so that different receivers can receive different information from the same observation.

papers.title: From picometre displacements to a three-dimensional lattice gas of polar skyrmions
papers.abstract: Polar skyrmions, the electric analogues of magnetic skyrmions, form arrays in PbTiO3/SrTiO3 superlattices that are known to be only short-range ordered, but how this disordered ensemble is organized in three dimensions, and how its microscopic structure underlies this organization, have remained largely inaccessible. Here, using three-dimensional difference pair distribution function (3D-ΔPDF) analysis of X-ray diffuse scattering, we show that the polar skyrmion bubbles form a three-dimensional lattice gas: they occupy discrete sites, but their order extends over only a few neighbours and is two to three times stronger across the SrTiO3 spacers than within a layer. This interlayer coupling is consistent with the polarization of the bubbles extending into the spacers. Within each bubble, the polarization rotates in a predominantly Néel-type manner, and Pb and Ti rotate together with comparable picometre displacements, demonstrating that both A- and B-site cations take part in the polar distortion.

papers.title: Feeling the generalised rough SABR boundary
papers.abstract: We provide an in-depth analysis of a generalised rough version of the SABR volatility model, widely used in the financial industry. We specifically focus on its behaviour at the origin, whether it can reach it and how fast it may do so.

papers.intro:
The stochastic alpha-beta-rho (SABR) model introduced in [13] has become a standard in volatility modelling. Its success is unusual in combining a parsimonious stochastic volatility specification with an explicit and remarkably effective approximation of implied volatility. The model is widely used, particularly in interest-rate and foreign-exchange markets and has generated a substantial mathematical literature on implied and stochastic volatility, and on asymptotic analysis. papers.title: EPRV Asteroseismology of the K dwarfs GJ 570 A and GJ 783 A with ESPRESSO. Empirical mode-amplitude scaling in tension with 3D convection simulations
papers.abstract: Solar-like oscillations in K dwarfs have intrinsically low amplitudes, making them challenging to detect in space-based photometry. The advent of Extremely Precise Radial Velocity (EPRV) instrumentation enables Doppler asteroseismology in the mid-K regime, providing a new opportunity to test mode-excitation and damping physics. We investigate the scaling of oscillation amplitudes with stellar parameters and assess whether 3D surface convection simulations reproduce the observed amplitude behavior. High-cadence ESPRESSO radial-velocity time series were obtained over five and six consecutive nights for the K dwarfs GJ 570 A (K4 V) and GJ 783 A (K2.5 V), respectively. We identified oscillation modes from weighted power spectra and extracted them via sine-wave fitting following spectral deconvolution. Peak mode amplitudes were measured from heavily smoothed power spectra. For comparison, we performed 3D radiative-hydrodynamical simulations including excitation and damping-rate calculations. We measured 6 modes for GJ 570 A and 24 for GJ 783 A ($\ell=0$-$2$, and $\ell=3$ for GJ 783 A). The peak radial-mode amplitudes are $2.57 \pm 0.52\:{\rm cm\,s^{-1}}$ and $4.90 \pm 0.81\:{\rm cm\,s^{-1}}$, respectively. These results support a transition from an $\sim(L/M)^{0.7}$ amplitude scaling to a steeper $\sim(L/M)^{1.5}$ scaling, occurring near the G/K-dwarf boundary toward decreasing $L/M$. In contrast, 3D simulations predict an $\sim(L/M)^{0.9}$ scaling for K dwarfs, revealing tension between observations and first-principles convection models. EPRV asteroseismology extends into the mid-K regime and exposes a steep mode-amplitude scaling that our 3D convection simulations do not reproduce. This discrepancy points to missing physics in our implementation of convection-pulsation coupling and/or limitations in the adopted modeling assumptions, motivating further theoretical investigation.

papers.intro:
Notable progress in asteroseismology has been made due to missions such as Convection, Rotation and planetary Transits (Baglin et al., 2006, CoRoT;), Kepler/K2 (Borucki et al., 2010; Howell et al., 2014), and the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (Ricker et al., 2015, TESS;). These missions have delivered high-precision photometric data from space, allowing for in-depth investigations of the internal structures of solar-type and red-giant stars, which exhibit solar-like oscillations driven by convection (Chaplin and Miglio, 2013; Aerts, 2021). Despite this, the small-amplitude solar-like oscillations in K dwarfs (Kjeldsen et al., 2008a; Verner et al., 2011, amplitudes below a few parts per million or, correspondingly, 10​cm​s−110\>{\rm cm\,s^{-1}};) remain extremely challenging to detect in space-based photometry (Mathur et al., 2017; Hatt et al., 2023). This difficulty persists even with access to multi-year Kepler (Campante et al., 2015; Lundkvist et al., 2016, e.g.,) and multi-sector TESS (Campante et al., 2016; Hon et al., 2024; Lund et al., 2025, e.g.,) observations. As a result, only a handful of dwarfs cooler than the Sun show oscillations in photometry, with detections dropping off sharply below ∼5500​K{\sim}5500\>{\rm K} (see Fig. 1).

Doppler velocity observations offer a viable alternative to space-based photometry. Stellar “noise” from activity and granulation is significantly lower in Doppler than in photometry (Harvey, 1988; Grundahl et al., 2007), resulting in a higher signal-to-noise ratio (S/N) over the typical oscillation timescales (Hon et al., 2024; Kjeldsen et al., 2025; Ádám et al., 2026). This motivated several pre-Kepler radial-velocity (RV) campaigns targeting late-G/early-K dwarfs (Kjeldsen et al., 2005; Carrier and Eggenberger, 2006; Teixeira et al., 2009, e.g.,), using then state-of-the-art spectrographs such as the High Accuracy Radial velocity Planet Searcher (Mayor et al., 2003, HARPS;) and the Ultraviolet and Visual Echelle Spectrograph (Dekker et al., 2000, UVES;). These pioneering efforts helped establish a lower effective temperature (TeffT_{\rm eff}) bound for cool-dwarf asteroseismology (see Fig. 1). However, limited RV precision and/or relatively small apertures restricted detections to the very brightest dwarfs.

Advances in Doppler precision, driven by the search for Earth-like planets, are providing a renewed opportunity for detecting low-amplitude oscillations, with Extremely Precise Radial Velocity (EPRV) techniques currently achieving 2020–30​cm​s−130\>{\rm cm\,s^{-1}} precision in a single exposure (Burt et al., 2026, for a recent review, see). The few-minute oscillation periods typical of K dwarfs demand a fast observational cadence, requiring exposures as short as ∼25​s{\sim}25\>{\rm s} (with the remaining cadence budget allocated to readout). Achieving the necessary RV precision within such short integrations calls for an optimal combination of instrumental stability and large collecting area. The last couple of years have witnessed a groundbreaking resurgence of observational campaigns targeting K dwarfs (see Fig. 1), fueled by EPRV instruments mounted on large-aperture telescopes, namely, the Echelle SPectrograph for Rocky Exoplanets and Stable Spectroscopic Observations (Pepe et al., 2021, ESPRESSO;) on the Very Large Telescope (VLT) and the Keck Planet Finder (Gibson et al., 2024, KPF;) on the Keck I telescope. ESPRESSO and KPF are among the very few instrumental setups capable of achieving this level of performance, with a coordinated all-sky effort to characterize cool seismic dwarfs currently underway, leveraging both facilities.

This followed an earlier claim of p-mode detection in the nearly ten times fainter K3 dwarf HD 40307 (Pepe et al., 2021), a result that was subsequently ruled out (Campante et al., 2024). Hon et al. (2024) later detected oscillations in the K0 V star σ\sigma Draconis using only a single night of observations with KPF. While 20-second cadence TESS photometry from 14 sectors also showed oscillations for this star, the KPF data revealed oscillation modes over a considerably broader frequency range due to their higher S/N. These results conclusively show that precise asteroseismology of cool dwarfs is now possible down to at least the mid-K spectral type, effectively opening a new domain in observational asteroseismology. This development carries significant implications for stellar astrophysics. In particular, mode amplitudes are determined by a delicate balance between energy supply and mode damping, both directly connected to the turbulent velocity field associated with convection (Houdek and Dupret, 2015). Measurement of oscillation modes in cool dwarfs will thus shed light on the dynamical coupling between pulsations and near-surface convection in a regime yet unexplored. Theoretical calculations have suggested a scaling of the amplitudes of solar-like oscillations in Doppler velocity of the form \varvosc∝(L/M)s\varv_{\rm osc}\!\propto\!(L/M)^{s} (Christensen-Dalsgaard and Frandsen, 1983; Kjeldsen and Bedding, 1995), where LL and MM denote the stellar luminosity and mass, and the exponent ss is expected to lie in the range 0.70.7–1.51.5 (Houdek et al., 1999; Samadi et al., 2005; Samadi et al., 2007). Recent observations suggest that, for K dwarfs, mode amplitudes favor the upper bound of the predicted range for the exponent ss (Campante et al., 2024; Hon et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025), consistent with a transition toward a steeper scaling as one moves from the G- into the K-dwarf regime, occurring at Teff∼5300​KT_{\rm eff}\!\sim\!5300\>{\rm K} (see also Verner et al., 2011, where a negative d​s/d​Teff{\rm d}s/{\rm d}T_{\rm eff} gradient was measured, based on a large ensemble of main-sequence and subgiant Kepler stars). Moreover, characterization of this scaling is key to accurately estimating the asteroseismic yield of the upcoming PLAnetary Transits and Oscillations of stars (Goupil et al., 2024; Rauer et al., 2025; Chaplin et al., 2026, PLATO;) mission, whose P1 and P2 (“bright”), as well as P5 (“statistical”) stellar samples extend down to spectral type K7.

papers.title: Approaching Backpropagation Accuracy with Weight Perturbation on MNIST
papers.abstract: Weight perturbation (WP) estimates learning directions from random parameter perturbations and a scalar change in loss, without backpropagating derivatives. We examine how batch size, training duration, and estimator stabilization affect its attainable accuracy in fully connected MNIST networks. In the shallow configuration, large-batch training reaches approximately 97\% test accuracy, compared with an early backpropagation (BP) reference near 97.5--98\%. The same comparison exposes a substantial efficiency gap: under a ten-epoch budget, shallow WP reaches 90.2\%, whereas the reported BP reference reaches 97.4\%. Epoch-indexed curves show diminishing returns from increasing batch size beyond 4,000. Learning-rate reduction and averaging independent perturbation-based updates also stabilize deeper networks, although their recorded results do not establish BP-level accuracy. We distinguish these empirical findings from a finite-horizon approximation argument: under stated regularity conditions, population WP can approximate a fixed gradient-descent trajectory arbitrarily closely at any fixed finite depth. Positive classification margins then suffice to preserve the reference predictions on a finite test set with arbitrarily high probability. Together, the results identify near-BP accuracy as a configuration- and budget-dependent possibility, rather than evidence of equal efficiency or an unconditional accuracy guarantee across depth.

papers.intro:
Learning from global performance feedback without transmitting error derivatives through neural circuitry is a central challenge in biologically plausible credit assignment. Backpropagation (BP) solves this problem computationally, but its conventional implementation relies on coordinated forward and backward computations, precise layer-specific error signals, and corresponding feedback pathways whose biological realization remains debated [1, 27]. Biological synapses, in contrast, exhibit spontaneous fluctuations and remodeling, while synaptic plasticity can be regulated by neuromodulatory signals associated with reward and behavioral outcomes [28, 29, 30, 31]. These properties motivate learning mechanisms that exploit local stochastic exploration and globally available evaluative signals to guide synaptic adaptation.

Learning from global performance feedback without transmitting error derivatives through neural circuitry is a central challenge in biologically plausible credit assignment. Backpropagation (BP) solves this problem computationally, but its conventional implementation relies on coordinated forward and backward computations, precise layer-specific error signals, and corresponding feedback pathways whose biological realization remains debated [1, 27]. Biological synapses, in contrast, exhibit spontaneous fluctuations and remodeling, while synaptic plasticity can be regulated by neuromodulatory signals associated with reward and behavioral outcomes [28, 29, 30, 31]. These properties motivate learning mechanisms that exploit local stochastic exploration and globally available evaluative signals to guide synaptic adaptation.

Weight perturbation (WP) offers a particularly direct approach to this problem. Synaptic weights are transiently perturbed, and the resulting change in task performance determines the direction of subsequent plasticity [2, 3]. Each synapse requires only information about its own perturbation and a shared scalar feedback signal. The learning rule operates without an explicit differentiable model of the network, backward error propagation, or symmetric feedback weights. WP therefore provides a model-free candidate for biologically motivated learning, connecting stochastic synaptic plasticity with gradient-based optimization [28, 8, 12]. Perturbation-based learning has also been combined with competitive Hebbian plasticity in sparse excitatory neural networks [25], illustrating its compatibility with additional biologically motivated learning mechanisms.

WP infers a parameter update from scalar performance differences, introducing substantial variance into the estimated learning direction. Scalar-feedback learning has a substantial history in model-free learning, stochastic error descent, and statistical gradient-following algorithms [2, 3, 5]. The relative efficiency of WP and node perturbation (NP) is not determined by parameter count alone. Analyses in linear networks identify dimension-dependent learning costs [11], whereas Züge et al. show that trial duration and effective task dimensionality can make WP comparable or superior to NP [12]. The 2023 journal article succeeds the 2021 preprint used in the thesis and is reproduced with its supplement in Züge’s 2025 dissertation [13]. For NP, Hiratani et al. identify diffusion-driven instability under model mismatch and a stabilizing role for normalization [14]. papers.title: SCARCE: Emergent Institutions in Long-Horizon Multi-Agent Coding Systems
papers.abstract: As autonomous agents become widely deployed, coordinating access to shared computing resources and services will become increasingly important. Recent incidents have already revealed unplanned coordination between agents, highlighting the safety implications of these interactions. Yet prior studies of agent negotiation often use stylized games and simulated bargaining, leaving open how these behaviors develop during sustained, long-horizon tasks. We propose SCARCE (Shared Compute ARena for Coding agEnts), a framework in which agents solve sequences of coding tasks under individual deadlines while negotiating access to a shared execution resource. This negotiation determines when and for how long they can inspect programs, compile code, and run tests. We find that agents spontaneously develop informal institutions: persistent rules and commitments grounded in reputation, reciprocity, and precedent. These arrangements, which we call institutional behaviors, carry across tasks and influence resource allocation, with agents sometimes forgoing immediate advantages to honor earlier agreements. We develop a 21-category taxonomy of negotiation strategies and emergent norms and use it to analyze eight models and audit more than 1,500 trajectories across different environmental settings. Among the models tested, newer frontier models exhibit more institutional behaviors than older or lightweight models. Alongside cooperation, we observe exclusionary coalitions and rare divide-and-conquer strategies. SCARCE provides a controlled setting for proactively and systematically auditing how these relationships emerge, shape access to resources, and affect the safety and coordination of multi-agent systems.

Emergent institution (following North (1990)): a rule, norm, or commitment that agents devise themselves, rather than receive from the environment, and that persists beyond the round in which it was formed to shape later resource allocation. Institutional behavior is any act of discovering, creating, citing, or honoring such a rule.

Accounts reconstructed after an incident cannot tell us when such arrangements form, what sustains them, or how they shape access to resources. That requires controlled settings in which agents interact repeatedly while performing other tasks. papers.title: Microwave spectroscopic evidence of a moiré-commensurate electron crystal in monolayer graphene
papers.abstract: We probe the conductivity of the lowest Landau level of a moiré-aligned monolayer graphene device by broadband microwave transmission through a coplanar waveguide ($\sim$50 mK, 15.4--18 T), isolating the longitudinal channel through a low-minus-high frequency band difference $D(ν)$. We resolve a series of minima in $D(ν)$ that drift with field along lines of fixed carrier density rather than fixed Landau filling, the hallmark of moiré-commensurate electron crystals. The strongest minimum is present at every field and matches no fractional quantum Hall or integer Hofstadter state. It lies at band filling $s=1/3$, one electron for every three moiré cells---the generalized Wigner crystal that DaSilva, Jung, and MacDonald predict as the most favorable fixed-density ($t=0$) commensuration. The weaker minima fall near neighboring commensurate fillings.

papers.title: Learn Only Where You Can't Compute: Structured Corrections to Gaussian Process Posteriors
papers.abstract: Physics-informed Gaussian processes (GPs) provide a principled framework for scientific inference by expressing uncertainty over empirical measurements, boundary conditions, and governing equations. However, they struggle to scale to larger datasets and nonlinear information. Conversely, diffusion models excel at learning complex distributions over functions from massive datasets, but struggle in scientific contexts where training data are scarce and physical or observational information must be incorporated. We propose a structured posterior-correction framework that combines a tractable Gaussian reference with data-driven corrections via generative learning. After a mean correction and covariance calibration, a diffusion model learns a targeted correction in a low-dimensional subspace selected to capture discrepancies from the reference, while the complement retains its Gaussian law. Across three scientific inference tasks, these corrections recover hidden modes, improve sample structure, and reduce prediction error relative to the Gaussian reference. Comparisons with full-field generative models reveal task-dependent benefits and tradeoffs between predictive accuracy and computational cost.
papers.intro:
Scientific inference often combines heterogeneous sources of information about an unknown function or state, such as noisy measurements, boundary conditions, physical laws, numerical models, and historical data. These sources typically leave the quantity of interest only partially determined, making uncertainty quantification an essential part of the inference problem (Stuart, 2010; Hennig et al., 2022). A central challenge is therefore not only to predict a function, but to construct a conditional distribution that combines the available information while remaining computationally tractable.

These sources typically leave the quantity of interest only partially determined, making uncertainty quantification an essential part of the inference problem (Stuart, 2010; Hennig et al., 2022). A central challenge is therefore not only to predict a function, but to construct a conditional distribution that combines the available information while remaining computationally tractable.

Probabilistic function-space methods provide a natural way to combine such information. Gaussian processes (GPs), in particular, place a distribution directly over the unknown function and admit analytic conditioning on linear information such as measurements, boundary values, or derivative observations (Rasmussen & Williams, 2005; Raissi et al., 2017; Pförtner et al., 2024). Probabilistic numerical methods extend this perspective to information supplied by differential equations and numerical computations (Hennig et al., 2022; Schmidt et al., 2021; Krämer et al., 2022). The resulting Gaussian posterior can encode substantial prior, physical, and observational structure before any learning from data is required. It provides both a predictive mean and a structured representation of the uncertainty that remains.

It provides both a predictive mean and a structured representation of the uncertainty that remains.

Such a probabilistic model is nevertheless only as expressive as the assumptions from which it is constructed. Incomplete physics, unresolved scales, latent nonlinear effects, or model mismatch may cause the true conditional law to differ systematically from its Gaussian approximation. Some of this discrepancy amounts to an incorrect location or spread; other effects produce multimodality or dependencies that a Gaussian cannot represent. Expressive generative models offer a complementary route. Diffusion models, in particular, can learn rich distributions over fields and trajectories (Ho et al., 2020; Song et al., 2021; Rühling et al., 2023; Rozet & Louppe, 2023). Learning the entire conditional law, however, also asks the generative model to represent structure already available from the Gaussian posterior. When scientific training data are expensive to obtain, there is a particular incentive to make use of this information. This raises a question: how much of a scientific conditional distribution needs to be learned when a useful Gaussian approximation can already be computed?

A mean correction adjusts its predictive center across the whole field (middle). First, we formulate a correction framework that uses an available Gaussian posterior to reduce the part of the conditional distribution assigned to a generative model. Gaussian and subspace KL decompositions explain which discrepancies the corrections can repair and what remains outside the learned block. Second, we develop a data-driven subspace search based on estimated validation log-score improvement, making the value of a richer law the criterion for where to learn it. Third, we evaluate this restricted learning task on regression and smoke transport problems with tractable posterior references and on numerical trajectory reconstruction, using learning curves and measured run times alongside distributional scores. Small learned blocks improve on the calibrated scaffold and can improve the structure of individual draws even when marginal scores are similar. papers.title: Uncertainty-Aware Federated Learning for Joint Communication and Computation in XR Systems
papers.abstract: The convergence of communication and computation, empowered by artificial intelligence (AI) enhanced capabilities, emerges as a key enabler for realizing the promising functionalities of the sixth-generation of communication systems (6G). To this end, this paper investigates an AI-native, robust network, where multiple base stations (BSs) simultaneously serve several extended reality (XR) devices. The paper then presents an innovative distributed deep learning-based approach to simultaneously manage the transmit and computing powers, and computation allocation, amidst uncertainties in both channel and computing states information. Under such an interference network scenario, the paper proposes a robust approach for minimizing the worst-case delay across the served XR devices, subject to computation and power constraints. The paper leverages a deep neural network (DNN) that can be trained either centrally or in a federated manner to map estimated channels and computation requirements to optimized resource allocations per BS. During training, uncertainty samples, reflecting both channel and computing estimation errors, are injected after the DNN output to account for such joint uncertainties. Our results validate the enhanced robust delay performance and scalability of joint uncertainty injection as compared to uncertainty-agnostic methods and state-of-the-art benchmarks, with federated learning-based solutions achieving near-centralized performance while enhancing efficiency, privacy, and adaptability.

papers.intro:
As the number of consumers combining smartphones and extended reality (XR) devices is set to double within five years, with three-quarters seeking XR experiences beyond home settings, the demand for cellular XR is rapidly accelerating [2]. Delivering gigabit-per-second data rates, millisecond-level latency, and high computational efficiency, XR is expected to drive the sixth-generation of communication systems (6G) toward major architectural and operational advancements [3]. This evolution requires substantial amounts of remote data connectivity and processing, underscoring the need for an integrated communication and computation platform [4]. Additionally, 6G is envisioned to comprise widespread ultra-dense networks with numerous base stations (BSs) and devices [5]. Efficient coordination within these networks is essential to prevent communication backbone overload while mitigating large-scale interference in real-time. Consequently, automated joint management of communication and computing resources is critical for future decentralized systems.

In response, the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) steers future networks (6G and beyond) toward native integration of machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI), enabling AI-native air interfaces and ML-driven resource management [6]. Deep learning, in particular, offers efficient and near-optimal wireless resource management [7], but often assumes perfect knowledge of channel conditions and computing requirements [8]. In practice, robust resource allocation strategies must be uncertainty-aware, i.e., explicitly account for uncertainties in both communication (e.g., missing or outdated channel state information [9]) and computation (e.g., fluctuating processing demands [10]). While prior works have addressed either communication or computation uncertainty separately, only a few have considered their joint effects [11]. From an AI/ML perspective, such uncertainties further propagate into learning-based decision-making. Since training data is often imperfect, ML-based architectures, as explored in [7], must operate under uncertainty in estimated channel states. However, a systematic approach to jointly handling communication and computation uncertainties in AI-driven optimization remains largely unexplored. To bridge this gap, this paper addresses such issues via a joint uncertainty injection scheme in a multi-BS, interference-limited network scenario, generalizing the single BS scenario considered in [1].

As 6G networks tend to embrace data processing decentralization, e.g., by pushing intelligence toward the edge, the paper proposed solutions are poised to provide a valuable data-driven, robust framework for managing multi-BS deployments [12]. In such decentralized networks, relying on traditional centralized learning would require transmitting raw data to a central entity, which is impractical due to privacy issues, excessive bandwidth consumption, and scalability limitations. Federated learning (FL) addresses these challenges allowing individual BSs to train local models using their own data and share only model updates with a central server [13, 14, 15]. This decentralized paradigm significantly reduces communication overhead while enhancing both scalability and security. Although FL aggregates model parameters globally, the resulting allocations remain heterogeneous across BSs, since each BS performs inference on distinct local data, e.g., local channel estimations. Thus, FL harmonizes training without enforcing identical allocation policies [16].

papers.title: Retrofitting Recurrent Vision-Language Models from Pretrained Backbones
papers.abstract: Recent work shows that depth recurrence can be retrofitted into pretrained language models. In this work, we adapt this paradigm for visual understanding, using depth recurrence to reduce the parameter footprint of a pretrained vision-language model (VLM). To this end, we prune layers from the language backbone of the VLM and loop over a subset of the remaining layers. At each step of the loop, a linear adapter merges the block's output with the token representations from the preceding layers and projects the fused representation back into the block. As the pruning impacts the original model performance, we propose a three-stage recovery training: first, we leverage a language-only pretraining to recover the performance of the language backbone, followed by an alignment of the vision-language projector, and a full fine-tuning of the model via visual instruction tuning. In the first and the last stage, we distill the outputs of the pretrained non-recurrent model into the recurrent model, which further improves the recovery. We evaluate the proposed approach on the TinyLLaVA-1.4B backbone without introducing any new vision-language data during retrofitting. We further show that the proposed retrofitting recurrence outperforms the setup of converting a recurrent LM into a VLM on the same data. Additionally, our ablations show how design choices, such as the adapter between recurrences and a larger recurrent block, lead to the improved performance of our approach. Finally, we find that our proposed model gains on reasoning-oriented benchmarks, whereas its performance on basic visual understanding benchmarks remains on par with the baseline.

papers.title: Environmental dependence in the halo model informed by the FLAMINGO simulations
papers.abstract: Galaxy-galaxy lensing (GGL) measurements around galaxy samples in different environments provide valuable information about the galaxy-halo connection. In such studies the halo model is commonly used to estimate physical parameters from the lensing signal, but the impact of environment is generally not considered. Our aim is to adapt the halo model to allow a density-split GGL analysis and to understand the environmental dependence of the elements of the model. We use the FLAMINGO suite of cosmological hydrodynamical simulations to construct samples of halos in underdense and overdense regions. Environment density is assigned to halos based on halo counts within an aperture, employing different aperture sizes to probe both local and large scales. We utilize spherical apertures with radii between $1 h^{-1} {\rm Mpc}$ and $10 h^{-1} {\rm Mpc}$. We find a strong dependence on environment for the halo mass function (HMF) and the halo bias. To account for this, we propose an empirical modification that can be applied to existing HMF prescriptions. We find that after a density split, the halo bias is approximately constant with mass. There is also an environmental dependence for the stellar-to-halo-mass relation (SHMR), the conditional stellar mass function, and the mass-concentration relation, all of which can be addressed with existing models. We evaluate the impact of overlooking environment on halo occupation distribution (HOD) parameter inference, finding that it leads to biased estimations of the SHMR and the satellite fraction. These results emphasize the need to review the assumptions adopted in the halo model when working with samples of galaxies binned by environment, and consequently, by galaxy properties that correlate with environment, such as morphology and color.

papers.intro:
The environment that halos and galaxies inhabit plays a fundamental role in their formation and evolution. Consequently, many of their physical and observational properties exhibit correlations with environment. The best-known example is the morphology–density relation identified by Dressler (1980), who showed that elliptical galaxies preferentially inhabit high density environments. Subsequent observational studies have reported similar environmental trends in properties such as stellar mass (Kauffmann et al., 2004; Li et al., 2006, e.g.), color (Blanton et al., 2005; Baldry et al., 2006; Li et al., 2006, e.g.), star formation rate (Lewis et al., 2002; Gomez et al., 2003; Kauffmann et al., 2004, e.g.) and stellar population age (Trussler et al., 2021; Zheng et al., 2017, e.g.), among others.

Consequently, many of their physical and observational properties exhibit correlations with environment. The best-known example is the morphology–density relation identified by Dressler (1980), who showed that elliptical galaxies preferentially inhabit high density environments. Cosmological simulations have been used to also identify correlations between environment and properties of dark-matter halos, such as concentration and spin (Avila-Reese et al., 2005; Maccio et al., 2007; Jeeson-Daniel et al., 2011; Hellwing et al., 2021, e.g.). In particular, halo mass shows a strong dependence on environment, with the most massive halos found mostly in high-density regions. This dependence is important when interpreting environmental trends in other galaxy and halo properties. Correlations between these properties and environment do not necessarily imply a direct environmental dependence; instead, they may be explained by the variation of the halo mass function (HMF) with environment and the dependence of the properties on halo mass (Lemson and Kauffmann, 1999; Abbas and Sheth, 2006; Crain et al., 2009; Briggs et al., 2026, e.g.). Consequently, disentangling genuine environmental dependencies from effects produced by a varying HMF can be a challenging task (Jeeson-Daniel et al., 2011). Many studies have analyzed the HMF for different cosmic environments (Lemson and Kauffmann, 1999; Sheth and Tormen, 2002, e.g.), although few attempts have been made to model them. The excursion set formalism and the effective universe approach were utilized for this purpose by Alonso et al. (2015) to model the HMF of the different elements of the cosmic web; however, neither reproduces the results obtained from simulations. The clustering of dark matter halos has also been shown to depend on environment; the excess in clustering compared to dark matter is described by the halo bias. This dependence of the halo bias on secondary halo properties other than halo mass is known as assembly bias (Gao and White, 2007; Dalal et al., 2008). Multiple works (Pujol et al., 2017; Shi and Sheth, 2018; Han et al., 2019) have found that the halo bias not only depends on environment, but also that its halo mass dependence may instead be attributed to environment. The connection between dark matter halos and the galaxies they host has also been observed to depend on environment. Halos in overdensities host on average more massive central galaxies (Tonnesen and Cen, 2015; Zehavi et al., 2018), given a fixed halo mass. Using the cosmological simulation TNG50, Xu et al. (2026) recently found that both the slope and normalization of the conditional stellar mass function (CSMF) of satellite galaxies depend on cosmic environment, with the CSMF of central galaxies presenting a more subtle environmental dependence.

Many of these environment-dependent properties are components of the halo model (Seljak, 2000; Cooray and Sheth, 2002; Asgari et al., 2023, e.g.) that describes the distribution of matter in the universe as contained exclusively in dark matter halos. This framework is frequently used in the modeling of weak lensing (WL) (Mandelbaum et al., 2006; Mishra et al., 2023; Dvornik et al., 2023, e.g.), the regime of gravitational lensing where the shapes of background galaxies are only slightly distorted as their light is bent due to foreground matter. As these distortions are very subtle, it is only possible to detect them statistically by averaging over multiples sources. The case where the distortions are measured around a foreground galaxy is referred to as galaxy-galaxy lensing (GGL). The halo model is able to predict these measurements and can be used in the estimation of cosmological parameters and in the study of properties of dark matter halos and the galaxy-halo connection. The latter provides insight into galaxy formation and, similarly to halo properties, is expected to depend on environment. GGL studies with density-selected samples would offer insight into this dependence; however, even though halo model ingredients are known to depend on environment, this is not usually accounted for and generally has not been modeled such that it can be incorporated into WL analyses. This modeling has been addressed in a number of works in different manners. Mandelbaum et al. (2006) performed GGL measurements for a low-density and a high-density sample, assuming that the halo bias of the former sample is negligible. Burger et al. (2025) instead introduced a density dependence into the stellar-to-halo-mass relation. However, the environmental dependence of the majority of the halo model’s components is not typically addressed in GGL works. This gap in the modeling needs to be addressed to facilitate GGL analyses with environment-selected samples.

papers.title: The $L\log L$-Luxemburg Discrepancy for Nonnegative Weights Suffers from the Curse of Dimensionality
papers.abstract: We study the normalized discrepancy in the Luxemburg norm generated by $Φ(s)=s\log(1+s)$. For arbitrary nonnegative quadrature weights, we prove that the associated information complexity suffers from the curse of dimensionality: for every $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, there exist constants $c_\varepsilon>0$ and $d_0=d_0(\varepsilon)\in\mathbb{N}$ such that \[N_{Φ,+}(\varepsilon,d)\ge c_{\varepsilon} d^{-1}(1.07735\ldots)^d \qquad \mbox{for all } d\ge d_0. \] The result therefore also applies to equal-weight quasi-Monte Carlo rules.

papers.title: Low magnon damping of a EuSe film down to millikelvin temperatures
papers.abstract: The rapid development of quantum magnonics over the past decade has created a demand for magnetic materials that keep their magnon losses low at millikelvin temperatures and add functionality beyond that of the established iron garnets and ferromagnetic metals. The europium chalcogenides are natural candidates $-$ they are magnetic semiconductors whose moment of $7\,μ_{\mathrm{B}}$ per Eu$^{2+}$ ion stems from a half-filled $4f$ shell with zero orbital momentum, so that spin-orbit coupling and intrinsic damping are expected to be weak. Here we characterize an epitaxial film of the metamagnet EuSe on diamagnetic BaF$_2$ by magnetometry and broadband ferromagnetic resonance from 10 K down to 30 mK. EuSe combines a saturation magnetization of 1100 kA/m with antiferromagnetic, ferrimagnetic and ferromagnetic phases that are reached with fields below 0.25 T. In contrast to a Gilbert-damped ferromagnet, the linewidth of the field-aligned film decreases with increasing frequency and field, and below 750 mK it no longer depends on temperature. At 30 mK, 68 GHz and 1.8 T, it reaches 5.5 mT, close to the values of bulk single crystals, which corresponds to a magnon lifetime of 2 ns and to an upper bound of $1.1\times10^{-3}$ for the Gilbert damping parameter. These properties make EuSe and the europium chalcogenides promising materials for hybrid quantum systems and quantum magnonics.

papers.title: The derived category of a generalized complex torus
papers.abstract: For any translation invariant generalized complex structure J on a torus we construct the derived category D(J) generalizing the derived category of coherent sheaves on a complex torus and the affine/convergent Fukaya category of a symplectic torus. The category is defined in terms of a non-commutative curved deformation of the Dolbeault algebra of a complex torus. We show that this category is independent of the chosen deformation path, which we prove using non-commutative Fourier-Mukai duality. We also prove that the action of O(2n,2n; Z) on the space of generalized complex structures leaves the category D(J) invariant. In particular, T-duality acts trivially on D(J). We construct concrete objects associated to affine Lagrangians in the derived category associated to a symplectic torus and show that their spaces of morphisms are given by Floer cohomology. We show that our construction is consistent with the homological mirror symmetry conjecture (including its non-commutative version).

papers.title: Sb-5$p$-mediated antiparallel Nd-Fe coupling in Nd$_3$Fe$_3$Sb$_7$
papers.abstract: We uncover the microscopic mechanism underlying the antiparallel Nd-Fe coupling in the intermetallic 4$f$-3$d$-5$p$ compound Nd$_3$Fe$_3$Sb$_7$ by means of high-field x-ray magnetic circular dichroism (XMCD) spectroscopy, complemented by magnetization measurements and density-functional-theory (DFT) calculations. This coupling is unexpected for intermetallics composed of light rare-earth and transition-metal elements. Sb $M_{4,5}$-edge XMCD measurements indicate a clear spin polarization of Sb 5$p$ states antiparallel to the Fe 3$d$ moments. DFT calculations reveal the site-dependent character of the Sb moments and, together with the Fe-Sb antiparallel alignment seen by XMCD, identify a Fe 3$d$-Sb 5$p$-Nd 5$d$ hybridization pathway for the antiparallel Nd-Fe coupling. Pulsed-field XMCD reveals a field-induced spin reorientation through the evolution of the $c$-axis projections of the Nd and Fe moments. Nd$_3$Fe$_3$Sb$_7$, thus, provides a platform for exploring antiparallel rare-earth-transition-metal ($R$-$T$) coupling mediated by transition-metal 3$d$-ligand $p$-rare-earth 5$d$ hybridization in light-$R$-$T$ intermetallics with $p$-elements.

papers.title: FeaTok: Feature-Loss Tokenization for Image Generation
papers.abstract: Discrete image generators learn the distribution of tokens produced by an image tokenizer. These token representations should be easy for generators to model, not merely enable faithful image reconstruction. Yet these tokenizers are commonly trained to reconstruct pixels, which prioritizes low-level fidelity and may disrupt representation structure useful for generation. Motivated by feature-predictive self-supervised learning, we introduce feature-loss tokenization (FeaTok), which trains discrete tokens by reconstructing pretrained features rather than pixels. Ablations across SigLIP, SigLIP2, DINOv2, and DINOv3 show better generative performance with FeaTok. In class-conditional generation, FeaTok advances the quality-compute Pareto frontier, reducing gFDr6 at 256x256 by up to 29 percent over the strongest discrete baselines and outperforming the strongest unguided continuous baseline (RAEv2) with 38 times less sampling compute. FeaTok also achieves higher human-preference reward-model scores than prior art without reward-based training and surpasses continuous and discrete text-conditional baselines on three benchmarks with only 500 fine-tuning updates after pre-training.

Image generation quality depends on discrete tokens that are both expressive and easy for a generator to model. Previous discrete tokenizers focus on reconstruction performance, which targets the first property, expressivity. However, generation also depends on the second property, which we call generative learnability: how easily a generator fits the token distribution at a given budget. These two properties do not always align, as observed for both continuous and discrete image tokenizers and generators (Gu et al., 2024; Yao et al., 2025; Ramanujan et al., 2025).

We refer to the representations of encoders trained with SSL objectives in feature space as pretrained visual features (see Def. 1). Moreover, RAE (Zheng et al., 2026b) and RAEv2 (Singh et al., 2026) show that the benefits of pretrained visual features go beyond representation learning and successfully transfer to image generation.

papers.title: Sparse Federated Echo State Networks for Time-Series Classification via Smooth-L1 Regularization
papers.abstract: Echo State Networks (ESNs), as lightweight implementations of reservoir computing, provide efficient solutions for temporal data processing in resource-constrained environments. While standard ESNs offer computational efficiency, their dense readout layers inflate the stored model and the per-sample inference cost. This paper introduces a Smooth-L1 regularized ESN (SL1ESN) that promotes sparsity in the readout layer while preserving differentiability for gradient-based optimization. The method employs a twice-differentiable Smooth-L1 approximation compatible with Newton's method, which we exploit both for centralized training and for a second-order (Newton-step) federated aggregation scheme. Under a single fixed shrinkage threshold shared by every dataset and both settings, experiments on seven time-series classification benchmarks show that SL1ESN learns readouts that are 77-95% sparse in the centralized setting and 75-95% sparse in the federated one. On five of the seven benchmarks, the mean accuracy of the sparse readout over ten seeds differs from that of the stronger dense baseline by at most 0.7 points in the centralized setting and 1.6 points in the federated one, differences of the same order as the seed-to-seed variation, while on the remaining two it trails by 2.4-5.8 points. The second-order federated update converges in only a few rounds. The resulting sparsity compresses the stored model, the per-sample inference cost, and the server-to-client broadcast by a comparable factor. These results demonstrate the practical value of sparse readouts for edge computing and IoT deployments.

papers.intro:
Machine learning has become a cornerstone for extracting patterns from complex datasets. While a large share of applied machine learning operates on tabular, independently sampled records, an important class of problems is instead inherently sequential, in the sense that the measurements arrive as a time-ordered stream and the ordering itself carries the information. Sensor and IoT telemetry, physiological recordings such as ECG, industrial process traces, and financial series all fall into this class, and they are also precisely the settings addressed in this paper, where the data are generated continuously and often on distributed, resource-constrained devices. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) have long been a natural choice for such temporal processing because their hidden-state dynamics allow them to capture dependencies across time. However, traditional RNNs are often difficult to train reliably on long sequences and can suffer from vanishing or exploding gradients, which hampers the learning of long-range dependencies (Pascanu et al., 2013; Zucchet and Orvieto, 2024; Tiezzi et al., 2026). Gated architectures such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997) and Gated Recurrent Units (GRU) (Chung et al., 2014) alleviate some of these optimization challenges, and more recent designs continue this line. The xLSTM architecture (Beck et al., 2024) augments the LSTM cell with exponential gating and matrix memory to recover much of the scaling behavior of Transformers while retaining a recurrent, constant-memory inference path, and deep state-space models pursue a similar goal from the linear-dynamics side (Tiezzi et al., 2026). All of these nevertheless remain fully trained sequence models. They introduce a large number of trainable parameters and require backpropagation through time, with the associated computational and memory demands. These costs can become prohibitive in resource-constrained or real-time deployment scenarios, where compact and efficient temporal models remain especially desirable (Lu et al., 2025; Cordova-Cardenas et al., 2025). Echo State Networks (ESNs) offer a fundamentally different response to the same difficulty. They are not a reaction to the recent architectures above but a parallel development. Introduced by Jaeger (2001) at essentially the same time as gated recurrent models were becoming established, they sidestep the training difficulties of RNNs rather than engineering around them, and they remain a highly efficient class of recurrent models within the broader paradigm of Reservoir Computing (RC) (Lukoševičius and Jaeger, 2009). The core idea of RC is to separate the system into a fixed, randomly initialized recurrent layer, known as the reservoir, and a trainable output layer, called the readout. The reservoir acts as a high-dimensional dynamic memory that nonlinearly transforms the input signal into a rich state space. In standard ESNs, only the readout-layer weights are trained, often via ridge regression. By decoupling recurrent state generation from output-layer optimization, this design avoids direct training of recurrent connections and thereby reduces many of the optimization difficulties commonly associated with conventional RNNs. As a result, ESN training is typically much faster and often more stable than that of fully trained recurrent architectures (Liu et al., 2026; Matzner and Mráz, 2025; Yadav et al., 2024). Despite these significant advantages, standard ESN implementations employ a dense readout layer, meaning every reservoir neuron is connected to every output unit. While this ensures full utilization of the reservoir’s representational power, it carries several drawbacks. First, dense readouts are prone to overfitting, since every reservoir neuron, including redundant ones, contributes to the output. Second, dense readouts increase the model’s memory footprint and computational cost during inference. These limitations are particularly relevant in resource-constrained environments such as edge devices and Internet of Things (IoT) sensors, and in distributed or federated computing scenarios where communication bandwidth is often a bottleneck (Dritsas and Trigka, 2025; Akhtarshenas et al., 2024; Polato et al., 2026).

To address these issues, sparsity-promoting methods in neural networks have been extensively studied (Haugstvedt et al., 2023; Liu, 2020; Villmann et al., 2010). Applying L1 regularization to the readout layer of an ESN yields a sparse model that is more memory-efficient and better suited for efficient inference. Sparsity is often also motivated by interpretability; because the reservoir features are strongly correlated, however, many different supports realize an equally sparse and accurate readout, so throughout this paper we claim compression rather than feature selection (Section 6.4). However, the L1 penalty is non-differentiable at zero, which complicates gradient-based optimization. While specialized algorithms such as Least Angle Regression (LARS) (Efron et al., 2004) and Coordinate Descent (CD) (Wright, 2015) solve the LASSO reliably in a centralized setting, they fit poorly into distributed optimization frameworks such as FedAvg (McMahan et al., 2017), a Federated Learning (FL) approach whose aggregation step is an average of locally computed, smooth parameter or gradient updates. The mismatch is structural rather than a matter of implementation. First, both algorithms are path- or coordinate-sequential, since LARS builds the solution by adding one variable to the active set at a time and CD updates one coordinate while holding the others fixed, so neither exposes a single descent direction over all coordinates that a client could compute locally and a server could average. Second, their state is a discrete active set rather than a vector in a linear space; clients trained on different local data return different supports, and the average of models with disjoint supports is neither sparse nor the solution of any of the local problems, so the aggregation step loses the very property the penalty was introduced to obtain. Third, and specific to our setting, neither method produces the curvature information that a second-order server update requires. Because the L1 term is non-differentiable at zero, no Hessian of the full objective exists that clients could compute and sum.

papers.title: Deep Reinforcement Learning for HPC Job Scheduling: A Statistical Evaluation
papers.abstract: Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) offers learned job selection for High-Performance Computing (HPC), but performance against heuristics alone does not establish value beyond action masking. Six DRL treatments are compared: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), Advantage Actor-Critic (A2C), and Deep Q-Network (DQN), each with and without masking. Three heuristics and a seed-paired masked uniform random control provide baselines across ten seeds on two real Slurm (Simple Linux Utility for Resource Management) workload traces, one homogeneous and one heterogeneous, under a common non-parametric framework. All masked treatments complete evaluation, whereas unmasked treatments are truncated. On the homogeneous trace, no masked DRL treatment significantly improves average waiting time or average and maximum bounded slowdown over the control. On the heterogeneous trace, MaskablePPO improves all three metrics relative to the control. Its average waiting time is equivalent to that of the three heuristics within a 10% margin, and its maximum bounded slowdown is 22% lower than that of Last-Come, First-Served (LCFS). MaskablePPO has the leading average waiting-time rank among complete treatments on both traces, but Nemenyi comparisons detect no significant difference from MaskableA2C. Among masked variants, MaskablePPO has the lowest recorded mean training time, while MaskableDQN has the lowest mean decision latency. These findings distinguish completion from baseline-specific scheduling gains and support including a masked random control when assessing the value of learned selection.

papers.intro:
High-Performance Computing (HPC) job schedulers determine when jobs run and which resources they receive [15]. Increasing workload and hardware diversity complicates the balance between waiting time and resource utilisation [15]. Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) offers learned scheduling policies as an alternative to traditional heuristics [5, 25]. Their practical value, however, depends on whether learning improves schedule quality enough to justify training and decision-time costs.

Existing studies benchmark individual DRL schedulers against traditional baselines [18, 16], leaving limited evidence for choosing between DRL algorithms under a common experimental protocol. A structured review of 53 papers identifies Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) family methods in 40% of the sample, but this prevalence does not establish their superiority. Moreover, performance against a heuristic alone does not establish that learned selection adds value beyond action masking. A controlled comparison must therefore examine algorithm choice and masking together, evaluating schedule quality alongside computational cost.

Action masking excludes infeasible choices before action selection. MaskablePPO, MaskableDQN, and MaskableA2C apply this restriction to their corresponding base algorithms. The objective is to compare DRL algorithms in terms of schedule quality and computational cost, and to assess learning value beyond action masking. The comparison includes six DRL variants: PPO, Deep Q-Network (DQN), and Advantage Actor-Critic (A2C), each with and without masking. Three heuristics and a masked random control provide baselines on two Slurm (Simple Linux Utility for Resource Management) workload traces. Waiting time, slowdown, turnaround time, and resource utilisation are assessed through non-parametric comparisons [2]. The investigation is guided by three research questions (RQs): 1. What does action masking contribute to schedule quality and evaluation completion? 2. Does PPO’s schedule quality and computational cost relative to A2C and DQN justify its prevalence in recent HPC scheduling literature? 3. How does the performance of learned policies relative to heuristic and masked random baselines differ between the homogeneous and heterogeneous workload traces, considering training and decision-time costs?

papers.title: $p$-Laplace Serrin problem on planar annuli
papers.abstract: We prove a rigidity result for the problem $Δ_p u=-2$ defined on a ring-shaped domain in $\mathbb{R}^2$, when homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions are imposed and $p\in(1,2)$. This problem admits a natural physical interpretation, as it describes the steady laminar flow of a generalised Newtonian fluid exhibiting shear-thinning behaviour. Our symmetry result is obtained assuming that the set of maximum points, denoted by $Σ$, is a smooth closed curve, and there are no other critical points outside it; moreover, an appropriate asymptotic expansion of the solution near $Σ$ is required. Although our approach is inspired by the comparison strategy of [arXiv:2505.04458], the main ingredients used there are intrinsically linear and have no direct counterparts for the $p$-Laplacian. This requires the introduction of new ideas and techniques.

papers.title: Does Compression Imply Generalization? A Minimum Description Length Perspective
papers.abstract: A central question in modern learning theory is what notion of compression, if any, explains why over-parameterized neural networks generalize. Existing answers measure complexity at different levels, ranging from weights to representations; however, estimating the associated quantities either requires held-out data in principle or relies on the challenging (ultra) high-dimensional mutual information estimation. To overcome these challenges, we approach the question through the minimum description length (MDL) principle, and specifically, we propose the prequential regret as a complementary signal that is computable from the training trajectory alone. We establish that, in the (nearly) interpolating regime, the expected prequential regret upper-bounds the description length of the trained parameter under the algorithm-induced distribution, and that this description length translates into a high-probability generalization bound in the PAC-MDL setting. Along the way, we show that the encoder-complexity correction recently added to the algorithm-level information bottleneck (IB) is upper-bounded by an MDL parameter description length, \new{bringing together} the two views of compression from MDL and IB. Empirically, the prequential regret tracks the generalization error on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, with Pearson correlations exceeding 0.9.

Three mainstream approaches make this complexity precise as a coding cost. First, PAC-Bayes [28, 15] bounds generalization by DKL(Q∥π)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q\|\pi) between a posterior QQ over learned models and a prior π\pi, which by the bits-back argument [23, 24] is the code length of transmitting a sample from QQ induced by π\pi [17]. Second, the information-theoretic line [33, 42] replaces the prior with the data-marginal and bounds generalization by I⁡(S,W)I(S;W), measuring how much information the weights WW retain about the training set SS. Since I⁡(S,W)I(S;W) can be infinite for deterministic algorithms, the supersample/CMI variants [38, 19, 20] introduce a pooled sample Z~\tilde{Z} of 2​n2n points together with a uniform selector UU that assigns half to training and half to a ‘ghost’ test set, and bound generalization by I⁡(W;U∣Z~)I(W;U\mid\tilde{Z}), capturing how much the weights leak about the train/test assignment given the pool. Third, the information bottleneck (IB) [39, 40, 37] asks how much the internal representations ZZ retain about XX, with I⁡(X,Z)I(X;Z) or I⁡(X;Z∣Y)I(X;Z\mid Y) [39] as the coding cost of the representation. Recent work observes that vanilla IB implicitly assumes a fixed encoder and can fail when the encoder, i.e., the map from an input to its internal representation, is itself learned from data [18]; Kawaguchi et al. [25] hence addresses this by extending IB to the algorithm level, adding an encoder-complexity term that penalizes how much the trained encoder depends on the training set.

While these three lines capture different aspects of compression, they have the following shortcomings when we want a compression signal directly tied to fixed algorithms for training networks. On the conceptual side, what is being compressed is different across the literature: PAC-Bayes and the I⁡(S,W)I(S;W) line compress at the level of weights, while IB compresses at the level of representations, and the two notions have evolved separately, leaving it unclear whether they are facets of one underlying property or distinct phenomena that share a name. Further, even granting a notion of compression, whether Occam-style reasoning survives for over-parameterized neural networks is itself debated [45, 36, 30].

We summarize our main contributions as follows. • We connect MDL parameter compression to the algorithm-level information bottleneck, showing that the encoder-complexity correction added to obtain the first rigorous IB-based generalization bound is upper-bounded by an MDL parameter description length, which relates the two views of compression from IB and MDL (Section 3). • We prove that, in the (nearly) interpolating regime, the expected prequential coding regret upper-bounds the description length of the trained parameter under the algorithm-induced distribution over parameters given the data (Section 4). • We further show that this description length translates into a generalization bound in the PAC-MDL setting, with the algorithm-dependent content carried entirely by the prequential regret. papers.title: On the uniform-in-time propagation of chaos for the Motsch-Tadmor model
papers.abstract: We consider the Motsch-Tadmor model, a modification of the Cucker-Smale model for flocking dynamics that incorporates asymmetric communication weights. In the case of uniformly positive interactions, we consider the validity problem for the limiting kinetic equation, proving a uniform-in-time propagation of chaos result in the moving frame given by the consensus velocities. The result is obtained by studying the reversibility of the communication weights and by implicitly characterizing the asymptotic consensus.

papers.title: Coherent and Incoherent Time-Resolved Diffuse Scattering Intensity from First Principles
papers.abstract: Time-resolved diffuse scattering from X-ray free-electron lasers and ultrafast electron diffraction gives access to the nonequilibrium lattice dynamics of photoexcited solids in reciprocal space. Existing interpretations have often relied on simplified models. Here we present a first-principles formulation of the time-dependent first-order diffuse intensity in which coherent and incoherent contributions emerge on equal footing. By assuming the probe-pulse coherence time to be longer than the characteristic electronic timescales, but shorter than those of the ionic motion, we work in the density-matrix formalism and derive equations of motion for the displacement-displacement correlators in a basis of instantaneous, out-of-equilibrium Born-Oppenheimer normal modes. We show how the incoherent contribution, governed by the phonon occupations, and a coherent contribution, governed by the anomalous phonon correlators, emerge. The non-trivial coherent dynamics is shown to be induced both by the photoinduced phonon-frequency shift and by electron-phonon scattering off the nonequilibrium carrier distribution. We implement the resulting equations using Wannier interpolation in the \textsc{EPI}q code and apply them to photoexcited germanium. The calculated diffuse intensity reproduces both the oscillation frequencies and the rising incoherent background observed experimentally, opening the way to a systematic interpretation of time-resolved diffuse scattering in ultrafast experiments.
