papers.intro:
The investigation of lattice dynamics is fundamental to understanding the macroscopic properties of solids, from thermal conductivity to structural phase transitions. X-ray and neutron scattering are leading experimental techniques for measuring phonon dispersion relations, as they provide access to structural information via the Bragg peaks and to vibrational properties via the thermal diffuse background. Because the thermal diffuse scattering cross section is far smaller than that of the Bragg peaks, this connection became broadly exploitable with the advent of bright X-ray sources. At equilibrium, and within the Born-Oppenheimer and harmonic approximations, the first-order thermal diffuse scattering intensity is proportional to the atomic displacement-displacement correlation function, so that fitting force-constant models to the measured pattern yields the eigenfrequencies and eigenvectors characterizing the vibrational spectrum [26, 3, 22, 50, 51].

Recent advances have greatly expanded our ability to perform femtosecond-resolved experiments. High-brightness X-ray free-electron lasers (XFELs) and ultrafast electron diffraction (UED) sources can be used in a pump-probe configuration to monitor the thermal diffuse scattering intensity across large volumes of reciprocal space with sub-picosecond temporal resolution [46]. Ultrashort probe pulses reduce temporal averaging enough to capture nearly instantaneous snapshots of the displacement-displacement correlators, opening the possibility of directly probing the phonon spectrum of a photoexcited, out-of-equilibrium system. A characteristic dynamical signature is an oscillation of the thermal diffuse scattering intensity at a given momentum transfer at twice the phonon frequency of the corresponding reduced wavevector. The Fourier transform of the time trace therefore yields the phonon dispersion, with an energy resolution primarily set by the length of the delay scan [53].

Time-resolved diffuse signals contain a great deal of information about ultrafast atomic motion, and it is now well established that they exhibit two qualitatively distinct types of temporal modulation. The first is comparatively slow, developing over a few picoseconds, and reflects the gradual heating of the lattice as electrons and phonons exchange energy following the pump: the phonon occupations increase and the diffuse intensity grows with the amplitude of the thermal fluctuations [42, 38]. The second is a faster oscillatory component superimposed on that background, which carries direct information on specific phonon modes and signals the emergence of coherent phonon correlations. Both are clearly visible, as exemplified by the measurements on germanium samples of Refs. 46 and 53, where the Fourier transform of the oscillatory component shows dominant weight at twice the frequency of the lowest phonon branches.

Both are clearly visible, as exemplified by the measurements on germanium samples of Refs. 46 and 53, where the Fourier transform of the oscillatory component shows dominant weight at twice the frequency of the lowest phonon branches.

Subsequent experiments established time-resolved diffuse scattering as a probe of the coupling between the lattice and other degrees of freedom and revealed features that go beyond a simple photoinduced frequency renormalization. In PbTe, additional spectral components appear that cannot be assigned to the double-frequency overtone of a single branch, but instead correspond to sum and difference frequencies of transverse optical and transverse acoustic modes [23]. These features were interpreted as evidence of the photoinduced modification and coupling of phonon eigenmodes. In bismuth, the usual overtone signal coexists with additional weight on branches satisfying the resonance condition 2​ω𝐪​ν=ωA1​g2\omega_{\mathbf{q}\nu}=\omega_{A_{1g}} with the coherently driven A1​gA_{1g} optical mode, a signature of strong anharmonic decay of that mode into correlated phonon pairs at 𝐪\mathbf{q} and −𝐪-\mathbf{q} [45]. Related measurements have resolved phonon squeezing, anisotropic lattice cooling, and the decay of coherent optical phonons into acoustic modes [27], uncovered the real-time dynamics of the ultrafast structural phase transition in VO2 [49], and identified a nonthermal bonding origin [20] for the photoexcited lattice instability of SnSe [21, 31, 10].

The theoretical description of these experiments has often treated the coherent and incoherent components of the signal using separate approaches. The incoherent background is usually described by the two-temperature model of Allen [1] and its multi-temperature extensions. In this approach, the lattice is assigned one or a few effective temperatures whose evolution follows rate equations with an electron-phonon coupling constant expressible through the Eliashberg function [6], or by more refined Boltzmann equation approaches tracking the dynamical evolution of electronic and phononic occupations in time [4, 33]. More recently, first-principles nonequilibrium formulations have been developed that describe phonon occupations and anomalous phonon correlations on the same footing [41]. Population-based approaches give an intuitive and often quantitatively adequate account of the slow rise of the diffuse intensity, but do not by themselves describe the coherent oscillations. A widely used description of the oscillatory component is the sudden-quench model of Johnson et al. [24], building on the treatment of harmonic oscillators with time-dependent parameters of Kiss et al. [25] and on the identification of light-driven squeezed lattice states in second-order Raman scattering [12]. Within these frameworks, the normal-mode frequencies are assumed to change instantaneously from their ground-state to their photoexcited values, and the resulting impulsive squeezing of the vibrational wavepacket produces an oscillation of its variance, and hence of the diffuse intensity, at twice the new frequency, while the mean displacement is unchanged. This model picture, while qualitative, gives a useful description of the coherent oscillations and has served as a standard interpretive guide for experiments [47].

papers.title: Stability Analysis in IBR-Dominated Grids: Model-Based and Data-Driven Methodologies
papers.abstract: Stability issues in converter-dominated grids have a multifold nature, where static, small-signal and large-signal phenomena can influence each other. Capturing the interplay among these different stability aspects requires a rethinking of conventional modeling and analysis tools for power systems. As a further complication, Intellectual Property protection among manufacturers and system operators makes detailed converters and grid models unattainable. This motivates the use of data-driven approaches for stability analysis and control, nevertheless achieving an insightful representation of static, small-signal and large-signal phenomena from data still leaves many open questions. This paper discusses model-based and data-driven methodologies for stability analysis of converter-dominated grids. The instability mechanisms of static, small-signal and large-signal phenomena are conceptually explained, and the capability of different modeling and analysis tools to investigate them is examined. The effectiveness of data-driven methodologies to analyze instability phenomena in their multifold nature is debated, and the challenges on data completeness, model generalization under untrained conditions, physical interpretability, and uncertainty awareness are discussed.

In the last decades, the role of power electronics in electric grids has been elevated from a sole power conversion stage for small renewable generation units to a smart and multifunctional interface for multi-MW power plants with grid stabilizing capabilities [1, 2]. With the increasing adoption of grid forming control, Inverter-Based Resources (IBRs) are taking more and more responsibility in establishing the voltage and regulating the grid frequency, taking over the traditional role of Synchronous Generators (SG) [3, 4, 5].

In the last decades, the role of power electronics in electric grids has been elevated from a sole power conversion stage for small renewable generation units to a smart and multifunctional interface for multi-MW power plants with grid stabilizing capabilities [1, 2]. With the increasing adoption of grid forming control, Inverter-Based Resources (IBRs) are taking more and more responsibility in establishing the voltage and regulating the grid frequency, taking over the traditional role of Synchronous Generators (SG) [3, 4, 5].

This paradigm shift toward a power electronics-dominated grid led to the emergence of new and diverse stability issues [6], increasingly observed in recent blackouts, including undamped oscillations and voltage regulation problems (e.g. Spain 2025 [7]), low inertia (e.g. South Australia 2016 [8, 1]), and large-scale tripping of renewable power plants due to loss of synchronism (e.g. Texas Odessa [9]). The mechanisms behind converter-driven grids instability events are highly complex and multifold [6], i.e. they can simultaneously involve small-signal phenomena (e.g. undamped oscillations), large-signal phenomena (e.g. loss of synchronism due to current limitation) and static phenomena (e.g. insufficient long-term reactive power support) [6, 10, 11]. To ensure grid stability under all points of view, recent grid codes – especially with the emerging grid forming converters – are updating IBR functional requirements considering concurrently multiple aspects, e.g. oscillation damping capability, voltage regulation policies, grid supporting functionalities, Fault-Ride Through (FRT) behaviour [4, 12, 5].

Analyzing all these diverse aspects and meeting all IBR requirements simultaneously is a tough problem, which requires analytic tools able to perform static, small-signal, and large-signal dynamic analyses [13, 14]. A formidable challenge for model-based analysis tools is to capture the interplay among different aspects of grid stability. As an example, long-term reactive power regulation in IBRs is commonly used for improving static grid operation, yet it concurrently affects also IBR oscillation damping capability and grid small-signal stability, by changing the grid equilibrium point [14]. Furthermore, large-signal instability, usually considered as a dynamic problem, is often driven by the non-existence of a post-fault equilibrium point, whose assessment is rather a static problem [15, 16].

Analyzing IBR-based grid stability, embracing the interrelation between static and dynamic aspects, is further complicated by Intellectual Property (IP) protection among different manufacturers, system operators and other stakeholders [17]. That makes detailed analytical models of power electronics-dominated grids unattainable, and heavily limits the applicability of conventional model-based methodologies [18]. To overcome this issue, data-driven methodologies for stability analysis and control of IBR-dominated power systems are gaining increasing attention [17, 19]. However, capturing the interplay among different aspects of the stability with data-driven methods is even more difficult than with model-based methods, and leaves still nowadays many open questions.

The instability mechanisms of static, small-signal and large-signal phenomena are firstly elaborated (see Table I and Fig. 1). Then, the responsible factors behind these three types of instabilities in IBR-dominated grids are unveiled, focusing on the impact of IBR control system dynamics, IBR physical constraints (e.g. current limitation) and interaction with AC grids and with other IBRs (see Table II). What emerges from the discussion is that several dynamics and constraints of IBRs and power grids affect different types of stability simultaneously. Additionally, for some control dynamics e.g. synchronization, the guidelines for improving different aspects of the IBR stability are even conflicting: slow synchronization improves the small-signal stability [14, 16], nevertheless it deteriorates the large-signal stability [20, 21]. These considerations motivate a profound rethinking of IBR stability analysis tools to offer a more holistic perspective on stability, i.e. be able to study the interplay among static, small-signal and large-signal aspects.

With model-based methods, properly representing the IBR nonlinearity and performing combined static/dynamic stability analyses are of utmost importance to capture this interplay [14].

With model-based methods, properly representing the IBR nonlinearity and performing combined static/dynamic stability analyses are of utmost importance to capture this interplay [14].

With data-driven methods, in addition to the two aforementioned factors, assessing the completeness and informativeness of the collected data plays a critical role [19]. For small-signal analyses at a single operating point, for example, IBR impedance measurements over a wide frequency range in dd and qq channels are sufficient [22]. However, to capture the interplay between small-signal stability and static equilibrium point, a much larger amount of data across multiple operating points are required [19]. Studying transient stability issues from data is even more difficult, since quantifying the completeness and informativeness of the collected data in presence of complex nonlinearities is challenging [23, 24]. Once data are collected, a further issue is to find a proper model structure and computational method to fit data into models with high accuracy and generalizability [17, 19]. The generalizability of data-driven models for unseen operating conditions or unseen IBR configurations is indeed always limited; transfer learning has been proposed to partially mitigate this issue by embedding domain knowledge into the learning process [17, 25]. Moreover, purely black-box data-driven models may still violate fundamental physical constraints, and they lack the interpretability of first-principle models familiar to engineers, reducing their trustworthiness in safety-critical applications.

papers.title: Observing minimal submanifolds with isolated singularities on open sets of metrics
papers.abstract: We develop a perturbative theory for minimal submanifolds with only (strongly) isolated singularities, with respect to varying background Riemannian metrics. As an application, we obtain a general "sporadic persistence" criterion, thus naturally complementing the non-persistence theorem by the authors. In particular, such a criterion is satisfied by the spherical suspension in $\mathbb{S}^{3m+2}$ of the Veronese embedding of $\mathbb{K}\mathbb{P}^2$ for $\mathbb{K}=\mathbb{R},\mathbb{C},\mathbb{H},\mathbb{O}$ (the normed division algebras) in the round spheres of dimension $3m+1=4,7,13,25$ respectively, thereby providing families of continuously varying $(2m+1)$-dimensional stationary varifolds with isolated singularities that are observable on an open set of metrics. By our previous results, these phenomena cannot possibly occur in the codimension one scenario.

papers.intro:
The purpose of the present manuscript is to contribute to the study of minimal submanifolds with isolated singularities (that is, in the language of [4], of MSI), obtaining some results that complement (essentially: in the opposite direction) those contained in our previous work on the subject. More specifically, motivated by a question posed by Neves in relation to Hsiang’s solution of the spherical Bernstein conjecture [9], we proved in [4] that non-smooth MSI (albeit easily constructible in space forms, e. g. by spherical suspensions of closed, minimal submanifolds) are generically not observable (namely: they do not exist for a Baire-generic choice of the background metric) except for some potentially persistent ones that are singled out by the property of saturating certain inequalities pertaining to the geometry of the links at their singularities. Our scope here is to provide a general, verifiable criterion for actual persistence of MSI on open sets of metrics (see Theorem A for a precise statement) and then to present instances where such a criterion is actually satisfied (see Corollary B). We recall that the aforementioned inequalities in fact never hold in the codimension one case, which rules out any sort of “cheap” examples, and that they rely on the actual computation of the Morse index of (smooth, closed) minimal submanifolds in round spheres, that is a notoriously challenging task in its own right.

The previous existence results are obtained by developing a perturbation theory for MSI. Since – among other reasons – most examples of MSI are in space forms, it is immediately clear that one is naturally confronted with the symmetries of the ambient manifold, which results in obstructions to a direct application of the implicit function theorem in suitable (albeit a priori not obviously determined) functional spaces. What we do is rather, in general terms, a Lyapunov-Schmidt reduction “in the large” of the problem with respect to nonlinear constraints. As a byproduct, we also obtain multiplicity results of Morse-theoretic character, which we work out explicitly in the special case of the (codimension two) spherical suspension of the Veronese embedding of the real projective plane ℝ​ℙ2\mathbb{R}\mathbb{P}^{2} in the round four-dimensional sphere. That example, which is perhaps the simplest possible instance of application of our theory, already displays a number of interesting features.

papers.title: Statistical Laws of Human Mobility under Large-Scale Behavioural Shock
papers.abstract: Human mobility follows robust statistical laws, but whether these laws persist under large, sudden behavioural shocks remains unclear. Here we analyse privacy-enhanced GPS trajectories of over one million users in California and 180,000 in Massachusetts from January to September 2020, spanning the onset and easing of COVID-19 restrictions. During restrictions, individual ranges contracted below a characteristic scale of about 5 km, while short- and medium-range trip lengths and rare long-distance trips persisted. Exploration slowed from super-diffusive to near-diffusive, and visits concentrated on a few habitual locations. Trajectory shape, once rescaled, was preserved, and the entropy reduction is largely explained by fewer visited locations rather than more regular routines. Recovery after reopening was heterogeneous rather than a uniform return to baseline, and the decline began before mandatory orders. These results suggest that restrictions reorganised, rather than simply rescaled, individual mobility, with implications for mobility-based epidemic models.

papers.intro:
The COVID-19 pandemic raised fundamental questions about how to contain the spread of a novel disease [1, 2] and about the collateral effects of containment strategies [3]. In the absence of vaccines, Non-Pharmaceutical Interventions (NPIs) were the primary tool adopted by governments to limit transmission [4, 5, 6], significantly reshaping human behaviour and mobility patterns [7]. Importantly, a substantial share of these behavioural changes preceded formal mandates, driven by voluntary responses to risk information [8, 9, 10], a distinction with direct consequences for how mobility-based models should be calibrated. This context produced a large-scale observational perturbation of routine mobility and provided the scientific community with new challenges to model epidemic spread under changing behavioural regimes [11, 12, 13, 14, 15].

In the absence of vaccines, Non-Pharmaceutical Interventions (NPIs) were the primary tool adopted by governments to limit transmission [4, 5, 6], significantly reshaping human behaviour and mobility patterns [7]. Importantly, a substantial share of these behavioural changes preceded formal mandates, driven by voluntary responses to risk information [8, 9, 10], a distinction with direct consequences for how mobility-based models should be calibrated. This context produced a large-scale observational perturbation of routine mobility and provided the scientific community with new challenges to model epidemic spread under changing behavioural regimes [11, 12, 13, 14, 15].

Aggregate and anonymised mobile phone data have long been shown to support the modelling of epidemic geography [16, 17], while individual GPS trajectories are seen as a possible resource to improve adaptive estimates of contact patterns and spatial transmission dynamics [18, 1, 19, 20, 21]. The COVID-19 pandemic catalysed an unprecedented release of such data, from aggregated public indices [22, 23] to privacy-enhanced individual-level datasets [20, 24], enabling analyses at scales previously unavailable. These datasets are nonetheless subject to demographic sampling biases that must be accounted for when drawing population-level inferences [25, 26, 27], moreover, the choice of data source and processing pipeline can itself substantially alter the inferred mobility patterns [28]. Mobility data are often partial, aggregated, or available at mismatched spatial scales [29, 30, 31], leading studies to complement them with probabilistic mobility models [32, 33, 16, 34]. If restrictions alter exploration and visitation patterns in addition to the scale of individuals’ movements [24, 35, 36], models that only rescale baseline mobility may fail to reproduce some features of the observed epidemic trajectories.

The reduction in mobility was itself heterogeneous: sharp differences have been documented along income gradients [37, 35], urban–rural divides [38], and partisan lines [39, 40]. Recovery dynamics after restrictions were lifted showed similar heterogeneity across jurisdictions and political contexts [41, 42]. Understanding this variability, and whether standard statistical descriptions of human mobility remain valid under forced restrictions, is the central motivation of this work.

Motivated by this limitation, in this work we focus on improving the characterisation of changes in mobility patterns, through geometric measures (radius of gyration, straight line distance), visitation patterns, and information-theoretic complexity, rather than trying to infer transmission patterns from mobility measures.

In this paper, we laverage a large dataset describing individual mobility in the U.S. and we divide the observation period into three phases: pre-restriction (15 January – 15 March), restrictions (15 March – 15 May), and post-restriction (15 May – end of September), and we focus our analysis on the states of California and Massachusetts. We adopt these boundaries as a national-level reference, consistent with the period during which the majority of U.S. states progressively enacted and later eased shelter-in-place measures [45].

We measure the radius of gyration [46] and compare distributions across different county-level political affiliations, degree of urbanisation, and pandemic phases. We fit power-law models to the tail of the trip-length distribution and compare the fitted tail parameters across the different phases. The rate of discovery of new places follows a diffusive power law [47], and the rank structure of visitation frequencies [47, 48]. We further compute stop-point distributions in each trajectory’s intrinsic reference frame [46]. For trajectory complexity, we use three entropy measures — random, Shannon, and Lempel-Ziv real entropy [49, 50] — which progressively add sensitivity to visit frequency, sequential structure, and the regularity of return behaviour [51, 52]. Whether complexity reduction during restrictions reflects a structural change in trajectories or simply fewer visited locations is one of the central questions we address. Finally, we apply a returner–explorer framework [53] to characterise shifts in habitual versus novel movement.

Whether complexity reduction during restrictions reflects a structural change in trajectories or simply fewer visited locations is one of the central questions we address. Finally, we apply a returner–explorer framework [53] to characterise shifts in habitual versus novel movement.

Our results show that the restriction phase was not a simple rescaling of pre-pandemic mobility. Individuals moved within a smaller spatial range, with a characteristic contraction scale of about 5 km. Short- and medium-range trip lengths were largely unchanged, and rare long-distance trips persisted. Mobility also reorganised around a small set of habitual locations. The discovery of new places slowed from a super-diffusive to a near-diffusive regime, and a larger share of visits concentrated on the two most frequented locations. Once scale and orientation were removed, the geometric shape of trajectories stayed essentially the same across phases. Trajectory entropy dropped during restrictions, but this drop is explained mainly by the smaller number of visited locations rather than by more regular or periodic routines. After restrictions were eased, mobility did not simply return to its pre-restriction state. The rebound was asymmetric, favoured shorter-range habitual mobility, and was more complete in California than in Massachusetts. Mobility began to decline before the statewide mandatory orders. Users in rural counties kept larger ranges than urban users throughout the period, while differences between county political groups were small. Taken together, these findings suggest that mobility-based epidemic models that only rescale baseline movement volumes or distances may miss relevant changes in exploration and visitation behaviour. Such features may need to be re-estimated when mobility data are used to describe behavioural regimes during large disruptions.

papers.title: From Individual Songs to Music Corpora: Evaluating Explainable Harmonic Decision-Making on HookTheory
papers.abstract: Automatic melody harmonization is often evaluated through individual compositions or data-driven corpus models. This study examines whether an explainable harmonic decision model developed for individual songs can be applied to independently collected human annotations without changing its rules. We evaluate a frozen Explainable Melody Harmonizer (EMH) on selected HookTheory excerpts containing aligned melody and chord annotations. EMH generates chord sequences from melody alone using explicit criteria for melodic compatibility, harmonic function, persistence, cadence, meter-aware segmentation, and Viterbi-like optimization. Human chords are withheld during generation and used only for post-hoc comparison. Nineteen excerpts yielded 439 evaluable harmonic segments. Exact chord agreement reached 20.50%, chord-root agreement 31.66%, and harmonic-function agreement 47.62%, with functions assessed relative to the key inferred by EMH. Decision-level analysis identified 203 segments (46.24%) where the human chord lay outside the model's candidate vocabulary and 146 (33.26%) where it was available but not selected. These findings distinguish representational limitations from differences in chord selection without treating the human reference as the only musically valid solution. The study demonstrates a reproducible, interpretable approach to corpus-based evaluation of harmonic decision-making.

papers.title: Can LLMs Anticipate Their Cruxes?
papers.abstract: To use language models to help us make decisions we would like to understand the rationale behind the language model's outputs. In principle, the language model provides its rationale as part of its text output. However, the sheer volume of text makes this hard to use in practice. In this paper, we are interested in extracting the cruxes that lead a model to recommend one action over another. We take a crux to be a sub-question that a model's rollouts disagree on, where changing its value may have altered the conclusion. A crux is therefore a property of the distribution of a model's rollouts, not of any one rollout. We consider three strategies of increasing computational cost. First, we just ask a model to identify, a priori, what the cruxes of a decision will be. Second, we have the model actually go through the process of generating a response and then extract the cruxes that arose in its reasoning. Finally, we generate many responses and extract the cruxes by comparing the reasoning across the rollouts. We make this last procedure computationally tractable with cheap calls to a reranker, an estimated 86 times less compute than a judge. We then conduct an extensive empirical evaluation to assess whether the computationally inexpensive options are sufficient. They are not. Across domains and models, we find that a model's a priori assessment of the cruxes has little relation to the factors that are actually identified as important a posteriori. Using a single rollout helps, but is still inadequate for identifying the full set of cruxes. Accordingly, for high-stakes decisions (and to understand the space of language model decision making) the many rollout procedure is unavoidable.

papers.intro:
Consider using a language model to aid in decision making. For example, someone asking a chatbot whether to end a relationship, a patient weighing an AI-assisted diagnosis, or a researcher considering an agent-implemented change to their codebase. To decide what the right decision is, we would like to reduce the overall argument to the critical subquestions that lead to the conclusion. These subquestions are the cruxes of the argument (Sabien, 2017). They should surface the assumptions and reasoning that influence the conclusion. For example, suppose a coding agent skips every input that crashes its pipeline. The agent has decided, without saying so, that the skipped inputs do not matter. Whether the skipped inputs matter is a crux of the researcher’s decision to accept the change. How might the researcher identify this implicit crux if the agent does not volunteer it?

We can do this a priori—just ask in advance what the relevant subquestions will be—or a posteriori—have the language model generate a decision, and then look at its chain of thought to determine what the key subquestions were. The a priori case matters because cruxes named in advance say what to find out before deciding. For example, a priori cruxes let a language model ask for clarification before carrying out a task. The a posteriori case would hopefully be useful to sanity check the model’s reasoning. Both the a priori and single-rollout methods are appealing for their simplicity and inexpensiveness. Is either of these adequate?

To study this question, we introduce a method for extracting cruxes by contrasting many rollouts aimed at the same decision (Figure 1, whose run is described in Section D.3). Intuitively, the idea is that if a question is a crux of the reasoning then we should actually see variation across independent reasoning of the decision! To make this concrete, consider the forecasting question of whether Frontier Airlines files for bankruptcy. A priori, the bot identifies “whether Frontier keeps enough cash to avoid a distress filing” as an important factor. Given a single rollout, the bot might actually end up focusing on “whether Frontier has enough cash to meet its obligations”, adding another crux. Given multiple rollouts, if the bot always had the same belief about Frontier’s cash position, that belief would not be a crux of the reasoning! But if the rollouts vary in how much credence they give to a rival airline’s recent bankruptcy, that is a crux (Figure 2, right). The question is whether we really need the multiple rollouts, or whether LLMs are already capable of identifying, a priori or after a single rollout, the cruxes of their own reasoning. To address this: 1. We propose an elegant (but naively, expensive!) method for extracting the cruxes of a model’s conclusion from multiple rollouts. Informally, the idea is to contrast each pair of rollouts looking for important distinctions in the reasoning. Equivalent paraphrases of the same crux are then clustered. 2. We make this multiple-rollout method affordable. A reranker, which scores a pair of cruxes in a single forward pass, replaces an LLM judge for deciding whether two cruxes are equivalent. It matches every pair of the main evaluation in 6.4 GPU-hours, an estimated 86 times less compute than a local judge, and still agrees with it on most pairs and rarely merges two cruxes it called distinct (Sections 5.1 and B.2). 3. We evaluate the a priori and single-rollout methods against the multiple-rollout method. A method could score well merely by naming more cruxes, or by naming one crux many ways, so the overlap between two sets is read against a permutation baseline, which reshuffles the same labels over the same clusters (Section 5.2). The comparison runs on two sources of forecasting problems, four model families and three definitions of semantic similarity. Simply asking for the cruxes is plainly inadequate; the models do worse than a random shuffle (Figure 2). Further, using only a single rollout typically misses many cruxes. Accordingly, for high-stakes decisions, the multiple-rollout approach is necessary.

papers.title: Compression of Uniformly Distributed Unit Quaternions
papers.abstract: Unit quaternions are widely used in computer graphics making their efficient compression critical for reducing memory consumption and bandwidth requirements. In this paper, we present a novel method for encoding uniformly distributed unit quaternions. Our thorough analysis of several quaternion parameterizations compares their theoretical error properties, quantization behavior, computational cost, and memory efficiency and provides both an analytical and empirical characterization. We show that an infinity-norm parameterization with our optimized warp function consistently offers the smallest maximum error and the best storage efficiency, at a decompression cost equal to or lower than that of parameterization methods found in practice. We demonstrate the practical benefits of the proposed approach in several graphics applications, including tangent-space normal mapping, skeletal animation with blend weights, and Gaussian splatting.

Unit quaternions are a standard representation of 3D rotations in computer graphics. They are compact, avoid gimbal lock, interpolate smoothly, and are cheap to compose and to convert into rotation matrices. Consequently, they appear throughout real-time and offline pipelines: skeletal animation stores one quaternion per joint and key frame, the tangent frames of mesh vertices can be stored as quaternions for normal mapping, and 3D Gaussian splatting stores the orientation of millions of anisotropic Gaussians as quaternions.

papers.title: Co-designing a Layered Control Architecture
papers.abstract: Layered control architectures (LCAs) are ubiquitous in complex engineering systems. However, in practice they are largely designed ad hoc and mostly dictated by the experience of the designer. This is because there is currently no systematic and practically applicable theory available to holistically design LCAs. Hence, systematically reasoning about the optimality, stability, and feasibility of the LCA design is not possible. We set a first step toward such a theory by presenting a framework for co-designing a two-layer LCA for a linear time-invariant plant. The resulting co-design problem optimizes over architectural design variables (e.g., reduced order model dimension and sampling ratio between the layers) and tuning-based design variables (e.g., the numerical values of the feedback gain or the matrices of the reduced order model), all subject to constraints that ensure stability, feasibility, and compute properties of the closed-loop LCA. The proposed formulation allows to make informed tradeoffs along the Pareto front traced over different axes of optimality, e.g., speed, accuracy or computational effort. We demonstrate the effect of making various tradeoffs in a simple numerical example.
papers.intro:
Intricate designs of interconnected controllers operating at different levels of abstraction and on multiple timescales are at the core of the high-performance operation of complex, autonomous, cyber-physical systems, including robotics, aerospace, high-tech mechatronics, and power grids Matni et al. (2024). While such layered control architectures (LCAs) are a near-universal design pattern, in practice they are still designed largely ad hoc: governed by the experience of the designers, and each layer designed and tuned in isolation. This often necessitates multiple (expensive) redesigns of the LCA to ensure system requirements are met, because interactions between the layers are often only verified a posteriori. The main reason for this design process is the absence of a systematic and theoretically founded theory of control architecture design, making it in fact impossible to make a priori formal statements about the optimality, stability, or feasibility of the LCA design. Such a control architecture design theory must enable the joint design of layers in an LCA, i.e., a way to reason about LCA design and co-design the layers to trade off different performance aspects of the LCA. In this work, we aim to get a better understanding of the fundamental relations in LCAs by instantiating the co-design philosophy on a simple, linear, two-layer example, providing a tractable starting point. This results in a concrete co-design problem, allowing us to make systematic tradeoffs in LCA design.

Related work: We build on the ideas proposed in Matni and Doyle (2016); Matni et al. (2024), which consider joint and/or systematic design of LCAs. Complementary to these more abstract and system-theoretic approaches to LCA theory, several works design and certify a given (two-layer) architecture in the context of multi-rate model predictive control (MPC) Rosolia and Ames (2020); Csomay-Shanklin et al. (2022); Rosolia et al. (2022), hierarchical MPC Scattolini (2009), abstraction-based hierarchical control via (approximate) simulation relations Pappas et al. (2000); Girard and Pappas (2006), simulation functions Stamouli et al. (2025); Girard and Pappas (2009); Stamouli et al. (2026); Fainekos et al. (2009), reference governors Garone et al. (2017), contract theory Incer et al. (2024); Mazo Jr et al. (2024); Takayama et al. (2026), and reachability-based methods Herbert et al. (2017). All these works provide successful approaches to design the individual controllers of an a priori given LCA by providing careful analysis of the interactions between the layers, and tune the resulting controllers based on these analyses. However, the important architectural choices in the LCA (e.g, multi-rate sampling time ratio, reduced model order, control horizon length), which dictate the feasible design space, are left out of the design process. The aforementioned approaches manage the models and constraints in the higher layers through satisfaction of exact consistency conditions (e.g., using abstractions and simulation relations), Lyapunov-based contracts, or barrier certificates. In our work, we explicitly make such architectural choices part of the design process. This is in line within the more abstract mathematical theory of co-design Censi (2015); Zardini (2023); Zardini et al. (2021), which uses category theory to arrive at (Pareto) optimal designs of interconnected, heterogeneous systems through monotone maps. In this work, we take the view point of the design meta-problem (DMP) in Verhoek and Matni (2026), which quantifies the tradeoffs in single/intra-layer control design. We combine this with the concepts in the MPC and co-design literature, which results in an explicit, quantifiable co-design problem. This problem allows designers to systematically make tradeoffs in LCA design subject to both the architectural choices and the usual controller design parameters of the individual layers.

This path provides explicit and computable conditions to determine whether a set of ϕ\phi and θ\theta variables results in a stable and feasible LCA design, i.e., it enables a priori certification and comparison between candidate architectures defined through ϕ\phi and θ\theta. Concretely, we derive the closed-loop LCA error dynamics on both the timescales of the LCA, all in terms of ϕ\phi and θ\theta. While efficiently solving the co-design problem remains still open, we demonstrate in a simple numerical example that we can search over the architectural choices, intuitively illustrating the different behaviors of Pareto-optimal LCA designs.

papers.title: RAT-EC: Introducing a New Open-Source 3D Volume-Integral Eddy-Current Module
papers.abstract: We present RAT-EC, an open-source volume-integral eddy-current module for unstructured meshes, driven in the time domain by coils of arbitrary winding geometry. It is the first openly available code of this kind and part of the open-source RAT suite. Because only the conductor is meshed, neither the surrounding air nor an artificial outer boundary has to be modelled, which simplifies model preparation and brings problems with thin gaps and intricate air regions within reach of standard hardware. The formulation combines a semi-analytical evaluation of the singular and near-singular inductance terms, a multi-level fast multipole method that accelerates both the far-field inductance action and the coil field, topology-aware constraints for multiply connected conductors, and a matrix-free, GPU-accelerated time integration. The implementation is verified against closed-form solutions for a conducting sphere and a conducting ring, and is validated on the TEAM-7 benchmark. At 50 Hz, RAT-EC reproduces the measured field as accurately as finite-element solutions. At 200 Hz, it agrees with a converged finite-element model, but both deviate from published measurements, which suggests that this benchmark point should be re-examined. RAT-EC provides an open platform for volume-integral eddy-current simulation and method development.

papers.intro:
Eddy currents are induced wherever a conductor is exposed to a time-varying magnetic field. Computing them in large three-dimensional (3D) structures remains one of the most demanding tasks in electromagnetic design. They dominate the losses in electrical machines and transformers, limit the switching speed of the gradient coils in magnetic-resonance scanners, and are the working principle of induction heating, non-destructive testing and wireless power transfer. In superconducting magnets, they shape the current and field transients during ramps and quenches. Reliable quench-protection simulation, the main bottleneck in the design of high-temperature superconducting (HTS) magnets, therefore requires accurate knowledge of the eddy currents induced in the surrounding conducting structures [1, 2, 3, 4]. Realistic models combine several complex coils with extended conducting volumes, making both the field computation and the eddy-current simulations expensive. A useful simulation tool must therefore be accurate, keep the modelling effort low (as model set-up consumes most of the engineering time), solve large problems efficiently, handle realistic 3D coils, model conductors with holes, allow thin gaps and multiply connected regions, and be openly available.

Eddy currents are induced wherever a conductor is exposed to a time-varying magnetic field. Computing them in large three-dimensional (3D) structures remains one of the most demanding tasks in electromagnetic design. They dominate the losses in electrical machines and transformers, limit the switching speed of the gradient coils in magnetic-resonance scanners, and are the working principle of induction heating, non-destructive testing and wireless power transfer. In superconducting magnets, they shape the current and field transients during ramps and quenches. Reliable quench-protection simulation, the main bottleneck in the design of high-temperature superconducting (HTS) magnets, therefore requires accurate knowledge of the eddy currents induced in the surrounding conducting structures [1, 2, 3, 4]. Realistic models combine several complex coils with extended conducting volumes, making both the field computation and the eddy-current simulations expensive. A useful simulation tool must therefore be accurate, keep the modelling effort low (as model set-up consumes most of the engineering time), solve large problems efficiently, handle realistic 3D coils, model conductors with holes, allow thin gaps and multiply connected regions, and be openly available.

In practice, these problems are most often solved with finite-element (FE) methods, which resolve eddy currents in arbitrary 3D conductors and can cope with complex coil shapes [5, 6]. Their cost, however, lies outside the conductor. The surrounding air has to be meshed, and the unbounded exterior has to be truncated by an artificial boundary. In addition, the thin insulation layers and narrow gaps of magnet windings are the most laborious part of the model to build. For the eddy-current problem, the volume-integral method (VIM) avoids these costs by meshing only the conducting domain and treating the free space analytically. Several efficient implementations have been reported. Rubinacci and co-workers accelerated 3D eddy-current computations with a fast multipole method, making large models tractable [7]. Bettini, Passarotto and Specogna developed a formulation on general polyhedral meshes [8], and the Udine group later placed the family of volume-integral eddy-current methods on a common rigorous foundation [9]. Meunier, Chadebec and Guichon in Grenoble solved the same eddy-current problem within an unstructured partial-element equivalent-circuit (PEEC) framework, representing the current density in the conductors with facet elements [10, 11], and Torchio extended the approach from low to high frequencies with a volume PEEC formulation [12]. Equivalent-circuit and distributed-network models reduce the effort and the model complexity further, but they require the current paths to be assumed in advance, which reduces flexibility and accuracy on complex 3D geometries [13]. Several of these methods are openly available as fast-Fourier-transform-accelerated codes on regular voxel grids [14, 15, 16]. The uniform cell size required by the transform, however, imposes a single resolution on the whole model and precludes local refinement of thin features. Related open codes gain speed by restricting the current path: the inductance extractor FastHenry discretizes conductors into current filaments [17], and thin-wall codes for the conducting structures of fusion devices confine the current to thin shells [18]. All of these openly available codes are formulated in the frequency domain or, when in the time domain, resolve no variation of the current through the conductor thickness. The time-varying field of the coils is often computed with a current line model (CLM), which represents each coil as a set of current-carrying line segments and evaluates the Biot–Savart law directly, giving a precise coil model without meshing.

An efficient, openly available tool for transient eddy-current problems on unstructured meshes, driven by windings of arbitrary shape, is still missing. This paper introduces RAT-EC, the eddy-current module of RAT (Rotation of vector potential A in Tesla), an open-source simulation suite [19] used by research groups for superconducting magnet design and simulation [20, 21, 22]. RAT-EC extends the suite from magnetostatic to magnetodynamic problems. It is written in parallelized and vectorized C++ and distributed as a Docker container that runs unchanged on a workstation or on a batch system such as HTCondor [23]. RAT-EC combines established techniques: semi-analytical polyhedral integrals for the singular near and self terms [24, 9], a cohomology basis for conductors with holes [25, 26], multipole acceleration of the far field [27, 28], and physics-based preconditioning of the Krylov iteration [29]. A single multipole engine evaluates both the impressed field of the winding, represented by a CLM, and the inductance operator, and both the far-field action and the sparse near-field product can be executed on a graphics processing unit (GPU). Since only the conductor is meshed, the module handles large problems with little modelling effort and moderate memory. Its application to a complete superconducting magnet is left to future work. Here, three verification and validation cases demonstrate that RAT-EC reproduces analytical references and the measurements of the TEAM-7 (Testing Electromagnetic Analysis Methods) benchmark [30] at the 50 Hz operating point. At the 200 Hz operating point, RAT-EC and an independently converged commercial finite-element model agree closely, but both deviate from measurements published in 1990, which indicates that this benchmark point should be re-examined. A reproducibility repository [31] regenerates every figure and table of this paper. RAT-EC is designed modularly: each numerical component is accessed through a defined interface and can be replaced without modifying the rest of the code, which makes RAT-EC a platform for method development.

papers.title: Rethinking Routing Exploration in Modern Mixture-of-Experts
papers.abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models have become an important approach for scaling model parameters. Modern MoE architectures increasingly combine two design choices: fine-grained expert segmentation and shared experts. The former increases expressiveness by enabling more expert combinations at a fixed activation ratio, and the latter introduces experts that are active for every token. We identify an exploration dilemma between these designs: shared experts can make routing less exploratory by reducing the variability of token representations. This conflicts with the greater need for exploration induced by fine-grained expert segmentation due to the combinatorially enlarged routing space. Consequently, the additional expressiveness offered by fine-grained segmentation may not be fully realized in practice. MirrorMoE is proposed to reconcile this exploration dilemma by shrinking the exploration space through token-adaptive suppression of unnecessary experts. MirrorMoE consistently improves performance across model scales.
papers.intro:
Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models have been instrumental in scaling large language models (LLMs) to trillions of parameters and beyond (Lepikhin et al., 2020; Fedus et al., 2022). MoEs adopt a sparse conditional-computation paradigm, where each token activates only a subset of experts, or subnetworks. During pretraining, recent work has shown that MoEs can outperform their dense counterparts under matched total parameter counts, compute, and data budgets (Li et al., 2026). At inference, sparse activation allows computational cost to grow sublinearly with total parameters. Thanks to these advantages, MoEs have become a core architecture underlying model families such as DeepSeek (Dai et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024), Kimi (Team-Kimi, 2025; Team-Kimi, 2026), and Qwen (Team-Qwen, 2024b; Yang et al., 2025), among many others (Jiang et al., 2024; Abdin et al., 2024).

MoEs adopt a sparse conditional-computation paradigm, where each token activates only a subset of experts, or subnetworks. During pretraining, recent work has shown that MoEs can outperform their dense counterparts under matched total parameter counts, compute, and data budgets (Li et al., 2026). At inference, sparse activation allows computational cost to grow sublinearly with total parameters. Thanks to these advantages, MoEs have become a core architecture underlying model families such as DeepSeek (Dai et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024), Kimi (Team-Kimi, 2025; Team-Kimi, 2026), and Qwen (Team-Qwen, 2024b; Yang et al., 2025), among many others (Jiang et al., 2024; Abdin et al., 2024).

At the core of MoEs is the MoE layer, which consists of a router and EE experts, each implemented as a feedforward network (FFN). For each input token, the router selects KK experts (K<EK<E) for sparse activation (Lepikhin et al., 2020; Fedus et al., 2022). Building on this basic design, recent MoEs have increasingly adopted two notable architectural advances. The first is fine-grained expert segmentation (Team-Kimi, 2026; Liu et al., 2024). Recent MoEs tend to use larger numbers of both total and activated experts, i.e., larger EE and KK. For example, at the same activation ratio K/EK/E, (E,K)=(64,8)(E,K)=(64,8) is often preferred over (E,K)=(8,1)(E,K)=(8,1). Since there are (EK)\binom{E}{K} expert combinations, the latter yields richer routing space for more expressive token representations (Elango et al., 2026). The second advance is shared experts. Activated for every token, shared experts capture common knowledge that would otherwise be learned redundantly by routed experts. This allows routed ones to devote more capacity to specialization. The combination of the above architectural choices have become standard in modern MoEs (Dai et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024; Team-Qwen, 2024b).

This work reexamines the interaction between these two trends from the angle of routing exploration. The goal of exploration is to search for alternative expert combinations during pretraining to identify (near-)optimal routes for each token. On the one hand, realizing the expressive potential of fine-grained expert segmentation requires exploring a combinatorially larger routing space within each MoE layer. For example, the number of expert subsets increases from 88 when (E,K)=(8,1)(E,K)=(8,1) to (648)≈4.4×109{64\choose 8}\approx 4.4\times 10^{9} with (E,K)=(64,8)(E,K)=(64,8), i.e., several orders of magnitude increase. On the other hand, our analysis reveals an asymmetry during pretraining: shared experts dominate the learned token representations, leaving routed experts with less influence on the layer output. Consequently, even activating different routed experts only leads to limited variation in the learned features, making alternative routes harder to distinguish and thereby undermining the goal of exploration.

This exploration dilemma has tangible consequences for shared-expert MoEs. To see this, we train matched MoE models with and without shared experts at 4 scales, ranging from 100M to 2.4B total parameters. At each scale, we fix the total number of experts EE and vary the number of (total) activated experts KK over {6,8,10}\{6,8,10\}. A larger KK simultaneously increases model expressiveness and demands more strategic exploration due to enlarged routing space. As shown in Fig.1, shared experts no longer provide benefits over their non-shared counterparts as KK increases. More strikingly, the performance of shared-expert MoEs can even degrade as KK increases in Figs.1(b) and 1(d), suggesting that the inefficient exploration hinders realization of the additional expressiveness from larger KK.

papers.title: Multi-Method Machine Learning Classification of Astronomical Sources with Rubin Data Previews: a Spectroscopy-Free Approach with DP1 and DP2
papers.abstract: We present a multi-method machine-learning study for the binary photometric classification of point-like and extended sources in the Rubin Observatory Data Preview 1 (DP1) and Data Preview 2 (DP2). The workflow runs on the Rubin Science Platform using DP1 and DP2 ugrizy photometry, the DP1 ancillary photometric-redshift catalog, and the Monster astrometric and photometric reference catalog, without relying on external spectroscopy. Six methods (SVM, Random Forest, XGBoost, k-Nearest Neighbors, an Artificial Neural Network, and a soft Voting ensemble) are benchmarked in the deepest DP1 field, the Extended Chandra Deep Field South. These methods reach 10-fold cross-validation macro-F1 scores of 0.95-0.97 on the balanced training subset and test macro-F1 scores of 0.87-0.92 on the imbalanced held-out set, with RF and the SV ensemble tied at the top (0.918); the differences among the leading methods are within the statistical uncertainty. Permutation importance identifies FWHM as the dominant feature, and the six methods agree on 79.5% of the full catalog. The same pipeline is then applied without retuning the settings to the two other DP1 fields with full ugrizy coverage and photometric-redshift support, Euclid Deep Field South and the Low Galactic Latitude Field. Together, the three fields span a factor of approximately 7 in E(B-V) and approximately 10 in stellar density, yet headline macro-F1 remains above 0.87 in every field. We then apply the same pipeline to four DP2 fields (ECDFS, COSMOS, EDFS, and ELAIS-S1). Using colors and morphology, the best method reaches a test macro-F1 of 0.83 to 0.88 across these fields, and the six methods agree on 77 to 86% of each catalog. Adding the per-band photometric uncertainties as features raises the best macro-F1 to about 0.95 in ECDFS DP1 and 0.97 in ECDFS DP2 (and to approximately 0.97-0.98 in the other fields).

papers.intro:
The classification of astronomical sources into point-like and extended populations is a basic step in the construction and scientific use of large imaging-survey catalogs (Vasconcellos et al., 2011; Fadely et al., 2012; Krakowski et al., 2016; Nakoneczny et al., 2019). This task is especially important for the Vera C. Rubin Observatory’s Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST), which will repeatedly image the southern sky in six broad optical bands (u​g​r​i​z​yugrizy) over a 10-year survey and produce catalogs of billions of sources (Ivezić et al., 2019). Before the first annual LSST data release, Rubin’s Early Science Program will release commissioning data products through a series of Data Previews (Guy et al., 2025). Data Preview 1 (DP1), based on observations with the 9-CCD LSST Commissioning Camera (LSSTComCam, ∼0.4\sim 0.4 deg2) and processed with the LSST Science Pipelines, provides the first opportunity to benchmark source-classification workflows using on-sky Rubin imaging data (NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory and others, 2026a; SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory and NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory, 2024b; Rubin Observatory Science Pipelines Developers, 2025). Data Preview 2 (DP2) data products are based on images taken primarily during “on-sky commissioning”, supplemented by overlapping observations through early Jan 2026 with the full 189-CCD LSST Science Camera (LSSTCam, ∼9.6\sim 9.6 deg2) NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory and others (2026b); Plazas Malagón et al. (2025a).

Accurate star–galaxy separation is a cross-cutting requirement for Rubin/LSST science. Many analyses require clean stellar samples, clean galaxy samples, or well-characterized contamination between the two. For example, searches for ultra-faint dwarf galaxies (UFDs) rely on identifying sparse resolved stellar populations against a background of compact and unresolved galaxies (Simon, 2019; Mutlu-Pakdil et al., 2021), and reliable star–galaxy separation at faint magnitudes is essential to the UFD detection efficiency, as shown for the Virgo III satellite in DP2 by Pai et al. (2026). Conversely, weak-lensing and cosmic-shear analyses require source-galaxy samples with controlled stellar contamination and selection effects, while studies of galactic structure, stellar streams, variable sources, transients, and photometric redshifts can all be affected by source-type misclassification (Soumagnac et al., 2015; The LSST Dark Energy Science Collaboration et al., 2018).

A common starting point is morphology, because point sources and resolved galaxies differ in size and profile shape. However, purely morphological cuts become increasingly incomplete or contaminated near the survey limit, where compact galaxies, atmospheric seeing, blending, and lower signal-to-noise make the distinction ambiguous (Fadely et al., 2012; Soumagnac et al., 2015). Machine-learning (ML) methods offer a complementary approach by combining colors, fluxes, uncertainties, and morphological measurements in a single multi-dimensional feature space. Yet supervised ML also faces a practical limitation: spectroscopic labels are highly non-uniform across the LSST footprint, so classifiers trained on externally assembled spectroscopic samples may inherit field-dependent selection biases.

In this work, we present a spectroscopy-free, cloud-native ML pipeline for binary classification of point-like and extended DP1 & DP2 sources. The workflow runs entirely on the Rubin Science Platform (RSP) at data.lsst.cloud, the web-based integrated platform where Rubin Data Rights Holders can access Rubin and LSST data. It uses RSP-resident or RSP-accessible data products (and third-party software that can be installed at the RSP): DP1 & DP2 u​g​r​i​z​yugrizy photometry from the dp1.Object and dp2.Object table, the DP1 ancillary photometric-redshift (photo-zz) catalog of Charles and others (2025) and, for DP2, the RAIL photo-zz catalog of Charles et al. (2026), accessed as a Hierarchical Adaptive Tiling Scheme (HATS) catalog with the Large Scale Database (LSDB) package, and the Gaia-anchored Monster astrometric and photometric reference catalog. This design is intended to be reproducible by Rubin users and transferable to LSST fields with adequate multi-band photometry and photo-zz support, without requiring local spectroscopic training sets.

The primary analysis uses the Deep Drilling Fields (DDF) Extended Chandra Deep Field South (ECDFS), available in DP1 & DP2, and we then apply the same workflow without retuning the settings for DDF Euclid Deep Field South (EDFS) with DP1 & DP2, DDF COSMOS in DP2, the Rubin Science Validation (SV) Low Galactic Latitude field with DP1, and the ELAIS-S1 Field with DP2. papers.title: Pixels to Tokens: Token Space Efficient Active Learning for Low-Budget Semantic Segmentation
papers.abstract: While foundation models and vision transformers (ViTs) have redefined visual representations, current active learning (AL) strategies for these backbones largely operate at the patch or region level, where annotation requirements remain high due to extensive pixel labeling. Extending ViT-based AL to the pixel-level, low-budget regime is uniquely challenging: with as little as one pixel query per image, a method must simultaneously identify the most informative locations and train a reliable decoder head from an extremely sparse signal. We introduce TEAL (Token-space Efficient Active Learning), the first pixel-level AL framework built around ViT representations. TEAL uses a frozen ViT backbone and performs diversity-based selection directly on its native token lattice, avoiding the artifacts introduced by interpolating token embeddings to dense pixel resolutions. Our framework applies a two-level MaxHerding strategy over multi-layer token descriptors to select representative candidates, followed by margin-based uncertainty refinement on a finer decoder grid. Across CamVid, Cityscapes, ADE20K, and Pascal Context, TEAL consistently outperforms previous baselines under extreme label scarcity, improving over the strongest baseline by up to +24.36 mIoU with a single labeled pixel (px) per image, and reaching up to 97% of fully supervised performance with just 10 px. To rigorously establish the source of the gains, we further show that the improvements persist when all baselines are equipped with the same DINOv3 backbone, demonstrating that coupling token-space selection with uncertainty refinement on the decoder grid makes ViT token geometry an effective foundation for extremely low-budget active segmentation.

Semantic segmentation assigns a class label to every pixel in an image, but training accurate segmentation models typically requires dense pixel annotations. Active learning approaches reduce this cost by querying only a small set of informative pixels for annotation. Large-scale self-supervised pretraining has substantially improved dense visual representations, making ViT features a competitive backbone choice for semantic segmentation Dosovitskiy et al. Pixel-level active learning offers a fine control over labeling cost yet this setting is difficult because the acquisition space is extremely large, highly redundant, and sensitive to the representation used for selection Mittal et al. A natural approach is to upsample ViT token features to a dense pixel grid via interpolation, apply pixel-level acquisition directly on the resulting features, and train a lightweight pixel classifier. However, we find that this can lead to suboptimal annotation candidates for both uncertainty- and diversity-based selection. Both selectors tend to pick pixels near token boundaries because their descriptors are more affected by neighboring tokens. However, the embedding diversity and segmentation uncertainty of such pixels are due to interpolation, not genuine semantic ambiguity or visual diversity. As shown in Fig. 1(a), pixel-space selection concentrates along grid-aligned boundaries, whereas token-space acquisition over native DINOv3 features lands on more representative interior regions, leading to better downstream segmentation (Fig. 1(c) vs Fig. 1(b)).

TEAL progressively moves from token-level coverage to pixel-level annotation. It first applies MaxHerding Bae et al. Our contributions are threefold. First, we present, to our knowledge, the first pixel-level active learning framework built on ViT representations, showing that ViT-based segmentation can learn from extremely sparse pixel labels, contrary to prior findings that ViT features underperform diffusion features in this regime (Kim et al., 2026). papers.title: $q_x$-Bass Martingales: Optimality, Existence and Convergence
papers.abstract: We introduce the class of $q_x$-Bass martingales, extending the notion of $q$-Bass martingales. These are martingale couplings with prescribed marginals whose transition kernels are closest to a given family of reference kernels $(q_x)_{x \in \mathbb R^d}$ in the sense of a suitable weak optimal transport problem. We show that $q_x$-Bass martingales are optimizers of this problem and establish a strong duality result. Building on this duality, we introduce an algorithm for their computation and, under compactness assumptions on the prescribed marginals, prove its convergence, thereby establishing existence. We then specialize to one-dimensional marginals and show that the algorithm reduces to a fixed-point iteration.

Given a target distribution ν\nu, Bass’ approach starts by mapping a Gaussian random variable monotonically onto ν\nu and then uses conditional expectations to construct a martingale with deterministic initial value and terminal law ν\nu.

papers.title: Adaptive Prescribed Performance Trajectory Tracking for Uncertain Autonomous Underwater Vehicles With Input Saturation
papers.abstract: Accurate trajectory tracking is essential for autonomous underwater vehicles operating with uncertain hydrodynamics and limited thruster authority. This paper develops a low-complexity adaptive prescribed performance controller for uncertain underwater vehicle dynamics with coupled and saturated inputs. The proposed method adapts the performance functions directly through the mismatch between the requested and saturated control inputs, enlarging the performance funnels only when the available actuation cannot meet the nominal specifications. A coupled invariant-set analysis establishes boundedness of all closed-loop signals, prescribed bounds on the filtered tracking errors, and explicit feasibility conditions. Comparative simulations on a BlueROV2 underwater vehicle show that the adaptive design maintains prescribed performance during a figure-eight maneuver, whereas conventional prescribed performance control loses feasibility under input limits. A real-time pool experiment further demonstrates stable trajectory tracking and the practical implementation of the proposed method on an underwater robotic platform.

papers.intro:
Autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) are increasingly expected to execute inspection, mapping, intervention, and environmental monitoring missions under limited actuation authority. In these operations, trajectory tracking accuracy is a robotic mission requirement: large transient deviations may compromise sensor coverage, vehicle safety, or the quality of collected data. Underwater vehicles also operate with uncertain hydrodynamics, restoring forces, disturbances, and hard thruster limits whose effects propagate through control allocation and coupled body motion. Experimental prescribed performance tracking of underwater robots [1] and open-water funnel control under input saturation [2] reinforce the need to jointly address tracking performance and actuation limits.

In these operations, trajectory tracking accuracy is a robotic mission requirement: large transient deviations may compromise sensor coverage, vehicle safety, or the quality of collected data. Underwater vehicles also operate with uncertain hydrodynamics, restoring forces, disturbances, and hard thruster limits whose effects propagate through control allocation and coupled body motion. Experimental prescribed performance tracking of underwater robots [1] and open-water funnel control under input saturation [2] reinforce the need to jointly address tracking performance and actuation limits.

Prescribed performance control (PPC) imposes transient and steady state tracking specifications through designer-selected performance envelopes [3], while funnel control achieves the same following a different design [4]. Barrier-like transformations of normalized errors can enforce convergence rate, overshoot, and residual error requirements without exact model identification. Actuator saturation, however, creates a feasibility conflict whenever a fixed performance envelope demands more control authority than the vehicle can deliver, particularly during aggressive maneuvers or in the presence of strong currents and other disturbances.

Input constraints have been studied through adaptive, robust, neuroadaptive, finite-time, and sliding-mode control [5, 6, 7, 8, 9]. Saturation-aware PPC and funnel designs include adaptive-gain and MIMO funnel controllers [10, 11, 12], bang-bang designs [13, 14], disturbance-regularity and bounded-gain methods [15, 16, 17], and approximation-free constrained PPC [18]. Flexible envelopes, switching mechanisms, auxiliary dynamics, observers, and neural or fuzzy approximators have also been employed [19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24]. Recent underwater-vehicle work combines prescribed performance with dynamic compensation, neural approximation, filtering, and velocity observation to handle saturation and uncertainty [25]. Although effective, the use of such structures increases implementation complexity on robotic platforms that usually operate with limited computational capabilities.

The MIMO adaptive performance design of [21] exploits the available control authority across the input channels. However, its adaptation mechanism contains the saturation mismatch divided by the normalized error |ξi|<1|\xi_{i}|<1, together with user-selected cross-channel coupling parameters. Consequently, its saturation-induced relaxation contains a term of order 𝒪⁡(|Δ​τi|/|ξi|)\mathcal{O}(|\Delta\tau_{i}|/|\xi_{i}|), where Δ​τi\Delta\tau_{i} denotes the mismatch between the saturated and required unsaturated input. The scalar design of [27] instead adapts the performance envelope directly through |Δ​τi||\Delta\tau_{i}|, avoids divisions by the normalized error, and yields an 𝒪⁡(|Δ​τi|)\mathcal{O}(|\Delta\tau_{i}|) degradation bound, but it does not address coupled MIMO dynamics. Reference modification methods preserve the nominal performance funnel by altering the commanded motion. In particular, [30] treats uncertain MIMO systems with coupled and constrained inputs and obtains a mismatch-dependent tracking bound through reference adaptation rather than performance adaptation. papers.title: The Komlós Problem in Matrix-Multiplication Time
papers.abstract: We give a randomized algorithm that, for an $m\times n$ matrix whose columns have Euclidean norm at most one, finds a signing with discrepancy below $99$ in expected $\widetilde O(L_{\mathrm{in}}+n^ω)$ bit operations, where $L_{\mathrm{in}}$ is the input encoding length and $ω$ is the exponent of matrix multiplication. The previous fastest algorithm with a constant discrepancy bound, due to Li, is deterministic and uses $O(mn+n^{ω+2}\log^3 n)$ arithmetic operations. We build on the spectral signing framework of Guo, Fang, and Lu and of Li, which rounds a single fractional coloring while one spectral potential controls every row. Li's potential tracks a top eigenvalue, and the gap below that eigenvalue, which can be of order $1/n$, limits the length of every step. We replace it with a resolvent potential that is smooth without any gap condition, and we draw step signs at random, so that the potential only needs to be concave while progress is measured separately. Our key insight is to reuse a single subspace of directions throughout a batch of steps, thereby using only one spectral computation, so that the more expensive linear algebraic operations are paid for only polylogarithmically often at each scale. Within a batch, we sample directions from a Gaussian completion matrix whose inverse we maintain under rank-one row replacements. Finally, we use a finite-precision analysis to prove stability of the algorithm and attain the bit-complexity bound.

papers.title: AdapTest: Supporting Designers in Authoring and Evaluating Environmentally Responsive User Interfaces for Extended Reality
papers.abstract: Extended Reality (XR) headsets increasingly host familiar 2D user interfaces as windows floating in physical environments. However, their usability depends on environmental conditions that designers cannot fully control. Current design workflows often separate how a variant is designed from how it actually looks in the target environment. We present AdapTest, an in-situ authoring and testing tool that lets designers select interface elements, define when and how they change, compare the resulting variations, and test their activation without coding. Based on prior research and a formative study with 12 interface designers, the system targets three key environmental variables: distance, lighting, and occlusion. We evaluated AdapTest against a desktop design and in-headset preview workflow in a within-subjects study with 12 designers. Compared with the baseline, designers accounted for a wider range of environmental factors, addressed more overlapping conditions, and repeatedly tested and revised their designs in place; there were no significant differences in workload or usability despite longer sessions. Our work contributes an integrated, designer-centered approach to adapting, comparing, and validating environmentally responsive XR user interfaces.

papers.intro:
Graphical user interfaces are moving off the screen and into physical space. Extended Reality (XR) headsets now render familiar 2D interfaces—dashboards, control panels, exhibit guides—as windows carried into immersive surroundings (Ens et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2026), with deployments spanning museums, homes, and workplaces (Khan and Lindlbauer, 2024; Pei et al., 2024). Unlike a phone or desktop screen, such an interface is at the mercy of its environment: the viewer walks away and body text becomes illegible (Harrison and Dey, 2008; Vogel and Balakrishnan, 2004); the room dims and low-contrast styling disappears against passthrough (Kim et al., 2019; Erickson et al., 2021); furniture or passersby occlude the panel (Bell et al., 2001; Li et al., 2024); cluttered backdrops erode the readability of overlaid content (Satkowski and Dachselt, 2021; Lee et al., 2024). Most interface design is fixed at authoring time, so designers have to anticipate these conditions as separate cases.

Unlike a phone or desktop screen, such an interface is at the mercy of its environment: the viewer walks away and body text becomes illegible (Harrison and Dey, 2008; Vogel and Balakrishnan, 2004); the room dims and low-contrast styling disappears against passthrough (Kim et al., 2019; Erickson et al., 2021); furniture or passersby occlude the panel (Bell et al., 2001; Li et al., 2024); cluttered backdrops erode the readability of overlaid content (Satkowski and Dachselt, 2021; Lee et al., 2024). Most interface design is fixed at authoring time, so designers have to anticipate these conditions as separate cases.

Current tools give visual designers partial control over how their interfaces adapt to the XR environment and limited means to test that behavior in place. Automated systems decide the adaptation at runtime—repositioning or anchoring windows to spatial context (Evangelista Belo et al., 2022; Li et al., 2024; Davari and Bowman, 2024), matching layouts to the surrounding scene (Cheng et al., 2021), varying information density (Lindlbauer et al., 2019), projecting onto nearby surfaces (Han et al., 2023; He et al., 2024), switching input techniques (Lai et al., 2025), or recoloring panels against their background (Santos et al., 2025). Because these decisions live in code and optimization objectives, designers cannot see or shape what the interface becomes under each condition, and often cannot picture it in advance (Krauß et al., 2022; Chen and Yoon, 2024). Design practice keeps that control in the designer’s hands but loses the tie to condition: designers hand-build each case as a duplicated static artboard (e.g., a dark-room, far-away, or occluded version (Krauß et al., 2022; Krauß et al., 2021; Ashtari et al., 2020)) and preview the copies in headset prototyping tools such as ShapesXR (Tvori, Inc., 2026). These copies let a designer inspect a mockup, yet they do not connect a condition to the change it should trigger, and confirming that one behaves correctly in place would mean coding, rebuilding, and redeploying to the headset—development work outside design practice (Ashtari et al., 2020; Numan et al., 2025). Designers are therefore left either to accept automatic adaptation or approximate it by hand, without a way to author their own condition-to-change mappings for the environmental conditions of a 2D interface in XR and test them in the room.
