To address this gap, we present AdapTest, an authoring tool that lets designers adapt the GUIs they already create to the environments those interfaces will inhabit. After opening a design in the headset, a designer places its screens around the room, examines them where they will be used, and decides when the interface should change as spatial conditions shift. To author that change, the designer selects an element, assigns an alternative style such as larger type, higher contrast, or fewer details, and defines when that style should apply: when the viewer is far, the room is dark, or the panel is blocked. Each rule’s outcome appears in a preview beside the default design, so the designer compares how the interface should adapt across conditions. The designer then tests the rules against the room’s actual conditions, observes each transition as it fires, and refines the thresholds and styling accordingly. In a within-subjects study, twelve designers created adaptive versions of multi-screen interfaces with AdapTest and with a current-practice baseline pairing a 2D design tool with in-headset preview. With AdapTest, all twelve participants authored explicit conditional rules, created design variants covering multiple environmental factors, and interleaved authoring with repeated Test Mode runs. Workload and usability remained comparable to the existing workflow. Participants noted that current tools represent adaptive behavior only as text beside the design, whereas AdapTest allowed them to author and experience that behavior as a working rule and reuse it across screens.

papers.title: Imaging defects in two-dimensional crystals by convergent beam electron diffraction
papers.abstract: Convergent beam electron diffraction (CBED), recently demonstrated on two-dimensional (2D) materials, offers a number of interesting applications such as imaging atomic in- and out-of plane shifts, interlayer distances, and individual adsorbates. In this study, we show how CBED allows for atomic-precision imaging of individual defects in 2D materials using one single-shot intensity measurement. In combination with structural calculations using density functional theory, we present simulated CBED patterns for various defects in graphene, each of which exhibits a unique fingerprint distribution. We also show how atomic positions, including the individual atomic defects in graphene, can be reconstructed by iterative phase retrieval from a single CBED pattern.

papers.title: Thermal Confinement in Plasmonic Nanoparticles under Generalised Pulsed Illumination
papers.abstract: Thermal confinement is a key parameter in photothermal applications, as it determines the spatial extent of the region affected by the generated heat. In this work, we develop a numerical treatment to quantify thermal confinement in spherical plasmonic nanoparticles under excitation conditions ranging from ultrashort pulses to the continuous-wave regime. The model combines generalized optical heating with a finite-difference solution of the transient heat equation and explicitly accounts for finite interfacial thermal conductance. To characterize the spatial distribution of heat, we introduce a thermal confinement radius defined from the temporal temperature envelope in the surrounding medium. We demonstrate that pulse duration acts as a highly effective, tuneable parameter to govern thermal confinement. Notably, we quantitatively show that finite interfacial thermal conductance can induce deviations of up to 20% in the spatial confinement radius and over 60% in the transient thermal construct under ultrashort excitation. By comparing the characteristic dimensions of representative targeting ligands with the resulting thermal-confinement length scales, we show how pulse duration can be precisely tailored to control target heating. These results provide a unified framework for predicting nanoscale heat localization paving the way for the rational design of high precision thermoplasmonic applications.

papers.title: Hierarchical universal open structure dataset for atomistic modeling
papers.abstract: Atomic-scale simulations have been transformed by machine-learning models that predict the properties of atomistic structures with the accuracy of quantum calculations, but at a small fraction of the cost. These models have increased dramatically in generality, thanks to the availability of synthetic datasets of ever-increasing size and scope. The proliferation of datasets, with properties often computed using different levels of electronic-structure approximation, is problematic, as there is often overlap between different datasets, and strong correlations between structures obtained with short molecular dynamics trajectories or geometry optimization. To address these problems, we introduce a protocol to stratify a dataset into a hierarchy of nested subsets, subsampling from the coarsest to the finest resolution based on an "ecumetric" built to reflect the latent space representation of several popular universal machine-learning interatomic potentials. We then use this approach to combine most of the open structural datasets currently available, consolidating them into MAD-COSMO, a well-organized collection of almost 1.7 billion structures, whose $2^{24}$ most diverse members form the MAD-CORE stratified coreset, which can be easily used for all sorts of tasks, from exploratory experiments to the training of foundation models at scale. We envision that this collection will guide and help coordinate future efforts, focusing them on the most relevant and/or undersampled regions of chemical and structural space, and that it will be further extended to incorporate the outcomes of the collective work of this community.

papers.intro:
Atomistic machine learning potentials have transformed materials simulation by providing near ab initio accuracy at a fraction of the computational cost of electronic-structure methods [1, 2, 3]. More recently, the emergence of universal machine learning interatomic potentials (uMLIPs) has extended this success across an unprecedented range of chemistries and simulation tasks, fundamentally reshaping the field [4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10]. A central driver of this progress has been the availability of large-scale datasets of density functional theory (DFT) calculations, many of which now contain millions of structures across diverse chemistries and application domains [11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19]. At the same time, the public atomistic data ecosystem has developed in a largely decentralized manner. Consequently, datasets and benchmarks are often aggregated from heterogeneous sources with different electronic-structure settings and convergence criteria, leading to inconsistent labels and substantial numerical noise [20, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26]. In addition, many datasets contain overlapping or near-identical structures, such that aggregating them can unintentionally over-represent certain regions of configuration space [27, 28]. Building a coherent and diverse dataset is then not just a matter of concatenation but rather a technically and conceptually non-trivial task [29, 30, 31, 32].

In this work, we address these limitations by constructing a hierarchical view of existing atomistic datasets, in which each level provides provable uniform coverage of the data it is built from, at increasing levels of resolution. The construction relies on an ecumenical metric, a distilled structural distance obtained by training a SPACE model [33] on the last-layer features of several popular universal interatomic potentials, obtaining a single learned consensus representation. We first construct the hierarchy on a dataset built based on the principle of Massive Atomic Diversity (MAD) [34, 35]. Then we systematically extend it to other datasets using an accretion algorithm that tries to preserve the initial ordering at every level, without rebuilding it from scratch, and continues selection as farthest point sampling. We apply this pipeline to a collection of almost 1.71.7 billion structures from a number of major public atomistic datasets, which we refer to as MAD-COSMO, and construct its nested coreset of 2242^{24} structures, MAD-CORE.

This multi-resolution representation can be helpful for several practical applications. The hierarchical ordering of the library can be used to effectively select representative structures for budget-constrained recalculations at different levels of theory, hyperparameter exploration, and architectural benchmarking. It also gives a quantitative measure of dataset completeness by identifying areas where new ab initio calculations can most efficiently improve the coverage of the represented configuration space.

papers.title: Learning Lean Feedback for Efficient Proof-Candidate Evaluation on GPUs
papers.abstract: Training language models for formal theorem proving requires large numbers of verifier calls. Slow checks and timeouts often leave GPUs waiting and withhold rewards from potentially correct proofs. We train neural evaluators to predict Lean 4 verdicts and compiler feedback on GPUs using 4.84M labelled programs. We compare two validity classifiers with a feedback model that annotates proof attempts with predicted goal states and error messages. A two-stage evaluator that screens candidates with a classifier and scores its positive predictions with the feedback model reaches 87.8% accuracy in predicting whether Lean accepts a candidate proof, evaluated on a 68,932-program benchmark collected from public provers. The combined evaluator processes 3.5 candidates per second on one H100, 4.2x the throughput of our 64-worker Lean baseline with environment reuse. Finally, we combine our evaluator with Lean verdicts to obtain a hybrid reward system that shortens GRPO training steps by approximately 31%. After one GRPO epoch with hybrid rewards, the prover achieves nearly the same miniF2F pass@1 as with Lean-only rewards (62.2% versus 62.4%) and a pass@32 of 72.4% versus 71.3%.
papers.intro:
Proof assistants provide automatically checked training signals for language models that generate formal proofs [6, 26]. Lean-based provers use these signals for supervised learning, proof search, and reinforcement learning [17, 18, 23, 30, 4, 11]. Checking candidates at scale creates a substantial computational workload. Existing systems reduce this overhead through parallel workers, reuse of loaded environments, and compiler optimizations [7, 11].

Even with these optimizations, slow checks can delay reward computation for an entire training batch. In our 8B prover’s Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) training [24] using the efficient verl framework [25], a 64-worker Lean pool takes about 420 s to score 1,024 candidate proofs with a 60 s timeout per proof, about 40% of a 1,050 s training step. Timeouts also withhold rewards from some correct proofs: in an audit with a larger verification budget, 58.1% of the resolved timeouts are valid (Section 6). A separate comparison with Kimina Lean Server finds similar verification times on 10,000 proofs, providing an external check on our pipeline’s efficiency (Appendix A).

papers.title: Learning Rewards in Strategic Games
papers.abstract: Understanding the objectives that drive agents' behavior is crucial in strategic environments, where multiple agents interact and adapt to one another. This challenge arises in domains such as cybersecurity, autonomous driving, and online markets, where agents' underlying incentives are typically unknown and must be inferred from their observed behavior. Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) provides a natural framework for this problem, but extending IRL to strategic multi-agent settings introduces a fundamental challenge: a reward that explains observed behavior does not necessarily induce optimal strategies when used for decision-making. In this work, we study this problem through the lens of \emph{strategic identifiability}, and show that learning from a fixed policy pair can be insufficient to strategically identify rewards, independent of the number of expert samples $K$. Motivated by this, we introduce an active IRL algorithm for two-player repeated Stackelberg games, in which the leader adaptively selects policies to elicit informative responses about the follower's reward. Combining maximum-likelihood estimation with experimental design, we derive finite-sample guarantees on the Stackelberg sub-optimality induced by the learned reward, matching up to polylogarithmic factors a new minimax learning rate of $K^{-1/2}$. Finally, we evaluate our approach in a realistic anti-poaching setting, demonstrating the benefits of active exploration for reward recovery and downstream strategic performance.
papers.intro:
Strategic decision-making often requires reasoning about agents whose objectives are unknown. A defender may need to anticipate the incentives of an attacker, an autonomous vehicle the preferences of other drivers, or a wildlife-protection agency the objectives of poachers. In such settings, agents’ behavior provides an indirect signal about their underlying incentives. Recovering these objectives is valuable not only for explaining observed behavior, but, crucially, for predicting how agents may respond to new policies or interventions.

Rather than requiring recovery of the ground-truth reward itself, we argue that reward learning should preserve the strategic consequences that matter at deployment. We study this question through the lens of strategic identifiability, relating ambiguity in the inferred reward to the sub-optimality incurred when using it for downstream strategic decision-making. We illustrate this objective in Figure 1 for a wildlife protection application, where an error in reward estimation from a ranger patrol can incur highly sub-optimal behavior at deployment.

A key difficulty is that passive observations may provide insufficient information for this objective. Observing an agent repeatedly against a fixed policy only reveals its preferences under that particular interaction. Distinct reward functions may therefore generate indistinguishable behavior while inducing substantially different responses to alternative policies. As we show in this work, this can prevent low strategic sub-optimality even with infinitely many observations. This limitation suggests a different approach: rather than passively observing strategic behavior, can we actively choose interactions that reveal the reward information needed for downstream decision-making?

We answer this question in repeated Stackelberg games, where a leader can adaptively select policies and observe the responses of a bounded-rational follower. This setting naturally allows the leader to trade off exploiting its current estimate of the follower’s reward with selecting interactions that are informative about the follower’s underlying objectives. We develop an active IRL approach that combines maximum-likelihood reward estimation with experimental design to progressively resolve strategically relevant reward ambiguity, and we provide finite-sample guarantees on the strategic performance induced by the learned reward.

Our work connects inverse reinforcement learning and learning in games. In single-agent settings, IRL has long studied the ambiguity inherent in recovering rewards from demonstrations (Ng et al., 2000; Abbeel and Ng, 2004). In multi-agent settings, recent work has focused on whether policies learned from demonstrations remain robust when interacting with strategic agents, typically through notions of exploitability (Tang et al., 2024; Freihaut et al., 2026a; Bergerault et al., 2026a).

In single-agent settings, IRL has long studied the ambiguity inherent in recovering rewards from demonstrations (Ng et al., 2000; Abbeel and Ng, 2004). In multi-agent settings, recent work has focused on whether policies learned from demonstrations remain robust when interacting with strategic agents, typically through notions of exploitability (Tang et al., 2024; Freihaut et al., 2026a; Bergerault et al., 2026a).

Emerging work on IRL in games has instead characterized sets of rewards compatible with observed strategic behavior (Freihaut and Ramponi, 2026; Barbara et al., 2026). We take a complementary perspective: rather than only characterizing which rewards are consistent with observed behavior, we ask which interactions provide the information needed to identify a strategically useful reward, and how such interactions can be actively selected with finite-sample guarantees.

papers.title: Hy-Memory-30B-A3B: Attributed Reinforcement Learning for Long-Term Memory Writing
papers.abstract: External-memory systems extend language-model applications beyond a context window, but their quality depends critically on the model executing the write path: deciding what to retain, how precisely to represent it, and how new evidence should update persistent state. Existing frameworks typically place a general-purpose large language model behind framework-specific prompts. This raises serving cost, and a writer specialized for one protocol does not transfer directly to another; a unified model that can operate across established memory frameworks remains largely unexplored. We present Hy-Memory-30B-A3B, a compact long-term-memory writer trained across Mem0, MemOS, and Hy-Memory. Memory On-Policy Distillation teaches framework-specific write protocols on student-generated states; Memory RL then optimizes downstream answerability using dense per-chunk probes, attributed cross-chunk rewards, over-storage controls, and chunk-level GRPO. Carrying policy-written banks across windows keeps training aligned with deployment. On fixed 20% benchmark subsamples, Hy-Memory-30B-A3B ranks first on all four evaluated harnesses, including held-out EverMemOS, with a 55.49% macro average versus 54.62% for Claude Opus 5.
papers.intro:
A long-term memory system for an LLM application usually contains three functional stages: (1) a writer converts an interaction into persistent memory operations; (2) a retriever selects records relevant to a future query; and (3) a reader or answer model uses the retrieved records to respond.

Systems such as Mem0, A-MEM, MemoryOS, and MemOS have expanded the design space of persistent memory through extraction, consolidation, hierarchical paging, linking, versioning, and lifecycle management (Chhikara et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025; Kang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025). Benchmarks such as LoCoMo and LongMemEval have also shown that long-term memory is not a single retrieval problem: it includes precise extraction, multi-session composition, temporal reasoning, knowledge updates, and abstention (Maharana et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025).

Despite this progress, the write policy is commonly implemented by placing a general-purpose LLM behind a long, framework-specific prompt. That model must simultaneously distinguish durable user information from greetings, assistant suggestions, and transient text; preserve exact names, numbers, versions, dates, paths, and other identifying details; represent a state transition without losing either the new state or what it replaced; reconcile new evidence with retrieved memories already in the bank; and emit valid operations under the framework’s schema and control flow.

The framework cannot recover information that the writer omitted, and a powerful downstream reader cannot reliably infer a fact that was never stored. Conversely, indiscriminately storing everything increases cost and retrieval interference. The desired writer is therefore not a generic summarizer: it is a policy for changing an external state under a long-horizon downstream objective.

Recent work has begun to train memory operations with reinforcement learning. Memory-R1 trains a memory manager and an answer agent with final-answer rewards (Yan et al., 2025). MemAgent learns recurrent textual compression from a terminal verifier (Yu et al., 2026). Mem-α\alpha combines downstream QA correctness with format, compression, and operation-quality rewards (Wang et al., 2025). MemCoE explicitly identifies sparse outcome reward as a weakness and adds guideline-aligned process feedback (Xu et al., 2026). These studies establish that memory behavior is learnable rather than fixed. They also expose a remaining problem: a final answer score usually supervises an entire sequence of heterogeneous memory actions, even though only a few actions supplied the evidence—or caused the failure.

Hy-Memory-30B-A3B focuses on this credit-assignment problem while preserving compatibility with existing memory frameworks. Our contributions are: • A framework-integrated memory writer. Hy3-30B-A3B replaces the LLM inside Mem0, MemOS, and Hy-Memory without moving their memory logic into a custom model architecture. • State-distribution-aligned training. OPD and RL both execute the policy inside the actual harness, and later writes observe banks produced by earlier policy outputs. • Failure-surface reward data. Training questions are constructed from concrete write failures, including omission, lost specificity, semantic inversion, stale-state confusion, secondary-fact loss, and over-storage. • Attributed, non-binary feedback. Local probes provide dense per-chunk evidence, while cross-chunk outcome questions use gold facts to map recovered evidence back to source chunks. • Chunk-level policy optimization. Advantages are normalized among rollouts at the same chunk position rather than over whole trajectories, so one rollout can be credited at one chunk and penalized at another. Each rollout casts one vote per chunk even when a framework makes multiple LLM calls. • Cross-harness and OOD results. papers.title: Disagreement-Guided Weak-to-Strong Routing
papers.abstract: Small language models are increasingly deployed on edge devices and robotic systems to meet cost and latency constraints, yet their limited capabilities can make reliable deployment challenging. Stronger models can provide assistance when needed, but deciding when to route a weak-model response to a stronger model often relies on signals of response correctness. In open-ended and agentic tasks, however, obtaining such signals can require costly ground-truth supervision that is difficult to obtain at scale. We revisit the foundations of weak-to-strong routing and ask whether routing decisions can instead be guided by signals that do not require ground-truth supervision. We first characterize the optimal weak-to-strong routing policy, while allowing for multiple weak-model responses generated through local inference. Building on this characterization, we derive a principled approximation to the optimal routing based on model-to-model comparison. In particular, we introduce a notion of model disagreement that can be measured directly from model-generated responses, without ground-truth supervision. Importantly, the approximation becomes increasingly accurate as the strong model becomes a better proxy for the ground-truth distribution. Across agentic and single-turn tasks, our approach effectively navigates the trade-off between routing cost and response accuracy without ground-truth supervision. Moreover, even when ground-truth correctness signals are available for training, disagreement-based routing can outperform methods trained directly to predict correctness

papers.title: Counterexamples to the ordinary Fried conjecture near hyperbolic metrics
papers.abstract: We give an LLM-assisted construction of counterexamples to the ordinary Fried conjecture, with real analytic metrics arbitrarily close to a hyperbolic metric in dimension three. For acyclic unitary line characters tending to the trivial character, the modulus of the Ruelle zeta function at zero divided by analytic torsion squared tends to zero.

papers.title: ACEdit: Stable Multi-Turn Image Editing via Asymmetric Conditioning
papers.abstract: Image editing models produce impressive results for individual edits, but their quality often deteriorates over multiple editing turns. Each editing turn introduces small distribution shifts that accumulate over successive edits, creating a gap between the input distributions encountered during the editor's original training and multi-turn inference. We introduce a training scheme that makes multi-turn image editing stable under this accumulating distribution shift. A key is to force the editor to operate on its own outputs from previous editing turns during training, bringing the principle of Self-Forcing to image editing. The main challenge is that self-generated editing trajectories deviate from ground-truth trajectories, making direct supervision unreliable. We address this challenge through a distillation objective that leverages a teacher image editor to provide a reliable training signal when the model operates on its own previous outputs. We introduce an asymmetric conditioning scheme: while the student performs edits sequentially on its own outputs, the teacher remains anchored to the original clean image and receives a compound editing instruction. Experiments show substantially reduced degradation over long multi-turn sequences while maintaining editing quality and instruction adherence.

papers.intro:
Image editing with modern generative models has reached an impressive level of quality, enabling complex modifications while faithfully preserving the appearance and content of the input image [26, 49, 44, 6, 24]. Yet, practical editing is rarely a single operation. Users often refine an image through a sequence of edits, where the output of one edit becomes the input to the next. This setting is commonly referred to as multi-turn image editing. With current image editing models, each editing turn introduces small distribution shifts that accumulate as the model repeatedly operates on its own outputs. These shifts create a growing gap between the input distributions encountered during the editor’s original training and multi-turn inference. This gap leads to accumulating artifacts, loss of fine details, and unintended changes in appearance (see Figure 1). Effective image editing therefore requires not only high-quality individual edits, but also stability across successive editing turns.

Several approaches have been proposed to mitigate degradation in multi-turn image editing. Inference-time methods target specific sources of degradation [62, 27, 38, 47], but may incur computational overhead and are limited by the complexity of distribution shifts in multi-turn editing. Other approaches train models on multi-turn editing sequences [39, 52, 16, 61]. Training on ground-truth sequences leaves a gap between training and inference, while training on self-generated sequences poses supervision challenges, leading to inconsistent targets, restrictions on training sequences, or objectives that do not explicitly address distribution shifts.

papers.title: Progressive Misalignment Can Emerge from Benign Recursive Self-Distillation
papers.abstract: Training models on their own outputs has attracted widespread attention as a possible route to advance AI capabilities. One prominent approach is self-distillation, where a model is trained to match the token-level predictions it would have produced when given access to additional context, such as a cue, feedback, or instruction. However, the safety properties of this training procedure are poorly understood. In this paper, we present a surprising safety failure of recursive self-distillation, where each self-distilled model becomes the teacher for the next round of training. We observe that when a safe model is recursively self-distilled on its own (safe) generations while receiving an additional non-harmful cue, it becomes increasingly misaligned across a diverse set of harmful queries; we call this Progressive Misalignment. We show this failure mode in both the Qwen3 and Phi-4 model families on SORRY-Bench and StrongREJECT. Progressive misalignment also occurs in a more realistic setup, where the fixed cue is replaced by feedback from a simulated user with benign intent. Using a gradient-based method, we are also able to find benign prompts that lead to progressive misalignment when applying recursive self-distillation, showing that harmful training prompts are not necessary for this failure mode to emerge. We hope our work encourages future investigations of the safety properties of AI systems recursively trained on their own data.

Undoubtedly, the advancement of AI has been rapidly accelerating in recent months. Many believe that new systems will soon emerge with capabilities that come with unpredictable consequences, both in terms of promises and risks for humanity. Ensuring that AI systems are safe and aligned with our intended objectives (Russell, 2019; Hubinger et al., 2019; Ngo et al., 2024; Anthropic, 2026; Bengio et al., 2026; OpenAI, 2026) has therefore become even more pressing. Model safety, however, has been shown to be particularly brittle. papers.title: spora: A Unified Multimodal Dataset and Platform for Spatial Proteomics
papers.abstract: Spatial proteomics (SP) captures the molecular composition and spatial organization of tissues at single-cell resolution, opening a direct view of the cellular ecosystems that drive disease. Protein panels, acquisition platforms, and tissue contexts differ from one cohort to the next, and a coherent picture of tissue biology can only emerge from models trained to bridge this heterogeneity. Foundation models offer the natural path forward, but their training depends on large, harmonized corpora that span platforms, panels, and cohorts. No public resource currently approaches that scale; available data sit in small, narrowly scoped releases with incompatible formats and conventions. We present $\texttt{spora}$, a large-scale multimodal SP dataset of 13,546 standardized multiplex images from 5,477 patients across 35 cohorts and five major SP technologies. Curated with biomedical experts, $\texttt{spora}$ provides model training-ready formats together with cell and tissue segmentations, structured clinical metadata, and, where available, paired H&E enabling the training of virtual staining models. It is complemented by $\texttt{spora [io]}$, a unified interface for tiling, sampling, and standardization across all cohorts and modalities, and $\texttt{spora [bench]}$, a benchmark suite spanning cell phenotyping, diagnostic and therapeutic prediction as well as virtual staining tasks across twelve cohorts that places current SP foundation models on common ground against task specific baselines.

papers.intro:
Tissue function arises from the molecular states of individual cells and their spatial organization. Spatial proteomics resolves both at single-cell resolution, measuring dozens of proteins across intact tissue sections through technologies such as imaging mass cytometry (IMC), CODEX (now PhenoCycler), MIBI, and Orion (Giesen et al., 2014, Black et al., 2021, Keren et al., 2019, Lin et al., 2023a). The resulting images expose immune cell phenotypes, checkpoint expression, stromal composition, and the architecture of the tumor microenvironment (Wu et al., 2024, Nature Eds., 2024). These features are increasingly relevant to questions in translational oncology, including immunotherapy response prediction, microenvironment characterization, and the identification of spatial patterns associated with recurrence and treatment resistance (Cords et al., 2023, Salié et al., 2025, Xiao et al., 2022). Across these applications, SP is moving from research use into clinical decision support (Quail and Walsh, 2024, Liu et al., 2026).

Protein panels, acquisition platforms, and tissue contexts differ from one cohort to the next, so the corpora needed to train such models can only be built by aggregating across studies. Foundation models (FMs) (Bommasani et al., 2021) are the clearest expression of this paradigm, pretrained at scale on diverse data and applied to specific downstream tasks, and their development has consistently followed the same pattern where large standardized (public) corpora enable successive waves of model development (Campanella et al., 2025): In histopathology, the Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) (Tomczak et al., 2015) and HistAI (Nechaev et al., 2025) provide hundreds of thousands of standardized hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) whole-slide images, seeding a generation of general-purpose FMs (Chen et al., 2024, Zimmermann et al., 2024, Saillard et al., 2024, Nechaev et al., 2024). In spatial transcriptomics, HEST-1k (Jaume et al., 2024) and STOmicsDB (Xu et al., 2024a) consolidate paired transcriptomic and histology samples in standardized formats and supported the first FM pretraining and benchmarks for the modality. In single-cell RNA sequencing, CELLxGENE (CZI Cell Science Program et al., 2025) aggregates millions of cells from thousands of studies into a single queryable resource, providing the basis for cross-study atlases and FMs.

In this work, we present the Spatial Proteomics Reference Atlas (spora), the first unified, multimodal, AI-ready resource for spatial proteomics, and, to our knowledge, the largest publicly available SP corpus assembled to date (Fig. 1). spora brings together a large body of publicly released SP cohorts under a common resolution, file layout, and metadata schema, with cell and tissue segmentations, structured clinical annotations, and paired H&E provided wherever the source studies allow. By unifying SP at this scale, spora not only enables FM training across panels, technologies, and tissues, but also lays the groundwork for spatial tissue atlases: reference maps that capture how cells are organized within tissues across health and disease. Such atlases would provide reference frames for interpreting new patient samples, expose microenvironmental archetypes that recur across cancers and organs, and document how treatments reshape tissue at single-cell resolution. The accompanying library spora [io] exposes the dataset as an AI-ready interface, and spora [bench] evaluates current SP foundation models against task-specific baselines on a set of cell- and tissue-level tasks. papers.title: A clump population framework for star formation across galactic scales
papers.abstract: Whether star formation across different spatial scales and galactic environments follows universal laws remains poorly understood. We investigate cloud-scale star formation in 30 dwarf and disk galaxies. Molecular clouds are identified using a dendrogram algorithm, and their molecular gas masses ($M_{\rm H_2}$) and star formation rates (SFRs) are derived from integrated CO and mid-infrared emission, respectively. We find a consistent $M_{\rm H_2}$--SFR relation across all galaxies, with little sensitivity to galactic environment. Extending the analysis to Milky Way cloud substructures down to sub-parsec scales and 311 diverse nearby galaxies, we find that this relation persists across ten orders of magnitude in molecular gas mass and SFR. A theoretical model in which star formation occurs within dense clumps embedded in molecular clouds reproduces this observed relation. The weak environmental dependence of star formation at the clump scale provides a possible explanation for the nearly universal $M_{\rm H_2}$--SFR relation across galaxies. This framework establishes an observationally grounded connection between star formation in the Milky Way and external galaxies.

papers.title: FutureLift: Lifting Trajectory Proposals into Bidirectional Future Graphs for Motion Forecasting
papers.abstract: Accurate motion prediction is critical for safe autonomous driving, yet even strong forecasters leave residual errors in their multimodal proposals. Existing refiners compress complete proposals or update their segments sequentially, preventing the full proposed future from serving as explicit relational context for correction. We introduce FutureLift, a backbone-agnostic refiner that represents each multimodal proposal as a heterogeneous future graph, with spatially grounded temporal nodes connected to agent histories, map elements, alternative modes, and, for joint prediction, other agents future trajectories. Bidirectional temporal edges allow later evidence to revise earlier segments in a single pass, and the updated nodes predict residual coordinate and confidence corrections. Requiring only proposals, scores, and scene context, FutureLift provides a common refinement interface for structurally different forecasting backbones. On Argoverse2 and the Waymo Open Motion Dataset, it consistently improves frozen proposals and outperforms native and specialized refiners across marginal and joint forecasting. On the WOMD motion-prediction leaderboard, FutureLift ranks first in minADE (0.5049m) and minFDE (0.9942m) among the compared standard-input methods, without LiDAR or ensembling, while achieving a competitive 0.4874 Soft mAP.

Accurate motion forecasting enables autonomous vehicles to anticipate traffic participants and plan safely. Given agent histories and an HD map, models must represent multiple plausible futures over an extended prediction horizon. Modern methods use vectorized scene representations [13, 4], graph- or attention-based context encoders [23, 20, 5], and expressive trajectory decoders [32, 10]. Yet even strong predictors leave residual displacement and ranking errors in their multimodal proposals.

Accurate motion forecasting enables autonomous vehicles to anticipate traffic participants and plan safely. Given agent histories and an HD map, models must represent multiple plausible futures over an extended prediction horizon. Modern methods use vectorized scene representations [13, 4], graph- or attention-based context encoders [23, 20, 5], and expressive trajectory decoders [32, 10]. Yet even strong predictors leave residual displacement and ranking errors in their multimodal proposals.

Trajectory refinement can correct such errors without redesigning the underlying predictor. Existing refiners encode trajectory features, retrieve context around selected anchors, or model trajectory–trajectory and trajectory–lane relations [31, 26]. However, compressed embeddings, sparse anchors, and pairwise summaries do not spatially instantiate the complete proposed horizon. This is especially limiting for temporal correction: within a causal segment-wise sweep, later evidence cannot revise an earlier segment [31, 10]. Iterative relational refiners can revisit predictions [26], but require repeated computation and still reason primarily at the trajectory level. We instead argue that the complete proposed future should be explicit before correction, allowing every segment to interact jointly with the map, agent histories, alternative modes, and other predicted agents while exchanging evidence in both temporal directions.

FutureLift discretizes each trajectory proposal into spatially grounded temporal nodes connected to agent histories, map elements, alternative modes, and compatible predictions of other agents. This graph represents a hypothetical future scene rather than a compressed trajectory token. A bidirectional graph network refines the complete horizon in one pass and predicts residual coordinate and confidence updates. Requiring only proposal coordinates, scores, and scene context, FutureLift attaches to structurally different backbones without modifying their proposal mechanisms. The same interface supports marginal and coherent joint-world proposals, enabling social future relations only for the latter.

papers.title: $L^\infty$-regularity thresholds for a generalized Gross-Pitaevskii equation: dispersive blow-up vs. nonlinear stability
papers.abstract: We study a generalized Gross-Pitaevskii equation arising in the mean-field description of exciton-polariton Bose-Einstein condensates. The dynamics close to macroscopic wave functions $r_0e^{iω_0 t +ik_0x}$ is governed by a stabilizing relaxation mechanism without suppressing dispersive blow-up. We show that this competition yields $L^\infty$-regularity thresholds. More precisely, we construct solutions for which arbitrarily small perturbations from $C^4_b$ can develop finite time blow-up in $C^3_b$ whereas perturbations from $C^{4+η}_b$ for every $η>0$, satisfy a global-in-time $C^3_b$-stability estimate. The stability analysis is carried out in modulation spaces $M_{\infty,1}^k$.

papers.title: OnBodyAI - Why the Next AI Needs a Body
papers.abstract: The next AI will not win by knowing more about the world. It will win because it knows you: because it lives on your body, works for you and answers to you. That is what the term OnBodyAI stands for. It describes what happens when large language models are given a body, and what research and industry need to make that happen. This article is based on my talk in the Industrial Panel at UbiComp/ISWC 2026 in Shanghai (October 13, 2026) and follows its ten key statements.

papers.title: Identification of ultra-high-energy neutrinos in vertical air showers with surface detectors
papers.abstract: We investigate the potential of surface detector arrays to identify ultra-high-energy neutrinos using vertical air showers with zenith angle $θ\leq 60^\circ$, a region largely unexplored in current searches. The method exploits the enhanced electromagnetic component at ground level arising from energetic leptons produced in neutrino interactions. Using detailed air-shower and detector simulations, we show that observables sensitive to the electromagnetic and muonic content provide genuine discrimination between neutrino-induced and hadron-induced showers. This is demonstrated both with idealized shower quantities and with realistic detector-level signals based on water-Cherenkov and scintillator detectors. The corresponding neutrino identification efficiency is used to derive the effective mass and, primarily, the effective area of the array under background-rejection requirements appropriate to targeted multi-messenger searches. Although not competitive with inclined-shower searches under the stringent background rejection factors required for diffuse-flux analyses, this approach establishes the feasibility of a vertical detection channel, extending the field of view of surface arrays and providing a complementary tool for multi-messenger observations of transient sources.

papers.intro:
Neutrino astronomy provides a unique window into the most extreme phenomena in the Universe. In particular, the detection of ultra-high-energy (UHE) neutrinos, with energies above ∼1017\sim 10^{17}\,eV, would provide crucial information on the long-standing question of the origin of the UHE cosmic rays, on the environments in which hadronic acceleration takes place, and on the interactions undergone by these particles both at their sources and during propagation. UHE neutrinos are expected to arise both from the interaction of cosmic rays with cosmic microwave background photons, leading to the so-called cosmogenic neutrino flux Berezinsky and Zatsepin (1969), and from interactions taking place inside powerful astrophysical accelerators such as active galactic nuclei and gamma-ray bursts Halzen and Hooper (2002). Combined with observations of photons, cosmic rays, and gravitational waves, they constitute a fundamental component of the multi-messenger approach to the high-energy Universe Guépin et al. (2022). In particular, coincident observations of ultra-high-energy neutrinos and gravitational waves have been proposed as a powerful probe of transient sources, such as binary neutron-star mergers Farrar (2025). Neutrinos are especially valuable in this context because, being electrically neutral and weakly interacting, they can reach the Earth from dense and distant environments that may be opaque to photons.

Several techniques are being exploited to detect UHE neutrinos Mammen Abraham and others (2022); Ackermann and others (2022). Among them, searches for UHE neutrinos with large surface particle detector arrays rely primarily on very inclined air showers Aab and others (2019); Aab and others (2015a); Alvarez-Muñiz et al. (2022) with zenith angle θ≥60∘\theta\geq 60^{\circ}. In this regime, the efficiency of neutrino identification is enhanced. Neutrinos can penetrate deeply into the atmosphere before interacting and develop showers close to the ground with a significant electromagnetic component. In contrast, hadronic cosmic rays interact in the upper layers of the atmosphere and at large zenith angles produce showers that are mainly dominated by the muonic component at ground level. The Pierre Auger Observatory, for instance, exploits two such channels: the Earth-skimming channel, sensitive mainly to tau neutrinos interacting in the Earth’s crust and producing upward-going showers, and the downward-going channel, which targets neutrinos of all flavors interacting in the atmosphere at large zenith angles Aab and others (2015a); Aab and others (2019). In both cases, discrimination against the overwhelming cosmic-ray background relies on the difference between ordinary hadronic showers at large zenith angle, which are predominantly muonic, and deeply initiated neutrino-induced showers, which are electromagnetic-dominated.

papers.title: Strong coloring numbers of grids
papers.abstract: For positive integers $n$ and $d$, the $d$-dimensional grid of side length $n$ is the graph $G(n,d)$ with vertex set $[n]^d$, in which two vertices are adjacent if they differ by $1$ in exactly one coordinate and agree in all the other coordinates. We determine, for every fixed $d$, the asymptotic growth in $r$ of the $r$th strong coloring numbers of these grids. More precisely for $n$ large enough, ${\rm scol}_r(G(n,d)) = Ω_d\bigl(r^{d-1}\bigr)$ as $r\to\infty$. This matches an upper bound given by a volume packing argument, which holds more generally for touching graphs of unit balls in $\mathbb R^d$. For the lower bound, we construct in $G(n,d)$ a bramble of order $Ω_d(n^{d-1})$ with each element of radius at most $dn$. This construction was found by OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol.

papers.title: Hydrodynamic limits of finite range exclusion processes
papers.abstract: We consider variants of the simple symmetric exclusion process (SSEP) where particles are 'large'; while in the SSEP, each lattice point is either occupied or not occupied by a single particle, in our model each particle is represented by a fixed shape, and the dynamics is so that shapes cannot overlap. In one dimension, this reduces to a finite range interaction that prevents particles from coming closer to each other than a certain distance. In this case, we prove the existence of the hydrodynamic limit, and identify the relevant macroscopic PDE, which is a porous medium equation. In two dimensions, we have no rigorous results, but instead rely on numerical simulations to approximate the diffusion matrix. Under the assumption that the hydrodynamic limit exists in two dimensions, we derive properties of the diffusion matrix based on the shape of the particles.
papers.intro:
The simple symmetric exclusion process (SSEP) is a fundamental interacting particle system, and its large scale behaviour is well understood. The process consists of a collection of particles performing continuous time, simple symmetric random walks on ℤd{\mathbb{Z}}^{d}, but interacting through a hard core exclusion condition: if a particle attempts a jump to a site that is already occupied, that jump is not made. The hydrodynamic limit consists of rescaling the lattice ℤd{\mathbb{Z}}^{d} so that neighbouring lattice sites have a distance of 1/N1/N, at the same time observing the process for a time t​N2tN^{2} with t>0t>0, and then letting N→∞N\to\infty. If the initial configuration of particles (interpreted as atomic measures with unit atoms at the position of the particles) weakly converges to a measure u⁡(x,0)​d​xu(x,0){\rm d}x with a smooth Lebesgue density uu, then for any time s​⩽​ts\;\leqslant\;t, the configuration of the process at time s​N2sN^{2} also converges to a similar measure u⁡(x,s)​d​xu(x,s){\rm d}x, and its Lebesgue density is the solution of the heat equation ∂tu⁡(x,t)=Δ​u​(x,t)\partial_{t}u(x,t)=\Delta u(x,t). papers.title: Are $E>B$ regions essential for particle injection in relativistic magnetic reconnection?
papers.abstract: During relativistic magnetic reconnection, X-points ($E>B$ regions at vanishing guide field) have been proposed to play an essential role in injecting particles into the nonthermal population. Using fully kinetic particle-in-cell simulations at a range of magnetizations $σ\equiv B_0^2/(4πn_0 m_e c^2) = 12$--$800$, we study in detail how the particle energy gains up to the injection threshold $γ_{\rm inj} = σ/4$ are partitioned into work done inside $E>B$ regions (unmagnetized), within one gyration after exit (re-magnetizing), and at all other times (magnetized). The magnetized channel supplies the largest part of the energy gain for $\sim 95\%$ of injected tracers at $σ= 12$ and $\sim 65\%$ at $σ= 800$. Most of the tracers in this magnetized majority never enter an $E>B$ region before injection. We also compare these injection shares with the earlier studies that proposed an essential role for $E>B$ regions. We conclude that $E>B$ regions are neither necessary for injection nor the dominant direct contributors to pre-injection work by injection share in two-dimensional, nonradiative pair-plasma reconnection at vanishing guide field.

High-energy emission in the Universe often originates from relativistic particles with a nonthermal power-law spectrum. Relativistic magnetic reconnection, which converts magnetic energy into plasma heating and particle acceleration, has been proposed as a source of such spectra (see Guo et al., 2024; Sironi et al., 2025, for recent reviews). Fully kinetic particle-in-cell simulations find that, in the strongly magnetized regime σ≡B02/(4​π​n0​me​c2)>1\sigma\equiv B_{0}^{2}/(4\pi n_{0}m_{e}c^{2})>1 (i.e., when the magnetic energy per particle rest-mass energy is large), reconnection produces abundant nonthermal particles with a power-law distribution f∝ε−pf\propto\varepsilon^{-p}, where ε\varepsilon is the particle kinetic energy and pp approaches unity as σ\sigma increases (Zenitani and Hoshino, 2001; Sironi and Spitkovsky, 2014; Guo et al., 2014; Guo et al., 2015; Werner et al., 2016).

In the weak guide-field regime bg≡Bg/B0≪1b_{g}\equiv B_{g}/B_{0}\ll 1, the role of the nonideal electric field En≡E+u×B/c\textbf{{E}}_{n}\equiv\textbf{{E}}+\textbf{{u}}\times\textbf{{B}}/c (where u is the bulk plasma velocity) in producing these power laws remains under debate (Zenitani and Hoshino, 2001; Guo et al., 2014; Guo et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2019; Guo et al., 2020; Sironi, 2022; Guo et al., 2023; French et al., 2023; French et al., 2026). Zenitani and Hoshino (2001) suggest that acceleration in electric-dominant regions (electric field larger than magnetic field, hereafter E>BE>B) generates the power-law distribution, and they attribute its slope to the balance between E>BE>B acceleration and particle escape from those regions. Sironi and Spitkovsky (2014) propose a similar idea that nonthermal particles originate from X-points and are then accelerated to higher energies elsewhere in the reconnection layer. These authors argue that X-points are important in establishing and determining the power law, while the rest of the reconnection layer only further extends the power law. In two-dimensional pair-plasma simulations, Nalewajko et al. (2015) identify acceleration at X-points and between merging plasmoids, while Kagan et al. (2018) attribute the spectral shape and cutoff saturation to X-point acceleration limited by secondary islands. Guo et al. (2014); Guo et al. (2015) find that a Fermi-like mechanism facilitated by particle curvature drift motion in the motional electric field Em≡−u×B/c\textbf{{E}}_{m}\equiv-\textbf{{u}}\times\textbf{{B}}/c dominates the energy gain in their simulations, and argue that a power-law distribution forms as particles are injected into and accelerated in the reconnection layer. Later analyses find that acceleration in the broader reconnection layer determines the spectrum slope and maximum energy (Guo et al., 2019; Hakobyan et al., 2021, e.g.,). In two-dimensional pair plasmas, continued energization by plasmoid compression allows the high-energy cutoff to grow with time (Petropoulou and Sironi, 2018). Models also connect the spectral shape to acceleration and plasmoid trapping (Uzdensky, 2022), and to the coupled injection, acceleration, and escape processes (Li et al., 2023).

Following these studies, attention turned to injection, i.e., the initial energization that lifts particles from the thermal population into the power law, and to whether E>BE>B regions provide it. Sironi (2022) argues that nonideal fields control injection and are a necessary prerequisite for later acceleration. The main evidence is that particles reaching high energies have usually encountered E>BE>B or other nonideal regions. An encounter does not measure how much energy a particle gains inside those regions. Interpreting this evidence as a measure of injection therefore assumes that the encounter supplies the energy that injects the particle. Guo et al. (2023) show that a substantial fraction of injected particles do not pass through E>BE>B regions before injection. Particles that do enter E>BE>B regions typically stay too briefly to be injected there (Guo et al., 2023). French et al. (2023) find that motional-field mechanisms such as Fermi reflection and pickup dominate the injection share in weak-guide-field reconnection. Totorica et al. (2023) make the broader claim that exact nonideal fields, not necessarily E>BE>B regions, dominate particle energization until particles first reach a threshold kinetic energy of σ​me​c2/4\sigma m_{e}c^{2}/4, close to the injection threshold discussed below. They base this claim on the particles with the highest final energies. This conclusion assumes that the particles reaching the highest final energies were injected in the same way as the injected population as a whole. However, particles injected by some mechanisms could reach higher energies than those injected by others, either through the injecting mechanism itself or through later acceleration, and would then be over-represented at the highest energies. Gupta et al. (2025) ask a related but narrower question by measuring the work done inside E>BE>B regions before that threshold is reached. In their analysis, the largest E>BE>B work fractions also come from particles with the highest final energies, so the same assumption applies. French et al. (2026) extend the injection-share measurement to three dimensions, where Fermi reflection provides the largest injection share at bg=0.3b_{g}=0.3. This debate has recently been summarized by Guo et al. (2025). Whether E>BE>B regions play an important role in injection has not been settled.

papers.title: FastVLA: Task-Conditioned and Temporally Adaptive Visual Token Compression for Efficient Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models present a promising paradigm for general-purpose robot manipulation, but closed-loop deployment is often limited by inference efficiency: at each timestep, high-resolution, often multi-view images are encoded into hundreds of visual tokens that dominate transformer computation and latency. Token compression via attention is a natural solution but is challenging for VLA control because (1) decision-critical tokens are determined by the task, not generic visual saliency, and (2) the token budget varies substantially across steps, so static metrics and budgets waste computation or discard control-critical tokens. We introduce FastVLA, a training-free, task-aware, and temporally adaptive visual token compression framework. At each step, FastVLA scores token importance via task-to-vision attention and adaptively sets the compression rate from the importance-distribution uniformity, measured by an inverse-Simpson metric with online sliding-window calibration. We evaluate FastVLA on OpenVLA, OpenVLA-OFT, and CogACT across LIBERO and SIMPLER, and on a physical Franka Research 3 robot. In simulation, it reduces LLM-backbone FLOPs by 35-59\% and action latency by 9-32\% (a 1.09$\times$-1.46$\times$ speedup) while maintaining task success, achieving a comparable or better efficiency-performance trade-off than existing plug-and-play token compression/pruning/reuse baselines. On the real robot, it cuts action-prediction latency by 20\% (1.25$\times$ speedup) at comparable success. Code is available at https://github.com/jiuyixu25/FastVLA.

Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have recently emerged as a compelling paradigm for general-purpose robot manipulation, enabling policies to predict low-level actions conditioned on natural-language tasks and visual observations [30, 15, 4, 11, 7]. By leveraging large-scale pretraining and large vision-language backbones, VLAs demonstrate strong generalization across objects, scenes, and task specifications, making them increasingly attractive for deployment in versatile manipulation systems. Despite their impressive capabilities, deploying these models in closed-loop control is often limited by inference efficiency [9]. At every control step, high-resolution (e.g., 224×\times224) and frequently multi-view observations are encoded into hundreds of visual tokens [16, 3] that dominate the compute and latency of the vision-language-model (VLM) backbone during action prediction, far outweighing the few text tokens of a short task.

Despite their impressive capabilities, deploying these models in closed-loop control is often limited by inference efficiency [9]. At every control step, high-resolution (e.g., 224×\times224) and frequently multi-view observations are encoded into hundreds of visual tokens [16, 3] that dominate the compute and latency of the vision-language-model (VLM) backbone during action prediction, far outweighing the few text tokens of a short task.

Yet not all visual tokens contribute equally to action prediction. In a typical manipulation step, only a small subset of tokens carries decision-critical information (e.g., the target object/place or the gripper–object contact region), while the rest are redundant or even distracting [26, 27, 12]. Reducing the number of visual tokens processed by the large-language-model (LLM) backbone, without sacrificing task performance, has therefore become a key direction for accelerating VLA inference [22, 23, 25].

Reducing the number of visual tokens processed by the large-language-model (LLM) backbone, without sacrificing task performance, has therefore become a key direction for accelerating VLA inference [22, 23, 25].

However, directly applying VLM-specific token compression methods [5, 8, 29] to robotic control is often suboptimal, because these methods are designed for single-shot vision-language understanding, where the objective is to preserve global semantic content for perception tasks such as detection, captioning, or generation. Unlike image-based VLMs that process a single image, or video-based VLMs that encode a fixed sequence of frames, a VLA interacts with the environment through actions that directly shape its subsequent observations: at each step the agent receives a new observation conditioned on its previous action and predicts the next one. Visual tokens are thus not representations of a static scene but components of a sequential decision process, which sets token compression for VLA apart from its VLM counterpart in two respects. The first is that token relevance is governed by the task rather than by generic visual saliency (now standard practice in language-guided pruning), which we adopt as our importance signal rather than claim as a contribution. The second, and the focus of this work, is that the amount of decision-critical visual information varies drastically across control steps: some steps (e.g., target localization) rely on broad scene context, whereas others (e.g., grasping or contact) depend on a small, localized region. A single fixed compression rate is therefore inherently mismatched, wasting computation when the useful information is concentrated, and discarding necessary context when broader information is required.

Motivated by this, we propose FastVLA, a training-free visual token compression framework for efficient VLA inference whose core is a temporally adaptive, per-step compression rate. At each step, FastVLA scores visual-token importance with task-to-vision attention which is a training-free signal that a controlled comparison shows is more reliable for action prediction than vision-to-vision or all-to-vision attention and then, crucially, decides how many tokens to keep from the shape of the resulting importance distribution. Specifically, it estimates the effective number of tokens the decision depends on via an inverse-Simpson uniformity measure, and maps this quantity through an online sliding-window calibration to a timestep-dependent compression rate: when the current step concentrates on few tokens relative to its recent history it prunes aggressively, and when the decision draws on broader context it prunes conservatively. By allocating the token budget where each decision needs it, FastVLA reduces LLM-backbone computation, speeds up action prediction, and improves closed-loop responsiveness, without caches or training.

papers.title: MJev-Spatial: System One Spatial Intelligence via Native Attention Matching
papers.abstract: Spatial intelligence lets an agent perceive and act in the physical world, and many of its judgments must be made at interaction rates: which spatial relation holds, how far an object is, or where to place it. Vision-language models (VLMs) produce these answers by free-form text generation, paying for autoregressive decoding and answer parsing even though the output space is compact: one of a few options, a scalar, or a 2D point. In light of this, we introduce MJev-Spatial, a System 1 multimodal decision model that tackles all three types of spatial understanding tasks within a unified classification framework. Specifically, MJev-Spatial treats each candidate as a class and scores it using the backbone's pretrained query and key projections, without adding parameters. The candidates are the given options for choice tasks, or value bins and image regions refined through coarse-to-fine classification for numerical and point prediction, respectively. At inference, each classification decision takes a single forward pass and generates no answer tokens. To train on heterogeneous spatial data efficiently, we supervise all coarse-to-fine stages jointly with teacher forcing in one forward pass, and combine this with length-aware global batching and cross-GPU load balancing, raising training throughput by 30.8% over the original batching strategy. Built on Qwen3.5-4B and trained on 12.3M question-answer pairs converted from existing spatial datasets, MJev-Spatial achieves the highest overall score (65.64%) among eight tested models, ranks first on seven of twelve benchmarks, and outperforms its unmodified autoregressive base model on all twelve, while running 2.5 times faster than the fastest autoregressive baseline and 5.6 times faster than the base model.

Many of these interactions require timely spatial judgments. Vision-language models (VLMs) support these capabilities by answering spatial questions grounded in visual observations. Such questions may require selecting an option that describes a spatial relation (Ray et al., 2025; Tong et al., 2024; Fu et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2026), estimating a numerical quantity such as distance (Cai et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2025a; Yang et al., 2025b), or identifying a point for object placement (Zhou et al., 2025a; Yuan et al., 2024; Song et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2025).

This couples learning the spatial answer with learning its textual form, including formatting and boilerplate when present, introducing supervision beyond the task-relevant prediction itself. At inference, the model must generate the answer tokens sequentially, after which the resulting text must be parsed to recover the spatial prediction, adding decoding and parsing overhead. This motivates a System 1 approach to spatial understanding: using pretrained visual and linguistic knowledge to make spatial judgments directly. Jev provides a precedent for this approach by returning probabilities over specified candidates without generating answer text (TypeSafe AI, 2026). At the same time, we observe that all three common spatial output types can be represented as finite candidate sets: answer options are already finite, while numerical values and image locations can be discretized within a specified range and resolution. Building on these insights, we introduce MJev-Spatial, a multimodal decision model specifically tailored to spatial understanding.

MJev-Spatial unifies the three output types by casting prediction as classification over finite candidate sets. Each class represents a supplied answer option, a numerical bin, or an image region, depending on the task. Selecting a class gives the chosen option, predicts which bin contains the target value, or predicts which region contains the target point. To choose among these classes, MJev-Spatial encodes their descriptions together with the observation and question, then reuses the final attention layer’s pretrained query and key projections to compute class scores. A softmax over these scores gives the class probabilities, without additional prediction heads or trainable parameters. At inference, each classification decision scores all its candidates in one forward pass. Furthermore, to obtain fine-grained values and coordinates without evaluating a large number of classes at once, we subdivide the selected numerical bin or image region and classify again. Numerical prediction uses up to two stages; single-point prediction uses three stages, re-encoding the selected image crop before each later decision to recover local visual detail. The final selection is decoded to a numerical value or image coordinates. Conditional tree expansion evaluates multiple region paths to extend the same trained point predictor to multiple points without additional training.

papers.title: An Adaptive-Horizon Graph Neural Operator for coupled surrogate morphodynamic modelling
papers.abstract: Morphodynamic simulations require repeated coupling between hydrodynamic solvers, sediment transport modules, and bed updating. For long duration, multi-scenario simulations on large unstructured meshes, such coupling is computationally demanding. This study proposes an Adaptive-Horizon Graph Neural Operator (AH-GNO) that formulates bed evolution as a graph operator learning problem from recent hydrodynamic and topographic states to predict future bed elevation increments. The model operates directly on the native unstructured meshes. The approach integrates area-weighted graph learning, historical state selection, and forecast horizon estimation, allowing the effective history length (K) and update interval (B) to vary with the evolving flow and bed state. Using Telemac2D/GAIA solutions as supervised numerical references, the framework is evaluated on the official Bump and Yen bend benchmarks and on a field-scale application (Waiho River, New Zealand). Results show that the AH-GNO reproduces the main patterns of bedform migration, bend-scale erosion and deposition, and localized bed adjustment. Across the three cases, the tested CPU-GPU deployment reduced post-training bed-update workflow time from 12~1204 s with GAIA to 0.08~3.34 s with AH-GNO. This improvement corresponds to deployment-specific accelerations of approximately 150~360 times relative to 4-core GAIA CPU configurations, and with 105~186 times gains for 20-core CPU configurations. These results suggest that, while retaining hydrodynamic feedback from TELEMAC-2D, a learned operator for bed updating can provide an efficient acceleration component for morphodynamic scenario analysis and rapid coupled simulation.

papers.intro:
River-bed evolution is a fundamental process in fluvial morphodynamics with continually changing bed elevation and channel geometry under the combined effects of erosion, sediment transport, and deposition. Changes in the riverbed both respond to and influence the flow (Paul & Biswas, 2019), by modifying water depth, velocity, bed shear stress (Deal et al., 2023), and flood conveyance. Reliable simulation of river-bed morphodynamics is important for river engineering, flood-risk assessment, and sediment management (Afan et al., 2016).

River-bed evolution is a fundamental process in fluvial morphodynamics with continually changing bed elevation and channel geometry under the combined effects of erosion, sediment transport, and deposition. Changes in the riverbed both respond to and influence the flow (Paul & Biswas, 2019), by modifying water depth, velocity, bed shear stress (Deal et al., 2023), and flood conveyance. Reliable simulation of river-bed morphodynamics is important for river engineering, flood-risk assessment, and sediment management (Afan et al., 2016).

Several mature process-based models are now used for riverine, estuarine, and coastal morphodynamic simulation. Delft3D has been widely applied to coastal and fluvial morphodynamics (Vundavilli et al., 2021, 2024), and Delft3D-FM further supports three-dimensional morphodynamic modeling on flexible unstructured meshes (Mayerle et al., 2015). BASEMENT provides modules for river hydrodynamics and morphodynamics, including two-dimensional formulations based on the Saint-Venant equations and Exner-type bed evolution (Vanzo et al., 2021). HEC-RAS includes sediment-transport and movable-bed capabilities for engineering applications (Foda et al., 2025). In the TELEMAC-MASCARET system, the GAIA module computes sediment transport and bed evolution and can be coupled with TELEMAC-2D on unstructured meshes (Tassi et al., 2023). Although these models are physically interpretable and widely used, computational cost remains a major limitation in process-based morphodynamic modeling. Resolving events such as large floods, which can reorganize channel morphology over short periods (Yu et al., 2025), requires repeated hydrodynamic solution, sediment-transport calculation, bed updating, wetting–drying treatment, and stability control, and this cost becomes more pronounced for large domains, refined or unstructured meshes, and realistic river geometries (Hu et al., 2022; Reyns et al., 2026). Practical applications often require many repeated simulations for calibration, sensitivity analysis, uncertainty quantification, flood-scenario comparison, and engineering-design assessment, making exhaustive process-based modeling difficult for routine decision support (Cheng et al., 2023; Kroon et al., 2025). Morphological acceleration factors can reduce part of the computational burden by accelerating bed evolution (Reyns et al., 2026), but these factors introduce additional assumptions about the relationship between hydrodynamic forcing and morphological response, and their reliability can depend on flow unsteadiness, spatial scale, and sediment-transport regime (Morgan et al., 2020).

Hydrodynamic surrogates to predict flood inundation, water depth, velocity, discharge, and reach-scale water levels are being increasingly developed. These approaches use deep neural networks, convolutional and recurrent networks, U-Nets, graph neural networks, and physics-informed neural networks to approximate processes governed by the shallow-water equations or high-fidelity two-dimensional flood models (Bentivoglio et al., 2023; Sun et al., 2021; Taghizadeh et al., 2025). These efforts range from purely data-driven networks trained on the output of SWE-based hydrodynamic models (Haces-Garcia et al., 2025) to physics-informed formulations that embed the two-dimensional shallow-water equations directly in the learning framework (Liu et al., 2026; Qi et al., 2024), to deep-learning surrogates used for bathymetry inversion of shallow-water solvers (Liu et al., 2024), and to hybrid strategies that correct low-fidelity flood-inundation models through spatial analysis and Gaussian-process learning at reduced cost (Fraehr et al., 2022). Recent reviews have also examined how such tools are selected, developed, and compared across flood-related geospatial analysis more broadly (Pourzangbar et al., 2024).

Bed-elevation change, however, follows sediment mass conservation. In Exner-type formulations, the change equals the divergence of the sediment flux, a quantity defined by spatial gradients rather than by the hydraulic state at a single point, and the flux depends nonlinearly on water depth, velocity, bed shear stress, grain size, bed slope, and sediment supply (Paola & Voller, 2005). This constraint makes bed evolution harder to predict than single-step water levels or point-scale sediment transport. For sediment transport and morphodynamics, machine learning has more often targeted bed-load transport rate, suspended-sediment load, sediment concentration, sediment yield, and local scour depth, using approaches that span machine-learning regression models for open-channel sediment transport (Abid Almubaidin et al., 2023), large-sample data-driven and ensemble or tree-based regressors for river bed load (Hosseiny et al., 2023; Mir et al., 2024), and physics-informed networks that encode sediment-transport dynamics for pipe-flow prediction (Tipu et al., 2025). Across these studies, sensitivity and SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) analyses have repeatedly identified dimensionless bed shear stress and the Shields parameter as dominant predictive variables. Reviews of the wider field report the same emphasis on transport rates and point-scale morphological indicators rather than on distributed bed-elevation fields (Goldstein et al., 2019).

The data-driven and physics-informed models capture nonlinear relations among hydraulic and sediment variables and are effective for local parameterization, empirical-formula replacement, or offline component approximation. Their targets are scalar quantities at a point or a cross section, and they generally do not operate as mesh-based bed-update modules inside the time-stepping loop of a fully coupled hydro-morphodynamic solver (Fathi et al., 2026). If the bed is updated independently of the hydrodynamic solver, the predicted trajectory can drift from the physically constrained path because the surrogate is repeatedly evaluated on states affected by the cumulative errors (Kochkov et al., 2021). A more appropriate strategy is therefore not to replace the process model outright, but to embed the surrogate within a coupled workflow as an accelerated bed update, while the solver continues to provide hydrodynamic feedback and preserve the coupled flow–sediment–bed evolution structure.

papers.title: CoRGI in MaNGA - II. NGC 5717: cold-gas accretion and disk growth in a BGG
papers.abstract: Large-scale stellar counter-rotation, in which two coplanar stellar components rotate in opposite directions, is usually interpreted as a signature of external gas accretion. Such systems are most often found in relatively sparse environments, where cold gas can be acquired and remain dynamically undisturbed long enough to settle into a disk. It is less clear whether this channel can operate in massive central galaxies, whose group or cluster environments can heat, strip, or perturb cold gas. Here we present NGC 5717, one of the most massive galaxies known to host a counter-rotating stellar disk and the first identified case in a brightest group galaxy. Using integral-field spectroscopy from SDSS-IV Mapping Nearby Galaxies at Apache Point Observatory (MaNGA), together with CFHT imaging, ancillary HI data, and SDSS/DESI spectroscopy of the surrounding group, we show that the galaxy contains a dynamically cold counter-rotating disk embedded in an old dynamically hot elliptical component. The disk is young ($\sim 1.3$ Gyr), metal-poor ([Fe/H] $\sim -0.7$ dex), extended ($h \sim 2.4$ kpc), and massive ($\log M_\star/M_\odot \sim 9.9$); the associated ionized gas co-rotates with it, while the available HI data indicate no significant remaining reservoir of neutral atomic gas ($\log M_{\mathrm{HI}}/M_\odot \lesssim 9$). These properties support an in situ origin of the secondary component from externally accreted gas. The chemical evolution model favors gas accretion from a cosmic filament, which is consistent with the surrounding cosmic-web geometry, and indicates highly efficient burst-like star formation with substantial metal-enriched outflows. NGC 5717 may therefore represent a rare example of disk growth in a massive central galaxy, enabled by external cold-gas accretion during an earlier phase of the group assembly history.

Kinematically decoupled gaseous and stellar components provide important tracers of external accretion and galaxy assembly. In particular, misaligned, polar, and counter-rotating (CR) gas disks are commonly interpreted as the result of externally acquired cold gas, which may subsequently settle and form secondary stellar components (Davis et al., 2011; Corsini, 2014; Katkov et al., 2014). Large samples of such systems make it possible to constrain the origin of the accreted material and the physical conditions under which it can survive and form stars (Moiseev et al., 2011; Young et al., 2020; Gasymov et al., 2025).

NGC 5717 stands out in our “Stellar Counterrotating Galaxies Identified in the MaNGA Survey” sample (CoRGI in MaNGA; Sloan Digital Sky Survey IV Mapping Nearby Galaxies at Apache Point Observatory, SDSS-IV MaNGA) of galaxies with counter-rotating stellar disks (Gasymov et al., 2025) as an exceptional system. Unlike most galaxies with stellar counter-rotation, it appears to be a massive elliptical galaxy (log⁡M⋆/M⊙=11.20\log M_{\star}/M_{\odot}\,=11.20; Table 1) hosting an embedded large-scale counter-rotating stellar disk within an old, weakly rotating spheroidal body. Although this morphological classification differs from those adopted in other catalogs (S0–Sa; Vázquez-Mata et al. 2025), we demonstrate the spheroidal nature of the dominant component in Appendix References. A cross-match with the group catalog of Yang et al. (2007) further shows that NGC 5717 is the brightest galaxy in its host group. The formation of a young, dynamically cold counter-rotating disk in such a massive central galaxy is therefore challenging, as it requires cold gas to be acquired, survive the group environment, settle into an ordered configuration, and form stars.

The role of environment is important to galaxy evolution. Galaxy properties are known to correlate with local density and halo mass, from the classical morphology–density relation to the distinct assembly histories of central and satellite galaxies (Dressler, 1980; Peng et al., 2010; Somerville & Davé, 2015). These correlations extend to the most massive central galaxies: the properties of brightest cluster and group galaxies (BCGs and BGGs) are connected to the global properties and dynamical state of their host groups and clusters, including the mass, shape, and orientation of the surrounding halo.
