papers.title: The Pristine survey XXIX. Data Release 2: Photometric metallicities for 15 millions stars down to $G\sim 20.5$
papers.abstract: Tailored narrow-band photometric observations are an efficient way to measure the metallicity of Milky Way stars. The Pristine survey has been mapping the northern sky since 2015 using narrow-band $CaHK$ photometry obtained with the MegaCam imager on the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope (CFHT). Data Release 1 (DR1) provided a high-precision absolute calibration of the survey observed before October 2022 using \Gaia DR3 XP synthetic photometry, yielding photometric metallicities over $\sim$6,500 deg$^2$, but was limited in depth to the availability of \Gaia spectro-photometry ($G \lesssim 17.65$). We present the Pristine Data Release 2 (DR2) that includes all Pristine observations until January 2025, corresponding to an additional 1,500\,deg$^2$ of coverage, and including all faint sources down to $G\sim20.5$. This release aims to exploit the full depth of the Pristine observations to uncover the faint metal-poor halo. We process all images observed from the start of the survey in March 2015 through to January 2025 following the methodology presented in DR1. The core of the calibration utilizes the subset of bright stars with \Gaia synthetic $CaHK_\mathrm{syn}$ magnitudes to train the \texttt{PhotCalib} neural network. We then derive photometric metallicities using the established Pristine ($CaHK, G, G_{\rm BP}, G_{\rm RP}$) to [Fe/H] model. The resulting catalogue covers approximately $\sim$ 8,000 deg$^{2}$ and provides photometric metallicities for 15 millions FGK stars, which show good agreement with recently published, independent Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) metallicities. With its increased coverage and access to a significantly fainter regime compared to DR1, DR2 significantly increases the volume of the survey. We report more than 200,000 and 6,500 very and extremely metal-poor star candidates, respectively.

papers.intro:
The search for low-metallicity stars in the Milky Way is a search for the fossil record of the early Universe; these stars serve as unique probes for understanding the formation and evolution of primordial stellar systems. A continuing effort to find and identify these rare objects dates back to the HK survey (Beers et al., 1992) and the Hamburg-ESO survey (Christlieb et al., 2008). These pioneer surveys demonstrated the success of utilizing prism spectroscopy in the region of the Ca H & K lines (3900–4000A∘\;\mathrel{\mathop{\kern 0.0pt\rm A}\limits^{\circ}}) to efficiently select low-metallicity stars. Over the last couple of decades, this approach has evolved through the use of narrow-band filters covering the same Ca H & K region, mounted on wide-field cameras to systematically map the sky. Combined with readily accessible optical broadband photometry, the narrow-band photometry provides reliable metallicity estimates for the numerous FGK stars of the Milky Way. Such observations prove more efficient at probing the very metal-poor (VMP, [Fe/H]<−2\mathrm{[Fe/H]}<-2) and extremely metal-poor (EMP, [Fe/H]<−3\mathrm{[Fe/H]}<-3) regimes than when using only broadband photometry ( i.e., Ivezić et al. 2008, Ibata et al. 2017). Two main surveys started building on this narrow- and medium-band photometry strategy a decade ago: the SkyMapper survey, in the south, with its vv-band filter (Keller et al., 2007; Wolf et al., 2018; Onken et al., 2019; Chiti et al., 2021; Onken et al., 2024), and the Pristine survey (Starkenburg et al., 2017; Martin et al., 2024). The latter utilizes a custom narrow-band filter centered specifically on the Ca H & K lines, mounted on the MegaCam imager at the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope (CFHT) located at Mauna Kea. Such surveys have been shown to be particularly suited at finding the rare stars at the low end of the metallicity distribution function ([Fe/H]<−2.0{\rm[Fe/H]}<-2.0; e.g., Aguado et al. 2019; Da Costa et al. 2019). Other surveys that use similar strategies have since started (e.g., MAGIC Placco et al. 2025), sometimes complemented with additional narrow-band filters that allow for the determination of other stellar parameters (e.g., J-PLUS –Cenarro et al. 2019– or S-PLUS –Mendes de Oliveira et al. 2019).

papers.title: Nonlocal Gravity, Restricted CPL Dynamics and DESI Constraints
papers.abstract: Nonlocal modifications of gravity provide a theoretically motivated framework in which cosmic acceleration can emerge dynamically without introducing a fundamental cosmological constant. We revisit the cosmological predictions of the Maggiore--Mancarella nonlocal $R\,\Box^{-2}R$ model, with particular emphasis on its background dynamics and observational viability in light of recent DESI baryon acoustic oscillation measurements. A key feature of the theory is its predictive character: for fixed standard cosmological parameters, each value of the nonlocal parameter determines a specific effective pair $(w_0,w_a)$, so that the model traces a restricted trajectory in the Chevallier--Polarski--Linder plane rather than spanning the full phenomenological parameter space. We construct this mapping explicitly and confront the model with observations by implementing its cosmological dynamics in a Boltzmann solver and performing a Markov chain Monte Carlo analysis using Cosmic Microwave Background, supernova, and DESI BAO data. We find that current datasets constrain the nonlocal parameter close to the $Λ$CDM limit, with no statistically significant preference for nonlocal deviations.

papers.intro:
General Relativity (GR) provides an extremely successful description of gravitational phenomena over a vast range of scales, from laboratory and Solar System tests to the large-scale dynamics of the Universe. Combined with the cosmological principle and a cosmological constant, it leads to the standard Λ\LambdaCDM model, which provides an excellent fit to a broad set of cosmological observations, including the cosmic microwave background (CMB) [2], large-scale structure, and supernova distance measurements [44]. Despite this empirical success, the physical origin and the observed small value of the cosmological constant remain theoretically unexplained, giving rise to a severe fine-tuning problem. This has long motivated the exploration of theoretically consistent alternatives in which cosmic acceleration emerges dynamically rather than from a fundamental cosmological constant [3, 11].

Combined with the cosmological principle and a cosmological constant, it leads to the standard Λ\LambdaCDM model, which provides an excellent fit to a broad set of cosmological observations, including the cosmic microwave background (CMB) [2], large-scale structure, and supernova distance measurements [44]. Despite this empirical success, the physical origin and the observed small value of the cosmological constant remain theoretically unexplained, giving rise to a severe fine-tuning problem. This has long motivated the exploration of theoretically consistent alternatives in which cosmic acceleration emerges dynamically rather than from a fundamental cosmological constant [3, 11].

Recent observational developments further reinforce the importance of testing departures from Λ\LambdaCDM. In particular, the latest baryon acoustic oscillation measurements from the DESI collaboration have reached unprecedented precision and show a mild preference for dynamical dark-energy parametrizations when combined with other cosmological probes [1]. While the statistical significance of these deviations is still under active assessment, see e.g. [29, 14], they provide a timely opportunity to confront theoretically well-defined models of dynamical dark energy with high-quality data [31, 49, 42, 47, 12, 15, 16]. In this context, predictive models, in which the dark-energy evolution is not freely adjustable but instead follows from the underlying theory, are especially valuable.

An important distinction must therefore be made between phenomenological evidence for an evolving dark-energy component and evidence for a specific theory of cosmic acceleration. While the CPL parametrization allows the present value and time dependence of the dark-energy equation of state to vary independently, a fundamental theory generally correlates these quantities through its equations of motion. Consequently, even a model capable of generating a time-dependent equation of state need not reproduce the particular evolutionary pattern favored by observations. Assessing this compatibility requires confronting the correlations imposed by the underlying dynamics with the data, rather than merely establishing the existence of an evolving dark-energy component.

Among the proposed extensions of GR, nonlocal gravity constitutes a well-motivated class of modified theories [41]. Nonlocal interactions naturally arise in several approaches to quantum gravity. In string theory, for instance, gravitational interactions are expected to acquire a nonlocal character at the Planck scale [45, 13]. From an ultraviolet perspective, nonlocality has also been investigated as a possible ingredient for improving the high-energy behavior of gravity and constructing ultraviolet-complete theories [9, 8, 37]. Nonlocal modifications, however, are not restricted to the ultraviolet regime. They can also emerge at large distances from several infrared mechanisms, including quantum corrections to the effective gravitational action [48, 4, 20, 6], effective field theories obtained after integrating out light degrees of freedom [18, 27], more fundamental formulations of Euclidean quantum gravity [46, 5], effective descriptions of massive-graviton theories [32, 36], theories involving multiple metrics [19], and extensions based on post-Riemannian affine geometry [30]. The phenomenological implications of nonlocal gravity have also been explored in astrophysical settings, including compact stellar objects [43].

The phenomenological implications of nonlocal gravity have also been explored in astrophysical settings, including compact stellar objects [43].

At the level of the gravitational action, nonlocality is typically introduced through curvature invariants involving either infinitely many derivatives, encoded in non-polynomial functions of the d’Alembertian operator [8], or inverse differential operators such as □−1\Box^{-1} [20] or the inverse conformal anomaly operator [38]. The latter approach was pioneered in the context of cosmology by Deser and Woodard (DW) [20], who proposed one of the first nonlocal models aimed at explaining the late-time cosmic acceleration without explicitly introducing a cosmological constant. The DW model modifies the evolution of cosmological perturbations in a way that was initially considered to be in tension with observations [26]. Subsequent studies, however, showed that this tension could be alleviated [40], although a comprehensive confrontation of the model with observational data remains outstanding.

In this work, we focus on the nonlocal R​□−2​RR\Box^{-2}R model introduced by Maggiore and Mancarella (MM) [35]. In this framework, deviations from GR are controlled by a single mass scale and manifest themselves at cosmological scales as an effective dark-energy component. The model modifies the large-scale gravitational dynamics while preserving the successful local predictions of GR and yielding a matter power spectrum compatible with current observations [24, 23, 25]. More generally, the MM model and related realizations of nonlocal gravity have been shown to admit viable cosmological backgrounds and consistent perturbation dynamics without the need for an explicit cosmological constant [22, 21]. An important feature of the MM model is its predictive character: once the realization of the inverse d’Alembertian operator is fixed through the initial conditions of the corresponding auxiliary fields, the cosmological evolution is no longer freely adjustable but is restricted to a narrow family of trajectories controlled by a nonlocal mass parameter [7]. Consequently, the theory does not span the full space of phenomenological dark-energy parametrizations; instead, its underlying dynamics impose a definite relation between the present-day value of the effective equation of state and its time evolution.

papers.title: The ALMA-QUARKS Survey. IV. Core Mass Function and Evolutionary Trends in Core Formation Efficiency and Chemistry
papers.abstract: The ALMA-QUARKS (Querying Underlying Mechanisms of Massive Star Formation with ALMA-Resolved Gas Kinematics and Structures) survey targets 139 massive protoclusters selected from the ATOMS survey. The targets were observed at 1.3~mm wavelength with an angular resolution of $\sim0.3^{\prime\prime}$, corresponding to $\sim10^3$~au at the sample's median distance of $\sim3.8$~kpc. Using \texttt{getsf}, we identify 3374 dense cores and classify them as starless, protostellar, hot core, or H{\sc ii} region candidates based on spectral-line diagnostics (e.g., H30$α$, CH$_3$CN, and CH$_3$OH) and CO outflow associations. The resulting catalog provides core physical properties and enables statistical investigations of dense core populations in massive protocluster environments. The derived global core mass function (CMF) after excluding H{\sc ii} region candidates, which is biased by distance effects, has a relatively flat power-law slope at the high-mass end ($\mathrm{d}N/\mathrm{d}\log M \propto M^{-γ}$, with $γ=0.98\pm0.03$). In contrast, the measured high-mass slopes in individual distance bins are approximately Salpeter-like, while their fitted lower mass limits increase with distance. We further examine the core formation efficiency (CFE) across the full sample and find that it positively correlates with the luminosity-to-mass ratio of the parental clumps, consistent with an evolutionary increase in the fraction of mass concentrated into dense cores. We also investigate the detection rates of different molecular tracers and find systematic chemical variations with evolutionary stage. Compared with the ASHES survey, we find that the detection rates of deuterated species vary significantly even for cores at the same evolutionary stages, suggesting an important environmental influence on the chemical evolution of cores.

papers.title: The optical colors of hidden spiral-like features in nine Virgo early--type dwarfs
papers.abstract: Dwarf early-type galaxies (ETGs) are abundant in nearby clusters and provide a key laboratory for studying environmentally driven galaxy transformation. Although dwarf ETGs were once considered structurally simple, deep imaging has revealed embedded spiral-like features (e.g., bars and spiral arms) in some of them, contributing only a small fraction of the total light. Their origin at dwarf scales remains uncertain. As a pilot study, we investigate spiral-like features in nine Virgo dwarf ETGs with clear embedded arms, using optical colors to test whether these features differ from the surrounding diffuse component, which would constrain their formation pathways. Using deep g- and i-band NGVS images, we apply a residual-based method to separate excess light associated with the spiral-like component from the diffuse host. The residual images define arm and interarm regions, enabling direct measurements of light fractions and g-i colors for both components. The spiral-like features contribute only a few percent of the total light (about 1.5-5.5% in i and 1.7-3.7% in g). We find a diverse range of colors across the sample: four galaxies host spiral-like features redder than their interarm regions, four show no robust arm-interarm color difference, and one exhibits a distinctly bluer spiral-like component. The latter is consistent with a recently quenched transition object, while the redder and color-uniform features are consistent with older or more metal-rich stellar populations. Spiral-like features in Virgo dwarf ETGs thus exhibit a surprising diversity in their photometric properties, implying multiple evolutionary channels rather than a single one. This pilot analysis also demonstrates readiness for the much larger NGVS sample of dwarfs with potential spiral-like features.

papers.intro:
In the local Universe, small, low-mass dwarf galaxies represent the most numerous class of galaxies (Binggeli et al., 1985; Ferguson, 1989). Morphologically, dwarfs are commonly divided into two broad categories based on their global colors and level of star formation activity (Sandage and Binggeli, 1984): dwarf early–type galaxies (dETGs) and dwarf late-type galaxies (dLTGs). Both are characterized by low luminosities with the bright end being MB≈−18M_{B}\approx-18 (Ferguson and Binggeli, 1994) and low stellar masses (M⋆≲109−9.5​M⊙M_{\star}\lesssim 10^{9-9.5}\,{\rm M_{\odot}}).

Dwarf LTGs exhibit blue colors, ongoing star formation, and substantial reservoirs of gas and dust. They typically show irregular morphologies ( e.g., Carignan and Beaulieu 1989; Skillman et al. 1989; Conselice et al. 2003; Skillman 2005; Ann et al. 2015) or spiral-like features containing spiral arms or bars (e.g., Grebel 2001) and they are preferentially located in the lower-density outskirts of galaxy clusters, where dwarfs tend to rotate more strongly than those in the inner cluster. In contrast, dwarf ETGs are largely quenched systems with little gas or dust, resulting in their globally red optical colors and generally smooth morphology. Historically divided into dwarf ellipticals (Ferguson and Binggeli, 1994; Graham and Guzmán, 2003), dwarf lenticulars (Sandage and Binggeli, 1984; Binggeli and Cameron, 1991), and dwarf spheroidals (Harbeck et al., 2001), dwarf ETGs dominate the galaxy population in dense environments (Binggeli et al., 1985; Kurzner et al., 2025), while their occurrence in the field is very rare, with a probability below ∼0.06%\sim 0.06\% (Geha et al., 2012).

Dwarf ETGs, despite their seemingly simple appearance, have been discovered to harbor a range of intricate structural and stellar population complexities. Many are not well described by a single Sersic profile (Sersic, 1968), exhibiting multiple components (Janz et al., 2012; Janz et al., 2014; Su et al., 2021); moreover, spiral arms and bars have been detected in several cluster ETGs (Jerjen et al., 2001; Barazza et al., 2002; De Rijcke et al., 2003; Graham and Guzmán, 2003; Ferrarese et al., 2006; Lisker et al., 2006c; Penny et al., 2014; Venhola et al., 2019; Michea et al., 2022). Color imaging has revealed that some of these galaxies contain blue central regions indicative of recent or ongoing star formation, even though the class as a whole resides on the red sequence of the color–magnitude diagram (Hodge, 1973; Vigroux et al., 1984; Peletier, 1993; Lisker et al., 2006b; Pak et al., 2014; Urich et al., 2017; Hamraz et al., 2019). These "blue-cored" dwarf ETGs are preferentially located in the lower-density outskirts of galaxy clusters where dwarfs tend to be rotating more strongly than dwarf in the inner cluster (Lisker, 2009; Toloba et al., 2009). Almost all ETGs have negative metallicity gradients (Urich et al., 2017; Sybilska et al., 2017; Bidaran et al., 2023). Some of these steep gradients are linked to past dwarf-dwarf merger events (Taibi et al., 2022), while others are associated with the presence of shells in certain cluster members (Paudel et al., 2017). In the literature, these pathways are generally grouped into two broad classes: "nature" and "nurture" scenarios. In the nature scenario, the properties of dwarf ETGs reflect their intrinsic formation histories, such as early collapse, gradual mass assembly, or minor mergers that can heat or reshape their stellar components. In nurture, environmental mechanisms acting after infall into a group or cluster are responsible for quenching star formation and transforming LTG progenitors into ETGs. Several processes can contribute to such transformations, including starvation or strangulation, which halts the supply of fresh gas as the galaxy falls into high-density regions (Larson et al., 1980; Boselli et al., 2008); ram-pressure stripping by the hot intracluster medium, which efficiently removes cold gas (Gunn and Gott, 1972; van Zee et al., 2004; De Rijcke et al., 2010); and tidal harassment from high-speed encounters or the global cluster potential, which primarily leads to dynamical heating and thickening of stellar disks (Smith et al., 2010; Smith et al., 2015) and can perturb internal structures (Moore et al., 1998; Moore et al., 1999; Michea et al., 2022).

Early systematic efforts, most notably by Lisker et al. (2006c), used an iterative technique similar to unsharp masking on SDSS imaging to identify and study spiral-like substructures such as bars and spiral arms in Virgo dwarf ETGs. These studies first established that a nonnegligible fraction of Virgo dwarf galaxies exhibit embedded spiral-like components, and that residual-based decomposition can delineate where those components lie within a galaxy. While their contribution to the total galaxy light is typically modest (between 5%5\%–15%15\%), it can rise to nearly half in some dwarf ETGs.

papers.title: Modal estimation of high-order wavefront drifts on coronagraphic testbeds for high-contrast direct imaging of exoplanets
papers.abstract: Long-term wavefront stability will be critical for the upcoming Habitable Worlds Observatory which aims to directly image exo-Earths. Mechanical and thermal instabilities induce slow, high-order wavefront errors which can degrade the contrast and in turn, the scientific yield of the observatory. Dark zone maintenance (DZM) has been proposed as a high-order wavefront sensing and control strategy to maintain contrast despite wavefront error drifts. This approach uses an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) to estimate the electric field at each pixel in the dark zone of the science camera. However, relying on individual pixel information to estimate wavefront errors can discard information stored in the underlying wavefront. This is a fundamental limitation on the best achieved contrast compared to the model based theoretical bounds derived from photon noise. An alternative EKF can incorporate more holistic information by estimating the drifting wavefront modes present in the system. In this work we analyze the performance of this Modal EKF on the High-contrast Imager for Complex Aperture Telescopes (HiCAT) simulator at the Space Telescope Science Institute. A parameter scan is performed across key variables: deformable mirror (DM) drift, the direct photon rate at the telescope aperture governing the mean number of photons in the dark zone (DZ), and the dither magnitude used to provide phase diversity. While prior studies explored a range of dither magnitudes, this work introduces a covariance-based approach within the Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) framework to optimally determine the probe magnitude required. Results from the modal EKF demonstrate a 15-fold improvement in contrast relative to the single-pixel DZM experiments, reducing the gap to within a factor of 2-3 of the theoretical bounds.

papers.intro:
The Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO), scheduled for launch in the 2040s, is envisioned as the next flagship large-aperture observatory tasked with directly imaging Earth-like exoplanets, as recommended by the 2020 Decadal Survey on Astronomy and Astrophysics. Imaging exoplanets in the habitable zone, where liquid water may exist, requires suppressing starlight that is approximately 101010^{10} times brighter than the planetary signal [27]. Coronagraphs, optical systems composed of a focal-plane mask to occult starlight and a pupil-plane mask to mitigate diffraction, have been demonstrated by NASA to achieve contrasts of 4×10−104\times 10^{-10} when combined with two deformable mirrors (DMs) [22]. This enables the formation of a high-contrast region in the image, known as the dark zone (DZ), by compensating for static aberrations in the telescope system.

The Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO), scheduled for launch in the 2040s, is envisioned as the next flagship large-aperture observatory tasked with directly imaging Earth-like exoplanets, as recommended by the 2020 Decadal Survey on Astronomy and Astrophysics. Imaging exoplanets in the habitable zone, where liquid water may exist, requires suppressing starlight that is approximately 101010^{10} times brighter than the planetary signal [27]. Coronagraphs, optical systems composed of a focal-plane mask to occult starlight and a pupil-plane mask to mitigate diffraction, have been demonstrated by NASA to achieve contrasts of 4×10−104\times 10^{-10} when combined with two deformable mirrors (DMs) [22]. This enables the formation of a high-contrast region in the image, known as the dark zone (DZ), by compensating for static aberrations in the telescope system.

The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope (RST) will provide the first in-space demonstration of this technology, targeting contrasts of 10−810^{-8} with its coronagraph. In Roman’s observing strategy, a bright reference star is used to generate the DM commands needed to suppress aberrations and establish a DZ before slewing to the science target. However, thermal and mechanical instabilities degrade the DZ over time, requiring repeated slews back to the reference star to refresh DM commands [5]. This approach reduces the effective observing time and is not practical for HWO, which demands a higher and more stable contrast over long durations.

To meet these requirements, high-order wavefront sensing and control (HOWFSC) techniques are needed. HOWFSC enables continuous observation of the science target while simultaneously correcting quasi-static aberrations, which manifest as speckles in the image [17]. One such technique is Dark Zone Maintenance (DZM), which uses science exposures directly as measurements to estimate and null aberrations to maintain high contrast in the DZ [13, 18].

Several algorithms have been developed to maintain contrast in the dark zone, including Linear Dark Field Control (LDFC) [8] and implicit electric field conjugation (iEFC)[4] among others. DZM is one such approach, and has consistently demonstrated the ability to sustain contrast in the DZ despite continuous disturbances acting on the system.

DZM is one such approach, and has consistently demonstrated the ability to sustain contrast in the DZ despite continuous disturbances acting on the system.

In DZM, science exposures are used directly as measurements for the Extended Kalman Filter (EKF), which serves as the primary estimator of the open-loop electric field at every pixel of the focal plane. The EKF output is then passed to the Electric Field Conjugation (EFC) controller, which combines the electric field estimate with the system Jacobian to compute DM commands that null the field via least-squares minimization [3]. EFC is also widely used to dig the DZ when paired with pair-wise probing (PWP), which estimates the electric field by differencing images taken with positive and negative probe commands applied to the DMs [2]. While the PWP and EFC combination has been shown to effectively create high-contrast dark zones, the large number of exposures required makes it inefficient for contrast maintenance during science observations.

One of the primary metrics for evaluating contrast maintenance algorithms is their performance under contrast-limiting factors. These factors can be broadly classified into environmental and wavefront sensing and control (WFSC) variables. Environmental factors arise from the telescope and its operating environment, while WFSC factors are tied to the specific algorithm being applied.

papers.title: The energetic atmosphere of the Sun
papers.abstract: Understanding the mechanisms that heat the Sun's chromosphere and corona to temperatures far exceeding those of the solar photosphere below remains one of the central challenges in solar physics. Small-scale, rapidly evolving processes - including shocks, turbulence, magnetohydrodynamic waves, reconnection-driven jets, and nano-flares - are thought to contribute significantly to the heating budget. However, direct observational constraints on their spatial, temporal, and spectral signatures remain hard to obtain. At millimeter wavelengths, optically thick thermal emission provides a comparatively direct measure of gas temperature. While the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) already provides unique diagnostic capabilities, offering temperature diagnostics and high-cadence imaging, the current capabilities are still limiting the study of such dynamic, small-scale phenomena. Improved spatial resolution, enhanced uv-coverage, and simultaneous multi-band observations, as proposed for ALMA2040, would enable transformative progress in capturing dynamic processes across multiple heights and enable time-dependent three-dimensional thermal and magnetic tomography of the chromosphere. Combined with complementary diagnostics and simulations, these measurements would test how small-scale processes contribute to atmospheric heating.

papers.title: JWST reveals a highly ionized nebula powered by an ultraluminous X-ray source with a massive black hole in the metal-poor galaxy Holmberg II
papers.abstract: Recent James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) observations have revealed fine-structure lines of ions with ionization potentials ${\gtrsim}50$\,eV, such as [Ne\,{\sc v}] and [O\,{\sc iv}], in nebular spectra of some low-metallicity galaxies, raising questions about the nature of the ionizing sources. Ultraluminous X-ray sources (ULXs) have been considered as potential contributors, but direct evidence linking individual ULXs to highly ionized nebulae is limited. Here we present JWST IFU spectroscopy of the nebula surrounding the template ULX Ho\,II\,X--1 in the low-metallicity galaxy Holmberg\,II, already known to emit He\,{\sc ii}\,$\lambda4686$ and [O\,{\sc iv}]\,25.89\,$μ$m lines. We resolve the infrared nebula on spatial scales of ${\sim}15-25$\,pc and report the first detections of [Ne\,{\sc v}] and [Ne\,{\sc vi}] in this source. We find anisotropic ionizing conditions: emission from the highest-ionization species arises from compact regions offset from the ULX toward the previously detected radio knots, whereas lower-ionization species trace the wider nebula. The preferential alignment of the highest-ionization emission with the radio axis suggests anisotropic escape of the ionizing continuum and a physical connection with jet-ejection activity. Spectral lines across the nebula are narrow and consistent with the instrumental resolution, indicating kinematically quiescent gas and disfavoring shocks as the dominant ionization mechanism. Together, these results provide direct evidence linking an individual ULX to a highly ionized nebula in a low-metallicity galaxy. These JWST observations of Ho~II~X--1 show that an accreting black hole in a low-metallicity galaxy is responsible for the extreme ionization of the surrounding nebula on ${\sim}100$\,pc scales.

The ULX nebulae, which are usually observed in optical and radio, have a wide range of excitation and kinematic properties. While some nebulae display shock-excited expanding shells with velocities of several hundred km s-1, other nebulae are quiescent and their spectra are dominated by narrow lines consistent with photoionization [43].

Distinguishing between shock and photoionized nebulae is not easy and does not provide a unique diagnostic of the accretion regime operating in the X-ray source. Photoionization is always present, and may dominate in some locations or trace phases of the gas even in the shock heated nebulae. Shocks can be driven by jets or disk winds. Hence, a nebula which is predominantly photoionized does not necessarily imply the absence of mechanical feedback. Emission-line ratios and ionization structure provide important constraints on the dominant excitation mechanism, while spatially resolved spectroscopy adds the ability to connect local ionization conditions with the kinematics of the gas [1, 28].

papers.title: ALMA observations towards M83 reveal N2H+ tracing dense gas
papers.abstract: Galactic observations have shown that N2H+ intensities preferentially trace star-forming dense molecular gas compared with HCN or HCO+, which are conventionally used as dense-gas tracers in extragalactic studies. In this study, we aim to verify this trend in the nearby star-forming galaxy M83. Using ALMA, we observed the J=1-0 transitions of N2H+ and HCN, along with the 1-mm and 3-mm continuum, and analyzed the archival CO(1-0) data. The data achieved a spatial resolution of 48 pc in the southwestern bar-end region of M83, covering an area of 2.1 kpc x 1.8 kpc. N2H+ and HCN intensities are approximately linearly correlated, indicating that HCN luminosity can still reasonably predict the amount of dense gas as well as N2H+ luminosity does. However, in regions with high column densities, N2H+ becomes a super-linear function of HCN, suggesting that the N2H+ emission is more sensitive to dense gas than HCN. We employed a radiative transfer model that predicts line intensities as a function of column density, adopting parametric column density probability distribution functions (N-PDFs) to describe the underlying column density distribution. The model demonstrates that the observed linear or superlinear trend can be explained by a log-normal distribution only or a log-normal and a power-law tail distribution in the N-PDF. Furthermore, the N2H+ intensity is significantly more sensitive to the power-law tail than the HCN intensity. In addition, our analysis incorporating archival data shows that N2H+ is a less reliable tracer of dense gas in galactic center regions, where warmer temperatures may promote N2H+ destruction.

papers.intro:
Within molecular clouds, there is a hierarchy of density structures. The densest parts are directly associated with star formation, as they are most favorable for gravitational collapse. It has been suggested that there is a density threshold for star formation. Some observational studies proposed a specific volume density (n∼104n\sim 10^{4} cm-3) or column density [43, N∼1022N\sim 10^{22} cm-2;], whereas there are theories that consider the threshold as a function of the mean density, Mach number, and the virial parameter [41]. More recently, the star formation threshold has been shown to be linked to the minimum line mass of molecular filaments, which fragment to dense star-forming cores [2, 60]. While it is possible to resolve these dense cores, filaments, and clumps in Galactic star-forming regions, it is unfeasible in extragalactic observations except in the most nearby galaxies using currently available observing capabilities whose beam sizes are typically on the order of 10 pc or more. Instead of directly resolving these dense cores, certain molecular transitions with high critical densities can be useful in measuring the amount of dense gas in extragalactic sources.

Yet, it is important to investigate the emission in these regions since they host less extreme physical conditions than galactic centers, which are characterized by high cosmic-ray ionization rates, high pressure, and high temperatures. Watanabe et al. [83] conducted a line survey towards two spiral arm regions with different star formation rates in M51, and detected a number of species including N2H+. Jiménez-Donaire et al. [30] observed N2H+ and HCN JJ=1–0 transitions towards five selected positions in a double-barred spiral galaxy NGC 6946 using the IRAM 30-meter telescope. This study found that the N2H+/HCN intensity ratio is constant among these positions on the kpc scale. If the N2H+/HCN ratio is constant in different physical conditions and across spatial scales, then it would be reasonable to use HCN emission as a tracer of the dense gas instead of the fainter N2H+ line. However, this ratio starts to deviate from a constant at a higher spatial resolution. papers.title: Generic Mean Curvature Flow With Rough Weights
papers.abstract: We prove the generic existence of mean curvature flows in spaces with rough weights. Our weak solutions are both unit-density Brakke flows and distributional solutions. Such a generic statement is optimal in the sense that we consider weights that are too rough to have well-defined traces on every hypersurface.

papers.title: An HST survey of photometry and multiplicity of brown dwarfs and planetary-mass objects in the field of Taurus
papers.abstract: We present a photometric and multiplicity survey of 26 young objects with masses between 6 Mj and 37 Mj and spectral type later than M8 in the Taurus star-forming region with the Hubble Space Telescope. We search for companion candidates using two methods: a dedicated photometric technique based on the combination of colours from multi-band photometry and point spread function fitting. No companion candidates are detected beyond 30 au. With an updated membership and age identification, we determine luminosity, temperature, and mass for the 26 young objects using evolutionary models. We demonstrate that our HST observations are sensitive to companions down to masses of 1 Mj and even lower for some targets by artificial star injection tests. After survey completeness correction, we derive a binary frequency < 6.5% for this sample in the 68% confidence interval for companions with mass ratios between 0.1 and 1 and separations between 30 and 7,000 au. We find no significant difference in binary frequency among planetary-mass objects in Taurus, Upper Scorpius, and the field. These findings support that the binary frequency of planetary-mass objects is settled at young ages, probably younger than 1--10 Myr, suggesting that the formation of wide-orbit planetary-mass binaries is inefficient and the disruption of them likely occurs at a very early stage in a low density environment.

papers.intro:
The formation of brown dwarf binaries and planetary-mass binaries remains mysterious, although several formation channels have been proposed, including direct collapse and turbulent formation of dense cores resembling the formation of stellar binaries (Larson, 1972; Goodwin et al., 2004; André et al., 2019), gravitational instability in discs (Adams et al., 1989; Bonnell, 1994; Kratter and Lodato, 2016), and dynamical capture (Ostriker, 1994; Moeckel and Bally, 2007; Bate, 2012) and triple-system disruption (Reipurth and Mikkola, 2015). Each mechanism leaves imprints on the multiplicity fraction, separation distribution, mass-ratio distribution, and eccentricity of the resulting population. Thus, multiplicity is a key diagnostic of formation processes.

Each mechanism leaves imprints on the multiplicity fraction, separation distribution, mass-ratio distribution, and eccentricity of the resulting population. Thus, multiplicity is a key diagnostic of formation processes.

The fraction of objects found in binary or multiple systems in the field decreases with the mass of the primary: about half of solar-type FGK stars are in multiple systems (Raghavan et al., 2010), compared to 20–30% of M dwarfs (Janson et al., 2012; Ward-Duong et al., 2015), and less than 20% for brown dwarfs and planetary-mass objects (Bouy et al., 2003; Fontanive et al., 2018; Fontanive et al., 2023). Understanding the origin of this decline is critical for distinguishing whether stars, brown dwarfs, and free-floating planetary-mass objects form through common or distinct mechanisms. Moreover, because this trend is established primarily for field populations (age >1>1 Gyr), it remains unclear whether it is primordial or the result of dynamical evolution. Surveying brown dwarf and planetary-mass binaries across different evolutionary stages is therefore crucial for constraining their formation pathways.

Although the first multiplicity surveys of very low-mass stars and brown dwarfs date back to the 1990s (Fischer and Marcy, 1992), the population of known binaries in this regime has remained small. Nevertheless, observations reveal that very low-mass binaries differ from stellar binaries in both orbital separation and mass ratio distributions (Duchêne and Kraus, 2013; Offner et al., 2023). Burgasser et al. (2007) found that for systems with primary masses below 0.1 M⊙M_{\odot} in the field, their mass ratios strongly peak near unity, even after correcting for observational biases. The orbital separation distribution of very low-mass binaries is narrower than higher mass systems: the separation of the majority of very low-mass binaries is found within 10 au via spectroscopic observations (spectroscopic binaries) and high angular resolution observations (visual binaries) (Reid et al., 2002; Basri and Reiners, 2006; Burgasser et al., 2012; Maxted and Jeffries, 2005; Allen et al., 2007). This indicates that brown dwarf and planetary-mass binaries are more likely to be found in equal-mass binaries at close separations, suggesting formation channels that favour similar-mass pairing with the greater dynamical stability of such configurations.

Wide, very low-mass binaries have low binding energy and are subject to dynamical disruption after formation. (2023) constrained the binary fraction of late-T and Y-type brown dwarfs in the field with age >> 1 Gyr to be smaller than 4.9%. De Furio et al. Comparing multiplicity in various regions can examine the environment’s impacts on binary formation and evolution. Simulations have found that high stellar density can disrupt binaries (Ivanova et al., 2005). As one of the youngest star-forming regions in the solar neighbourhood, Taurus is a low-density environment consisting of sub-regions with an age of 1–10 Myr (Kenyon et al., 2008; Luhman, 2023) as well as older moving groups with ages of 10–60 Myr (Kraus et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2021). papers.title: Data World: Scaling Data Environments from Scratch
papers.abstract: Data agents use code to process heterogeneous files and derive analytical insights. Scaling their training faces costly environment curation, privacy and intellectual-property restrictions, and difficulty verifying open-ended findings without known generative truth. Our core insight is to specify the world behind the files before generating the files themselves. We introduce Data World, a multi-agent engine that synthesizes environments, tasks, and rubrics from explicit mechanisms. Independent audits check target recoverability from observed files; rubrics support evaluation and RL rewards. Human preference-based curation for question realism selects 100 tasks across 50 held-out worlds and 16 domains for DataWorld-Bench. The engine also yields 2,135 training tasks from 1,037 disjoint worlds. Evaluation of ten frontier models shows that the benchmark remains challenging, particularly for insight discovery, with a consistent computation-insight gap. RL-zero training on the synthesized tasks produces DataWorld-35B-A3B from Qwen3.6-35B-A3B without trajectory distillation. Under matched evaluation, it improves over its base by 7.06 points on DataWorld-Bench, 14.28 on DAComp, 20.90 on DABstep-Hard, and 12.13 on JobBench, a broader occupational benchmark.

papers.intro:
Data agents use code to inspect heterogeneous files, compute quantities, and derive evidence-supported analytical insights (Huang et al., 2024; Hong et al., 2025). Their data environments often contain multi-source structured data distributed across CSV and Excel tables (Dong et al., 2026b; Hasegawa et al., 2026). A task may ask an agent to explain a change in an outcome or trace its downstream implications, requiring more than correct computation alone. Training and evaluating these agents therefore require both diverse environments for multi-step analysis and feedback that distinguishes supported conclusions from errors. As agentic LLM post-training scales, this joint supply of environments and supervision becomes a central constraint (Huang et al., 2025a; Wang et al., 2026; Tu et al., 2026; Tian et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026).

Synthetic data has long served as an important complement to real data when the latter is costly or restricted (Walonoski et al., 2018). Yet for data agents, two obstacles limit this supply. First, diversity and accessibility: acquiring and annotating real workflows is costly, while privacy and intellectual-property restrictions constrain reuse (Dong et al., 2026b; Walonoski et al., 2018). Second, verifiability: the data-generating process behind real files is often unavailable, so open-ended findings rely on curated references or approximate matching (Gu et al., 2024; Sahu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026). Exploring these files to write tasks and rubrics ties supervision to what the curator or mining model discovers (Ramrakhya et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026). For example, consider an expert or strong model given food-delivery records collected from an online platform and asked to write a rubric for evaluating analyses of declining sales. Inspecting these records, it may identify expired promotions as a contributor but overlook reduced restaurant opening hours. An agent uncovering the latter may then receive no credit because the rubric omits that explanation, even when the records support it. Indeed, ten experts or strong models could offer ten different explanations for the same decline, as data complexity and inadequately controlled confounders can leave the underlying mechanism ambiguous. How can we scale diverse data environments with grounded supervision while retaining open-ended analytical depth?

Our core insight is to specify the world behind the files before generating the files themselves. Analysis depends on statistical and relational structure that explicit mechanisms can instantiate in code. This enables varied environments without private source records, while known generative states ground checks of selected analytical targets. Synthesizing new environments and task-specific answers also reduces the risk of pretraining contamination associated with reusing public datasets. Figure 1 illustrates the resulting difference for a data agent: its targeted findings have aligned rubric criteria rather than depending on prior exploration of existing files. The key challenge is preserving target recoverability through imperfect observations without making the analysis trivial.

papers.title: Mixture of Multi-Sequence Feature Difference for Contrast-Enhanced MRI Synthesis
papers.abstract: Contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (CE-MRI) is crucial for accurately diagnosing and segmenting brain tumors. However, the acquisition of CE-MRI requires injecting contrast agents, which poses potential health risks and increases scan costs. Here, we propose a CE-MRI synthesis method from non-contrast sequences, reducing both risk and cost. Unlike existing methods that rely on channel-wise concatenation to fuse multi-sequence information for synthesis, we introduce a Mixture of Feature Difference (MoFD) module. The proposed module uses a dynamic weighting strategy to adaptively select and aggregate informative features from both individual source sequences and explicit differences among them. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms baselines in terms of image fidelity and perceptual quality on the UCSF-PDGM and UPenn-GBM datasets. Our method successfully reconstructs tumor regions and achieves segmentation performance comparable to that obtained with real CE-MRI. Our ablation studies show that although adversarial learning improves perceptual quality, a regression-based variant of our method achieves higher structural fidelity.

papers.intro:
Contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (CE-MRI) is a pivotal tool that uses a contrast agent injected into the bloodstream to enhance image clarity [51, 9, 29, 30]. Although non-contrast MRI is sufficient for observing anatomical structures, it often lacks the sensitivity needed to identify vascular conditions and subtle tissue discrepancies. It is difficult to distinguish tumors or inflammation from healthy tissue on non-contrast scans because these conditions often have similar intensities [10]. CE-MRI addresses this issue by using contrast agents that make blood vessels and lesions hyperintense on T1-weighted images. This hyperintensity enables the precise identification of the location and extent of these lesions [38]. As shown in Fig. 1, tumor boundaries are ambiguous in other non-contrast MRI sequences, whereas the contrast-enhanced image clearly delineates the tumor region. Despite these advantages, administering contrast agents raises safety concerns because gadolinium may not be fully excreted, potentially leading to accumulation in the brain and bones [25, 40]. Furthermore, CE-MRI requires longer acquisition times and incurs higher costs.

To address these issues, recent studies have explored generative model-based medical image translation for synthesizing CE-MRI from non-CE images [32]. In particular, Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) [17] and diffusion model [21] based generative models have been widely investigated for synthesizing target modalities by concatenating source modalities along the channel dimension as input [53, 48, 11, 13, 28]. Ea-GAN [53] is a 3D Pix2Pix [23]-based model that integrates edge information, effectively preserving structural details. MM-GAN [48] utilizes a 3D GAN framework that combines information from all available MRI sequences to simultaneously synthesize arbitrary missing sequences. Chen et al. [11] have proposed a 3D convolutional network designed using a fusion method that extracts unique information feature maps through independent encoders for each input modality and then combines them in the channel direction to synthesize CE-MRI within the regression framework. ResViT [13] has been introduced as a GAN-based generative model for multi-modal image synthesis that combines Vision Transformers [15] with the convolutional networks to leverage global context. ALDM [28] applies a 3D Latent Diffusion Model [46] incorporating switchable SPADE [42] blocks within the latent space, enabling the translation of a single source image into various target images. Recent studies [44] have suggested that, in medical image translation, fidelity is more critical than perceptual quality because generative models for restoration tasks are subject to the perception-distortion tradeoff [4]. Accordingly, regression losses can be more important than adversarial learning, which primarily aims to improve perceptual quality [44].

[11] have proposed a 3D convolutional network designed using a fusion method that extracts unique information feature maps through independent encoders for each input modality and then combines them in the channel direction to synthesize CE-MRI within the regression framework. ResViT [13] has been introduced as a GAN-based generative model for multi-modal image synthesis that combines Vision Transformers [15] with the convolutional networks to leverage global context. ALDM [28] applies a 3D Latent Diffusion Model [46] incorporating switchable SPADE [42] blocks within the latent space, enabling the translation of a single source image into various target images. Recent studies [44] have suggested that, in medical image translation, fidelity is more critical than perceptual quality because generative models for restoration tasks are subject to the perception-distortion tradeoff [4]. Accordingly, regression losses can be more important than adversarial learning, which primarily aims to improve perceptual quality [44].

Most approaches concatenate multi-sequence images along the channel dimension for use as input. This often overlooks the distinct contrast characteristics of each sequence. For example, T1-weighted images depict fat as hyperintense, while water, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), edema, and inflammation appear dark [43, 16]. T2-weighted images depict water, lesions, and fat as hyperintense, while air and blood appear hypointense [43, 3]. T2-FLAIR images also highlight lesions and fat, but water and CSF appear dark [14]. Furthermore, the contrast enhancement of pathologies such as inflammation and edema varies significantly across these sequences, serving as an important biomarker [12]. These abnormal regions can be explicitly modeled using difference maps between sequences, making them useful for accurate contrast-enhanced image synthesis. Therefore, to accurately synthesize contrast-enhanced regions, it is crucial to explicitly incorporate the diverse contrast variations of distinct sequences and their explicit differences rather than relying on channel-wise concatenation. Because channel-wise concatenation captures pixel-level relationships between source modalities, it can be sensitive to intensity scaling and noise. In contrast, modeling differences in a feature space can provide an enhanced contextual representation of inter-sequence contrast changes.

We propose the Mixture of Feature Difference (MoFD) module that effectively leverages the complementary information from multiple sequences for CE-MRI synthesis. Unlike conventional methods that concatenate sequences across channels, our approach uses an encoder to extract sequence-specific features from each input sequence capturing unique contrast characteristics. We further calculate the feature differences between sequences and dynamically allocate importance to sequence-specific features and their feature differences, enabling flexible and selective feature integration instead of fixed averaging. We validate our method with regression-based and GAN-based approaches to investigate the impact of adversarial training on improving perceptual quality. We also evaluate tumor segmentation performance on the synthesized images using nnU-Net [22] to assess synthesis quality in tumor regions.

papers.title: Bias Mitigation in Audio-Enabled LLMs through Adversarial Training and Distillation Methods
papers.abstract: Audio-enabled large language models (AuLLMs) allow users to interact with them simply by talking to them, without the need for an intermediate transcription. This expands the model's accessibility and capabilities by encoding non-verbal cues. However, using non-verbal cues may lead to biased behaviour based on the attributes inferred (or assumed) from them. In this work, we focus on the gender attribute and show that models' perception of it can be unlearned using adversarial methods without a loss in performance on other benchmarked tasks. Such models are useful in situations where gender inference is unwanted. However, in other practical settings, gender perception (without bias) may be desired.As a less radical measure, we distil the gender-agnostic model, creating a model that perceives gender but responds similarly to the gender-agnostic teacher, unless explicitly asked.We apply our newly proposed methods to three AuLLMs and obtain satisfactory results in the gender-unlearning part and partially satisfactory results in the distilling part.

papers.title: Reflective Compositional Grounding for Natural-Language-to-SPARQL
papers.abstract: Natural-language query generation over large knowledge graphs embodies the classical vocabulary problem in human-systems communication. Questions express concepts through wording and compositions that can differ substantially from the target schema, while limited model context requires selective access to schema information. We present an NL2SPARQL framework that places conceptual compositionality at the center of query interpretation and connects it to the relational composition required for binding and query construction. A fixed concept encoder represents compound expressions jointly, and schema candidates are ranked using semantic similarity, type compatibility, and hierarchy proximity. Reflective refinement critically examines how the grounded meanings are realized through argument bindings, joins, and operator scope. Diagnosed semantic discrepancies guide revisions to the responsible stage. We formalise a monotone refinement discipline that accumulates scoped interpretation requirements and establish conditions under which changes to the composed process preserve previously validated interpretations. Across five benchmark/knowledge-graph targets, mean schema recall@10 increases from 0.712 to 0.837. With retrieval held fixed, reflective prompt rewriting adds 2.27-3.33 answer-F1 points. These experiments evaluate the grounding and refinement mechanisms, while the formal analysis specifies the stronger requirements for conservative adaptation across queries.

papers.intro:
Natural-language access to databases faces a vocabulary problem. Users express information needs through concepts and relations that can differ in wording and conceptual structure from the target schema (Freitas, 2015; Freitas et al., 2012), a gap that widens in large, heterogeneous knowledge graphs with overlapping concepts and contextual ambiguities (Freitas et al., 2015). Large schemas can also exceed a language model’s available context, making selective, structurally-aware retrieval necessary, which is itself a form of conceptual interpretation at scale, since relevant schema elements may share little lexical overlap with the question. Query generation must therefore construct a relevant schema context, ground the question’s concepts within it, and compose their interpretations into an executable query; conceptual interpretation and compositionality are thus central to the end-to-end mapping.

papers.title: A Sample of Thick-Disk Stars Hosting Hot Jupiters
papers.abstract: We present a homogeneous analysis of 268 confirmed and candidate transiting hot-Jupiter host stars with 4800K < Teff < 6200K. We combine high-resolution TRES spectra, Gaia, 2MASS and WISE photometry, and Gaia astrometry to determine these stars' Teff, log g, Rstar, [alpha/Fe] and [Fe/H]. Based on their [alpha/Fe] and [Fe/H], we classify the stars as members of the Milky Way's low-[alpha/Fe] thin disk, high-[alpha/Fe] thick disk or an ambiguous intermediate population. We identify two confirmed hot Jupiters (WASP-81 b and TOI-5322 b) and three candidate hot Jupiters (TOI-3118.01, TOI-2728.01, and TOI-5781.01) as orbiting previously-unrecognized members of the high-alpha thick disk. We compare the properties of the confirmed planets in the three populations and note two indications of a potential difference between the populations: both high-[alpha/Fe] confirmed planets and eight out of the eleven ambiguous-disk confirmed planets are less massive than the median low-[alpha/Fe] planet, and none of our high-[alpha/Fe] or ambiguous confirmed planets have orbital periods shorter than 2.7 d, when 22% of our low-[alpha/Fe] population do. These differences may reflect variations in giant-planet formation across galactic environments, evolutionary effects, or differing stellar properties between the high- and low-[alpha/Fe] populations. Our catalog is the largest sample of chemically-identified high-[alpha/Fe] thick-disk confirmed and candidate hot-Jupiter host stars. These ancient systems, with ages > 8 Gyr, may allow for a better understanding of how the formation of hot Jupiters depends on galactic environment, and how their orbits evolve over very long time scales.

papers.intro:
The Milky Way comprises three broad stellar populations: the thin disk, the thick disk, and the halo. Thin-disk stars have circular and low-inclination orbits relative to the galactic midplane, thick-disk stars have eccentric and moderately inclined galactic orbits, and halo stars form an extended shroud out to large distances [23, 12]. These three populations reflect different epochs and conditions of star formation throughout galactic history, as reflected in their age and chemistry: thin-disk stars are characterized by their youth (age <8<8 Gyr), [Fe/H][\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{H}]-enhancement (−0.8≲[Fe/H]≲0.4-0.8\lesssim[\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{H}]\lesssim 0.4) and [α/Fe][\alpha/\mathrm{Fe}]-depletion ([α/Fe]≲0.2[\alpha/\mathrm{Fe}]\lesssim 0.2), thick-disk stars are older (age >8>8 Gyr), [Fe/H][\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{H}]-poor ([Fe/H]≲0.2[\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{H}]\lesssim 0.2) and [α/Fe][\alpha/\mathrm{Fe}]-rich ([α/Fe]>0.12[\alpha/\mathrm{Fe}]>0.12), and halo stars are the very oldest and most metal-poor, thought to be accreted from past mergers with dwarf galaxies [47, 59, 34, 58]. The planets that orbit stars belonging to each of these populations have been affected by both their formation environment and their age. Metallicity and external radiation influence protoplanetary disk chemistry and lifetimes, while the passage of time reveals which planets survive long-term dynamical and tidal processes. In this work, we focus on the Milky Way’s high-α\alpha thick disk as a laboratory for exploring these effects, as its combination of ancient age, distinct chemical enrichment pattern, and dynamical history uniquely preserves signatures of planet formation in the early Galaxy.

Thick-disk stars, and their planets, also formed earlier in the history of the galaxy than their thin-disk counterparts. This earlier period in the galaxy’s history, known as “cosmic noon,” was characterized by its high star formation rate, and the increased radiation experienced by nascent thick-disk stars could have shortened the lifespan of their planet-forming disks and contributed to the dearth of planets we observe around them today [24]. Even though these proposed effects are thought to cause an even greater reduction in giant planets than smaller planets, most studies of thick disk exoplanets thus far have focused on smaller planets.

Focusing on hot Jupiters, Hamer and Schlaufman 25 used galactic kinematics as a proxy for relative stellar age and found the average hot Jupiter host star to be younger than the average field star, suggesting that hot Jupiters are tidally distrupted and destroyed during the span of their host star’s main sequence lifetime. Chen et al. 10 also found that hot Jupiters are preferentially hosted by relatively younger stars in the Galactic thin disk, whereas warm/cold Jupiters do not exhibit this trend. They further found that the difference in metallicity between the younger and older stars in their sample was not the dominant cause for the difference in age distributions of their different planet populations, supporting the conclusion that tidal decay destroys hot Jupiters during the course of their hosts’ lifetimes. Thick disk stars are all older (≥8\geq 8 Gyr) and so are a key population for understanding the results of exoplanetary system evolution.

Thick disk stars are all older (≥8\geq 8 Gyr) and so are a key population for understanding the results of exoplanetary system evolution.

papers.title: A QED Functional Formulation of Relativistic Many-Body Perturbation Theory in Atoms
papers.abstract: We systematically derive relativistic many-body perturbation theory (RMBPT) from the two-particle irreducible effective action of quantum electrodynamics (QED) in the Furry picture, giving an organisational and diagrammatic framework for both correlation and radiative corrections in many-electron atoms. We further discuss that RMBPT is a well-defined subset of QED effects evaluated on a redefined vacuum, such that the interplay between correlation and radiative effects becomes transparent. We use this to derive QED corrections to the interelectronic interaction of atomic systems, yielding the transverse (frequency-dependent Breit) photon-exchange corrections, including retardation. Of those corrections, we numerically evaluate the first-order transverse photon-exchange corrections, which complement the conventional RMBPT based on the Dirac-Coulomb no-pair Hamiltonian.

Many-body methods [21, 31] and quantum electrodynamic (QED) [34, 39] approaches to atomic systems are historically two separate fields. While the former is mostly concerned with correlation corrections in many-electron systems, the latter is mostly applied to radiative corrections in few-electron systems such as H- to B-like ions. As a consequence, radiative corrections in many-electron atoms are usually a posteriori considerations on top of existing many-body methods.

This is an issue that has been partially tackled by Lindgren et al. in the past, using their covariant evolution operator formalism in [25, 24] to resum interelectronic interaction diagrams with the inclusion of retardation and radiative effects. Our goal in this work is different in scope. Rather than attempting to treat QED to all orders, we argue that both approximations can be derived from the QED effective action of the atomic system at hand, as a stationary functional of the electron propagator rather than an energy-dependent effective Hamiltonian on a model space. As a consequence, the Dirac-Hartree-Fock-Coulomb (DHFC) equations and RMBPT can be extracted as well-defined instantaneous, no-pair truncation schemes to this full effective action. Thus, the complement of the truncation, that is, what is left out at every given order of RMBPT, is readily accessible without any additional diagrammatic input. Consequently, this framework makes the interplay of correlation and radiative corrections apparent. It also gives systematic access to corrections that any conventional many-body treatment omits, including the radiative sector. We further note that reformulating the atomic many-body problem within the framework of the quantum effective action opens it up to the plethora of methods developed for such functionals in other fields, such as condensed matter theory, in future work. This has already been done for nonrelativistic density functional theory and the functional renormalization group by Polonyi and Sailer [28].

Such studies are also motivated by recent applications of atomic structure calculations, one example being the determination of isotope masses for high-precision searches for physics beyond the Standard Model. Isotope-shift measurements in clock transitions are sensitive to a new force acting between electrons and nucleons because the contribution from the new interaction can depend on the neutron number of the nucleus. For several isotope pairs, a King plot can be constructed, in which a new mediator boson can manifest itself through a nonlinear isotope-shift relation [15]. An important ingredient in such analyses is the precise knowledge of the isotope masses. In Penning-trap mass-spectrometry experiments, the masses of highly charged ions (HCIs) can nowadays be determined with uncertainties at the eV or even sub-eV level [38, 16]. Atomic theory is required to account for the mass defect of the electronic binding energies of the corresponding HCI. Another application is the determination of the neutrino mass through electron capture [2, 3]. The QQ value for this process can be determined from Penning-trap measurements with the mother and daughter ions [32]. Here, again, theoretical calculations are required to account for the binding energies of the removed electrons. In both applications, a clean separation and an accurate treatment of the individual physical contributions is essential for reliable predictions.

In this article, we show that the order-by-order computation of diagrams in the LW skeleton expansion recovers the RMBPT matrix elements and the Dirac-Hartree-Fock-Coulomb (DHFC) equations from a single organisational principle, namely, the QED Luttinger-Ward functional in a Furry-picture reference vacuum. This provides a functional criterion for separating instantaneous correlation, retardation, negative-energy, self-energy, and vacuum-polarization contributions. The no-pair approximation enters naturally as a splitting of the electron propagator into positive- and negative-energy contributions; pair corrections are then transparent.

We further show that RMBPT is a subset of QED corrections evaluated on the core vacuum: correlation corrections are precisely the instantaneous Coulomb, no-pair limit of the self-energy and vacuum polarization diagrams. We show this explicitly through second order (Secs. III and IV); for higher-order diagrams it follows by construction. This identification establishes a systematic scheme for including radiative corrections on top of correlations and vice versa. We note that in this work, we follow standard usage and reserve the term radiative corrections for self-energy and vacuum-polarization loops with respect to the QED vacuum, which appear already for hydrogenlike ions and require renormalization. Photon exchange between electrons, including its retarded and negative-energy (pair) parts, is referred to as interelectronic interaction or screening effects. On the core vacuum, both types of contributions arise from diagrams of self-energy and vacuum-polarization topology.

papers.title: Energy Flow Shapes the Decomposition Dynamics of a Reactive Atmospheric Intermediate
papers.abstract: The unimolecular dynamics of Criegee intermediates depend strongly on their internal energy, which can differ substantially between nascent atmospheric species and laboratory-prepared reactants. Here, the decomposition dynamics of {\it anti-}CH$_3$CHOO are investigated using molecular dynamics simulations on a neural network-based potential energy surface under thermal and mode-selective vibrational excitation. Simulations were performed at internal energies representative of those released during ozonolysis (chemical/thermal preparation, TP) or following vibrational excitation (VibEx) along the CH-stretching mode with two or three quanta, as can be done in laboratory studies. These excitation conditions strongly affect reaction yields and kinetics, with VibEx promoting passage across the initial cyclization barrier. For TP, 35 kcal/mol of internal energy are required to form molecular products, whereas for VibEx, 27 kcal/mol are sufficient. Although TP and VibEx ensembles access largely the same fragmentation pathways with comparable relative yields, the absolute product yields, characteristic timescales, and kinetic behavior differ substantially. Methyldioxirane is found to be a kinetic trap along the pathway. The resulting molecular-level description of {\it anti-}CH$_3$CHOO decomposition provides guidance for interpreting experiments and contributes to a broader understanding of energy-dependent Criegee-intermediate dynamics.

papers.title: Monte Carlo Framework for Physics-Based Design and Optimization of X-Ray Compressive Ghost Imaging Systems
papers.abstract: X-ray ghost imaging has emerged as a promising computational imaging modality capable of forming images from spatially integrated measurements. Unlike optical implementations, image formation is governed by multiple energy-dependent photon-matter interactions: photoelectric absorption, Compton scattering, and fluorescence. The relative contributions of these interactions depend on the source spectrum, sample geometry and composition, and detector configuration. We present a FLUKA-based Monte Carlo framework that models photon transport and predicts bucket signals generated by binary illumination patterns. The framework couples a physical scaling analysis, which converts the simulated bucket signals into photon numbers, tube loading and absorbed dose, with a ghost imaging reconstruction analysis of image quality and convergence. Our framework helps assess whether a given configuration is limited by the source output, the mask modulation or the reconstruction before any measurement is made. We evaluate the reconstruction for a centimeter-scale imaging system for an iron crown using one transmission detector and three off-axis scattering detectors over a range of source spectra. The results reveal how source characteristics and detector geometry influence reconstruction quality and radiation dose, providing quantitative guidelines for future X-ray ghost imaging system design. More broadly, this work establishes a predictive design framework for application-specific X-ray ghost imaging systems.

papers.title: Series and Parallel Dependency Links: Vitality for Interdependent Networks of Networks
papers.abstract: In a network of networks, a dependency link runs from a supplier to the node it serves and binds the supplier's failure to the node's failure. Indices computed from the graph topology leave aside the service each edge carries, but in real interdependent systems that service decides how failure propagates: a pumping station requires electricity and telemetry, and losing either stops it; a district fed by either of two reservoirs survives the loss of one. Building on this observation, we label each node of the network with the service it provides. We then measure how far this qualitative input can change the node's vitality ranking: by fixing the graph topology we show that changing only the labels moves the Mean Operativity Loss from $0.023$ to $0.114$, while a ranking computed from the unlabelled graph topology is blind to the difference. The links give a node its suppliers; the labels group those suppliers into alternatives within one service and joint requirements across services. These labels should belong to the description of an interdependent system alongside the links themselves for a fidelity vitality measure

papers.title: On the Robustness of Gossip Protocols in Modern Blockchains
papers.abstract: Modern platforms such as Ethereum and Polkadot nowadays execute Byzantine fault-tolerant consensus protocols over large validator committees, often comprising hundreds of nodes. At this scale, complete graph topologies for connecting nodes are impractical, leading systems to adopt various gossip mechanisms, often in an ad hoc manner. In this paper, we study the robustness of widely deployed gossip protocols used in committee-based blockchains against realistic network adversaries. We show, both analytically and through extensive empirical measurements, that the graph parameters commonly chosen to instantiate random graphs are insufficient to guarantee that enough honest nodes receive consensus messages for quorum formation in existing protocols. Motivated by this finding, we empirically assess the robustness of Bitcoin's Erdős-Rényi (ER) graphs, Polkadot's grid topology, Ethereum's GossipSub, and Solana's chunk- and tree-based disseminations. Our results reveal surprising tradeoffs: Solana's dynamic trees are bandwidth-efficient in benign settings but fragile under adaptive attacks; Polkadot's grid achieves strong robustness at the cost of high bandwidth overhead; GossipSub is both bandwidth-efficient and resilient to adaptive adversaries, yet highly sensitive to parameter choices; and ER graphs provide a strong robustness-efficiency tradeoff, e.g., when the (average) fanout degree exceeds 15 for networks up to 5000 nodes.

papers.intro:
Decentralized platforms are rapidly gaining ground as a key technology in blockchain deployments, machine learning (e.g., federated and decentralized learning [1, 2, 3]), social networks (e.g., federated social networks such as Mastodon [4, 5]), file storage (e.g., IFPS [6]), and content and music distribution (e.g., Odysee [7] and Audius [8]). At the core of almost all decentralized deployments lies a peer-to-peer (P2P) network that is responsible for reliably propagating critical information and metadata to all nodes. For instance, the security analysis of blockchain protocols often assumes a synchronous model where messages arrive at all nodes within a bounded delay window [9]. Any partition in the P2P network, however, can break these guarantees [10], potentially causing major forks [11].

The interplay between the network layer and the consensus layer has been largely overlooked, with most existing designs treating these two components almost in isolation. This separation appears to be an artifact of the field’s development. Historically, BFT protocols were deployed on only a small number of nodes. With such a limited scale, a complete graph was the natural choice: every node could communicate directly with every other, keeping overhead tolerable. Today, however, platforms such as Ethereum, Polkadot, and Cosmos run BFT-style consensus across large validator committees. For the first time in decades, BFT protocols operate at scale, involving hundreds or even thousands of participants—for example, Ethereum and Polkadot maintain validator committees of roughly 9​t​r​u​e​0009true000 and 600600 nodes, respectively. This substantial increase in committee size renders the reliance on complete graphs impractical. Consequently, modern decentralized platforms have replaced them with more sophisticated dissemination protocols, adapted from the P2P networking literature, to enable validators to exchange information efficiently and reach consensus at scale. Ethereum, for example, uses GossipSub [12] to organize nodes into a mesh network in which full messages are pushed across peers, complemented by metadata-only links that periodically advertise information about recently seen messages. Polkadot, in contrast, uses a grid-like dissemination protocol that guarantees a maximum two-hop distance between any two nodes, ensuring rapid and efficient information propagation.

We address these questions as follows. First, we introduce a novel framework that captures both the robustness and the efficiency of existing gossip protocols once peer discovery has completed and the overlay topology has formed (Section II). The framework incorporates a practical threat model with targeted attacks and mobile adversaries, which can release corrupted nodes and corrupt others as the network evolves. Such adversaries adapt their choice of corrupted nodes based on readily available information about node placement within the network. Leveraging our framework, we analyze the robustness of random graph topologies and show, both analytically and empirically, that the default parameters used in currently deployed random graph topologies (such as Bitcoin’s fanout degree of 88, or the de facto standard fanout degree of ln⁡(n)\ln{(n)} in random graphs of size nn [13]) are ill-suited for composition with classical Byzantine Fault Tolerance (BFT) protocols (Section III).

papers.title: Well-posedness of 2D stochastic parabolic-parabolic Keller-Segel system with logistic source
papers.abstract: We consider a stochastic, fully parabolic Keller-Segel system with multiplicative noise in non-divergence form and a logistic source in a two-dimensional bounded domain, subject to random initial data. We construct a global-in-time, non-negative martingale solution by means of a suitable regularisation procedure, combined with Banach fixed-point arguments, a localisation procedure, and a stochastic compactness method. We further establish pathwise uniqueness and uniqueness in law for martingale solutions, and prove the existence of a unique global-in-time, non-negative weak solution without imposing any smallness condition on the initial data.
