papers.intro:
The Keller–Segel system, introduced in [26, 36], is one of the cornerstones of mathematical biology. It describes the chemotactic aggregation of cells, for instance, the amoeba Dictyostelium discoideum, in response to a chemical signal that the cells themselves secrete. In two space dimensions, the classical deterministic system exhibits a striking mass-dependent dichotomy driven by the competition between diffusion and aggregation: in the absence of logistic terms, sufficiently small initial mass ensures global existence, whereas sufficiently large initial mass may lead to finite-time blow-up; see, for instance, [21, 22, 23, 47]. The addition of a logistic source with quadratic damping will change fundamentally this picture: in the deterministic setting, it suppresses finite-time blow-up and ensures global existence even for arbitrarily large initial mass; see, e.g., [28, 43, 46, 49]. This damping mechanism models the saturation of the cell population due to limited resources. A central question is whether its stabilizing effect persists under random perturbations. Such perturbations arise naturally in biological and physical environments and can influence both cell-population dynamics and the evolution of the chemical signal, motivating the study of stochastic Keller–Segel systems. An early stochastic formulation was proposed by Chavanis [6], building on the approach introduced by Dean [11]. To examine this question, we introduce stochastic forcing into both the cell-density and chemical-concentration equations. papers.title: The Self-Improvement Problem
papers.abstract: With the rise of large language models, agentic systems are becoming increasingly autonomous, as they write code, call tools, revise prompts, and propose modifications to their own components. This autonomy raises a fundamental question for safe self-improvement: can an automated gate like a reward model or an automated reviewer reliably decide whether a proposed update should be accepted? The difficulty is structural. The gate must be a terminating, computable procedure, while the property we ultimately care about, namely whether an update is a genuine semantic improvement, depends on potentially unbounded program behavior. We formalize this mismatch by modeling agents as programs and defining improvement in terms of a semantic score that need not be computable. We study two evaluation abstractions. The first is a certifier that approves or rejects an update. The second is a search procedure that, given access to a proposal generator, attempts to output some improving candidate if one exists. We show that, in the fully general setting, no terminating procedure can simultaneously guarantee reliability (never accepting a non-improvement) and non-conservatism (never missing an available improvement): self-referential constructions can force any such gate or searcher to fail. Randomized gates with bounded error face the same limit. We then identify a standard decidable regime used in practice (bounded evaluation and a finite proposal budget) under which exhaustive simulation yields a terminating search procedure with the desired guarantees. We also show the limit of this recovery: a chain of accepted updates can raise the bounded score in every round while the true score falls. Our results draw a boundary between unbounded, universal settings where correctness guarantees collapse and bounded settings where they can be recovered by design.

papers.intro:
Many modern “agentic” pipelines follow the same pattern: an agent proposes a self-update (a code patch, prompt rewrite, new checkpoint, tool policy, etc.), and an automated gate decides whether to apply it (Lu et al., 2024; Yamada et al., 2025). The gate may be a reward model, a regression test suite, or an automated reviewer that must terminate and output accept/reject. The intended notion of improvement, however, is semantic: whether the updated agent is genuinely better depends on unbounded program behavior, long-horizon interactions, and open-ended tool use (Wang et al., 2023). This mismatch creates a concrete failure mode that is now routine in practice: once the proposal mechanism can anticipate or condition on the gate, it can “optimize the gate” rather than the intended objective. In other words, the proposer can exploit the evaluator as a predictable part of the environment.

In other words, the proposer can exploit the evaluator as a predictable part of the environment.

This paper formalizes that failure mode and proves a sharp boundary: in a fully general setting, no terminating gate or search procedure can be both reliable and non-conservative. The core obstruction is not statistical; it is structural. If candidates can depend (directly or indirectly) on the gate’s decision, then self-reference yields diagonal constructions in which any total computable gate must fail, either by accepting a non-improvement or by rejecting (or missing) an available improvement.

papers.title: MYOPIA: Understanding the Limits of Tree-Based Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Decision trees can make vision-language model (VLM) classification interpretable by replacing a single prediction with a sequence of root-to-leaf questions. However, the accuracy cost of this greedy, non-backtracking procedure remains unclear. We introduce \textbf{MYOPIA}, a benchmark comprising four LLM-generated, human-refined decision trees for GTSRB, MNIST, CIFAR-10, and MSCOCO, together with matched prompts, diagnostic protocols, and an evaluation harness. Across GPT-4o, Qwen-VL Max, and LLaMA-3.2 11B Vision, tree traversal underperforms zero-shot prompting in all 12 dataset--model pairs; paired bootstrap analyses consistently favor zero-shot. Our diagnostics characterize interacting failure modes associated with this gap. Models often recall tree-encoded class attributes more accurately than they ground the same attributes in images: the mean label--image accuracy gaps are 9.5, 13.8, and 12.6 points for GPT-4o, Qwen-VL Max, and LLaMA, respectively. Incorrect local decisions then irreversibly exclude the correct class, while answer extraction introduces additional model-dependent loss. A node-level audit of the four trees finds that split entropy is weakly but consistently associated with lower node accuracy, whereas depth, branching factor, and within-node grounding differences are less stable. \textbf{MYOPIA} therefore provides a framework for diagnosing hierarchical visual classification and motivates testing tree designs that prioritize perceptual answerability and recovery from early errors. Code is available at https://github.com/islammesabah/VLM_Classification.

papers.intro:
Vision-language models (VLMs) can classify images without task-specific labeled examples. Pretrained on large image–text corpora, models such as CLIP, GPT-4o, and the Qwen-VL family perform strongly across a range of zero-shot visual tasks [32, 30, 5]. Nevertheless, two challenges remain. First, VLMs often struggle with fine-grained recognition that requires distinguishing subtle visual differences, such as traffic-sign variants, medical image subtypes, and car models [12, 4, 41]. This limitation is especially consequential in safety-critical domains. Second, opaque zero-shot predictions provide little insight into systematic errors [14].

Decision trees offer a potential way to address both challenges. A tree decomposes a difficult classification decision into a sequence of simple, interpretable questions [28, 36]. Each answer narrows the label set until one class remains, and the resulting path explains the prediction. This rationale is intuitive, but it assumes that the model can answer every local question reliably. An early error excludes the correct class, prompt wording can alter intermediate answers, and longer paths create more opportunities for failure. Whether the added interpretability justifies these accuracy and inference costs has not been systematically evaluated.

We test this premise by comparing greedy, non-backtracking tree traversal with zero-shot prompting across three VLMs, four datasets, and several prompting variants. In the primary comparison, traversal underperforms zero-shot prompting in all 12 dataset–model pairs. We investigate this gap by separating class-attribute recall from visual grounding, distinguishing path-selection errors from answer-interface failures, and examining tree structure and inference cost. These findings do not show that hierarchical visual inference is inherently ineffective. Instead, they characterize the limitations of a common implementation and provide guidance for designing more reliable alternatives.

Our main contributions are: 1. We introduce MYOPIA, a benchmark for evaluating tree-based reasoning in VLMs. It includes four LLM-generated, human-refined decision trees; matched zero-shot and tree-based prompt templates; paired class-attribute-recall and visual-grounding diagnostics; a reusable tree-generation pipeline (Section 3.1); and a complete evaluation harness. 2. In the primary comparison, greedy tree traversal underperforms zero-shot prompting in every dataset–model pair, even when models can recall the relevant class attributes. Paired bootstrap analyses support this gap, and a GPT-4o pilot that adds the global label list to each tree prompt yields only limited and inconsistent gains (Section 5.1). Thus, this implementation of greedy traversal does not reliably improve visual classification. 3. We diagnose traversal failures by separating class-attribute recall from visual grounding (Section 5.3) and path-selection errors from answer-interface failures (Section 5.3). A node-level analysis examines associations between tree structure, grounding gaps, and node accuracy across the four evaluated trees (Section 5.4), while prompt and cost analyses identify further design tradeoffs for interpretable VLM classifiers.

papers.title: Temporal Specification Guidance for Text-to-Video Generation
papers.abstract: Text-to-video models often generate the visual concepts requested in natural language prompts but fail to satisfy their intended ordering, timing, and persistence requirements. We propose representing these requirements as specifications in a formal Temporal Logic, and introduce Temporal Specification Guidance (TSG), a training-free inference-time framework that turns temporal specifications into executable objectives for guiding video generation during sampling. TSG scores traces of visual concept evidence using differentiable quantitative semantics and uses the score's gradients to construct a specification-guided denoising direction. We instantiate this framework with video-text attention traces, efficient differentiable scores for Metric Temporal Logic, and gradient-derived attention biases. This instantiation requires neither an external concept classifier nor backpropagation through the video transformer. Its attention-steered forward pass yields a denoising direction that augments classifier-free guidance (CFG). On a benchmark of 220 prompts spanning 11 categories of temporal constraints, including ordered object entry and state transitions, this instantiation improves specification satisfaction accuracy over CFG by 9.5-20 percentage points across five models, with minimal memory overhead. These results demonstrate the potential of temporal specifications and differentiable satisfaction objectives as a flexible interface for controlling video generation.

Text-to-Video generation has seen tremendous progress in recent years, with models such as Gemini Omni (Google DeepMind, 2026), Runway Gen (Esser et al., 2023; Runway, 2025), Wan (Wan et al., 2025), and CogVideoX (Yang et al., 2025) producing videos with improved visual quality and semantic fidelity. Classifier-Free Guidance (Ho & Salimans, 2022) was introduced to improve adherence to natural language prompts in image generation and is now widely adopted by video generation models (Ho et al., 2022b; Ho et al., 2022a). However, adherence to temporal constraints remains challenging (Choi et al., 2025; Schiber et al., 2026). Figure 1 shows two examples of such failures with CogVideoX-5B. While the model broadly incorporates the semantic concepts described in the text prompts (e.g., the presence of a traffic light or a drone), it fails to follow the required ordering, persistence, and timing requirements. In these examples, the model misses the intended timed color progression and the eventual appearance of a hiker or a flare signal, respectively.

In this work, we propose expressing temporal requirements as specifications in formal Temporal Logics. Formal temporal specifications can precisely express requirements that are implicitly described in natural language prompts. Frame-level visual concepts, such as the presence of a traffic light or the associated colors, can be represented as atomic propositions. Temporal Logics offer standard Boolean operators (negation, conjunction, and disjunction) and temporal operators such as Always (𝐆\mathbf{G}), Until (𝐔\mathbf{U}), and Eventually (𝐅\mathbf{F}) to express persistence and ordering requirements. In this work, we present a specification language adopted from Metric Temporal Logic (Koymans, 1990) to express temporal requirements with different degrees of timing precision. Representations of temporal requirements from prior work, including timed binary masks (Schiber et al., 2026) and untimed Temporal Logic formulae (Choi et al., 2025), can also be written as specifications in this language.

We propose Temporal Specification Guidance (TSG), a training-free inference-time framework for improving adherence to temporal specifications with transformer-based video generation models. Our key insight is that temporal specifications provide an executable objective for guiding video generation during sampling. TSG makes this practical through differentiable specification scores and attention interventions that avoid backpropagation through the video transformer. Concretely, TSG computes traces of visual concept evidence using video-text attention from the video transformer. For every attention head, TSG computes biases as gradients of a differentiable specification score, steers the attention scores with these biases, and computes the specification-guided direction from the steered forward pass through the video transformer. Our use of attention as a proxy for visual concept presence builds on prior work on attention-based semantic guidance in image and video generation (Chefer et al., 2023; Schiber et al., 2026). The use of video-text attention mitigates the need for an external concept classifier during generation. Because differentiation is restricted to the attention-derived traces and their specification scores, TSG avoids backpropagation through the video transformer, reducing the associated computational and memory demands.

We compute a differentiable specification score over attention traces using a quantitative semantics for Metric Temporal Logic. Inspired by efficient log-domain quantitative semantics for Linear Temporal Logic (Khare et al., 2025), our quantitative semantics aggregates support for the temporal witnesses and alternatives admitted by a specification. Its log-domain form provides differentiable guidance and can be efficiently evaluated in time linear in trace length for a fixed specification. We establish monotonicity in independent literal-support inputs and predictable concept-score gradient signs under consistent polarity.

We evaluate TSG on a benchmark of 220 prompts spanning temporal constraints from 11 categories, including timed state transitions, entity appearance and disappearance, persistence, and choice. Across five models from the CogVideoX (Yang et al., 2025) and Wan (Wan et al., 2025) families, TSG improves specification satisfaction accuracy by 9.5–20 percentage points over CFG-only sampling. We also evaluate TSG with Wan 2.1 1.3B on strictly-timed prompts from the TempoControl object appearance benchmark (Schiber et al., 2026), where it outperforms CFG sampling by up to 22 percentage points in temporal accuracy and matches the state-of-the-art method on that benchmark with approximately 62% lower peak GPU memory. Together, these findings support specification-guided attention steering as an effective and memory efficient approach to temporal control in video generation.

papers.title: Optimal energy conversion -- A port-Hamiltonian approach
papers.abstract: This paper studies optimal energy conversion in port-Hamiltonian systems. We analyze state- and control-constrained finite-horizon optimal control problems that maximize energy conversion efficiencies. Under suitable reachability conditions, we show that the asymptotic optimal efficiencies exist and coincide with the corresponding optimal cyclic efficiencies. For a class of port-Hamiltonian systems describing coupled storage-conversion components, we further derive intrinsic limits on achievable energy conversion and establish a generalized Carnot-type efficiency bound. Our results provide an optimal-control framework connecting asymptotic optimal operation, cyclic operation, and fundamental efficiency limits for port-Hamiltonian systems.

papers.intro:
Energy conversion is a fundamental mechanism in a wide range of engineering systems, including electromechanical devices, power electronic converters, and thermodynamic processes. In thermodynamics, cyclic operation provides a natural paradigm for analyzing energy conversion, where operating cycles are typically designed a priori and idealized as quasi-static to characterize the maximum achievable efficiency. Modern engineering systems, however, often operate dynamically under state, control, and physical constraints, raising the question of how such dynamic operation can be optimally controlled to achieve maximal energy-conversion efficiency. In this context, energy-based modeling provides a natural framework for describing conversion systems and their interactions. In particular, port-Hamiltonian (pH) systems offer a structured representation of energy storage, interconnection, dissipation, and external power exchange, thereby enabling a unified treatment of multi-physics systems (Duindam et al., 2009; van der Schaft and Jeltsema, 2014). The pH framework has proven particularly effective for the design of passivity-based controllers (Ortega et al., 2002; Zhang et al., 2018; Macchelli, 2023).

The pH framework has proven particularly effective for the design of passivity-based controllers (Ortega et al., 2002; Zhang et al., 2018; Macchelli, 2023).

On the control side, optimization-based methods have been widely used to improve the performance for constrained dynamical systems (Mayne, 2014). Recent contributions have extended optimal control formulations to pH systems by incorporating energy-, entropy-, and exergy-related objectives (Schaller et al., 2021; Philipp et al., 2024). Moreover, dissipativity-based analysis and turnpike theory have revealed that long-horizon optimal operation is often closely related to steady-state or periodic behavior (Damm et al., 2014; Zanon et al., 2017; Köhler et al., 2018; Trélat et al., 2018; Faulwasser and Grüne, 2022).

Energy conversion in port-Hamiltonian systems has recently been studied from a structural perspective (van der Schaft and Jeltsema, 2021; van der Schaft and Jeltsema, 2022). These works relate the transfer of energy between two ports to the interconnection topology. In particular, without direct interconnection between the state components associated with injection and extraction, energy cannot be converted while keeping the injection-side output constant. This motivates generalized Carnot cycles alternating between different constant injection-side outputs and constant-state phases.

More broadly, van der Schaft (2021) motivates extending concepts from classical thermodynamics to systems and control. There, First and Second Laws of Thermodynamics are interpreted in terms of cyclo-losslessness and cyclo-dissipativity, respectively, and the classical Carnot bound is derived from the Kelvin formulation of the Second Law. This treatment raises the question of whether analogous bounds can be established for two-port systems beyond thermodynamics.

Despite these developments, optimal operation has not been characterized. Indeed, van der Schaft and Jeltsema (2021) explicitly identify the formulation of optimal energy conversion and the extension of Carnot cycles to more general cyclic processes with a notion of efficiency as open problems. Moreover, although a Carnot-type efficiency is derived for the generalized Carnot construction, whether it bounds the optimal efficiency remains open.

Motivated by these observations, this paper investigates constrained energy conversion in two-port port-Hamiltonian systems from an optimal control perspective. We study the relation between finite-horizon optimal operation, optimal cyclic operation, and fundamental efficiency limitations. The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows: i) We formulate finite-horizon optimal control problems for two complementary notions of energy conversion efficiency and characterize their asymptotic optimal performance. ii) Under suitable reachability conditions, we prove that the asymptotic optimal efficiencies coincide with the corresponding optimal cyclic efficiencies. iii) Building upon the energy-conversion framework of van der Schaft and Jeltsema (2021); van der Schaft and Jeltsema (2022), we investigate a class of block-diagonal port-Hamiltonian systems representing coupled storage-conversion components. We identify structural restrictions on achievable energy conversion and, under an additional scalar structural restriction, establish a generalized Carnot-type efficiency as a rigorous upper bound.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 states the energy conversion problem within the two-port port-Hamiltonian framework. Section 3 formulates the corresponding optimal control problems and derives general bounds on the conversion efficiencies using the available storage function. Section 4 establishes the asymptotic characterization of the optimal efficiencies and their relation to optimal cyclic operation. Section 5 investigates energy conversion in block-diagonal port-Hamiltonian systems, while Section 6 establishes a generalized Carnot-type efficiency bound under an additional scalar structural restriction. Section 7 presents numerical examples, and Section 8 concludes the paper.

papers.title: Isaac's Condition (TU) is false
papers.abstract: In 2006 Isaac reduced the simple normality to base $2$ of $\sqrt s$, for $s$ not a perfect square, to a property of dyadic expansions that he called Condition~(TU): the upper frequency of the digit~$1$ in $\sqrtν$, along any subsequence, depends only on the tail of the expansion of $ν$. We show that Condition~(TU) is false, already for the full sequence. We give two proofs. The first is elementary and turns Isaac's own reduction against the condition. The second uses the theorem of Kaufman and Mosquera--Shmerkin on the Fourier decay of smooth images of self-similar measures, and gives counterexamples for almost every point of a Cantor measure. All results are machine-verified in Lean~4; the second proof uses the two cited theorems as hypotheses.
papers.intro:
A real number is simply normal to base 22 if the digits 00 and 11 occur in its dyadic expansion with asymptotic frequency 1/21/2 each. Whether 2\sqrt{2} is simply normal to base 22 is open. Isaac [Isa06] claimed that s\sqrt{s} is simply normal to base 22 for every natural number ss that is not a perfect square [Isa06, Thm. 1]. His proof has two parts. In [Isa06, §2] he shows that Theorem 1 follows from a property he calls Condition (TU) [Isa06, Thm. 2]. In [Isa06, §3] he argues that Condition (TU) holds. A later paper [Isa11] restates the condition and offers “a simpler direct proof that Condition (TU) is true” [Isa11, Thm. 1(b)].

papers.title: Optimization of multi-resolution observation strategies for cosmic microwave background experiments
papers.abstract: Cosmic microwave background (CMB) observations are increasingly performed by using a combination of both small aperture telescopes (SATs) and large aperture telescopes (LATs) to extract information across a wide variety of angular scales. The observation strategy of the telescopes must balance the restrictions of the observing site, instrument constraints, and a variety of science goals. We present a general framework for simulating the performance of different observation strategies. Using this framework, we focus primarily on the inflationary science goal and determine the optimal LAT coverage for delensing SAT measurements and present a novel deep scan strategy for an experiment in Chile that improves observation efficiency in the deepest 3% of the sky by 26%. Finally, we present considerations for future surveys to consider to further increase their observing efficiency.

papers.intro:
The cosmic microwave background (CMB) holds a wealth of scientific information on both large and small angular scales. If inflation occurred, it would have left a signal in the B-mode polarization on degree angular scales [17]. The B-mode signal also has a contribution from E-modes being gravitationally lensed into B-modes by large scale structure on arcminute scales [24]. These arcminute scales also enable high-resolution measurements of the CMB and galaxy clusters, which can constrain the sum of the neutrino masses ∑mν\sum m_{\nu}, the effective number of light relics NeffN_{\rm eff}, dark matter, dark energy, and additional cosmological parameters [2, 8, 3]. In recent years observations at high resolution have also been used for galactic science and detecting millimeter wave transients, opening a new discovery space [2, 8, 3].

Initially the CMB-S4 project envisioned leveraging the strengths of both the South Pole and Chile sites to maximize the scientific potential. At the South Pole, the same patch of sky is always available but there is limited sky area available, making it well suited for deep inflationary measurements. Meanwhile, the mid-lattitude location of the Atacama Desert in Chile enables access to 70% of the sky, but the rising and setting of the sky means that observation targets are not always available, making it well suited to the arcminute scale science cases. papers.title: EvolvingBrain: An Adaptive Skill System for Multi-modal Agents Self-Evolution in Open Worlds
papers.abstract: Multi-modal agents have made significant progress in interacting with open worlds. However, their ability to self-evolve remains limited. Supervised fine-tuning enables imitation but not active experience organization, while outcome-based reinforcement learning promotes exploration yet underuses intermediate trajectory information. Therefore, we propose EvolvingBrain, which uses an adaptive skill system as the brain for agent self-evolution, consisting of two following components. Stratified Skill Self-Evolution: extracts Procedural Patterns and Problematic Patterns from model-specific trajectories, summarizes experience by generating skills, and evolves through multiple interactions with the open world, ultimately forming a Stratified Skill Architecture consisting of Domain, Plan, and Action/Trap Skills, which provides the agent with a multi-granularity knowledge repository and a novel evolution approach. State-Aware Adaptive Execution: summarizes long-horizon interactions into Structured Abstractive Memory and uses it to guide the State-Aware Skill Fusion Strategy, enabling the agent to utilize knowledge according to its current state. Experiments on VAB-Minecraft and DiscoveryWorld demonstrate that EvolvingBrain improves success rates on open-world tasks and exhibits generalization capabilities. Our code is provided in the supplementary materials and will be publicly released in the camera-ready version.

Multimodal agents have made substantial progress in interacting with open worlds. However, their ability to self-evolve from interaction experience remains limited. Supervised fine-tuning teaches agents to imitate demonstrated behaviors but does not enable them to actively organize and consolidate experience (Zeng et al., 2024). An adaptive skill system offers a alternative for agent self-evolution: it can actively organize intermediate trajectory information into reusable knowledge and continuously refine this knowledge through interaction. However, existing skill-based methods primarily distill successful trajectories into procedural guidance (Che et al., 2026), leaving three key issues unresolved: how to learn from both successful and failed trajectories, how to validate and evolve the extracted knowledge through environmental feedback, and how to organize and retrieve knowledge at different granularities according to the current state. Stratified Skill Self-Evolution extracts Procedural Patterns and Problematic Patterns from model-specific successful and failed trajectories. Procedural Patterns capture reusable procedures, whereas Problematic Patterns characterize behaviors and obstacles that should be avoided or resolved. These patterns are summarized as Plan Skills for task-level planning, Action Skills for fine-grained multimodal operations, and Trap Skills for problem identification, avoidance, and recovery. The skills are applied and evolved through multiple interactions with the open world, while shared knowledge across tasks is further abstracted into coarse-grained Domain Skills. Together, they form a Stratified Skill Architecture that provides the agent with a multi-granularity knowledge repository and an evolution approach.

papers.title: Finite Volume Convergence for a Heat Equation with a Measure-Valued Source
papers.abstract: Past work with Tom Seidman analyzed the spatial convergence order of the numerical finite element method applied to time-dependent diffusion-reaction equations with a measure-valued source term. For smooth source terms, the numerical method has second-order accuracy, but the non-smooth source terms introduce a limitation of the order that depends on the spatial dimension. This work in honor of Tom extends the analysis to the finite volume method in its clas- sical two-point flux form and shows that the regularity of the source term reduces the convergence order to 1 in two and 0.5 in three spatial dimensions which is reduced from the nominal second-order and depends on the space dimension. Computational tests with a point source modeled by a Dirac delta distribution exhibit the behavior predicted by the analytical results.

Thus, one may summarize the state of the literature as follows. The heat equation with measure-valued right-hand side is solved at the PDE level. For finite volume schemes, the available convergence theory is well developed for L1L^{1} parabolic data, while the fully Radon-measure finite volume theory is clearly established in the elliptic case and seems less explicit in the standard parabolic finite volume literature. From the point of view of applications, heat equations with low-regularity/measure right-hand side appear in many models of the continuum mechanics of solids, as e.g. in modeling of shape memory alloys Kružík and Roubíček (2019).

papers.title: Casimir Sign Reversal from Finite-Range Bogoliubov Fluctuations
papers.abstract: We study the zero-temperature Casimir effect of a three-dimensional Bose fluid with finite-range corrections to its Bogoliubov spectrum. Beyond the universal acoustic contribution scaling as $L^{-3}$, the long-distance expansion contains a nonuniversal $L^{-5}$ correction that can compete with the phononic term. We derive this crossover analytically within a minimal isotropic finite-range model and test the asymptotic result against the full dispersion. A regulator-independent Poisson-resummed calculation confirms that sign reversals of the Casimir energy are possible, while showing that the apparent low-coupling zero inferred by balancing only the $L^{-3}$ and $L^{-5}$ terms is not quantitatively controlled. Robust sign changes instead occur in the stable regime close to roton softening, where the Casimir energy acquires an oscillatory finite-momentum contribution. Strongly dipolar atomic gases provide a natural motivation for microscopic interaction lengths in the nanometric regime. We further discuss how the resulting nonlinear force law could be probed through the frequency response of a driven nanomechanical resonator.

papers.intro:
Fluctuation-induced forces provide a direct probe of the spectrum of confined quantum fields. In the electromagnetic Casimir effect the force originates from the modification of vacuum photon modes by material boundaries [2, 15]. In a quantum fluid the relevant fluctuating degrees of freedom are instead collective excitations. For a weakly interacting Bose gas at zero temperature the low-energy modes are phonons, and the leading Casimir energy is therefore the scalar-field result with the speed of light replaced by the sound velocity [18, 7, 19]. This acoustic approximation, however, misses the finite-momentum structure of the Bogoliubov spectrum.

This acoustic approximation, however, misses the finite-momentum structure of the Bogoliubov spectrum.

Casimir energies in dilute Bose gases have previously been analyzed using the full Bogoliubov dispersion, including the crossover from the interacting phononic regime toward the ideal-gas limit [19]. More recently, the fluctuation contribution to the surface energy of a Bose gas near hard and soft boundaries was studied within a spatially resolved Bogoliubov treatment [10]. Oscillatory Casimir interactions have also been predicted between impurities immersed in a spin–orbit-coupled Bose condensate, where the finite-momentum scale is imposed by the spin–orbit coupling and the interaction can acquire both positive and negative parts [9]. The mechanism considered here is distinct: we study the zero-temperature boundary-induced Casimir energy of confined Bogoliubov modes, with the finite-momentum structure generated by a finite-range interaction and, close to instability, by the roton momentum.

Finite-range and nonlocal interactions modify the dispersion away from the strictly linear regime. They can generate curvature corrections, maxon-roton features, and, in more complete anisotropic models, supersolid behavior with vortices [3]. Such effects are especially relevant for strongly magnetic atoms, where dipolar interactions coexist with short-range scattering. Dysprosium is a natural example: measured ss-wave scattering lengths are of order as∼5​nma_{s}\sim 5\,\mathrm{nm}, and the dipolar length is also of order a few nanometers [20, 14]. These microscopic lengths are much smaller than the soft-core radius of Rydberg-dressed gases, which is typically micrometric, and are therefore more compatible with nanomechanical gaps. Here RcR_{c} should be understood as an effective microscopic range characterizing finite-momentum corrections to the interaction, rather than as a literal Rydberg blockade radius. For dimensional estimates we consider RcR_{c} in the nanometric regime characteristic of microscopic interaction scales in strongly dipolar gases; no quantitative identification of RcR_{c} with either the scattering or dipolar length is implied.

In this Letter we compute the zero-temperature Casimir energy of a homogeneous Bose fluid with a finite-range Bogoliubov spectrum. We deliberately use a minimal isotropic model, not a microscopic theory of a dipolar supersolid. Its purpose is to isolate analytically the effect of a finite interaction length on the confined quasiparticle zero-point energy. The full anisotropic dipolar problem, including roton softening and supersolid order, is the natural extension discussed at the end. We also compare the long-wavelength expansion with a numerical evaluation of the full spectrum. The purpose of this comparison is not to replace the analytical result, but to determine its range of validity and to identify finite-momentum contributions that cannot be captured by a small-qq truncation.

papers.title: Optimally large cuts in both directions
papers.abstract: We prove that for every integer $d\ge2$ and all sufficiently large $m$, every digraph with $m$ edges and minimum outdegree at least $d$ has a vertex bipartition for which each directed cut is of size at least \[\left\lceil\frac{d-1}{2(2d-1)}m+\frac{d^2}{2(2d-1)}\right\rceil.\] The bound is sharp for infinitely many $m$. This answers for large graphs a question of Scott and proves a conjecture of Lee, Loh, and Sudakov. For $d=2$ we prove that $\lceil m/6\rceil$ is achievable for all $m$. We also establish a stability result characterizing near-extremal graphs.

papers.title: Wavelength-selective bidirectional plasticity in self-powered Se/ZnMgO visual synapses
papers.abstract: Artificial visual synapses combine sensing, memory and processing in a single device, but most of them need an external voltage to read the synaptic weight and light is generally able to strengthen the weight rather than to weaken it. We report here Se/ZnMgO thin film photodiodes in which the photocurrent at zero bias writes and reads the synaptic weight, with a direction of change set by the photon energy alone. At equal photon flux, 365 nm pulses increase the photocurrent by 38 % while 455 nm pulses decrease it, and the depression reaching 30 % at higher flux, with up to 19 distinguishable levels per branch and no electrical energy spent. Spectrally resolved light soaking shows that short wavelengths potentiate while low-energy light erases. The interesting property is therefore the photon energy-dependent competition between potentiation and depression, the crossover being set by the defect population of the interface. Optical simulations show that both wavelengths are absorbed within the first tens of nanometres of Se, and the stored state is erased by a reverse bias in a voltage-dependent way and by sub-gap light, which indicates that potentiation corresponds to interface defects filled with electrons, in agreement with drift-diffusion simulations. The devices also show relearning, their response is modulated by bending on flexible substrates, and a network built from the measured weight updates reaches 89 % accuracy on handwritten digit recognition without noise and 85 % with the measured noise, against 97.5 % for floating-point weights.

papers.title: Encoded but Exposed: Language Embeddings can Reveal More Than They Should in Recommender Systems
papers.abstract: Language embeddings are increasingly used in recommenders to represent item content, but their privacy risks remain poorly understood. We study whether item embeddings can reveal item identities when an adversary has access to auxiliary item text from external sources. We show that a simple cosine-similarity attack can recover item identities with high mean reciprocal rank across language models and candidate-set settings on two real-world datasets. Leakage is strongest when the adversary's partial information overlaps with the victim representation, but it also persists through semantic alignment between independently sourced descriptions. We further show that item leakage can propagate to user re-identification from sparse ratings. Finally, we evaluate obfuscated descriptions as a mitigation and find a clear leakage-utility tradeoff.

papers.intro:

Recent advances in language models have made it possible to derive richer representations from natural language data, such as item descriptions, reviews, and queries [39]. Consequently, natural language embeddings are increasingly used in both research [16, 32] and industrial settings [15, 26, 6] to support more accurate and context-aware recommendations.

Besides improving downstream recommendation tasks, language embeddings are often perceived as privacy-preserving because they are high-dimensional and not directly interpretable by humans. For instance, embedding representations of users and items are frequently shared with third-party service providers [8, 11, 36]. However, this assumption can be particularly fragile in recommendation system scenarios [3, 4]. Although a potential adversary may not have access to the original corpus used to generate the embeddings, domain knowledge and the abundance of publicly available item data [9, 10, 35] can make attacks more feasible than in settings where the underlying information is entirely internal or difficult to obtain. Therefore, even if an attacker does not have access to the exact movie plots used by a streaming provider to generate such embeddings, publicly available movie datasets [27, 28] can be used to construct a similar corpus, enabling effective inference attacks. Our work focuses on studying the robustness of item embeddings generated by different language models in recommender settings by examining whether it is possible to identify which items correspond to a given set of embeddings.

Prior work shows that text embeddings can encode sensitive attributes even when the original text is unavailable [41], and similar leakage has been observed in computer vision embeddings designed for utility tasks [1]. Another line of work in RS privacy and security studies whether users or user-item interactions can be de-anonymized from recommendation data. Early work showed that sparse rating patterns are often distinctive enough to re-identify users in anonymized datasets [25]. Subsequent studies demonstrated that even without explicit demographics, rating behavior can reveal sensitive user attributes: for example, [34] infers user gender from ratings using only a small set of users with disclosed demographic labels. More recent work extends this perspective to membership inference, asking whether a user or a specific user–item interaction was part of a recommender’s training data [37, 40], and to cross-domain record linkage, where rating patterns are used to link user identities across datasets from different domains [31]. papers.title: Lipschitz-free spaces over separable Banach spaces and their complementability in the bidual
papers.abstract: We prove that the Lipschitz-free space over a separable Banach space is complemented in its bidual if and only if the underlying Banach space is isomorphic to a Hilbert space. This answers negatively a long-standing question of Godefroy, Lancien, and Zizler concerning the case of $\ell_1$. We also characterize the existence of a projection of norm one and extend both characterizations to nonempty open convex subsets. Our approach yields several further results which we believe may be useful for understanding the structure of Lipschitz-free spaces over Banach spaces. These include an isometric representation of such spaces as quotients of Bochner $L^1$ spaces constructed using Gaussian measures.

papers.title: Efficient KV Cache Migration for Geo-Distributed LLM Inference in Collaborative Edge Computing
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown exceptional capabilities but rely heavily on centralized cloud GPU clusters, leading to high bandwidth costs, latency, and privacy issues. Edge computing offers a solution by deploying LLMs closer to users on edge servers, yet single edge servers often cannot meet LLMs' heavy computational demands. Collaborative Edge Computing (CEC) addresses this challenge by integrating resources of multiple geo-distributed heterogeneous edge servers, which jointly host small model shards and associated Key-Value (KV) cache for distributed inference. However, edge servers may disconnect or easily become overloaded, making it essential to migrate stateful KV cache to other servers for ensuring continuous service. Existing cloud-based KV cache management methods, such as direct cross-GPUs transmission and recomputation from input tokens are ill-suited for bandwidth-constrained and resource-limited edge environments. In this work, we propose EdgeFlow, a novel hybrid KV cache migration scheme that integrates direct KV cache transmission with activation-based recomputation, leveraging parallel computation and communication to minimize migration time. On this basis, we formulate a multi-node KV migration optimization problem and design a 2-approximation algorithm based on improved linear programming relaxation and bipartite graph techniques. Extensive experiments on a real-world distributed LLM inference platform demonstrate that EdgeFlow reduces migration time by up to 45%, significantly enhancing the robustness and efficiency of distributed LLM inference in collaborative edge computing.

Their widespread adoption promises significant societal and economic benefits. However, current LLM inference predominantly relies on centralized cloud infrastructures with powerful, dedicated GPU clusters, leading to high bandwidth cost, long response time, and privacy concerns [3]. Edge computing is a promising solution to address these issues by deploying LLMs at the network edge (e.g., personal workstations, edge servers, community clusters) [4, 5]. However, LLMs are computation-intensive and resource-greedy, while edge servers are usually with limited resources.

To overcome this challenge, collaborative edge computing (CEC) has emerged as a promising paradigm. It integrates geographically distributed, often underutilized computational resources at the network edge (e.g., personal workstations, edge servers, community clusters), enabling efficient distributed processing of complex tasks [6, 7]. As shown in Fig. 1, CEC-enable distributed LLM inference involves partitioning the LLM into smaller, manageable shards and distributing these shards across participating edge servers at different geographical regions. Each server executes inference for its assigned shard(s), collaboratively generating the model’s output [8, 9, 10, 11]. This is a new paradigm of LLM inference. This approach offers compelling advantages: leveraging ubiquitous computational resources, reducing reliance on centralized clouds, and potentially lowering latency for geographically dispersed users. Pioneering projects like Petals [12, 13] and PolyLink [14] have connected hundreds of consumer-grade edge GPUs over decentralized networks to allow multiple users to collaboratively perform LLM inference and finetuning, which demonstrated the feasibility of this concept.

Despite potential, CEC-enabled distributed LLM inference introduces new system-level challenges. First, edge servers are heterogeneous and with relatively limited resources. When serving large amount of requests, some servers may easily become overloaded. Second, users may plan to disconnect the server from the network. In such scenarios, the Key-Value (KV) cache hosted on servers must be migrated to other servers to restore and ensure continuous inference service, as it accumulates contextual information during the generation of each token[15]. Managing the KV cache and minimizing the migration time to achieve fast service recovery is essential in CEC-enabled distributed LLM inference.

This is a novel new problem. Existing solutions for managing KV cache primarily target centralized cloud environments: 1) cross-GPUs transmission, such as Llumnix [16] and Mell [17]. These works directly transfer/copy KV cache among GPUs via high-bandwidth NvLinks or PCIes to achieve workload balance and inference acceleration. 2) KV Offloading. It moves parts of the KV cache from GPU memory to slower storage (e.g., CPU RAM or SSD) to free up GPU resources [18, 19, 20]. However, these two methods directly transfer large KV cache, which may incur prohibitive communication overhead between edge servers in typical resource-constrained, heterogeneous, and bandwidth-limited edge networks [3]. 3) Token-based Recomputation. Other works [21, 22] tend to recompute KV cache from the original and historical tokens. While this reduces memory footprint, token recomputation involves computation-intensive prefill phase. This approach is often infeasible for consumer-grade GPUs on edge servers, which lack the powerful computational resources for frequent, costly recomputation.

In this paper, we propose an efficient Hybrid KV Cache Migration scheme, named EdgeFlow, to reduce the KV Cache migration time. Rather than directly transmitting the KV Cache, we find that KV Cache can also be re-computed from the smaller intermediate activations of the transformer layer, as shown in Sec. II-B. papers.title: MindEval2: Clinically Grounded Patients and Rubrics for Evaluating Language Models in Mental Health Support
papers.abstract: With people increasingly turning to AI chatbots for mental health support, the need to evaluate these tools is becoming more pressing. Recent benchmarks attempt to mimic a realistic setting by simulating multi-turn interactions with synthetic patients and evaluating them with an LLM-as-a-judge. However, the usefulness of these methods is limited because simulated patients can be overly forthcoming and self-reflective, and judgments typically involve opaque Likert scales with unclear practical utility. To bridge these gaps, we introduce MindEval2, an evaluation framework that consists of two components: Mental Health Quality Rubrics (MHQR), for evaluation, and MindSim, for patient simulation. For MHQR, we collaborate with PhD-level psychologists to develop a set of rubrics that break down response quality into explicit operational criteria that are more interpretable and actionable than existing evaluation taxonomies. MindSim, in turn, is an LLM harness that combines carefully-designed patient profiles with tools, enabling more varied, challenging, and realistic interactions than existing baselines. The harness also contains a memory component that is updated between each interaction, enabling MindEval2 to model the longitudinal aspect of mental health. We evaluate 18 proprietary and open-weight models on MindEval2, finding that while frontier models have largely improved on issues related to surface level quality and boundaries, guidance calibration remains the dominant failure mode across all models, accounting for most of the quality gap.

papers.title: CogDrift-4D: Hierarchical Multimodal Modeling of Temporal Behavioral Decay for MCI Detection
papers.abstract: Early detection of mild cognitive impairment remains a critical bottleneck in dementia care, demanding scalable tools capable of capturing subtle behavioral decay. To capture the subtle temporal changes of cognitive decline, we introduce a behavioral dataset collected across seven unscripted multimodal interactions over an 18-month horizon. This dataset formalizes continuous, multi-session interactions into a dense 4D tensor (Batch * Session * Time * Feature) that explicitly preserves concurrent local dynamics alongside long-term changes. To effectively process these complex behavioral patterns, we propose CogDrift-4D: a novel, hierarchical 4D Transformer framework. To capture the complex trajectory of cognitive decline, CogDrift-4D implements a dual-level behavioral fatigue and drift modeling architecture. At the intra-session level, the model computes localized least-squares regression slopes to quantify the acute ``fading'' of frame-level facial action units and acoustic energy. At the inter-session level, a recursive cross-attention feedback encoder acts as a cumulative fatigue accumulator, mapping the patient's continuous behavioral drift across successive sessions. To mitigate environmental noise and track failures across sessions, a localized Quality Gate dynamically filters low-integrity features before final fusion, also an early fusion that integrates semantic insights with raw physical dynamics. Evaluated on structured verbal and linguistic interactions, our architecture successfully detects MCI with a classification accuracy of 0.733 +- 0.13 and an F1-score of 0.716 +- 0.14, outperforming advanced baselines. The framework provides a mathematically rigorous, scalable, and robust foundation for home-based, real-time dementia screening.

papers.intro:
Dementia is a major global public health challenge whose prevalence is rising with aging populations. Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) marks the transitional stage between normal age-related decline and early dementia, involving measurable deficits in memory, language, or executive function while daily independence is largely preserved. Individuals diagnosed with MCI are at increased risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease, with studies estimating that approximately 10% to 20% of adults aged 65 or older with MCI transition to dementia annually [28]. However, standard early screening tools such as the MoCA and MMSE depend on in-person clinical settings and trained administrators, limiting accessibility, longitudinal monitoring, and scalable early screening.

Motivated by the need for longitudinal monitoring approaches, we investigated the feasibility of tracking MCI progression by modeling long-term behavioral dynamics over an 18-month longitudinal horizon, in which participants completed standardized speech interaction tasks at consecutive 3-month intervals (7 sessions). Leveraging the continuous nature of human expression, this study captures physical facial dynamics, acoustic characteristics, and linguistic patterns. Fine-grained facial affect signals [10] and facial Action Unit (AU) activations [7] are extracted from video recordings to identify variations between cognitively healthy individuals and those with MCI. We track these behavioral and temporal signatures across successive sessions to evaluate longitudinal decline.

papers.title: Task-Centric Multimodal Learning for Cognitive Impairment Detection
papers.abstract: Dementia affects millions of older adults worldwide, yet early detection remains difficult outside clinical settings. Traditional models primarily rely on text or voice-based responses, capturing only a limited view of human cognition despite the inherently multimodal nature of human expression. This work proposes a contactless, multimodal screening framework that leverages video, audio, and text signals collected during structured voice-based interactions with Amazon Alexa. By incorporating these modalities, our approach captures a more holistic representation of human behavior encompassing speech patterns, vocal characteristics, facial expressions, and linguistic structure, which may enable more accurate detection of cognitive decline. Different participants completed three conversational tasks designed to probe spontaneous speech, comprehension, and recall. We pursued three objectives: (1) evaluate which of the three Alexa tasks provides the most informative cognitive signals, (2) compare the effectiveness of unimodal models, and (3) assess the benefits of multimodal fusion models. Task-level analysis shows that the video model achieves its best performance on Command-Reading, with an accuracy of 0.65 (AUC 0.69), while the audio model performs best on Question-Answering, reaching an accuracy of 0.67 (AUC 0.73). In contrast, the multimodal model demonstrates consistently stable performance across tasks, achieving an accuracy of 0.76 (AUC 0.75) on Command-Reading and 0.76 (AUC 0.73) on Question-Answering. Early detection is crucial, as timely intervention can significantly improve quality of life and inform effective care planning. papers.title: A Linear-Time Algorithm for the Unbiased Claw Game on Graphs with Maximum Degree 4
papers.abstract: We study the unbiased Maker-Breaker $K_{1,3}$-game, the unbiased claw game, played on the edge set of a general graph $G$. In this game, Maker and Breaker alternatingly claim edges of $G$, and Maker wins if his claimed edges contain a claw once no more edges are available. Graphs with maximum degree at least 5 are Maker's win. A graph $G$ is claw-connected if the hypergraph modeling the unbiased claw game played on $G$ is connected. We characterize Maker's win in the unbiased claw game on every claw-connected graph whose maximum degree is different from 3. Our main structural result is a complete characterization of Maker's win for claw-connected graphs with exactly one vertex of degree 4. The analysis is based on the fact that vertices of degree 4 act as forcing structures. Our characterization results in a linear-time algorithm for the unbiased claw game on claw-connected graphs with maximum degree different from 3. We also obtain a linear-time decomposition algorithm reducing the game on general graphs to a collection of pairwise edge-disjoint claw-connected subgraphs of maximum degree exactly 3, thereby isolating the only remaining case. This decomposition yields an $\mathcal{O}(|V(G)|^3)$-time algorithm for the unbiased claw game on general graphs, improving on the $\mathcal{O}(|V(G)|^7)$-time algorithm implied by the work of Galliot, Gravier and Sivignon (arXiv 2026). For a lower bound on the decision complexity, we prove that any agent deciding the game in the adjacency-array model makes at least $Ω(|V(G)|)$ queries in the worst case, indicating the optimality of our linear-time algorithm.
papers.intro:
A positional game is a two-player game in which the players take turns claiming vertices of a hypergraph. There are several variants with different winning conditions, including Maker-Maker, Maker-Breaker, and Avoider-Enforcer games; see [10] for an introduction to the area. We focus on Maker-Breaker games, which were introduced by Erdős and Selfridge [6], where Maker aims to occupy every vertex of a hyperedge while Breaker seeks to stop Maker from doing so. A common setting is to define the game on the edge set of an ordinary graph, treating its edges as hypergraph vertices and declaring certain collections of them winning, for example those edge sets forming a spanning tree, perfect matching, Hamiltonian cycle or a copy of a fixed graph HH. In this work, we investigate the Maker-Breaker K1,3K_{1,3}-game, the unbiased claw game, on general graphs. In the unbiased game, each player claims exactly one vertex in every round. For biased variants, in which Breaker is allowed to claim several vertices in each round, see [3, 1].

The computational complexity of Maker-Breaker games on hypergraphs has recently been fully classified. A hypergraph has rank kk if all of its hyperedges contain at most kk vertices and at least one hyperedge contains exactly kk vertices. In a seminal work, Schaefer [14] proved that Maker-Breaker games are 𝖯𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤\mathsf{PSPACE}-complete even when restricted to hypergraphs with rank most 11. In subsequent works, the rank bound was reduced to 6 by Rahman and Watson [13], to rank 5 by Koepke [11] and finally to rank 4 by Galliot and Sénizergues [8]. Galliot [9] also obtained the stronger result that 𝖯𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤\mathsf{PSPACE}-completeness already holds for 4-uniform hypergraphs, in which every hyperedge consists of exactly four vertices. In contrast, Maker-Breaker games on hypergraphs of rank at most 3 admit a polynomial-time algorithm for determining the winner of the game [7]. This extends the earlier result of Kutz [12], who obtained a polynomial-time algorithm for linear hypergraphs of rank at most 3. A hypergraph is linear if two distinct hyperedges intersect in at most one vertex.

papers.title: Two dissociable axes of brain hierarchical dynamics track universal and population-specific effects of mindfulness
papers.abstract: How mental training reshapes the temporal architecture of large-scale brain dynamics and how these mechanisms differ between healthy and clinically vulnerable populations remains poorly understood. Time-averaged neural measures collapse the multi-scale nature of brain activity, obscuring the dynamic processes through which behavioural interventions reorganise hierarchical brain function. Here, applying a sliding-window Temporal Irreversibility Index to source-reconstructed EEG across three complementary cohorts (n = 141), we decompose hierarchical brain trajectories into three orthogonal temporal descriptors and uncover two dissociable, mechanistically interpretable axes of intervention-induced plasticity. Cumulative meditation practice drives a universal, pan-cerebral reduction in the exploratory breadth of hierarchical dynamics, tracking dose-dependently with lifetime hours of practice. Temporal persistence is bidirectionally tuned by 8-week mindfulness-based interventions in a population-specific way: reduced in healthy meditators but increased in trauma-exposed individuals, revealing that comparable MBI protocols engage qualitatively distinct network mechanisms depending on baseline clinical status. A joint Hidden Markov Model further links these dynamical shifts to distinct microstate substrates, and longitudinal changes selectively track improvements in a single facet of mindfulness, attentional presence in daily life. Together, these findings establish a mechanistic framework for how behavioural training reorganises non-equilibrium brain dynamics, with direct implications for tailoring mindfulness-based interventions to individual clinical profiles.

papers.title: Awakening as a Trait-Level Transformation of Consciousness
papers.abstract: Awakening is reported across contemplative traditions yet remains poorly defined in science, where it is often conflated with transient states induced by meditation or psychedelics, obscuring its significance for theories of consciousness and cognitive architecture. We treat awakening as a functional construct capturing convergence across Hindu and Buddhist sources, phenomenological and psychometric findings, and neuroimaging evidence. Synthesizing these literatures, we find convergent evidence for reorganization across dimensions including self-related processing, affective reactivity, and temporal structure, while exposing limits of paradigms for detecting trait-level change. We argue that awakening is best understood not as a transient state but as a trait-level reorganization of experience, centered on a reduction in identification with mental contents rather than the acquisition of new content. To account for this contentless transformation, we propose the enactive-dereification model (EDM), which treats training and awakening as graded differences along a dereification gradient, from a reified to a relational mode of experience. We offer an operational definition that distinguishes awakening from state-dependent experiences and psychopathology, emphasizing dynamical flexibility and stabilization of a dereified mode. The framework yields falsifiable predictions linking independently assessed trait transformation to large-scale neural dynamics and provides a basis for distinguishing adaptive contemplative change from pathological ego-dissolution.

papers.title: $λ$-geodesic convexity of the squared sliced-Wasserstein distance
papers.abstract: The squared Wasserstein distance with respect to a fixed target measure is not a convex function along Wasserstein geodesics over $\mathbb{R}^d$ when $d\geq 2$. Still, in dimension $d=1$, this function is $2$-geodesically convex. We prove that the square of the sliced-Wasserstein distance (which is a distance constructed averaging one-dimensional Wasserstein distances) is $λ$-geodesically convex (possibly with $λ\leq 0$) on sets of measures satisfying upper bounds on their density, when the target measure satisfies some given geometric conditions. We also present some consequences of this result in the study of the sliced-Wasserstein flow.

papers.intro:
The modeling of vehicular traffic flow on a road network naturally leads to conservation laws with a discontinuous flux, since the macroscopic behavior of traffic typically changes abruptly at junctions, intersections, or points where the characteristics of the road itself (e.g., surface condition, number of lanes, speed limits, local regulations) vary. A classical and effective way to formulate such discontinuities is through the notion of flux limiter and the associated (A,B)-connection, which selects, among the infinitely many weak solutions of the scalar conservation law, the physically relevant one compatible with the behavior of vehicles crossing the junction.

papers.title: Finite-Time Guarantees for Constrained Reinforcement Learning under Partial Observability
papers.abstract: We study reinforcement learning in constrained partially observable Markov decision processes (CPOMDPs), where an agent maximizes reward subject to a cost constraint using only incomplete information about the underlying state. The lack of state observability may require optimal policies to depend on arbitrarily long observation-action histories, making planning and learning challenging. We leverage recent advances in finite-memory approximations of POMDPs and represent finite history windows as states of a constrained MDP. We then develop a primal--dual algorithm that provides the first non-asymptotic guarantees that jointly bound average reward suboptimality and constraint violation in the original CPOMDP. A key challenge is that this finite-window approximation affects both reward values and the set of feasible policies. Under a filter-stability assumption, we derive bounds relating optimality and feasibility in the finite-state model to those in the original CPOMDP, with approximation errors that decay geometrically with the window length. Experiments in partially observable gridworlds demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.

papers.intro:
POMDP model sequential decision-making problems in which an agent seeks to maximize its expected cumulative reward without directly observing the state of the environment. Instead, the agent acts on observations that provide only partial information about the underlying state. For example, a robot may not know the exact positions of surrounding objects and must instead rely on noisy camera observations (Lauri et al.,, 2022). Despite the success of POMDP in domains such as robotics and healthcare (Ding et al.,, 2018; Yu et al.,, 2021), maximizing reward alone does not ensure safe behavior, such as collision avoidance in robotics.

Despite their practical relevance and successful empirical applications (Hogewind et al.,, 2022; Carr et al.,, 2023; Huang et al.,, 2025), theoretical guarantees for learning in CPOMDP remain limited.

Despite their practical relevance and successful empirical applications (Hogewind et al.,, 2022; Carr et al.,, 2023; Huang et al.,, 2025), theoretical guarantees for learning in CPOMDP remain limited.

Existing theoretical work has focused primarily on planning with explicit knowledge of the model, providing guarantees on feasibility (Undurti and How,, 2010), approximate optimality and feasibility in time polynomial in the model size for any fixed horizon (Khonji et al.,, 2019), and finite-iteration bounds on reward optimality and constraint satisfaction (Kalagarla et al.,, 2022). Other work proposes an online Monte Carlo planning method that uses a black-box generative simulator and provides an asymptotic convergence result under additional assumptions (Lee et al.,, 2018). However, these methods do not provide finite-time guarantees for both reward optimality and constraint satisfaction when the model is unknown, and the agent learns solely through interaction with the environment.

Addressing this gap requires overcoming a fundamental difficulty inherited from POMDP. Since the agent receives only partial observations of the underlying state, an optimal policy need not be Markovian in the current observation and may depend on the entire history of observations and actions (Kaelbling et al.,, 1998). This history dependence makes both planning and learning challenging. Even with a known model, planning is computationally intractable in general (Papadimitriou and Tsitsiklis,, 1987); with an unknown model, learning a near-optimal policy requires exponentially many samples in the worst case (Krishnamurthy et al.,, 2016).

We extend finite-history methods to CPOMDP by representing finite history windows as states of a superstate CMDP (CMDP). Our goal is to learn policies in this model while guaranteeing reward optimality and constraint satisfaction in the original CPOMDP. This extension requires addressing three technical challenges. First, history truncation affects both reward and cost values. Thus, a policy that is feasible in the superstate CMDP may violate a constraint in the original CPOMDP. Second, comparing the optimal values of the two constrained problems requires more than bounding the error in individual policy values, since history truncation changes the set of feasible policies. Third, values in the superstate CMDP must be estimated from trajectories generated by the original CPOMDP, which introduces a mismatch that the learning analysis must account for.

papers.title: conformalForecast: An R package for sequential conformal prediction in time series
papers.abstract: Reliable uncertainty quantification is central to modern forecasting. Conformal prediction offers model-agnostic intervals with coverage guarantee under exchangeability, but existing software often targets general prediction problems or individual time series procedures rather than integrated workflows for multistep forecasting applications. We introduce conformalForecast, an open-source R package for constructing, updating, and evaluating conformal prediction intervals for multistep time series forecasts. The package separates point forecasting from calibration, accepts forecasts from diverse sources through a common interface, and preserves horizon-specific forecast errors and calibration states. It implements several conformal calibration schemes spanning empirical-quantile, feedback-based, and dependence-aware approaches, together with tools for assessing coverage, interval width, and interval scores over time and across horizons. Fitted objects can be extended as new observations arrive while retaining previously issued intervals and avoiding recomputation at earlier forecast origins. An application to short-term electricity price forecasting across five Australian regions illustrates the workflow. Aggregate coverage is generally close to the nominal level, while rolling coverage and interval efficiency vary across methods and horizons. In the reported experiment, incremental updating reproduces full-reconstruction intervals under identical forecasting and calibration settings while substantially reducing computation. conformalForecast provides a reproducible and extensible framework linking conformal methodology with sequential forecasting practice.

papers.intro:
Forecasting requires not only accurate point predictions but also reliable quantification of their uncertainty. In short-term wholesale electricity markets, for example, a nominal 90% price prediction interval supports hedging and operational planning only if it is well calibrated, with empirical coverage close to 90%, and sharp enough to distinguish different levels of price risk. Conformal prediction (Papadopoulos et al. 2002, Vovk et al. 2005) provides a general framework for constructing such intervals. Under exchangeability, it offers finite-sample, distribution-free marginal coverage guarantees (Shafer & Vovk 2008, Lei et al. 2018), and it can be applied on top of any point forecast, whether from a statistical/machine learning model, or a judgmental process, without specifying a predictive distribution.

Under exchangeability, it offers finite-sample, distribution-free marginal coverage guarantees (Shafer & Vovk 2008, Lei et al. 2018), and it can be applied on top of any point forecast, whether from a statistical/machine learning model, or a judgmental process, without specifying a predictive distribution.

Time series pose a fundamental challenge for this framework. Serial dependence, nonstationarity, and distributional shifts violate exchangeability, so the classical guarantee need not hold. One line of research extends conformal prediction beyond exchangeability under additional conditions on the form of the shift or dependence (Tibshirani et al. 2019, Chernozhukov et al. 2018, Xu & Xie 2021, Barber et al. 2023). A complementary line adapts calibration online as observations arrive, without modeling how the distribution evolves. Adaptive conformal inference adjusts the miscoverage level in response to past coverage errors (Gibbs & Candès 2021), and later developments include expert aggregation (Zaffran et al. 2022), adaptive regret minimization (Bhatnagar et al. 2023), dynamically tuned step sizes (Gibbs & Candès 2024), PID-based threshold updates (Angelopoulos et al. 2023), and multistep forecasting with dependence across horizons (Wang & Hyndman 2024). These methods turn calibration into a sequential task, and this sequential structure makes their implementation a forecasting-specific software problem.

Forecasting practice imposes requirements that extend beyond a generic regression interface. Forecasts are issued repeatedly as the forecast origin advances, often at several horizons, and their errors become observable only as outcomes are realized. A conformal forecasting workflow should therefore (i) accept point forecasts from any source, (ii) preserve the joint origin–horizon structure of the forecast errors, (iii) update calibration as new observations arrive without repeating earlier computations, and (iv) evaluate interval performance over time and across horizons.

Existing open-source software meets these requirements only in part. General-purpose tools such as pintervals (Randahl et al. 2026), marginaleffects (Arel-Bundock et al. 2024), and probably (Kuhn et al. 2025) within tidymodels workflows (Kuhn & Wickham 2020) in R; crepes (Boström 2024), puncc (Mendil et al. 2023), and TorchCP (Huang et al. 2025) in Python; and ConformalPrediction.jl (Altmeyer 2022) in Julia, target regression and classification problems. Other R packages address specific model classes or response structures, including conformalbayes (McCartan 2025) for Bayesian models, conformalInference.fd (Diquigiovanni et al. 2022) and conformalInference.multi (Diquigiovanni et al. 2025) for functional and multivariate responses, and LCP (Guan 2023) for localized conformal prediction. A small number of packages address the time series framework. In R, modeltime (Dancho 2026) adds Gaussian-residual and split-conformal intervals to tidymodels workflows, whereas caretForecast (Akay 2026) constructs horizon-specific intervals by rolling-origin calibration. In Python, sktime (sktime developers 2026) wraps arbitrary forecasters with empirical and conformal intervals. StatsForecast (Garza et al. 2022) and MLForecast (Morales 2026) calibrate multistep intervals for statistical and machine-learning forecasters, respectively, using rolling-origin residuals. MAPIE (Cordier et al. 2023) implements EnbPI and adaptive conformal inference through a dedicated time series regressor, while puncc and crepes also provide sequential procedures. Few of these combine the four requirements within a single model-agnostic workflow, so applying and comparing conformal methods across forecasting models and horizons still requires custom code.

This paper presents conformalForecast, an open-source R package whose design follows from these four requirements. Point forecasts may come from many sources, including operational systems outside R, so calibration is separated from forecasting and accepts any function that returns a forecast object. Forecasts issued at successive origins are stored with their errors in a common origin–horizon representation that respects the horizon-dependent delay with which errors become observable; five calibration schemes, including the multistep approach of Wang & Hyndman (2024), operate on it through a single interface. As new observations arrive, fitted objects are extended rather than rebuilt: with the forecasting function and calibration settings unchanged, updating reproduces the intervals of a full reconstruction and leaves previously issued intervals untouched. Finally, since calibration quality varies over time and with the horizon, coverage, interval width, and interval scores are reported overall, over rolling windows, and by horizon. The resulting objects integrate with the forecast ecosystem (Hyndman & Khandakar 2008, Hyndman et al. 2026).

papers.title: Variation of Shafarevich-Tate groups in Hida families
papers.abstract: Let $\mathbf{f}$ be a Hida family of cusp forms over a standard (power series) Iwasawa algebra. We determine the pseudo-isomorphism class of the big Shafarevich-Tate group attached to $\mathbf{f}$ over a suitable imaginary quadratic field by describing all its higher Fitting ideals; this description is given in terms of the universal Kolyvagin system of Howard's big Heegner points. As a second contribution, we study the variation of the structure of the Shafarevich-Tate groups of the classical specializations of $\mathbf{f}$.

The goal of the present paper is to study the variation of the structure of Shafarevich–Tate groups in a Hida family of modular forms. To explain the context and give some motivation for our results, recall that if EE is an elliptic curve over ℚ\mathds{Q} and KK is an imaginary quadratic field, then the group structure of the Shafarevich–Tate group X​(E/K)\mbox{\cyr{X}}(E/K) of EE over KK was first described, under suitable arithmetic assumptions, by Kolyvagin ([15]; cf. also [22]); more precisely, one assumes that all the prime factors of the conductor of EE split in the imaginary quadratic field KK and that the basic KK-rational Heegner point yKy_{K} is non-torsion (here yK∈E⁡(K)y_{K}\in E(K) is defined by taking the Galois trace of the Heegner point of conductor 11 on EE, which is rational over the Hilbert class field of KK). Under this assumption on yKy_{K}, Kolyvagin proves that X​(E/K)\mbox{\cyr{X}}(E/K) is finite; his description of the isomorphism class of X​(E/K)\mbox{\cyr{X}}(E/K) makes use of the collection of “derived” Heegner classes built out of Heegner points rational over ring class fields of KK and is obtained by studying divisibility properties of such a family. The case of higher (even) weight cusp forms was then considered by Masoero ([18]), who extended Kolyvagin’s techniques replacing Heegner points with Heegner cycles.
