The mechanisms of performance degradation extend beyond the deployment phase. In safety-critical applications like humanoid balance, it is often impossible to collect open-loop training data; a baseline controller must remain active. This closed-loop data collection introduces system identification challenges [44, 64, 24]. The correlation between the baseline control input and unmeasured environmental disturbances introduces an estimation bias during the offline learning phase. The scope of this paper focuses on supervised learning paradigms for neural network control. While Reinforcement Learning architectures incorporate online adaptation, the mathematical dynamics of offline-to-online distributional shift in supervised contexts remain a challenge. Recent advances in closed-loop system identification, such as Dual Input-Output Parameterization (IOP) [11], System Level Parameterization (SLP) [65], and Neural Identification of stabilized models [9], have proposed structural frameworks to mitigate this initial estimation bias while guaranteeing closed-loop stability. However, even if this initial bias is eliminated, the transition from offline training to static online deployment induces a secondary mathematical challenge. This paper therefore distinguishes between three sources of performance degradation: the initial Closed-Loop Identification Error, the distribution-shifting Action Error, and the continuous Tracking Error.

papers.title: When the next byte's type is fixed: why entropy patching skips computed values under tight budgets
papers.abstract: The Byte Latent Transformer (BLT) runs a large model once per patch and starts patches where a small model's next-byte entropy is high. Under tight budgets this rule skips computed values, such as the number after "= " in math. On BLT-1B at inference we trace the miss to the cue before a value: when the preceding bytes fix the next byte's type, the patcher's entropy is capped near log2 10 bits, close to a 10% budget's threshold. Entropy then starts a patch at 0% of values after a dollar sign and 19% after "= "; writing "is " instead of "= " raises the 19% to 66%. Version 1's two-byte lookup table, motivated by LZ novelty, acts as a learned detector of cues that tend to precede new values in its fitting text: on the solutions rewritten as prose it covers every value after a dollar sign and none after a plain space, and its margin over entropy falls from +42.1 to -8.9 points, partly because prose gives entropy more starts per value. In BLT-style models trained from scratch (1M-50M parameters, 128-byte context, 3 seeds per rule) and scored by teacher-forced exact match on answer spans, the table beats entropy at 50M by 36.8 points on computed results and 29.6 on final answers, which mostly copy the last computed result. A hand-written marker rule is not distinguishable from the table at 1M and 12M; its 50M control was not run. At 1M and 12M the table ran on a T4 GPU in fp16 and the baselines on an A40 in bf16; at 50M all ran on the A40. End to end, no 1M-50M model solves more than 2 of 100 GSM8K problems. A label-free probe of BLT-1B's patcher finds prose values, mostly after a dollar sign, but costs final answers. In six domains, no rule we tested beat entropy on exact match of whole words and numbers in more than one domain. The positive findings concern tight budgets on cue-formatted text. This version corrects version 1; the work is closed, with no venue intended.

Byte-level models avoid a fixed tokenizer by working on raw bytes and recover efficiency by grouping bytes into variable-length patches [Pagnoni et al., 2025, Slagle, 2024, Hwang et al., 2026]. In BLT [Pagnoni et al., 2025], a small byte-level language model estimates the entropy of each next byte, a patch starts where that entropy crosses a threshold, and the large global transformer runs once per patch. The guiding principle, shared by later work, is that compute should go where prediction is hard: Scratchpad Patching triggers extra global steps by next-byte entropy [Zheng et al., 2026], and SOMBRERO trains learned chunkers to place boundaries on high-surprisal bytes [Neitemeier et al., 2026]. Fewer patches mean less global compute. BLT’s own scaling runs use average patches of 6 and 8 bytes [Pagnoni et al., 2025, §5.1], so that about 12.5-16.7% of bytes start a patch, and at its default threshold BLT-1B starts a patch at 25.5% of the bytes of GSM8K solutions [Vera Zúñiga, 2026]. We study budgets of 10% and 15% of bytes.

papers.title: Locally indicable groups outside Brodskiĭ's quasivariety
papers.abstract: We provide a set of group properties that together obstruct membership in the quasivariety that Brodskiĭ constructed in his proof that torsion-free one-relator groups are locally indicable. There are examples of locally indicable groups with these properties, which implies that Brodskiĭ's quasivariety is strictly contained in the quasivariety of all locally indicable groups. This disproves a conjecture of Howie.
papers.intro:
A group is called locally indicable if each of its non-trivial finitely generated subgroups admits an epimorphism onto ℤ\mathbb{Z}. In [2], S. D. Brodskiĭ announced the first proof of the result that torsion-free one-relator groups are locally indicable. His proof was published four years later in [3]. Independent proofs of the same result were given by J. Howie around the same time in [6] and later in [8].

A group is called locally indicable if each of its non-trivial finitely generated subgroups admits an epimorphism onto ℤ\mathbb{Z}. In [2], S. D. Brodskiĭ announced the first proof of the result that torsion-free one-relator groups are locally indicable. His proof was published four years later in [3]. Independent proofs of the same result were given by J. Howie around the same time in [6] and later in [8].

The idea of Brodskiĭ’s algebraic proof is to show that a certain quasivariety of groups contains all free groups and is closed under taking one-relator products whose relator is not a proper power. A quasivariety of groups is a non-empty class of groups that is closed under the operations of taking subgroups, arbitrary direct products and ultraproducts. All classes of groups considered in this article are meant to be abstract in the sense that membership of a group GG in a class 𝒞\mathcal{C}, which we denote by G∈𝒞G\in\mathcal{C}, only depends on the isomorphism type of GG. The quasivariety in question is 𝔄~\tilde{\mathfrak{A}}, the smallest non-trivial quasivariety of groups that is closed under group extensions. Because the class of all locally indicable groups is a non-trivial quasivariety closed under group extensions, the class 𝔄~\tilde{\mathfrak{A}} is contained in the class of locally indicable groups.

papers.title: ARC-SORT: Adaptive, Robust, Compensated Multi-Object Tracking with Interacting Multiple Models
papers.abstract: Multi-object tracking in sports broadcasts is hard for two reasons: athletes move fast and change direction abruptly, and the camera pans and zooms at the same time. We present ARC-SORT (Adaptive, Robust, Compensated SORT), a tracking-by-detection tracker that trains nothing and runs in real time. Its design rule: the tracker measures its own uncertainty, and that measurement decides how it acts. An Interacting Multiple Model (IMM) Kalman filter gives every track a predictive covariance, and we turn it into a per-track search region: the less reliable the motion prediction, the larger the region in which a detection may match (uncertainty-adaptive Expansion IoU, EIoU). On identical inputs, this continuous coupling is what matters: the same covariance used as a hard Mahalanobis gate hurts at every threshold we swept, and richer covariance summaries add nothing measurable. When two tracks cross, the assignment cost itself reports whether the decision was close. ARC-SORT keeps such pairs under review and applies at most one corrective identity swap once post-crossing appearance evidence shows the first decision was wrong; this adds +1.0 HOTA (higher order tracking accuracy) on both the SportsMOT and DanceTrack test sets at under a millisecond per frame. For players who leave the frame for seconds, motion extrapolation carries no information, so our offline re-identification drops the usual motion gate and links tracklets by appearance alone. ARC-SORT reaches 81.82 HOTA on the SportsMOT test set with the fewest identity switches of the 69 leaderboard entries as of August 2026 and tied-third multi-object tracking accuracy (MOTA, 97.09), and 62.1 HOTA on DanceTrack test with the same association settings. On Deep-EIoU's public detections and embeddings it reaches 80.31 HOTA, +3.1 over Deep-EIoU. It runs at about 50 frames per second on a laptop RTX 3060 GPU. Code will be released.
papers.intro:
Tracking-by-detection splits multi-object tracking (MOT) into two steps: a detector finds object boxes in every frame, and an association step links those boxes across frames into tracks that keep their identities. The SORT family [7] performs the second step with a Kalman filter, which predicts where each track will be, and a matching cost, usually the intersection over union (IoU) between predicted and detected boxes, solved as a linear assignment. This paper is about the association step only: ARC-SORT takes the output of a fixed detector and trains nothing.

The SORT family [7] performs the second step with a Kalman filter, which predicts where each track will be, and a matching cost, usually the intersection over union (IoU) between predicted and detected boxes, solved as a linear assignment. This paper is about the association step only: ARC-SORT takes the output of a fixed detector and trains nothing.

Sports broadcasts concentrate the two failure modes of the SORT paradigm into one domain: athletes sprint, cut, and collide, violating the Kalman filter’s constant-velocity assumption, while the broadcast camera pans and zooms on top. The dominant response is to make association more tolerant, enlarging boxes by a fixed margin [43], schedule [21], or velocity heuristic [40], or else to learn motion per domain [27, 22, 2]. Meanwhile, two quantities that report how much the tracker should trust itself are computed every frame and discarded: the filter’s predictive covariance says how far the motion prediction can be trusted, yet overlap-cost pipelines either ignore it at association time or consume it as a hard Mahalanobis veto [42] (ground-plane costs [45] abandon overlap entirely); and the assignment’s own cost margin says how nearly it preferred the swapped pairing, yet nothing in the tracker’s state distinguishes a confident match from a coin flip.

This paper is built on a single principle: a tracker should let its own uncertainty govern its own decisions. We instantiate it twice, as search breadth and commitment firmness, and follow it to its limit. At short horizons the motion covariance acts as tolerance, not veto: our uncertainty-adaptive Expansion IoU dilates each track’s matching region by a continuous function of its predictive standard deviation, supplied by an Interacting Multiple Model (IMM) filter [8, 5]. At crossings, the assignment margin governs identity commitment: a pair whose swap would cost the assignment almost nothing was decided at the moment of worst evidence, so ARC-SORT marks it entangled, snapshots pre-crossing appearance, accumulates a permutation likelihood, and repairs the decision with at most one corrective swap per episode [32]. Past a multi-second out-of-view gap (football’s dominant failure; median camera exit 111 frames) the covariance has diverged and a search region wider than the frame is no gate at all, so the offline re-identification stage drops the motion gate and lets appearance alone link tracklets.

papers.title: A Simple Proof of I. Chowla's Theorem on Addition of Residue Classes
papers.abstract: We present a brief, elementary proof of a striking theorem by I. Chowla on the addition of residue classes (1937) which generalizes the famous result of Cauchy and Davenport to residue classes modulo a composite.

papers.title: Embeddings Are Overpriced? A Frozen 16 MB Vocabulary for Small and Ternary Language Models
papers.abstract: In a small language model the vocabulary is the single largest part. In Gemma 3 270M the embedding table holds 168M of 268M parameters, and because quantisation methods leave the embedding in 16-bit, it is also most of the file once the rest of the model is compressed. We ask what that table actually buys. We replace it with one frozen table of 512-bit codes, 16 MB, with no trainable parameters, derived once from a pretrained embedding by principal-component projection and sign binarisation, and we train the same Gemma-shaped body from scratch on the same 2.05B tokens with and without it. The learned table buys 0.20 nats of validation loss for 2.6 times the trainable parameters, but on LAMBADA, HellaSwag and PIQA the frozen-table model is better or tied; only ARC-Easy favours the learned table. With a ternary BitNet b1.58 body the whole model is a 46 MB file, still ties the float model on LAMBADA and PIQA, and on a laptop CPU generates 615 to 740 tokens per second in 62 MB of memory, five to six times the speed of the float model's 8-bit GGUF in llama.cpp at a seventh of the memory. The frozen table wins by 1.7 to 2.3 nats on rare words, accepts 10,000 new words after training with a 3% cost where the learned table collapses by 43%, and all of it is released with the weights, the data and every evaluation answer.

papers.title: Learning from Past Mistakes: AI-Assisted Analytics of Software Defects and Their Fixes for Future Defect Prevention - An Industrial Case Study
papers.abstract: Context. Despite advances in software testing and quality assurance, defects continue to recur in industrial software systems. Defect data are routinely collected in issue-tracking systems, but their use is largely confined to detection, reporting, and short-term resolution, leaving the knowledge embedded in historical defects and their fixes under-exploited for prevention and long-term improvement. Objective. This paper investigates how historical defect and defect-fix data can be analyzed, with AI assistance under human oversight, to identify the human-error origins of recurring defects and to feed that understanding back into prevention and QA improvement. Method. We developed an AI-assisted, human-in-the-loop analytics approach that classifies defects by failure type and by human-error origin across the SDLC, determines how each could have been prevented, and synthesizes engineer-focused capability-building insights. It was deployed and evaluated in a large software company through an industrial case study, using practitioner surveys and interviews, classification-reliability checks, and an effort-normalized analysis of defect density. Results. Practitioners and independent review judged the classifications accurate; the outputs were rated useful and actionable; and defect density decreased after the introduction of the feedback, a tentative association we interpret as consistent with, but not proof of, a positive effect, given the study's uncontrolled pre/post design. Conclusion. AI-assisted, human-governed analysis of defect-fix data can help shift organizations from defect detection toward prevention, continuous learning and improvement.

papers.title: Can a search hold its own bar? In-loop deflation and its exploits in autonomous strategy discovery
papers.abstract: Corrections for backtest overfitting such as the deflated Sharpe ratio are applied after a search ends: the searcher maximises raw performance and a separate procedure deflates the reported winner. Autonomous searches driven by large language models perform many implicit backtests before reporting, so this paper asks what changes when the correction moves inside the loop and the acceptance threshold is indexed to the running count and dispersion of the search's own trials. The threshold then becomes an object the search can optimise against: we show analytically that a naive in-loop bar admits a variance-dilution effect, in which mediocre near-duplicate candidates lower the bar because the ledger's dispersion falls faster than its trial-count factor grows. We propose two defences, a pre-registered variance floor and a monotone high-water-mark bar, and evaluate the construction under a protocol frozen before any run, with every in-loop decision replaying exactly from its recorded trace. Across 53 audited hundred-candidate searches over two frontier models, two universes, and two feature spaces, the gated search reports "no certifiable discovery" on 36 of 37 runs, un-gated controls report a strategy on all 16, and every arm's out-of-sample confidence interval includes zero. Supporting studies find that state-based stopping reaches the same outcome after 8 to 9 trials at about a twelfth of the trial budget while an adaptive budget adds nothing, that a controlled stress test reproduces the dilution effect and both defences, and that a hundred nominal trials collapse to 6 to 8 effectively independent return streams. We scope these results to the analysed system.
papers.intro:
A strategy that is chosen as the best of many candidates owes its measured score to two ingredients. One is genuine edge, which tends to repeat on data the search never touched. The other is selection luck, which does not. When a process auditions NN candidates and reports the best, the reported score is inflated by the luck that helped put that candidate on top. Empirical finance has long supplied instruments to correct for this, including the deflated Sharpe ratio, the probability of backtest overfitting, and multiplicity-adjusted hurdles (Bailey et al., 2017; Bailey and López de Prado, 2014; Harvey et al., 2016).11 1 The Sharpe ratio is a strategy’s mean return divided by the standard deviation of its returns, annualised throughout this paper. A backtest is a historical simulation of a strategy; point-in-time means universe membership as known on each historical date; SPY is an S&P 500 index fund, used here as the passive benchmark. These instruments share a common arrangement. The search runs first, and the correction is applied afterwards, to the reported winner. The searcher itself stays statistically naive: it maximises raw in-sample performance, and honesty is imposed on its output after the fact.

Autonomous search loops built on LLMs make this arrangement uncomfortable. A refinement agent that proposes, backtests, and revises candidate strategies performs its multiplicity inside the loop, quickly, guided by a critic that sees raw performance numbers. In prior work we instrumented such a system and applied the correction after the fact, finding that the apparent edge of every discovered strategy disappeared once its performance was deflated by the search’s recorded trial count (Gençay, 2026). That verdict is honest, but it arrives only after the search budget has been spent. A natural question follows, and to our knowledge no agent-loop system has made this move: what changes if the correction is moved inside the loop, so that the searcher’s own acceptance threshold, stopping rule, and feedback are indexed to the running count and dispersion of its own trials? Optimisation loops for LLM agents are now common, but they do not carry statistical accounting of this kind.

Moving the correction inside the loop is not simply a matter of relocating a computation, and the analytical core of this paper is to explain why. The live threshold, which we call the bar, is Bk=V^k​K​(Nk)B_{k}=\sqrt{\widehat{V}_{k}}\,K(N_{k}): the dispersion of the trial scores seen so far, multiplied by a factor for the luckiest of NkN_{k} draws. Read in words, the bar is an estimate of the best score that selection luck alone would be expected to produce, given how many candidates have been tried and how spread out their scores are. A candidate is accepted only if it clears this bar. Once the bar is part of the searcher’s environment, however, it becomes something the search can act upon. The trial-count factor K⁡(N)K(N) grows only like 2​ln⁡N\sqrt{2\ln N}, whereas a single near-mean trial shrinks the dispersion factor V\sqrt{V} at the faster relative rate 1/(2​N)1/(2N). Adding mediocre, near-duplicate candidates can therefore push the bar down rather than up. We call this variance dilution, state it as a proposition with explicit assumptions, and propose two defences: a pre-registered variance floor that limits how far the bar can be pushed down, and a monotone bar that is not allowed to fall at all.

The empirical program is pre-registered in the sense available to a systems paper. The full protocol, covering parameters, arms, primary endpoints, decision rules, and an acceptable-findings clause, was written into a versioned design document and frozen by commit before any run; the frozen parameters are checked by automated tests; and every in-loop decision of every run can be replayed exactly from its recorded trace. The primary endpoint is deliberately independent of the bar: each arm is judged by an external measure, the out-of-sample Sharpe ratio with a bootstrap confidence interval of whatever that arm selected. This avoids grading a system with the very instrument under study.

We report both what the system rejects and what it certifies. The central result is that the gate changes what is reported rather than what is found. Across 37 gate-active searches (arms whose acceptance objective includes the certification gate), spanning two frontier models, a 453-stock point-in-time equity universe, a 39-ETF transfer universe, and an exploratory fundamentals feature space, 36 end with “no certifiable discovery,” while un-gated controls report a selected strategy on every run. In every arm of the study, gated or not, the out-of-sample confidence interval of the selected strategy includes zero. The one certification, at the seed whose in-sample record was strongest, indicates that the gate is discriminating rather than trivially always-empty. Around this central result we place four supporting studies: a comparison of stopping rules, a study of what the critic is allowed to see, a controlled stress test of the dilution effect, and a diagnostic for statistical dependence among the trials. Their findings are summarised in the contributions below and reported in Section 6, with claims scoped to the analysed system.
